translations.text: Another discourse of Apollonius. These things grieve me deeply: a just king who dies, and a good governor who is dismissed,
a wise man who is despised, a righteous man who falls into sin, a rich man who becomes poor, and a freeborn man who serves as a slave,
and a good man who acquires an evil wife. Indeed, these things have caused me great sorrow and still do.
But these things astonished me, and anguish seized me: a fool who acquires wealth, and a slave who holds authority,
a man lacking understanding who is sent as an ambassador, someone who had nothing and now has possessions, and a slave woman who rules over her mistress [?],
and a son who dishonors his parents. But these things will bring me great joy when they come to pass.
I have rejoiced greatly and still rejoice over a fool who dies—if only he went from his mother's womb to the grave!—and over a tyrannical king who is killed,
an unjust governor who is dismissed, an adulterous woman who is publicly ridiculed, and a rich man who would not give relief and has become poor.
Do not honor a foolish man, because honor is not fitting for a fool. Whoever honors a fool angers God, and kindness to a fool is a great sin.
An evil wife is an evil treasure. Woe to whoever falls into her hands! A wicked and [?] man is a bad friend.
Disobedience is a troublesome possession, the source of all evils, and the likeness of the Evil One. Those who have drunk from it—it has strangled them.
Much talk is boasting, arrogance, and empty glory. An evil will is an evil companion. Again, concerning the wicked man and the [?].
I, Apollonius, from the city of Tyana, through the gift that was given to me, made talismans as my God enabled me.
With them I acted upon lions, leopards, wolves, cheetahs, bears, and wild boars,
wild asses, gazelles, foxes, hares, all wild animals, livestock, birds, and the fish of the seas and rivers,
and snakes and scorpions, and also gnats, flies, bees, and ants. I yoked every harmful creeping creature under the yoke of subjection.
I subdued them all and subjected them through talismans. I also rebuked prostitutes, subdued [?], and directed the flow of water.
But for the fool who lacks understanding, I found nothing that would help him, except that one should stay far away from him and out of his sight.
Another account by him, with its interpretation. Mount Olympus is entirely fire: its dust, its stones, its appearance, and even its smell.
It does not burn any of us who walks on it during the day, but it burns those who approach it at night.
Its interpretation is the body of a woman. It is entirely fire: her appearance, her likeness, and her speech.
All her limbs are ablaze with the fire of desire. But those whose souls are ablaze with divine fire,
who possess knowledge and whose minds are enlightened by the vision of wisdom, direct their spiritual gaze
and see, beneath a woman's outward beauty, loathsomeness, foulness, and uncleanness.
They do not wallow in her foul mud, and the fire of desire for her does not burn them.
The account is finished. Another account. All the birds on Mount Aaunpos [?] have the appearance of fire. They dwell in that fire and are not burned by it.
All that flame, its seething heat and its blaze, rises through them. They eat the roots that grow in that fire.
They drink the water heated by the fire. Their appearance is beautiful, and they are lovely. Whenever one bird [?] flies down from the mountain,
that appearance, radiant with beauty, is immediately taken away from it. And whenever one of them flies up to ascend that mountain,
the blast of that fire comes out and burns it. Its interpretation: Mount Attunpos [?] is heaven, and the birds are the angels who stand in fire
and are not burned by it. They are clothed in fire and shine with the appearance of flame. Their appearance is lovely
because they are clothed in glory. All their food and drink is spiritual, and they are nourished by the Spirit.
Satan himself, together with his fellow servants, flew down to earth. Immediately that appearance of fire and glory was taken away from them.
Whenever one of them flies to ascend on high, a blast of fire comes out and strikes him down, and he is hurled into the depths.
These three splendid qualities with which the demons once shone were taken away from them: light, fire, and the clothing of glory.
They acquired three disfigurements: they are naked, black, and ugly in appearance. The discourse of Apollonius is finished. And to him be glory.
The Histories of the Roman Emperors
God also rewarded him for his good conduct. He lay down on his bed of rest in this world, was gathered to his people, and was joined to his fathers.
After him, Julian the wicked took the throne, in the fifty-second year of the peace of the churches. Julian the tyrant rose to power over the whole Roman Empire.
He renewed the persecution of the Christian people. He ordered the temples of idols to be opened, their altars to be built, and carved images to be worshiped.
He also ordered meeting places for false teachings to be built and furnished. He closed the churches and plundered them.
He banished the bishops from their cities into exile, and the entire holy order was subjected to insult and mockery.
Some of them were handed over to imprisonment and beatings, to scourging and scraping. Some endured sufferings and afflictions. Some were persecuted.
Others were stoned. Others were stripped. Others were beaten on their bodies, and after they had been weakened by persecution,
they met the end of their lives from those wounds. Others were dragged through the streets like dogs, without the judges’ authorization.
Others changed their place of residence so that they would not change the truth of their Lord. Others had their possessions handed over to plunder
and were stripped of their property so that they would not be stripped of their Lord’s love. Others were banished to the region of Miletus and to distant lands
for the sake of their Lord’s name. There were also others who denied him during the struggle in a different way: when they saw the terrible afflictions and harsh tortures,
they shrank from the struggle of confessing their faith. They kept their faith within themselves and held back from this path [?] of martyrdom.
But others, whose faith was sound, did not conceal the truth. Instead, they made the truth of their faith shine before everyone’s eyes.
And they took upon themselves severe afflictions of many kinds, along with other varied and bitter torments of every sort.
Through their steadfast endurance they completed their crowns by confessing their faith. And since our account cannot now cover everything that was inflicted on us,
one can learn from the account of the victories of Mar Eusebius, bishop of Rome, whose name we have mentioned above,
what persecution was inflicted on us in the days of Julian the wicked. Our account, then, is brief and hurried
as we recount the deeds of this old man of wondrous victories. For he was the first, the firstborn in confessing the faith, and he opened his [?] to the arena of his contest,
like a well-prepared athlete trained in the maneuvers of combat. He threw the Evil One with a wrestling move and dashed him down.
He won the crown of victory from his unseen adversary. This old man, full of victories, deserves wonder and admiration,
for although he was very [?] in years, being nearly ninety years old,
like a man in the prime of his years, so he went out into it—like a man in the prime of his years, so he went out into the contest, resolutely and mightily.
He gained a good name and an outstanding victory. For he was alert in mind, eloquent in speech, rich in knowledge, and powerful in his words,
and accomplished in all the duties of reverence for God, and also in worldly matters. Why should we prolong our account of the story of this old man of wondrous victories?
For his story and the memory of his victories are recorded for the discerning people who lived in his time. They are much better acquainted with the toil of his way of life
and with the resolute struggle of this true shepherd, who showed an example in his own person and left his church a model to imitate.
In him was fulfilled what our Lord said in his Gospel: that the good shepherd cares for his flock and lays down his life in death for the church. This is truly the good shepherd,
who laid down his life—his life—to death for the flock entrusted to him. He went down courageously into the contest, began and [?], and received fulfillment and victory.
He inherited life that does not pass away and a bridal chamber that is not dismantled, in that kingdom
which endures forever and ever. Amen and amen. Here ends the account of the triumph concerning the faith of Constantine and his three sons who reigned
after him. The account of the victories of the blessed Eusebius, bishop of the church of Rome, in the days of Julian, the tyrant and uncircumcised man.
After the allotted days of the faithful, Christ-loving King Constantius had come to an end, and he had been gathered to his people in peace
and joined to his fathers, leaving behind a good name and an everlasting remembrance in all the churches under heaven,
Julian, the wicked and cruel man, succeeded him as emperor. In his madness and under the influence of demons, he denied God his maker.
He turned away from the true faith to which he had held from his youth, broke his covenant, and turned away from his truth.

He followed the error of demons, gave himself over to their divinations, and was drawn along by their will. He became wild and frenzied in the worship of demons and the adoration of idols, more than the pagan kings who had preceded him.
He renewed the persecution of Christians and ordered the temples of idols to be opened, their shrines rebuilt, idols set up, and carved images worshiped.
He also ordered the meeting houses of false teachings to be restored, which had been uprooted and demolished in the days of the Christian kings before him.
He became arrogant and rose up against the churches of Christ. He took their treasures, plundered their furnishings, and closed and sealed them.
He sent the bishops into exile from their cities and [?] against the community of God's holy one. But the sentence of justice quickly overtook him.
God did not allow him to prosper and succeed in his reign. Instead, he removed him from life early and shortened the span of his days,
[?] lest the measure of his sins grow much longer and greater. For this madman made God's servants endure many evils.
God justly repaid him for his evil deeds, and his destruction took place
in the land of the Chaldeans, just as God's martyr Eusebius, the blessed bishop of the church of Rome, had previously prophesied about him
while standing on trial before him. For he made this admirable, victorious old man endure considerable suffering, torture, and various afflictions of every kind.
He was not restrained or deterred by the dignity of the old man's years. For this old man was nearly ninety-seven years old
when he stood in the contest of confessing his faith. Despite all this burden of old age, he did not weaken in his steadfastness.
Nor did he shrink from confessing his faith, but like a strong young man standing in the prime of his years,
he went out into his contest resolutely and powerfully, and [?] a good name and victory.
He won the crown of his confession. This was the first martyr to suffer martyrdom at the beginning of our persecution. Like a mighty contestant,
he was the first to open the contest of spiritual combat, so that he might be a good model and example for those coming after him,
so that they might walk in his footsteps and emulate his struggle. For he was alert in mind, eloquent in speech, and powerful in his words,
discerning in his knowledge, perfect in his conduct, and admirable in his victories. For he was thoroughly trained in the discipline of worldly wisdom.
He was fully versed in the various branches of philosophical wisdom, endurance, and ingenuity.

He amazed many with the natural [?] wisdom with which he had been created. But what was more excellent and glorious than all these things was that he was also perfected beyond measure in divine wisdom.
He was wholly a source of benefit both to himself and to those who saw him. It is astonishing and amazing
that although this blessed old man was perfect and complete in everything, and lacked nothing in his fullness,
he was still eager and diligent to gather enough for his soul through the practice of righteousness, right up to his last breath.
Although he was already an old man, close to the end of his life, and stood at the beginning of the road of his departure, he never ceased
to increase his purse with the profit from his talents. For this was his concern in his old age:
to add provisions upon provisions for the long road of his departure. And when an opportunity for spiritual trade came his way,
like someone hungry and eager, he swallowed it down in his joy. In his old age he gained the good portion of confessing his faith,
which he had longed for from his youth. He journeyed victoriously to his Lord, carrying the goods of his trade on his shoulder.
And truly, this is the genuinely wise merchant, who knew enough to gain life for himself through trading: a good and diligent servant,
who can openly give his master an account of the talents entrusted to him; a perfect and diligent worker, who began his master's work in the morning.
With the vigorous strength of his youth he bore the burden of the day's heat and did not draw back from his master's work. And when the shadows of youth declined
and the evening of old age drew upon him, the toil of his work did not diminish. Rather, his righteous work increased in his old age beyond what it had been in his youth.
With his voice raised and his face unveiled, he receives from his master the wages of his work. And what praise can we offer
to someone who has no need of the praise of our words? His perfect conduct, his glorious deeds, and his wondrous victories themselves proclaim his praises at all times.
Therefore, so that we may not neglect to present the good testimony of this spiritual man
and do an injustice to the unceasing toil of his way of life and to the sufferings and tortures of his limbs, in his history
let us briefly describe the struggle of his confession of faith. It happened after Constantius died, as we wrote above,
that the tyrant Julian prepared to march down to Rome with a great army from the upper regions of Gaul, where he had been ruling,
so that he might establish his rule anew on the throne of Rome and become sole emperor over the entire Roman dominion.
When the blessed Eusebius became aware of these things, and learned and received confirmation from many people that the tyrant was reigning, he grieved within himself and groaned deeply in his heart.
He sighed and said, “Alas! Glory has departed from our church, and our sanctuary is being handed over to destruction,
and we are exposed to mockery, and our people to persecution.” For news of this madman's paganism had reached him.
Great sorrow had taken hold of this holy man of God, and in anguish, like Jeremiah, he wept for the Christian kings who had died.
He sighed over them, saying, “Alas for our kingdom, deprived of your guidance, you who upheld our faith and brought peace to the church!
Diligent farmers, you labored in a field full of thorns and uprooted from it the thicket of sin and the weeds of paganism.
You cultivated it with the [?] of your faith and sowed in it the good seed of your zeal, and it yielded fruit thirty[?], sixty, and a hundredfold.
And now the reward for your work is before you, and your good memory remains throughout the world.”
With many sorrowful expressions like these, and others resembling them, the blessed Eusebius remembered the Christian kings of the house of Constantine,
out of the brokenness of his heart and the anguish of his mind. And when he had relieved his mind a little through the tears of his eyes,
like a righteous shepherd who is distressed for his flock when a wolf prepares to ravage his sheep, and who calls out to the sheep and gathers them to himself,
so, in the same way, when the blessed old man heard about the coming of this defiled man, he took great care to send for and gather to himself the entire order of the church,
from the greatest to the least. He admonished them like beloved children, saying,
“Take heed, my children! Watch over yourselves, stand firm in your faith, persevere in your truth, and be courageous and strong.”
For the wolf is about to gain power over us, and a trial is to rise against the church.
Take care that you do not weaken in your steadfastness or lose heart in your trial, for the time is short and very brief.
Your trial will come to an end. For God does not withdraw his hand from his flock, which he purchased with his precious blood, nor does he abandon it entirely to the wolf.
For even if the accursed tyrant gains power over our kingdom for a time, to discipline us because we have sinned,
nevertheless, my sons, let this be certain and assured for us: his end follows close on the heels of his beginning. For God has never turned his gaze away from his church.
Rather, his eyes are always upon it for its good, even during his discipline. For when has he failed to deliver it in the time of its trial?
Therefore, do not be shaken or frightened by the news of this tyrant’s paganism. Today he is exalted and raised up, but tomorrow he passes away and is no more.
His memory will perish and be blotted out. But the memory that the steadfast gain through this, by our confession, will never fade from the world.
Therefore, rejoice and be glad, like mature and steadfast people, when trials assail you violently.
Just as fine gold displays its beautiful splendor in the furnace, and those who see it marvel at it, so the mature are tested in the furnace of trials.
Through the testing of their endurance, the steadfast are recognized. For without a contest, without triumph, and without persecution,
there is neither a crown nor victory. The mature are praised through the testing of their endurance, and at the end of their race, when they have won, they receive the prize.
The title of athlete brings an athlete no praise unless he demonstrates his proven vigor in the contest. Nor does the name of Christian bring a Christian praise,
if the testing of endurance [?] is completed in us. Endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame.
Therefore, as people who are assured and confident that they have a hope that does not put them to shame, cast off laziness, weakness, and discouragement.
Join battle with sin and break its stings. With the spiritual armor you possess, fight against error and blunt its onslaught. For strength is fitting for you,
and courage becomes you, because you learned the discipline of an athlete from the foundation of the church, the chief of the disciples.
You have practiced the exercises of the contest, and the evil one has no way at all to win a victory over you.
For you wear the breastplate of righteousness, and your mind is armed with spiritual weapons. However hard he strives to fight against you,
victory is denied him, and he becomes all the more insolent in his tricks. For he is an obstinate athlete who feels no shame: even when defeated, he fights again.
He never rests at all from his fighting. Against the strong and steadfast he fights with the disturbances and enticements of his cunning.
But over those who are weak and sick in their minds, he boasts as though victorious, seeking to deprive them of the grace of Christ.
He wears them down in their weakness, because by their own free choice they have become feeble in their contest.
Therefore, wake up, my brothers, and stand firm in faith. Be courageous and strong, and do not give way to the evil one, your enemy, allowing him to gain power over you.
For he is a feeble athlete against those whose faith is sound and whose love for God their maker is steadfast. The steadfast wear him out by their victory.
Whenever he wages war against them, because they do not fear or tremble at the tortures and afflictions he makes them endure,
at the hands of pagan kings and unjust judges, let us too, my children, be watchful and ready to make the good confession for Christ.
Let us not grow slack in the contest that demands our courage. For in the [?] and at the time of battle, whoever is strong in body and courageous in spirit exposes his body to blows,
and often even surrenders his life to death, so that he may receive a crown of victory and a glorious name.
In the same way, we too ought, like strong and courageous men, to be the first to enter the contest and take the lead in the struggle.
For this is also right: just as we have been placed first in the leadership given to us through Simon Peter,
so let us be the first to confess Christ when the occasion is given to us. Let us be a good example and a noble model for the faithful and steadfast,
who long for the exalted rank of confession. Let us give a good demonstration of [?], of our endurance, to the rest of the church whom we have left in our place.
For this is true and just: just as Simon Peter made us his partners, my brothers, in leadership and election,
so let us share in the suffering of his death and the fierce contest of his crucifixion. And let us share not only in his sufferings,
but also in the sufferings of his Lord, of whom the blessed Paul said, “If we share in his suffering, we also share in his consolation.”
For it is fitting for discipleship to embody the example of its [?]. The chief of the disciples himself embodied the example of his master and asked to be crucified upside down.
So precious was his Lord’s death in his eyes that, at the time of his own death, he asked to kiss the foot of his cross. We ought to emulate this spiritual merchant.
Although he was very rich in good works, flourishing and perfect in the practice of [?], and held the keys of the heights and the depths,
and was entrusted with the treasuries of the Godhead, with blessedness bestowed upon him, a throne promised to him, and glorious promises,
despite all these things he possessed, he did not grow weary or agree to rest from his labor. For he was not struggling for what he already possessed,
but running after what he did not yet possess. We ought to emulate these diligent men, who worked diligently and bought the kingdom above
with the profit from the money and talents entrusted to them. They preserved the deposit, together with its interest, for its giver, and traded with it to gain for themselves what no eye has seen,
no ear has heard, and what has never entered the human heart. While the blessed Eusebius still wished to continue his words of instruction,
Aphentus the deacon came into his presence and said to him, “My father, let your speech rest now, and attend to your contest. Sleep has been stirred, and the contest is pressing.
Already your old age has been found worthy of the exalted rank of confession.” The holy man of God rejoiced inwardly at what he heard and looked lovingly at that deacon.
He questioned him, saying, “What is your message, my son? Tell me.” Aphentus his deacon answered him, saying, “I was met at the outer gate
of the church concerning a matter involving Your Holiness. One of the king’s soldiers, whose name is Adauctus, is asking about your holy angel.
This man is one of the tyrant’s trusted servants, as I learned from those with him. With him are some well-known men
and ten priests of sin. In their hands is the king’s annual gift for Your Holiness, and in the hands of Adauctus is the tyrant’s drawn sword.”
For he wanted to enter through the church’s outer gate, but I did not allow him. I had the gatekeepers keep him back until Your Holiness learned of these things.
I was astonished at this sinner’s conduct: how patiently he bore it, without becoming angry or enraged at what I did to him. Nor did he insist on entering once he learned our wishes.
And now he is still waiting for your command.” When the blessed Eusebius heard all these things,
he was neither alarmed nor shaken. For he had been longing and yearning for the time when the door of confessing the faith would be opened to him.
For he always called those who had been found worthy of this gift blessed, whenever he read the accounts of their martyrdoms and reflected on their victories.
Although he was very glad and his mind rejoiced at this message that had been read to him, a little sorrow troubled his mind,
because of those in his flock whose instruction was still immature, since he did not know

how they would fare in their struggle. When he saw his flock dejected and anxious, he raised his hand and made the sign of the cross over the whole covenant community of the church, both men and women.
He encouraged and comforted them, saying to them, “Take courage, my children, and do not be afraid. Remember the words I have spoken to you.
Consider me: I am an old man of ninety years, and more than someone longs for cold water when thirsty,
so my soul thirsts and prays that I may be the first—the firstfruits of the struggle and the last fruits of our persecutors.
May the persecution of Christians begin and end with me. Through me may the anger of justice be appeased, and may God be reconciled to his people.
But you, my children, show goodwill toward God, and be ready and prepared to make the good confession for the sake of
Christ. If it is his will to act in his mercy as he usually does, and to remove the time of desolation from his churches,
your goodwill will be accepted just as it is. But if he considers it just to make his rod heavier for our discipline, let us not, my children, refuse discipline,
lest we be found to be outsiders and not children. This is what the blessed apostle said: ‘If we are without discipline, we have become outsiders and not children.’
For God disciplines those whom he loves, like a father who disciplines his children.” While he was strengthening his flock with these words of comfort,
Frontinus, the church’s gatekeeper, came in hastily and said to him, “Adauctus, Julian’s trusted official, has sent this message to Your Holiness through me, your servant [?]:
‘If Your Wisdom wishes me to tell you privately what I was sent to say to you, give the order, and I will come into your presence.
But if you wish me to pay honor to your old age before this assembled crowd, as I was instructed, that too is your choice.
Only let me know your wishes.’” But the blessed Eusebius said to those with him, “My children, let us not allow the unclean to enter
and trample the Lord’s house. Let us undertake to go out to them ourselves, especially for the sake of the crowds in the city.
Let us learn what the defiled man wants and what he has planned against our people and our churches. In response to what he has sent us,
let us send him back, through his messenger, a rebuke suited to his madness.” When the good shepherd set himself to leave his church,
his entire flock followed at his heels. He went at the head of the church’s covenant community, like a commander at the head of the flock.
Those who accompanied him and came out of the church with him were united in soul and mind, a gathering of men and women numbering about one thousand nine hundred and thirty people.
He was glad and rejoiced in his heart over the gathering of his church, and especially over the sound understanding they possessed.
He called them blessed and praised their faith. And when that blessed shepherd himself arrived,
with his flock, at the outer gate of the church, a beautiful radiance was poured over the face of blessed Eusebius, as though by the grace of God.
His appearance resembled that of an angel, so that when Adauctus saw him, he was greatly astonished and marveled at his appearance.
He questioned him as one would a kindly father, saying, “Are you Eusebius, who has been appointed overseer and leader of the Christian people?” But that pure and holy man of God
answered him openly and with great courage, saying, “I am the least of Christ’s disciples, if you want anything.”
“For we do not wish to diminish your honor in any way, as far as we can help it, because of your wisdom and the clarity of your knowledge.
For Julian, the emperor forever, holds authority over the world. Regarding you as an educated and wise man, pure in body and holy in thought,
he has appointed you high priest, to serve God all the days of your life. And through the renowned and honored priests of Zeus and Apollo,
he has sent you priestly garments, in which you are to serve and please the gods. And look, so that you may believe my words, here is the letter of our emperor, sent first to you,
as a leader of our province and a priest of the gods. From it you will learn what goodwill he has toward you.” He stretched out his hand and gave him the impious man’s letter.
He received it from him like a man who knew what he was destined to do. The following was the text of the letter sent to him by the tyrant:
“Since we have long had experience of your education and proof of your knowledge, it has been our wish
not to diminish your honor or bring you down from your high position, if you will quickly recover your senses and help yourself.
For it is not fitting for us, on account of occasions of transgression in various matters, to take men whose knowledge is sound and whose understanding is clear

and drive them away and cast them out from among us, when through the power of their knowledge they can assist us in the affairs of the empire or in matters that concern the gods. For we have examined these matters
with the clear eyes of our mind and have come to understand that unless pardon is granted to transgressors, our empire cannot grow strong.
For few would remain in it if we undertook to prosecute and investigate these things. We have therefore overlooked many things,
and require only this one necessary thing from everyone: that from now on the gods be worshiped, their temples be opened, their shrines be built, and no one withhold their sacrifices and offerings.
The old things have passed away, and we wish everything to be renewed from the beginning, so that each person may choose of his own accord
to worship and honor the immortal gods, whose mercy has overflowed even toward those who denied them praise. But do not be angry at these things, educated and wise man,
for in these matters we have not placed you among the foolish. You are a man of knowledge, and you have never conducted yourself contrary to the times.
And wherever they directed you, you [?], and you obeyed their rulers, even though the administration of those emperors who preceded me was confused.
Duty compelled us to obey their commands, conform to their will, and follow their error. This is the way of wise men.”
that they should submit their will to the rulers of the age. What I have written to you is enough for you to know and understand, from the indications in our letter, what our will is.
For our mind is not attached to the corrupt thinking of the house of Constantine, who, in their ignorance, imitated the madness of the Galileans.
They were drawn into their error, abolished the commands established by the kings before them, changed their laws, and threw their arrangements into confusion.
Yet those earlier kings far surpassed them in greatness, were rich in knowledge and clear in understanding—men whose wisdom enabled them to bring order to the world's confusion.
And if the will of these men, who astonished the world with their remarkable deeds, did not endure after the deaths of those who disrupted the noble arrangements
and the commands of the kings before them, and who arrogantly did away with the worship of the gods, who will uphold
their will after their death? Therefore, do not let your mind be caught up in their madness, lest your honor be diminished and you be brought down from your greatness,
about which I wrote to you above. Why, then, do you trouble me with so much? You are not a child who needs a rattle
and [?] lengthy explanations for your instruction. For I, as to a man of understanding—since you have been made head and overseer of the entire Christian people—
the first letter of our reign was sent to you as to a man on whom the whole religion of the Nazarenes depends. For this has not escaped our knowledge:
if you willingly obey our command and turn to the worship of the gods, the entire people will follow you without hesitation.
By your obedience you will gain your lives, and our majesty will also be spared having to shed much blood.
For we do not desire the destruction [?] of our dominion, nor that the number of our troops should decrease and be diminished. You will render our majesty a great service by doing this.
In return for this, we too are determined to repay you with many benefits. For I will make you a great man and an overseer for all your days.
I will appoint you [?] and chief priest of the holy gods, who love devout men like you. You will enter into the mystery of the gods and learn things hidden from ages past.
You will also learn the things that are to happen afterward. You will come to divine birth, renew your worn-out condition, and make your old age young. And what is greater [?] than all these things:
by adoption, you will become a son of the gods through grace. You will enter into the secrets of our kingdom as a confidant of the gods.
I will entrust to your hands all the treasures of the churches, as treasurer of the immortal gods.
So that my words may be believed by you and my promises confirmed to you, look: I have sent to you, in honor of your position, ten distinguished priests of Zeus and Apollo.
They will carry out in practice what we have written to you, for they have received our instructions concerning everything.
For the gods, the helpers of the world, may they instill [?] have received our instructions concerning everything. For may the gods, the helpers of the world, instill in your mind a helpful thought,
so that you may help yourself and find mercy in the eyes of our majesty. After the impious man's letter had been read before
all the people of the city, Adauctus gave the command, and those priests entered in their priestly attire.
They presented to the blessed Eusebius the gifts sent to him through them by Julian the tyrant—lavish gifts, as befitted a king's generosity—
and the implements for priestly service: splendid, magnificent royal garments, a laurel crown, and the complete regalia and attire of the chief priesthood.
But God's holy man would not look at them, the gifts of the unclean man. Instead, he turned his face away from them and despised both them and those who had sent them.
He rebuked those priests of sin, saying, “May Christ rebuke you and your father Satan,
whom you serve. Go and tell the madman who sent you that he and his gifts together should go to destruction.”
This was what God's apostle, the chief of the disciples, had said to Simon, his counterpart.
“You too, priests of sin and ministers of error, who have stolen away the simple and misled the innocent through those who peddle your madness:
destruction will come upon you suddenly, at a time you do not know and at an hour you do not expect.
Just retribution will be exacted from you, and the schemes you have whispered will recoil on your own heads.
The tyrant who sent you will be astonished and alarmed when news of your destruction reaches his ears.” Adauctus was inwardly amazed at these things and burned with anger.
Yet, seeking an opportunity to accomplish his mission, he continued to speak gently with him, saying, “You have not sought to honor us as we have sought to honor you, Father.
Is this justice? The ruler of the world, the ever-victorious king, treated you as his equal in his letters.
Because he honored your old age, he sent you a gift as to a good father. But in your arrogance you have pelted him, as though with stones, with insulting and abusive words.
Know that I am innocent of your blood. Nevertheless, I must carry out what I have been commanded.”
The tyrant drew his sword and held it out, unsheathed, toward Eusebius. He said to him, “These two things you see have been left to your choice
by the king. Choose one of the two for yourself: either the king's gifts, submitting to his will, and he will make you chief and overseer of all the priests of the gods,
just as you are now chief of all the bishops; or this sharpened sword, by your own free choice.
Now consider what answer you will send back to the king who sent me to you.” God's holy man was grieved in his soul and said to Adauctus,
“Truly, I am ashamed for you, because you call that madman a king rather than a tyrant.
He has abandoned God his Maker and bestowed worship on his creatures. The madman has fallen away from his truth and denied his faith.
He has become depraved and gone mad through worshiping demons and serving idols. What can we say now except what the prophet said to God:
‘For your sake we are killed every day, and we are considered sheep for slaughter’?” He bowed his head before him to be killed, offered his neck to the sword, and said,
“Come near, my son, and carry out what you have been commanded.” When Adauctus saw this, he recoiled and cried out loudly before the whole assembly of the city,
“I have not been ordered to kill you, but to warn you, just as the ruler of the world himself sent you a warning in his letters,
so that, while there is still room for pardon, you may rescue your life and save yourself. Here is his letter in your hands.” Zeal stirred God's holy man,
and he seized Julian's letter, tore it apart, and scattered its pieces to the wind. Then he turned and said to Adauctus,
“Just as your master has been torn out of this first letter he wrote, so may he be torn out of his kingdom. May he neither prosper nor succeed in ruling the Romans.”
But let his destruction take place outside their domain, because he dared to exalt himself against God his maker, withheld worship from him, and denied him thanksgiving.
Although he knows and is certain that all God's creatures owe worship to him as the creator of all, he has assigned his worship to demons and evil spirits,
who have never shown him any faithfulness. Like wild dogs, they eagerly watch for the moment when they can lick his blood at the hour of his destruction. For this
is the reward and repayment given to those who serve and labor with demons. When Adauctus and those with him heard these things and saw what had happened,
they groaned in their hearts and tore their clothes. They were greatly afraid because the imperial document had been torn up.
They threatened God's holy man, but they could do nothing to him: first, because of the assembled congregation of the church,
and second, because they had no order to kill him. They turned their faces away from him in anger
and turned toward the city's leading men. They argued fiercely with them, saying,
"Men of Rome, understand and see what you have done [?]. For the [?] that occurred today in your city was no small thing, and to you perhaps [?]
[?] was considered [?] you, and you do not bring [?] to mind the danger that arises from this
for you. For you yourselves heard with your own ears Eusebius's insult against the emperor and his blasphemy against the gods.
You saw with your own eyes the imperial document being torn up. Yet you did not groan within yourselves, feel distress, and seek redress for the insult to the emperor and the gods
from this wretched, ill-fated man, who [?] will soon perish from among the living. And you will rightly be called to account for his disgrace,
as people in whose eyes your master's writings were held in contempt, who disregarded his commands and defied the fear of his authority.
Perhaps it is because you have received favor in his eyes and are held in affection by him,
so that he wrote you letters as to brothers and friends, letters full of [?], proclaiming peace, gladdening the heart, and bringing joy to the soul.
Perhaps this is why his authority has become contemptible in your eyes, and you did not seek redress [?] for the insult done to him through his writings, which were torn up.
For if he had sent you writings in keeping with imperial authority and as its regulations prescribe, through angry men full of wrath and ready for the sword,
perhaps fear and trembling would by now have fallen upon them, and the writings of the one who holds authority
over the world would have been very precious in your eyes. But because he has not yet exercised his authority over you,
perhaps you have not even recognized that he is emperor. Now consider what you are doing, for the evil that occurred today in your city is no small thing. And if you wish,
there is a way for the danger to be removed from your city. Only give us your support so that we may act as we have been commanded, and then the danger will be removed from you,
and you will be free from blame. [?] But Volusianus, who was one of the leading men of Rome,
answered Adauctus, saying, "What have you been commanded by your master? Show me, so that we may know his will and support your action. [?]"
Adauctus said, "From what has just been read before you, which you heard with your own ears, you can learn the emperor's will."
“If you are willing, you have no need of questions....” Belsinus said, “The things that have just been read before us.”
“It was sent to Bishop Eusebius, not to us. He answered your questions as he wished and as seemed good to him.”
“But what business do you have with us?” Adauctus said, “We have only this one request to make of you: that, as the officials and governors of the city,”
“and also because we know that those assembled with Eusebius in the church are your brothers and relatives, you should issue orders”
“and persuade [?] to go, each person [?] and to his business, and lend a hand [?] of the emperor [?] to his command [?].”
“For while [?] we can [?] do something [?], so that no disturbance [?] occurs in the city and both we and you come under blame.”
Belsinus said, “We have received no written command from your master about this matter.”
“A law was laid down for us by the emperors who preceded you: we are to do nothing without the emperor’s command and written instructions.” Adauctus said,
“Were it not that I fear the danger arising from the offense committed [?], lest another letter be torn up like the first and I be exposed to the danger of transgression,”
“because I issued another letter after experiencing what happened to the first letter. You too have letters of your own with us from Julian, who holds authority over the world.”
Belsinus said, “We have never overstepped the bounds of our duty, nor have we done anything harmful to ourselves. So let no one suppose anything further about us.”
Then Adauctus reached out and handed Belsinus and his companions the letter of the defiled man. In it he had sent them many foolish words.
We need not record all of them in our history, but only those relevant to the course of our account. At the end of all his words, he wrote to them as follows:
“Since your city has always flourished through the presence of the gods—gods who departed from it throughout the reigns of the emperors before us—”
“it came close to ruin. But I, knowing your firm faith in the gods,”
“before the time of the house of Constantine, put myself forward on your behalf, and through my sacrifices and offerings [?] the gods’ anger against you. For we have not forgotten”
“the care and reverence you showed toward the immortal gods.”
“They recognize people’s faith not through ordinary, empty words, but through evident, glorious, and constant deeds.”
“Therefore, when the gods were pleased with the faith of your minds, and recognized and examined your inner thoughts and perceived your love for them,”
“they judged justly and decreed that your city deserved to blossom and flourish again through the presence of its gods,”
“to grow and become strong, to rejoice greatly, and to delight in their festivals. Show, therefore, your goodwill toward what the gods have resolved,”
“and lend a hand to Adauctus, the right hand of my imperial rule, and to the holy priests with him,”
“so that they may carry out the gods’ will and fulfill the plan they have devised. For this was the gods’ will:”
“that a great altar should be built for them at the gate of the great church of Rome, from where the error of the Nazarenes flared up and spread throughout the whole Roman dominion,”
“and that a sacrifice of reconciliation should be offered upon it for the atonement of your city and the forgiveness of its inhabitants.”
And if Eusebius repents and turns back from his error, comes to his senses, and submits to our will, let him first, as high priest of the gods,
offer a new sacrifice on a new altar for the peace of your city and the continued welfare of its inhabitants. But if he persists in his misguided way of thinking,
defies our command, and despises our authority, let him be held for a just judgment. And let the priests of Zeus and Apollo
perform the sacrifice to the gods. As king, I could have carried these things out by force, even against your will.
But because I learned of your love for the gods, and that you had been longing for this very thing for a long time,
I therefore left everything to your wishes, treating you as brothers and friends, so that, when you show us your goodwill,
you may receive good gifts from us, and benefits may be passed on to your children and your grandchildren for many generations....
When the vile man's letter was read before all the people of the city, some were happy and rejoiced, while others were sorrowful and distressed.
There was joy for the Jews and the pagans, but mourning and sorrow for the whole community of the house of God. The city's leaders were also distressed,
for they too were believers, and they did not know what to do because of the treasury affairs entrusted to them.
They said to Adauctus, “We have been appointed over the city's affairs, not over sacrifices to demons. If your master has commanded you to do something,
here is the whole city before you. Do everything you have been commanded to do. Do not implicate us. We neither oppose your master's will
nor fight against our brothers. For all those gathered with Eusebius in the church are our brothers and relatives.
It is not our business to build altars or to tear down churches.” ... Adauctus said to them, “You have plainly revealed
that you share the views of Eusebius and those with him.” ... Belusianus, speaking on behalf of all his companions, said to him, “Why
do you suppose that we should deny God our maker?” ... Adauctus said, “Who is the maker of everything?”
Belusianus said, “Christ, who was crucified for the sake of his creatures.” ... Adauctus said, “If this is your way of thinking,
how many terrible things you will have to endure!” ... Belusianus said, “Who has ever heard or seen anything like this?
The king has not yet seen us, has not yet sat on the throne of our kingdom, and his authority has not yet begun to rule over us,
yet his threats and menaces are already being proclaimed in the streets of our city instead of consular largesse and a royal gift. And what more is there than this? [?] change our country,
but not change the truth of our God; become foreigners to the entire Roman Empire, but not abandon the faith that our fathers handed down to us.
It is astonishing and amazing that, while your master is still in the upper regions, the news of his paganism has preceded him into every region of our dominion.”
Adauctus said to them, “Now that this is your wish, I am leaving for the king who sent me.
He himself will settle accounts with you for your insolence as he sees fit.” Now the Jews who had gathered to witness this discussion
railed against the leaders of Rome, saying, “Because your minds are attached to the religion of the Nazarenes,
You want to bring disaster upon us, and our city will be destroyed because of you, because you refuse to carry out the king’s will.
But be certain of this: the king’s will will be carried out even against your wishes. We, for our part, support the king’s will, and it will be carried out.
For joy has come to us only with difficulty and after a long time. How you would have liked it to have faded already! But far be it from our joy to fade!
For the time has come for Abraham’s daughter to be gathered together and comforted in her sorrow, and for her heart to rejoice and be glad at the gathering of her children
and at the joy of her temples. This is her day to clap her hands and stamp her feet, and to raise her voice and say, “Do not rejoice over me, my enemies!
Though I have fallen, I shall rise again, and the time has come for me to rise. You who rejoiced over me on the day I fell—look, today I rejoice at your humiliation!” These
were the expressions the Jews used openly before all the Roman people. They clapped their hands, stamped their feet, and danced.
They stirred up agitation and urged the pagans to build the altar. Jews and pagans followed Adauctus,
about three thousand men, saying, “We support the king’s will.
An altar to the gods will be built at the [?] of that arrogant, conceited woman, who overthrew the temples of the gods, uprooted their altars, demolished and devastated our [?],
and burned our synagogue. When, indeed, will the day come when we see her temples being demolished and jeer at her as our fathers jeered at her
in the days of the renowned kings Diocletian and Maximian, who demolished her lofty temples
and laid bare the foundations of her enclosing walls?” When the blessed Eusebius learned of these things, he sent word to Adauctus:
“Keep away from the boundaries of the church, for it is a charge entrusted to me. I would rather die for it than let a stranger trample it.
And if the Jews, our enemies, are inciting you against us, understand and consider what you are doing. For all the people who are with me
are ready and prepared, and they are determined to destroy and be destroyed.” When Adauctus heard this,
he summoned the Jews and the pagans and said to them, “Eusebius and those with him, as I have learned,
are ready and prepared to fight. Therefore, so that the undertaking is not delayed by a battle, accept the advice I give you:
shut the church’s outer gates against them and take up positions at them. Let Eusebius and those with him remain confined
until the altar is built and the sacrifices are completed. Once the king’s will has been carried out and the name of the gods has been invoked over their meetinghouse,
let the gates be opened. If they have the strength to face our attack, let them fight us.” This proposal pleased the Jews and the pagans.
They shut the church’s outer gates and took up positions at them on every side.
Eusebius and those with him were confined for two days. The Jews and the pagans began to build the altar. And when

the city’s leading men saw that Bishop Eusebius and all the church’s clergy, together with the believers who were with them, had been confined, and learned of the agreement between the Jews and the pagans,
that once the altar had been built and the sacrifices completed, the church’s gates would be opened.
And they would attack them with swords, without Adauctus’s orders, and slaughter them. The leaders of Rome were deeply distressed.
They were troubled to the depths of their souls, not knowing what to do, because they were afraid on account of the treasury offices they held.
And they could not reveal themselves. But he sent word secretly, and they informed the exarch of these monasteries.
They sent them this message: “Hurry to rescue your brothers in the church before the persecutors’ sword gains power over them.
For the crowd of pagans and Jews who have been set against them have seized the outer doors of the church.
They have imprisoned Bishop Eusebius and those with him, while a sacrificial altar is being built for Zeus and Apollo at the church door.
An agreement has been made between the Jews and the pagans that, when the altar is finished and the sacrifices have been offered, the church doors will be opened.
They will force their way in against them, without orders, and slaughter them. Now hurry to rescue them before the sword of the crucifiers gains power over them.
For we cannot make ourselves known openly because of the unjust authority we hold.” When the exarch learned of these things,
he cried out and wept bitterly, saying, “Alas! Our sins have made a wicked king reign over us!” He rose hurriedly, in great alarm,
and notified all the monasteries there. He gathered all the monks in Rome and its surroundings who were strong enough to face a fight,
about fourteen hundred men. They were all of one soul and one mind. They raised their voices and wept over the humiliation of the church
and the imprisonment of their brothers. They clasped one another’s right hands, pledging to die for their brothers in the church.
They strengthened and encouraged one another and put on strength and courage. They entered Rome with great boldness, equipped and carrying
clubs. About five hundred Roman men were also mingled with them. They were from Arta [?] in Mesopotamia. Out of zeal for God, these men
had changed their clothing for the clothing of monks. They cut their hair and entered Rome with them, armed,
without anyone recognizing them at all. The whole city was shaken at their approach. They headed straight for the church, where they had learned that the sacrificial altar was being built.
When the pagans and Jews saw them, they began to panic before them, for the Lord had cast fear and trembling upon the Jews and pagans.
They began fleeing from the monks in every direction. The monks fell upon them with clubs in the streets and struck them like dogs.
A great many Jews and pagans died that day. Only a very few of them escaped, hiding themselves in concealed places and recesses

and in the city’s sewers, and so they were saved. Not even one of the company of monks was injured, for the Lord spread his hand over them and protected them. When Adauctus saw that slaughter had begun among the Jews,
he said to the priests who were with him, “Where [?] among the Jews.” He said to the priests who were with him,
“Save yourselves wherever you can!” He himself mounted his horse and escaped alone.
When these priests saw that Adauctus had abandoned them and fled, fear and trembling fell upon them.
They wandered about, looking for somewhere to hide themselves. They found a large idol temple two miles away from the city.
They avoided him and hid themselves for a while, until an opportunity arose for them to flee from there.
When the sword had ceased and there was quiet, not a Jew or a pagan remained to be seen openly anywhere in the city.
Eudoxius said to his fellow monks, “Now that Christ has given us relief, and our eyes have seen the fate of the church’s enemies and those who hate the cross,
let us open the church’s doors and comfort the blessed shepherd and his flock.” So they opened the church’s doors
and went in and greeted Bishop Eusebius and those with him. And there was joy
throughout the city over the deliverance God had brought about for his church. There was, however, an inquiry among the brothers about what had become of those priests of sin.
When their inquiry had been investigated, it became known that not one of those priests had died.
They begged the blessed Eusebius to allow them to go out in search of them. God’s holy man said to them,
“My children, leave the dead to bury their dead, as our Lord said. Let us attend to our own struggle
and be diligent in this spiritual undertaking that has come upon us. Let us not, under the pretext of zeal, hinder our own struggle and find ourselves fighting against ourselves.
For God has called us to bear witness in the time of our trial, not to wage war against our persecutors.
For that all-conquering Power could have destroyed with the breath of his mouth those who seized him to crucify him.
But so that the course for which he came into the world would not be thwarted, he gave those who would crucify him the opportunity to seize him.
To show them that they had seized him by his own will, he released a slight flash of his divinity and surrendered himself to his captors. Though he was not subject to suffering or death,
in the nature of our body he endured the sufferings of crucifixion and tasted death in our nature. By his death he annulled the sentence against our humanity. And if that good Lord,
who is high and exalted above suffering and death, tasted our death and endured our sufferings for the sake of saving his servants,
how much more ought we, guilty servants who are mortal and subject to suffering, to taste the suffering of his crucifixion
through the sufferings and tortures of our confession, and not deny him. Let us withdraw from what has happened today and attend from now on to our own struggle.
For who knows whether, among those who died today, there were people who would have come to their senses, regretted their error, and attained repentance,
and gained their lives, instead of dying today in their paganism, departing in their sins, being deprived of their hope, and losing their lives? So it is with these priests.
Who can grasp the future and know whether there are among them people whom grace will call, whom repentance will reach, and who will gain their lives, just as
Sharbel the priest and others like him gained their lives?” While the blessed Eusebius had not yet finished his exhortation, someone came and informed him,
“As for those defiled men, the priests of sin, Pharcus the centurion went out in search of them, overtook them, and brought them in chains to the pyre they had built.
The whole crowd of the city is in an uproar, shouting that they should be burned on the pyre they built. I was sent to tell you this.”
The blessed Eusebius rose in great alarm, went out into the city, and found them in an uproar.
He motioned to them with his hand to be quiet. When they had become still, they spoke with them, and he said to them, “Men of Rome,
understand and consider what you are doing today. For this pagan tyrant has long been fiercely threatening our city
because of your true faith. All the more so today, when he hears what has happened to the followers of his error. In the madness of his paganism, he will destroy your city
and take your lives.” [?] The crowds of the city answered, saying, “Let our city be destroyed, and let us die!
And let those who defile our empire burn in the fire! For we have already, once and for all, set our faces toward death for the faith of the church.”
But Saint Eusebius gently admonished them with persuasive words, saying, “My children, what benefit will we gain from the death of these wretched people,
especially since they will go away in their error and die in their sins, and their opportunity for repentance will be lost? Instead, if you are willing and it seems good to you,
let them be placed in monasteries and taught the faith of the church.
Perhaps they will repent of their wickedness, turn away from their error, find repentance for themselves, and gain oblivion for their destruction and error. Therefore, let us not,
my children, hasten their death, if you are willing.” Then eloquent and wise men from the crowds of the city stood up and argued with Eusebius, saying,

“Repentance is not called for in the case of those who have themselves cut off the hope of their repentance: impure men who dared to build an altar in the holy place where a dwelling has been built for God Most High,
to demons and idols. What repentance can there be for these people, even if they promise to repent?
For their repentance would be a matter of cunning and deceit until the tyrant strengthened their power. Then they would prove their repentance false and turn back to take unjust revenge on us
for the death that we justly decreed against them. For they are an evil planting,
and their roots are planted beside the streams of error, and they bear no fruit of repentance at all.
Therefore, let the proclamation of John the Baptist apply to them: ‘Every tree that does not bear fruit
is cut down and goes into the fire,’ together with what our Lord also said: ‘Every plant that my Father in heaven did not plant will soon be uprooted.’

With these divine utterances proclaiming their destruction, who will stand against them except someone who agrees with their error? Therefore, let this evil planting be uprooted from our city before it produces a bitter shoot and poisons us. For Your Holiness is not unaware
of the care and vigilance with which our city holds to the faith that the apostles handed down to it.
Nor is it without cause or in vain that the crowds of our city threaten these unclean and defiled people,
who left the streets and squares of our city and built impure altars to demons and idols at the gates of our church.
Unless their offense is laid upon their heads, the simple and innocent will soon be led astray,
and we will justly be held accountable for them.” But although the blessed Eusebius heard these words,
he continued to strive with all his might to save these misguided people from death, so that he might establish them in repentance.
But the crowds of the city were displeased, and they began shouting at Eusebius, the orthodox man of the church.
Support the faith that our fathers, the apostles, handed down to us, for all the churches hold fast to you.
Christ has established you on the throne of Simon Peter, who, in his zeal for his faith, justly exacted punishment from Simon the magician
and from those who agreed with his madness. Follow his example and take vengeance on the unclean followers of his error.
And let Julian, who sent them, suffer distress because of them. Let the priests of sin, the enemies of truth, burn on the pyre they made.

Let those who hate the church be given to the fire as its portion. Let them themselves be offered as a sacrifice to demons. For through these things your faith is praised, noble and faithful shepherd.
Through these things your faith is glorified, radiant and holy priest. Through these things your old age is honored, you who bear the burden of his church and his flock.
Righteous shepherd, stand before your flock. [?] of the church, avenge her humiliation upon the contemptible men who entered and trampled the bridal chamber of her betrothed.
For Christ entrusted the church, his betrothed, to you. See that you do not neglect to exact punishment from those who mock her. Swing the sickle of your zeal and reap the heap of weeds.
Let them become fuel for the pyre they built. And if you have any fear about this, and shrink from the death of these defiled men, enter your church with honor.
We ourselves will take upon ourselves the danger of burning them and the punishment for their death.” While these cries were beating upon the holy man's ears from every side,
he was grieved in his soul and lifted his eyes to heaven. He raised his hands toward God and said, “You are sufficient, you who know hidden things.
You have examined my heart and searched my thoughts, knowing what means I sought to save these wretched men from death.
It was not because I shrank from the tyrant's anger and threats, as those who spoke supposed,
but so that your mercy would not demand from my hands the repentance of these misguided men at the time of their reckoning. And since this causes the Romans to stumble,
and the destruction of sinners is more acceptable to them than their repentance, my Lord, everything is entrusted to your will.”
With tears in his eyes, he returned to his church, bearing in his soul grief over the destruction of these guilty men,
who were now deprived of repentance. There was, however, a division among the city's crowds after the blessed Eusebius returned to his church.
Some of them regretted that they had thwarted the righteous shepherd's will. They discussed with one another how they might carry out the will of God's holy man. Others, however,
opposed their words, saying, “There should be no mercy for those who wrongfully dared to defile the Lord's house.”
The argument of those who threatened the defiled priests prevailed. In the heat of their zeal, they bound them and threw them onto the pyre.
They piled wood over them and burned them on the pyre they had built. When the flame had consumed their bodies until no trace of them remained,
they overturned the pyre and scattered its ashes. They dragged it away and threw it into the river that passes through the middle of the city. On that very day,
the leading men of Rome entered into a sworn covenant—well-known and distinguished men, the city's nobles and officials.
They made an agreement and took oaths that they would be of one soul and one mind, and would ask to be released from the administration of the city
and from the treasury affairs for which they were responsible, in one accord and complete agreement, and with one sincere love free from deceit,

[?] to declare openly before the tyrant that they were Christians, without denying their faith because of his authority or being frightened or shaken by his menacing threats, even if he forcibly pressured them to deny it.
They resolved to accept tortures and afflictions. They set before their eyes the confiscation of their possessions, the plundering of their property, and the surrender of their very lives,
rather than deny God their Maker. For they said to one another, “Our city is the capital of the entire territory of our kingdom, and if apostasy [comes] from us [?],
we will become a cause of stumbling [?] for all the lands under our authority. Responsibility for their apostasy and sin will fall upon us if we happen to falter.
Therefore, as people sound in their faith and steadfast in their truth, we ought to cast behind us worldly cares and concern for possessions,
and love and affection for wife and children, brothers and sisters, together with everything in the world.
Let us care only for our souls and our struggle, and for how we may please God by our confession,
so that we may look upon him openly and without shame, as he commanded us in his gospel. Like diligent and mighty competitors,
let us run this race set before us [?], fight against sin, and overcome it through steadfast endurance. Like resolute athletes, let us exert ourselves for a time,
and carry away from it the crown of victory. Let us become a source of benefit and a good example to all the lands
of our territory. For what will we gain from the world if we acquire it but lose our souls? This is what our Savior himself said in his gospel.”
They brought forward examples from the Holy Scriptures and testimonies from the people [?] that suited their circumstances.
They strengthened and encouraged one another. When the blessed Eusebius learned how concerned the leading men of Rome were
that the Church’s true faith should not be emptied of its power, and that they had offered themselves to death for the truth of their God,
he rejoiced, and his heart was glad at their zeal for the faith and the steadfastness of their resolve. This blessed old man did not grow weary, and in the divine love he possessed,
he got up and went to them where they were gathered, and greeted them.

He spoke to their hearts and comforted them. With many examples from the Scriptures, he encouraged them and strengthened their resolve, calling them blessed and praising their faith. When it was time, he instructed each of them to go home.
They approached, bowed before him, and received his blessing. He filled his mouth with blessing,
blessed them, and said to them, “You are blessed by the Lord your God, to whom you have entrusted yourselves, whom you have loved and cherished more than everything in the world.
You have committed yourselves to walking the path of his crucifixion, and you have fulfilled what our Lord said: ‘Whoever loves me, let him come after me.’
And, ‘Whoever does not deny himself, take up his cross, and come after me is not worthy of me.’ And so that we should not lose heart
when trials come upon us, and draw back from loving him, he urged us and said to us, ‘Remain in my love.’
Therefore, my children, let us remain in love for our Maker, and let us not lose heart in our afflictions.
For affliction that lasts for a time gains us everlasting life. Nor should we be frightened by the tyrant’s fury and threats.
For God does not abandon us completely, nor does he discipline us to destroy us. Let us listen to the apostle Paul, who said, ‘We are afflicted in every way.’
But we are not crushed. We are troubled, but not defeated. We are persecuted, but not abandoned. We are struck down,
but we do not perish,” together with the other divine sayings with which the apostle comforted those who were being persecuted in his time,
as we are. We too, my beloved, ought, through these same sayings proclaimed by the Holy Scriptures,
to comfort ourselves in our persecution and cast our care upon God our Maker. By his power he can quench the fury of our persecution,
and in his mercy, as is his custom, grant forgiveness for our guilt, deliverance to his churches, and new life in his kingdom to you who have willingly become witnesses.
After blessing them, he dismissed them to go home in peace, each to his own house. He himself returned to his church, rejoicing, giving thanks, and praising God.
Julian learned everything that had happened in Rome. He threatened the people of Rome fiercely and was filled with fury and anger against them.
He had set his face toward destroying them and exacting vengeance from them for the burning of his champions [?]. But someone was able to calm the tyrant’s mind:
Aplatus, through his knowledge. He was a man accomplished in wisdom and renowned among the philosophers. Although he was a pagan,
he gave just and upright advice. This man was one of the tyrant’s advisers,
and the advice he gave was accepted. Julian summoned him privately to obtain his advice about what he had planned.
He disclosed to him and explained what vengeance he intended to exact from the people of Rome, who had despised him and disregarded his writings. He threatened them harshly, saying:
“I am taking vengeance upon them as duty rightly demands—these rebellious slaves who, in their insolence, dared to lay hands on the priests of the divine power. They did not fear the vengeance

of the gods, whose priests they unjustly burned on a pretext they fabricated. Nor did they shrink before the just authority of our imperial rule and submit to discipline. Instead, they added to their wickedness
and ravaged and destroyed the Jewish people because they had complied with the will of our imperial rule, besides the countless evils and offenses they have committed. In response to these things,
what advice is there to give about them, you who are learned and wise and a lover of the gods?” But Aplatus, because he was a wise and peace-loving man,
began his speech by yielding to the tyrant’s intention in the matter, so that he might bring about a reversal and draw him toward his own intention.
For he said to the tyrant, “Your imperial authority extends both to destruction and to mercy. As king, you have authority to do whatever you wish,
since there is no one above you to condemn your will in what you do, except our holy gods, who do not desire the destruction of human beings.
For who among mortals would dare overturn the king’s will and still remain alive?” Julian said, “If I wanted to exercise my authority as you have said,
I would not have troubled you about what I had planned. For it had not escaped our notice that, as king, I have authority over everything.
But although I have that authority, I do not wish to do anything by force, so that in this too our uprightness may become known to everyone.
Therefore, as a learned and wise man, give just and upright advice about the matters on which we have consulted you.
Do not be intimidated by our authority and neglect your duty. Nor should you show unjustified mercy toward rebels and murderers who do not deserve it.”
Aplatus said, “Since I have received permission from Your Majesty and obtained an assurance that I should not neglect my duty: you do indeed have authority as king.
But along with this, let Your Majesty also know that even the powers of kingship are subject to the requirements of duty
and to the laws of justice. If anyone wishes to overstep the requirements of duty and trample on the laws of justice,
the title of king, which had brought him honor, is stripped from him, and the title of tyrant takes its place.
This bequeaths everlasting disgrace and shame to those who bear it. He can no longer be called a king, but rather a tyrant who conducts affairs without law.
But far be it from Your Majesty to transgress the laws of justice, since all the ordinances of duty proceed from you. Julian said:
“And what do the requirements of duty demand, or the laws of justice command, concerning rebellious and murderous slaves who have not kept the fear of their masters before their eyes?”
Aplatus said: “Your Divinity has granted freedom of speech to us lowly people, and we have been commanded by the authority of Your Might
to offer your understanding advice about whatever our lowliness can comprehend. It has seemed to us, then, O glorious and mighty king forever,
that, since Your Might has not yet sat upon the throne of the Roman Empire,
and the revered and glorious name of Your Awe-Inspiring Majesty has not yet been proclaimed over the Roman dominion,
and we have not yet received the [?] of our kingship in this city, which is the capital of our dominion and the mother of all the cities under our authority—
and those who do not receive the [?] of kingship in this city have a rule inferior to that of kings
and are outside the historical record of the Roman emperors—concerning this, O glorious and mighty one,
we submit an appeal and petition to the authority of Your Awe-Inspiring Majesty: let us be patient with this city for a while, because it is the capital of our dominion.
Let us not hasten to proclaim the sword against it before we reign, lest we be called enemies rather than rulers.
For it is not fitting for us, before we reign, to seize the royal throne through weapons, the sword, and war, through destruction and bloodshed,
lest we be regarded as tyrants rather than kings. But if Your Majesty wishes, and it seems good to Your Authority, let us restrain ourselves
and bear the affront of their wrongdoing for a while, until the kingdom is firmly established in our hands, we have gained strength against our enemies, we are victorious in our battles,

and we return triumphantly to our dominion in accordance with the law. Then, as a king and ruler, in keeping with the requirements of duty, Your Uprightness will take vengeance on the offenders, and there will be
a just reckoning with them for having crossed the bounds of duty. Each one of them will be repaid justly, as his offenses deserve.
For we, like lowly servants commanded by their masters, have submitted to Your Awe-Inspiring Majesty, in our earnest petition, what has seemed right to us. The decision now belongs to Your Divinity.”
Julian said: “Your advice seems very good to me, and I accept your words. Yet even if I disregard and set aside everything else, as for vengeance for the priests of the deity,
we cannot neglect it, lest the gods whom they served become angry at our neglect of vengeance for them.” Aplatus said:
“Leave vengeance for the priests to the gods, so that they may exact their vengeance whenever they wish. For who can search out the secrets of the gods,
enter into their hidden counsels, and comprehend what their will is concerning what has happened?”

Perhaps they used to approach their service contemptuously and mockingly? Or perhaps, again, they used to approach their mysteries in filth and corruption? Or perhaps they were committing thefts of the firstfruits?
And were they defrauding the gods of their vows through their greed and withholding their offerings, so that, because of the gods’ hostility toward them, this merciless lot fell to them?
But this is hidden from us. To the gods, however, it is clear why they neglected them while they were being tormented and did not help them while the flame was taking vengeance on them.
Let us therefore leave to the gods what lies with the gods, and to time what lies ahead of us, as far as we are able.
For now, let us take care to acquire a good and illustrious name through the administration entrusted to us. And he was pleased
—the tyrant—with the advice Aplatus had given, and he carried out his word. Now this accursed tyrant, when he arrived and reached Italy,
sent messengers ahead of him to Rome to announce his arrival. The whole city was thrown into confusion and alarm.
But the nobles of Rome, those who had entered into a sworn covenant, were not at all alarmed or disturbed. Instead, when they learned that the tyrant was about to arrive, they cast away
worldly cares and concern for possessions. They put their affairs in good order and attended to the poor, the needy, and also the orphans
and widows, providing generously for them, for they were wealthy men. The remainder of their property and whatever they possessed
they entrusted to the members of their households. They appointed trusted men and stewards over their property, both within the city and outside it. Before the tyrant came to their city,
they left their houses and withdrew from their dwellings, and they made their home in the church of God with the blessed Eusebius,
until the day when the tyrant entered their city and sent men to imprison them. Julian’s entry into Rome took place
in the month of Adar, in the year six hundred and seventy-three according to the reckoning of the Greeks, on the twenty-fifth day of that month,
when five months had passed since the death of Constantius. On this very day the tyrant entered Rome with a great procession of his troops,
with the might and strength of his army, with a multitude of legions, and with the [?] of their garments. He was carried away by arrogance and boasting,
and his mind was proud and exalted by the divinations of his paganism. In his madness, it did not even occur to him that he was a human being.
He wore a threatening expression on his face that made those who saw him tremble, intending to cast alarm and fear upon the inhabitants of Rome.
The people of the city were shaken at the sight of him. They fled and hid from him, and no one came or went through the city’s streets
for many days. When the tyrant saw that great fear had taken hold of the inhabitants of Rome,
he gave gifts to his troops, appointed commanders over them, and sent them away to other cities
until such time as they received orders. He sent his heralds through the city proclaiming peace and promising pardon.
Even so, they scarcely dared to appear before him. When quiet had returned, the sword was at rest, and the people were at peace, the tyrant ordered spectacles to be held and
all the people to assemble in the city’s theater, promising them under oath that from now on there would be peace and no danger of any kind.
When the whole city had assembled according to the wicked man’s command, and the theater was filled from end to end, Julian put on royal garments.
And he went up to sit on the royal throne. But the tyrant was waiting first to receive the acclamations of kingship from the city's assemblies, and only then to sit on the royal throne.
