Otherwise he might be recorded in the royal chronicles as a tyrant rather than a king. The Romans shouted to him, saying:
“If you demand the acclamations of kingship from us, promise to grant our requests, and receive the acclamations.” Julian said to them:
“What is your request?” They said to him, “That peace may reign over all our religions.” But Julian shook his head and remained silent.
They kept clamoring against him and shouting, “You want to sit on the throne of our kingdom!
Leave the religions to themselves, and remain in your own as you see fit. And if you wish to possess our city,
let the persecution of the house of Maximinus be removed from our midst, and then we are your servants. These are the things our city desires.
To these things our people agree. For kingship befits you when you make peace throughout your dominion. The crown and authority adorn you
when your compassion is spread equally over everyone.” And when they had persisted for a long time with these cries,
the tyrant waved his hand at them to make them quiet. When they had fallen silent and become still, he spoke to them and said:
“What is this wicked corruption that has seized your city? For the offenses and evil deeds committed in it are not few.
And if our Majesty were to investigate your offenses and your evil deeds, scarcely would there survive our sword
one-third of the inhabitants of your city. But because this is the beginning of our reign, it seemed to us most fitting
to pardon those who have been guilty up to this day and to pour out mercy upon offenders. But know this, Romans: once I have granted pardon
to your city, from now on there is no pardon, no mercy, and not even life for anyone who dares to trample upon the command of our authority
or persists in that former tyrannical intention. As for the peace you have requested from us concerning the religions, I do indeed intend to make peace,
provided that they too adopt a good disposition by devoting themselves to the worship and service of the gods,
taking care and making sure that sacrifices, offerings, and their firstfruits are not withheld. And once they have appeased the gods on their own behalf,
they too have our permission to practice the mysteries of their error as much as they wish, without any fear of anything
from us. As for the tyrant Eusebius, he had already been secretly in our thoughts,
and shortly afterward his sentence was revealed to him. But those tyrants with him, who were drawn into his madness,
who did not [?] from their evil deeds and did not repent of their offenses, but still persist in that same former tyrannical intention,
do not keep the fear of our authority before their eyes. To know that these things are so, observe that they have not even appeared
before us, because of their arrogance, so that their tyranny is revealed even by this. For these people, therefore, there is no mercy, no pardon, and not even life.
For from now on, as justice requires, I will exact vengeance from them for their offenses and the evil deeds committed by their hands.”

At that very moment he sent men to remove them from the church in great humiliation. They were pulled about and thrown down, and their captors stripped off and took away the honorable clothing of their order.
They dressed them in humiliating women's clothing, as the wicked man had commanded. By this command they brought them before him in this degrading attire.
But the tyrant did not look at them or question them at all. Instead, they put collars and chains on them.
He sent them to prison in great humiliation, until, he said, there would be time to give them a proper hearing.
All the people of the city were weeping bitterly over the humiliation and disgrace of men
who were distinguished and honored, leaders of all Rome. But those servants of God
felt no sorrow at all in their souls over this. Instead, they rejoiced and were glad at heart that they had been found worthy to begin the struggle of confessing their faith.
They gave thanks and praised God. But concerning the blessed Eusebius, the tyrant ordered that he should not appear before him.
Instead, he too was to go to prison, wearing his priestly attire but without iron fetters, until the day appointed for the festival of the gods.
They did to him as he commanded. Now the tyrant had conceived and devised a plan: at the festival of the idols they would offer the blessed Eusebius as a burnt offering on the altar,
in the attire and insignia of his priesthood, so that through this everyone would know that the chief priest of the Nazarenes
was himself paying the penalty demanded by the priests of the gods. As though to honor his idols, he spared the holy man the humiliation of fetters.
For he said, “It is not right for a man appointed as a sacrifice to the divinity, and once [?] consecrated to the gods, to suffer humiliation.”
But the blessed Eusebius was unaware of these things. Instead, in prison he continually offered prayer to God
for the peace of the churches and the salvation of their children, and for the struggle and endurance of those who were with him.
He strengthened their resolve and confirmed their faith with proofs from the Scriptures,
recounting to them the story of the victories of men [?] like themselves, who, just like them, had abandoned everything they possessed in a wonderful struggle
and in the good testimony they bore for Christ, and had reached the end of their lives in the days of the wicked Maximinus.
When the tyrant had spent four weeks in Rome, the madman ordered a great altar to be built at the entrance to the church of Rome,
where the former altar had stood. It was built as he commanded, and his heralds were sent throughout the city,
announcing, “Ten days from now, the great festival of the gods will take place. So let everyone attend to himself and whiten his clothes,
and purify his body, for the day of the gods is holy, as they are.” And while these mad proclamations
were being heard in the streets of Rome, all the people of the city were astonished at his paganism and amazed at his madness.
When nine days had passed, the tyrant gave orders, the drum was beaten, the horns sounded, and heralds went out through the city,
announcing that everyone, willingly and with a cheerful heart, should be ready and prepared at dawn to rejoice and enjoy himself at the great festival of the gods.
Especially at the divine festival of Zeus and Apollo, who remain exceedingly angry with us to this day, because we have not yet
avenged their priests. To these, then, who sustain the world, from whom help flows to our humanity,
we must offer a burnt offering of reconciliation to their divinity, hidden from all, which cannot be perceived by bodily eyes,
except through its [?] alone. To all these visible [?] of the hidden divinity,
we will dedicate a burnt offering upon their sacrificial pyre: Eusebius, the head of the religion of the Nazarenes, to become a burnt offering whose pleasing fragrance will satisfy the divinity,
and bring peace to your city and stability to its inhabitants, so that, when you serve the gods with all your heart,
times of rest and good years bearing joys will come upon you.” These utterances of madness
were ringing in the hearing of all the people of their city. But the Romans were mourning and grieving,
groaning inwardly over the grievous death of the blessed old man, and determined to die with him
or to save him from the fire of the sacrificial pyre by their outcry. The following day, in the morning,
Julius put on a magnificent royal robe, and over it he also put on another garment, a priestly one,
so that in both capacities he might officiate at the festival of his idols. He sent and summoned the defiled priests who shared his error,
and commanded them, saying, “Be ready and prepared, so that, when the drum sounds and the people of the city gather at the sacrificial pyre of the gods,
you take care that, with the splendid vessels of your ministry, Zeus and Apollo are carried honorably in procession upon the palms of your hands and come
in their glory, to the sound of praise from the choirs before them, while the whole blessed craft of musical instruments is stirred to sound at the time of their arrival.”

When the priests had received the command and gone out, the tyrant gave orders, and the drum was sounded. All the people gathered at the sacrificial pyre that the tyrant had built, hoping that they might be able
to save Eusebius from the burning of the sacrificial pyre by the sound of their outcry. When the tyrant learned that the entire population of the city had gathered,
he too came with a great procession of his troops. He went up and sat on the tribunal that had been prepared for him in front of the sacrificial pyre,
with his armed troops standing on his right and on his left. When the accursed man turned and looked at the crowds of the city,
and saw them mourning and grieving, dressed in shabby and humiliating clothing, he was deeply displeased. He lashed out at them and said to them angrily,
“Why have you appeared before our royal presence in this disgraceful attire and dishonored the great day of the gods?
You have dressed as though for a house of mourning for the dead and come to the festival of the gods! Because you have disregarded our command and despised what we proclaimed,
know, then, that by your insolence you have called down destruction upon your city and yourselves. But why is it that you are mourning and grieving?
Reveal your thoughts and make your wishes known, so that we too may know.” They remained silent and did not answer him a word.
While silence lay over them all, someone from among the crowds raised his voice and cried out, saying:
“Truly, we rightly and justly mourn and grieve, as we ought—that is, over your madness and your error.
For you abandoned God your Maker, who spread the wing of his mercy over you in the time of your distress and sheltered you from the sword of the righteous man.
But you, ungrateful man, denied him when you rose to greatness. You refused to acknowledge him, and became lawless and mad with love for demons
and the fumes of idols. Like a madman, you grew a beard for the priesthood of idolatry.
How could anyone not lament and weep over the blindness of your understanding? For God Most High is deprived of worship from his creatures through the madness of their rulers,
while demons are worshiped and idols are acknowledged. They feel no shame at shameful things and do not know how to accept correction, as the holy Scripture says.”
The tyrant became embittered and furious. He ordered a diligent search to be made for him and commanded that he be seized. When he had been seized and brought before him,
he ordered the cloak wrapped around his head to be removed, so that it might be known who this man was who had dared to do this.
When the covering was removed from him, everyone recognized that he was Eudoxius, the superior of the monasteries of Rome.
Julian was astonished and bewildered at what had confronted him from the beginning of his reign, especially in the city that was the capital of his dominion.
While he was considering the death of the faithful man, he asked him angrily and threateningly, “Are you indeed Eudoxius,
about whom I have learned from many people that you were responsible for the destruction of the priests of the divine power?”
Eudoxius said, “Far be it from us to betray the priests of the divine power! Rather, we worship and honor them.
But as for the priests of sin and the champions of error, before the assemblies of the city and before all your armies,
I openly acknowledge about myself that I was responsible for their destruction and also for their burning, if that is what you wish.” Julian said, “Today I wish
to celebrate the festival of the gods joyfully and to pay honor to their great day. After today—the gods themselves are my witnesses—I will take vengeance on you for your insolence
and bring down on your head your contempt and your blasphemy against the gods, so that through you I may frighten and terrify the entire people of the Galileans.” Eudoxius said,
“Because you have not yet gained experience of the Galileans or put their endurance to the test, you have supposed in your error that you can frighten them with your words
and terrify them with your threats. You are greatly mistaken and do not know it. If the gate of martyrdom is opened to them by your polluted hands

and becomes accessible to them through their confession, the Galileans will leave your madness astonished by their courage, their struggles, and their steadfast endurance, putting your weakness to shame
through their triumphant victory.” But since it was now time for the tyrant to perform the mysteries of his pagan religion, and he had resolved to burn God’s holy man,
Eusebius, on the pyre of his priests, and then complete the sacrifices to his idols,
for this reason the tyrant refrained from mistreating the blessed Eudoxius that day. He put him in irons
and sent him to prison until he had celebrated the festival of his idols and had a day available to hear his case.
After Eudoxius had been handed over to the prison, the tyrant sent for Eusebius and had him brought, so that they might offer him up in the fire as a burnt offering to his idols.
When all the people of the city saw the holy man of God being led like a lamb to slaughter, they all raised their voices and wept.
They cried out to Julian, saying, “If you seek the peace of our land and the preservation of our city, grant us and our city, as a gift at the festival of the gods,
a reprieve from the burning of this old man, out of respect for his age. If you do this for us,

we and our city will be indebted to your merciful kindness all our days. Trusting in your abundant mercy toward us, we present this appeal to your Majesty through our petition. It is now yours to show mercy out of goodwill.
Pardon is most fitting for your Majesty, especially on the great day of the gods.”
Julian was enraged by these words and answered them harshly, saying, “You rebels and stiff-necked people, calling destruction down upon yourselves!
How long must I be patient with you and put up with you? Our mercy has led you into great insubordination. What is this outcry of yours today,
you who harm yourselves through your zeal? For if the gods are not appeased by the burning of this wretch,
they will call down the sword and destruction upon you and your city. Now understand and consider
what you are doing. It is not just today that you began to act in a spirit of insubordination. We have had experience of you for a long time, and your insolence is well known to us. For
our Majesty has not lost sight of the ill will you showed toward us even before we entered your city, or of the offenses and evil deeds committed by your wicked hands
against the detachment sent by us to your city. Because it was the beginning of our reign,
we granted an undeserved pardon to evildoers and perpetrators of hateful acts, people deserving death who were not worthy of pardon.
Because our mercy overflowed toward you, it became your habit, whenever you committed another outrage with your shouting,
to come back like [?] and ask pardon for your offenses. But we have no such custom. Know, then, people of Rome,
that unless you restrain yourselves, mind your own affairs, and remain quiet, you will perish and your city will be destroyed.
Your possessions will be given over to plunder. Look, I have warned you beforehand!” But they cried out as though with one mouth, saying,
“Let our city be destroyed, let us perish, and let our possessions be given over to plunder, but do not lay your hands on the holy man of God. Look, we have warned you beforehand!
For we are all determined to die with him.” When Julian saw that they were neither restrained by his threats nor frightened by his menaces, he ordered his troops
to draw their swords and bend their bows, to frighten the crowds of the city until the will of the defiled man was carried out against God's holy and righteous man.
His troops did as they were commanded, but even so he could not silence them. They raised their voices against him and cried out to him, saying,
“We too are looking toward this very thing: to destroy and to be destroyed, if you lay your hands on the holy man of God.”
These words tormented and embittered the tyrant, but he held back from calling down the sword upon them,
because his entire army had not assembled around him. For the crowds of the city were strong and far more numerous than the force with him.
When the blessed Eusebius saw that the tyrant was threatening and the crowds of the city were rejoicing,
With zeal he addressed them and quieted them, and with his gentle, pleasant words he calmed them, saying:
“My children, you have shown us enough human affection until now. Let us not, because of our love for one another, fall short in our love for Christ,

who testified to us in his gospel and told us, ‘Whoever loves his own life more than me is not worthy of me. Whoever does not take up his cross and come after me is not worthy of me.’ In his gospel our Lord invited and called us to the path of his suffering and crucifixion.
“Take care, my children, lest we shrink back from his calling and become strangers to his promises.
“Be on your guard, then, my children, lest in your zeal you hinder me from the calling to which I have been called, and bring upon yourselves responsibility for my confession.
“For only with difficulty have I found this spiritual trade, which I have had my eye on ever since my youth.
“And now the Evil One, in his envy, is scheming under the guise of your zeal to deprive me of its profits. So, with persuasion and supplication and the divine love that I have for you,
my old age now implores you: children of my faith, do me this kindness and remain quiet.
“Let the will of the Lord be fulfilled in me, and not the tyrant’s will. We have not yet reached the contest; do not be alarmed.
“May God grant my old age the privilege of being worthy of that hour! Blessed shall I be when the voice falls upon my ears, saying:
“‘Give your hands and feet to the bonds, your body to the scrapers and [?], your back to the scourges, and your sides to the scrapers.’
“It is fitting, then, to rejoice and be glad at that hour, when these things happen in your city, which, like a faithful woman, was the first to send God the firstfruits of our persecution.”
Although Eusebius could not calm them amid these disturbances or silence their shouting, the accursed, impious man
was filled with fury and anger against this true shepherd. He shouted harshly at him, saying:
“Tell me, you insolent man who hates his own life: what is this boldness and arrogance of yours? Without our permission,
on your own authority, you have sown whatever comes into your mind and pleases you in the hearing of those who share your mistaken beliefs, without fear
or dread. Do you imagine, you troublemaking old man, that through these people’s shouting you will escape the fire of the burnt offering,
and be spared punishment for these things that you have unlawfully done with your own hands?
“Do you not know, wretched man, that even if the sound of their shouting rises to heaven, you will not escape the sentence I have pronounced concerning the priests of the deity?
“For this is the god’s will: as you have judged, you shall be judged, and as you have acted, you shall be repaid. Your blood is on your own head,
for by your own free choice you have called down upon yourself a merciless sentence.” But the blessed Eusebius laughed heartily at his words,
and answered him with words suited to the tyrant’s words, saying: “Do you really suppose, you senseless, mad tyrant, that you frighten me with your fire?
“No, by Christ the Son of God, who will soon strip you of your kingdom and make you an object of disgrace to the generations that come after you! I am not afraid of your threats,
nor do I tremble at your fire. Nor do I shrink from death, for I myself am ready to be offered as a pure sacrifice to the Deity,
and not to demons and idols, as you suppose.” Julian said: “You have nothing to boast about in this before the followers of your error, you madman.”
For this sentence has not been pronounced against you today because of the faith of your polluted religion, but because you burned the sanctuary of the holy priests.
This sentence of burning has come upon you today as your crimes deserve, so that you may have no glory or confidence before the god of your error,
nor any gratitude toward the gods for being burned on their account, so that from both sides [?] may come upon your old age.
Eusebius said, “Because of your foolish words, I am compelled to disclose things that I did not want revealed before they happened,
although they are to the praise of our people and the glory of our God. But to crush the boasting of your arrogance before the crowds of the city
and before the adherents of error, necessity has compelled me to declare openly, without concealment, before everyone’s eyes, that through the mighty power of our God, who accompanies
us, we will overcome your fire, trample on your threats, mock your menaces, and not shrink from your tortures.
For we have a God whose power is sufficient to help us in everything.” Julian said, “These are [?], you foolish and ignorant old man.
For they are the insipid tales of your error. But if there is any power in what you have said, shortly give proof that it is true.
When the sacrificial fire roars against you like a lion and the flame embraces your body, at that moment, if you have a god, you miserable man,
let him come to your aid and help you. Then your words will indeed be confirmed as true.” Blessed Eusebius answered and said, “You may rage with your fire, you madman,
just as you have taken trouble over your troops, and also over the burning of your combatants [?], so that you may know that we have a God who helps us. But learn this now, madman:
your fire will not harm us today, your desire concerning me will not be fulfilled today, and your plan will not come down upon my head,
so that you cannot boast and say that you offered us as a burnt offering to your idols.” Julian said, “Even if there were a possibility that this could happen, you miserable man,
I would have had grievous afflictions, harsh torments, and various tortures of every kind to make you endure,
as your crimes and the evil deeds you have committed deserve. But thanks be to the gods,
who have shown you their mercy and have already appointed you as a burnt offering for their sacrifice, so that your life may quickly come to an end
and you may escape what I had planned to make you endure.” Eusebius said, “Because of our [?], you are delaying our contest
and neglecting your sentence, madman. For what you have planned will come to nothing today, just as you have been told. [?] Julian said,
“You are greatly mistaken, you unfortunate man, to suppose this. For there is no power capable of overcoming the nature of fire, not even if you possess all the books of sorcery
and the precise moments of Chaldean calculations, and the craft and venom of magic. You could not accomplish what you have said. For you are not
more enlightened in knowledge or more distinguished in wisdom than Socrates the Athenian, who could not save himself from being burned by the Athenians’ fire.
For the nature of fire is a powerful nature, and it has a share in the divine nature. For it is exalted in its radiance, in the light of its flame,
and in its brilliance, by which the gloom of night is dispelled. And if the heavenly lights, which are the gods of creation, need an admixture of it,
even darkness, which itself also has substantial existence by its nature, cannot stand defiantly before a little gleam from it.”
You miserable, frail vessel! Can you really dare to stand before a blazing fire and save yourself from its fierce burning?
What pleasure or benefit will you gain by promising things greater and stronger than yourself, except shame? Wait a little and consider your words....
Eusebius said, “Who could fail to be astonished at you and weep over you? How your understanding has grown dull, and the eye of your mind has gone blind!
You have fallen away from God your maker. These false tales that you cling to are what have brought you to all this madness.
You have become like an animal without understanding. You have stopped attending to the matters that urgently require attention, and to how you will confront the great [?] of Assyria.
You have neglected these things, and look, you have exhausted yourself like madwomen with dancing, singing, and filthy howling that serves no purpose.
You remain idle and inactive in the affairs that sustain the territories of your dominion, while you are occupied and engrossed in the futile worship of idols.
Demons deceive you, and evil spirits mock you. Through those they possess, they give you false prophecies that never come true.
But if you want to learn, listen to me, for I am telling you the truth: from now on you will have no success in your reign.
Your time has already run out, and your end has hastened along with your beginning. The sentence of justice has already gone ahead of you to the land of the Chaldeans.
Your end awaits you there. Like a man driven out and cursed, you will perish outside the dominion of your kingdom, so that not even

your corpse will enter the royal burial place. For you did not understand your honored position or recognize that your authority was given to you from above, for a time, to discipline our people because we have sinned....”
Julian said, “This is common among murderers and evildoers: when they face the punishment of their destruction, they insult kings and blaspheme the gods.
They say whatever comes to them, like people who know that their hope of life has now been cut off. So now, too, as much as you please,
unleash your [?] and pour out your insults, until the fire catches the wood of the burnt offering....” But the blessed Eusebius mocked him, saying,
“When, then, priest of sin, will you offer the sacrifice of your uncleanness to your shameful god?
For look, today already [?] four years.” Julian became angry and proceeded to pronounce the sentence that the holy man should be burned, saying,
“Eusebius, who was the leader of the religion of the Nazarenes, who in the arrogant spirit of his tyranny exalted himself against the gods
and rose up against the king, and burned the holy priests upon the burnt offering of the gods—concerning this man our Majesty has decreed what the gods themselves have also commanded:
that as he has done, so it shall be done to him, and his recompense shall come back upon him. Through this, too, the justice of the gods toward everyone will be made known,
for their judgments are upright, as they themselves are.” After the sentence of burning had been pronounced against the holy man, the priests of Zeus and Apollo approached.
They petitioned the tyrant, saying that he should be offered as a burnt offering to the gods in his priestly attire and in the vestments of his ministry. Julian said to them,
“How long will you weary me with your petitions and wear me down by demanding vengeance for your companions? Look, your wish is granted.
Go quickly, and in whatever attire and vestments you wish, take this ill-fated man out of my sight, so that I may have relief from his wickedness.
For an evil lot has fallen to me from the beginning of my reign. I did not wish to stain my hands with the blood of these polluted people,
If not for the outrage they committed. These priests came forward and seized the blessed Eusebius, and began pulling out
the blessed old man's white hairs and putting them in his mouth. They mocked him, saying, “If you really have a God, let him come now and help you.”
They wove a crown of flowers and put it on his head. They mocked him with words fit for those who crucified the Lord, saying,
“Hail, high priest of the Nazarenes! Do not be distressed in your old age that you are offering a burnt offering and sacrifice not to a mortal man whom the Jews crucified,
but to Zeus and Apollo, who are gods by their very nature.” They also hurled other insults full of blasphemy at him. But God's holy man

remained silent and did not open his mouth, for he was contemplating his Lord's calm during his crucifixion. When they had mocked and ridiculed him as much as they wished, they set fire to the wood of the pyre.
They sprinkled resinous oil over it. Like those who crucified our Lord, the defiled priests stood around this martyr of God.
Like men preparing to consecrate themselves to their idols by burning the blessed Eusebius,
they stood resplendent in white clothes around the pyre. When the fire took hold of the wood of the pyre and was blazing and roaring,
the martyr of God sealed himself, making the sign of the cross on his chest and between his eyes. Of his own accord, without compulsion,
he sprang up onto the upper step. When his foot touched the pyre, the flame fled from before him and swept over the defiled priests,
who numbered thirty-two. It clung to their bodies, and they burned and were consumed until nothing remained of them.
When the flame had taken vengeance on them for their insults and abuse of the holy man and their blasphemy against God,
it gathered itself together, flew up, and rose into the air. It blazed in the air and roared,
so that the roaring sound of its burning filled all the pagans and unbelievers who had gathered and come to witness this event with fear and trembling.
But all the Christian people rejoiced, gave thanks, and praised God for the manifest deliverance he had shown toward
his servant, saving him from the burning flame. The blessed Eusebius knelt on the pyre and prayed earnestly to God
that he would soon make him worthy to taste the suffering of his crucifixion through the torments and suffering of confessing him. When he rose from his prayer, he turned and said to the tyrant,
“How long, you wicked and defiled man, will madness hold you captive and your mind be carried away into the deception of demons? Do you not perceive and understand
that idols are nothing and can do neither good nor harm?
For how have they been able to harm me, who insulted them, or to do good to their servants, who honored them? They were unable to save them from the burning fire,
whereas Christ rescued me and saved me from your burning fire, as your own eyes can see.” Julian said,
“[?] Do you suppose, you impure and defiled man, that what happened and took place today was through the power of that Nazarene whom you serve? For the gods brought this about,
because they were unwilling for you to go up as a burnt offering on their sacrificial pyres. For they drew their fire away from you as from a [?] and defiled man,
lest it be defiled by your impurity. They gave it leave, and it slaughtered their priests.”
because they offered you upon their altars. And when the anger of the gods was appeased by the burning of their ministers and their fury subsided, they commanded the air to be cool.
It mingled with the heat of the fire, and the intensity of its burning was also restrained within the cool embrace of the air, so that its burning would not grow fierce
and burn and destroy these crowds who had assembled to witness your deed.” But blessed Eusebius filled his hands with ashes from the furnace
and gave them to the tyrant, saying, “May this accompany you out of your kingdom, enemy and hater of God!
Even now, though you have seen with your own eyes the manifest miracle that God performed, you have refused to acknowledge that God performed it.
Instead, in the blindness of your heart and the deficiency of your understanding, you credited the miracle that occurred to demons like yourself and to evil spirits resembling
you. The prophet rightly said through the Spirit of God, ‘A foolish man does not understand this.’” Julian became angry and said to him threateningly,
“So you consider me a fool, you condemned man, and no longer a king and ruler who has authority over your death and your life, you wretch?”

But the holy man mocked him, saying, “Your crown and your purple robes are those of kings, but your heart and understanding are those of an animal. Your beard and the appearance of your head are those of a philosopher,
but your words and questions are those of madmen and fools. Indeed, the saying applies to you: ‘A fool speaks foolish things.’”
Julian became very angry at the words of blessed Eusebius and ordered one of the executioners to push him onto the altar.
When Platon the executioner approached to push him, the angel of the Lord struck him at that very moment. He fell before the altar and died.
Great fear came upon all the people of the city. The tyrant himself trembled and was greatly alarmed, and he ordered that the holy man
be put in irons and kept in the prison where the city's officials were confined, until he could decide what to do with him. They did to him as he commanded.
But when the tyrant saw that he had been made a laughingstock in every respect, and that the day he had appointed for celebration and rejoicing had instead become a day of mourning and distress,
he shrank from simply dismissing the city's assembly, for shame covered his face.
Then the tyrant devised a way to disguise his dejection and assumed a proud spirit before the assembled crowds of the city,
although his spirit was deeply cast down and suffering. The defiled man ordered all the churches of the Christians to be closed and the imperial seal to be placed upon them,
until he [?] his resolve to issue a sentence of destruction against them. And concerning all the bishops in the territory of the Romans,
he ordered that they be banished from their cities. Concerning God's holy man, the blessed archbishop Eusebius, the madman ordered
that his case be heard the following morning before the assembled crowds of the city, and that he undergo questioning and interrogation with various tortures and afflictions
of every kind, to discover by what power or authority he had insulted the gods and the kings
and dipped his hands in the sacred blood of the holy priests who ministered to the deity. As for the rest of the Christians, he ordered them not to hold an assembly
or celebrate the mysteries of their faith. If they ventured to hold an assembly in any form or by any means,
they were to be handed over to execution by the sword without questioning or investigation. But all the people of the city
They were filled with hostility and anger toward the tyrant, and they shouted at him, saying, “Now that you have revealed your paganism,
it is right for us also to reveal and make known our resolve: we worship Christ our God, and we confess both his divinity and his humanity.
Even if we must all die and our city be destroyed, we will not depart from the faith handed down to us by the Christian kings.
Nor will we turn aside from the true worship that the apostles entrusted to the Church. Where is your sword now, lying idle, [?] thirsty for our blood?
Let your sword rule over us, rather than you, a pagan, ruling over our city. Let us see our blood and our children’s blood shed rather than see idols worshiped in our streets.
Let our possessions and furnishings be given over to plunder rather than let us see our churches uprooted. You have heard this from us, if you care to listen.
Unless you worship Christ, whom the [?] before you worshiped, you will not be called king over us. Our city has no need for a foreigner to reign over it,
for its king is alive and enduring, and he will never pass away.” After making the wicked man hear these words, they turned and left him in great anger.
But the tyrant was utterly bewildered by these things because of what had been disclosed to him through his divinations. For Onqatar the Egyptian had already warned him,
being his diviner: “As far as you are able and have the power, be patient with this city and do not act harshly toward it.
Do not unleash your anger against this city, and do not act harshly toward it. Do not draw your sword against it or raise your hand against it.
For you have no authority over it from above. The God of heaven is helping the city, and two old men,
his priests, lie buried in it. How great is his power in them, and their [?] is mightier than you!
But if you can, through disturbances, persuasion, and clever maneuvers, obtain the [?] of kingship in this city, do so and then leave it.
For it has not fallen to you by lot. Your lot has sent you to Byzantium to reign there for a set time. Your departure is to the land of the Chaldeans,
and your destiny is with the kingdom of mighty men. The lot that has fallen to you in your war is revealed, for the beginning of your destiny is victory.
But the end of your destiny is hidden for now, and no one born of flesh can reveal and explain it before its time.”
The tyrant was deeply distressed because the outcome of his destiny had not been explained to him, and he became greatly anxious and preoccupied.
But when the blessed Eusebius heard in prison that the next morning he was to stand in the contest of confessing the faith, he rejoiced and his mind was glad.
He exulted and was joyful, like a man invited to [?] on high. He clapped his hands in prison and stamped his feet, saying,
“This is the day that the Lord has made for my old age. Come, let us rejoice and be glad in it! Clap your hands with me and rejoice, my wedding companions and guests!
The wedding day of my old age has arrived and is here. Rejoice and be glad with me, my young men! For the [?] of my [?] is watching for me, waiting for me to adorn myself with it.
You are invited, my friends, to a feast kept ready and rich for me. See to it for me that no one is absent from my banquet.”
Such was the joy and gladness of mind of this man of wondrous victories when he received in prison the good news that he would confess the faith.
For the blessed old man longed to confess the faith, and he wished, if it were possible, that morning might arrive at once, together with the news.
For that day's evening seemed long to him, and the length of that day weighed heavily on him. For he longed for morning to arrive,
so that he could stand in the contest of confessing his faith and give proof of his hidden struggle through the hidden contest of his endurance.
For the athletic struggle of this old man, whose victories were astonishing, was truly remarkable. Against a troop of forty tortures he set
himself to fight in the contest. The tortures failed against him and were defeated, but the tortures [?] of his faith did not fail or suffer defeat.
For who would not have marveled that an old man, ninety-seven years old, was like a mighty, vigorous man standing in the prime of his years?
Thus he went out into the contest like someone standing in the prime of his years. Thus he went out into the contest, as we wrote above.
He scorned the tortures, made light of the afflictions, trampled on death, endured, stood firm in his steadfastness, and wove the crown of his confession.
So remarkable was the contest of this faithful man that, through his courageous struggle, he amazed the tyrant himself, his officials, and everyone watching the contest.
They were also amazed by the astonishing victory of his endurance. For the tyrant brought cruel tortures of every kind upon him.
Like adamant, he gave proof of his steadfastness, and his faith was not harmed. For forty years the wicked man fought against him.
In all of them the defiled man failed against him, was defeated, and raised a finger. But to record individually in our history the tortures that God's martyr endured
would be needless labor on my part, since they had already been written down once, and records of his confession had also been set down
by Apentus, his disciple and attendant, who accompanied him in all his deeds. He wrote down the contest of his sufferings,
the tortures he suffered, the afflictions he endured, the tyrant's questions, and the faithful man's rebuke, uttered in a powerful [?] spirit,
and the astonishing miracles that God performed through his hands to put the tyrant to shame, and how death did not gain mastery over him at the tyrant's command,
and how the angel of the Lord brought Eudoxius out of prison and transported him to the wilderness of Egypt. Julian searched for him but did not find him.
He stayed with the fathers of Egypt until Julian died, and then returned to his monastery. Apentus, the holy man's attendant, wrote these things down,
for he was thoroughly acquainted with his master's contest. But these few things that were left—he was thoroughly acquainted with his master's contest.
But these few things omitted from this discerning man's account, which constitute the occasion for the contest of the blessed Eusebius,
we have added to our history so that their memory may be preserved for those who come after us. Now the accursed tyrant, after
making the blessed Eusebius endure tortures and afflictions of every kind, saw that he had not submitted to his will or relaxed his steadfastness.
He could not devise further tortures for him, for the holy man's body had been mangled by the tortures, afflictions, and blows.
The tyrant ordered him to be put to death by the sword. But even in this God did not grant the wicked man his desire.
When the executioner raised the sword to strike him, his blade melted and fell before him, as wax melts before a fire.
The holy man was not harmed, for the Most High had not given death permission to rule over the devout man until he heard the news of the wicked man's own destruction.
But when this accursed wretch realized from what had actually happened that neither had fire consumed him nor had a wild beast approached him, and that, through the forty tortures he had endured,
death had not pierced him at all, his sword too, stronger than anything and hard by nature, melted, became like water, and poured out before him.
When the tyrant considered all these things and understood and became convinced that the holy man's help came from heaven, he no longer dared to challenge him.
Instead, he restrained his anger, abandoned his prosecution, dismissed him from his presence, and put him in prison.
His body was torn open by blows, his sides by scraping instruments, and his limbs by tortures, so that he already looked like a dead man.
But Christ, for whose sake he had endured suffering, did not neglect him. That very night he visited him in prison, relieved his pains, and healed his wounds,
so that not even a single scar could be seen anywhere on his body. He poured into him and filled him with a spirit of strength and courage.
He brought him out of his prison through the locked doors and stood him before the tyrant, with heavenly radiance poured over his face.
His appearance was so astonishing that even the tyrant himself, when he saw him, trembled and was terrified before him, for he thought he was seeing a vision.
He was not convinced that it was really him until he sent someone to look for him in prison and did not find him. The tyrant was astonished
and bewildered at the wonders performed through the holy man. He was utterly perplexed within himself, since he did not know how to extricate himself from the affair.
For, as for simply releasing God's holy man, he was deterred by his troops and by all the people of the city.
And as for subjecting him to torture again, he was ashamed because of what had happened. While the madman was caught in these uncertainties, a thought occurred to him:
to grant a pardon to all the city's prisoners, so that, under the pretext of their pardon, Eusebius might be released and leave his presence through this clever maneuver.
Julian sent orders and first brought the nobles of Rome out of prison, and discussed their case with them.
He pardoned them as people who had been blinded by error, saying, "A sense of duty has urged me today
to imitate the gods in this mercy of ours, which today has been poured out equally upon everyone. Just as the mercy of the gods themselves extends over both the good and the wicked,
so too our imperial authority has granted a pardon throughout the whole dominion for the offenses committed in error up to this day.
But from now on, if anyone dares to follow his former habits of transgression, let him know
that by his own insolence he has called down upon himself punishment for the past as well." Julian sent orders and brought out all the city's prisoners.
Through this cunning device of his, Eusebius was released and left his presence together with these sixteen nobles of the city.
They gave thanks and praise to God. [?] But the blessed Eusebius openly and publicly declared that he was a Christian.
He did not cease his [?], and without fear or dread he served God in purity.
Day by day he advanced in his godly way of life, until his last breath. [?] The blessed Eusebius remained alive
until he heard the news of the death of the wicked Julian, and his spirit rejoiced and exulted in the deliverance God had brought about for his people.
And his old age was comforted by the opening of the churches, the return of their priests, and the gathering of their children. And in a good old age, upon his bed of rest,
his departure from the world took place in the year six hundred and seventy-three according to the reckoning of the Greeks.
This was the year three hundred and sixty-seven of the reign of our Lord Jesus among humankind.
To him, his Father, and his Holy Spirit be glory, honor, and worship, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Here ends the history and praise of Constantine, the faithful king, and his sons, and the history of the blessed Eusebius,
bishop of Rome. The letter that Abdeel the abbot wrote to Aploris, the trusted attendant of King Jovian,
who had been entrusted with the matter of the settlement between the kingdoms. Discerning people, my son, do not grow weary
when someone asks them for a gift—the kind that benefits both those who give and those who receive.
For just as a spring's flow grows richer the more people draw from it, and its fullness remains while it refreshes many with its water,
so a giver ought to labor without letting his giving cease. While it enriches people in need,
its fullness remains with its giver. Therefore, beloved son, the good legacy of a spiritual man, do not
grow weary of granting our request, which already holds benefit for both its givers and its recipients. For no small benefit have you gained for yourself
through the conversion of many souls, who turned back from their error through the admonition of the holy book that Your Excellency sent us. They turned away from
their error, embraced repentance, and came to the knowledge of the truth. For you know, my beloved, that we live in a land of pagans.
And just as a bird is lured into a trap by grain, so pagans too are caught and brought to repentance by the grain of instruction.

Therefore, my son, undertake the burden of our request, and give us the history and full account of the war that took place between the kingdoms, and its disastrous conclusion, which took the tyrant's life.
And along with these things, give us also the praise and greatness of Jovian your lord, as well as the struggle and humiliation of the upright and discerning men
who fought against the defiled, persecuting, and insolent man, and loved victory and triumph.
When Aploris received the writings of Abdeel the abbot, he placed them upon his eyes and kissed them.
And he began to write to him: In the days of Julian, the pagan and wicked man who had received the kingdom from the house of Constantine,
he had a steward whose name was Jovian, [?] a man of knowledge and understanding,
whose knowledge qualified him to be one of the tyrant's advisers. This man's parents were Christians.
In their care for him, they had him baptized from his childhood and entrusted upright conduct to him.
And they departed from the world in noble martyrdom for Christ, during the persecution under the wicked King Maximinus.
But this man, this wondrous chosen vessel, held within himself the [?] faith that his parents had entrusted to him.
He did not depart from their teaching, but was perfect in his godly conduct, like them, and abundantly rich in good deeds.
He secretly held the Christian faith within himself, while outwardly he wore the appearance of a pagan as a borrowed disguise, for the sake of expediency.
It was not because he feared the tyrant’s threats and menaces, nor because of the temporary service he held. He was restrained [?] of the tyrant.
Nor was it because of the temporary service he held that he refrained from revealing himself as a Christian, but so that he could deceive the tyrant

with an appearance borrowed for his stratagem, so that through his advice he might overturn the evil plans that the madman had devised against Christ’s churches, and the scheme he had conceived against God’s priests.
For the wicked tyrant listened to him and gladly accepted his words, as coming from a knowledgeable man whose understanding he trusted.

One must marvel and wonder at this man of God: how, through his knowledge, he was able to turn aside the sentence of destruction from the churches and keep the tyrant’s sword away from the Christian people
through his wise strategies. For after Julian became emperor and gained control over the whole Roman dominion, and his imperial rule was firmly established,
he grew exceedingly great and powerful. Fear and dread of him fell upon all the lands under his rule, and they were greatly afraid of him.
Then the accursed devourer prepared to belch out the gall of his paganism, which had long been festering within him, to make his will known and reveal about himself
that he stood opposed to God’s will. And the evil scheme he had conceived against God’s church and the entire Christian people—
he had carried it within himself for a long time, until the pagan festivals were being observed. But little by little he carried it out covertly, using various pretexts.
The tyrant himself ordered that the temples of the gods, together with the shrines where they dwelt, which had been uprooted and overthrown in the days of the Christian emperors before him,
should be rebuilt and restored, and that their expenses should be paid from the religious treasury in every region and city.
The vessels used in their worship and all their splendid ornaments were to be given to the house of idols, to adorn the temple of paganism.
For the madman raised the head of paganism, which had been cast down, and exalted it, placing it above all religions.
He subjected them to its worship, brought down the church’s exalted strength before empty religions, and afflicted her.
For in his madness he ordered that the exempt members of the church’s covenant should be placed under the burden of imperial taxation
and become subjects bound to his empire, constantly employed at the emperor’s court. As for the chaste and modest daughters of the church’s covenant,
the reckless tyrant ordered that their religious garb should be taken away, and that they should marry men and bear children.
The madman also planned to make the devout and holy bishops commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.
The troops entrusted to them were to be supported from the taxes levied on their churches, when the day came for him to place them in command. And amid all these things that happened,
the holy order of the churches was reviled, trampled on, and dishonored in every region and city. And more than all these,
the teachings of error that stand opposed to the church’s faith. Meanwhile, the insolent people of the crucifiers
rejoiced and boasted over the harsh times that had come upon the church. Although the decree of persecution had not yet been issued against us, already the sons of the crucifixion—
They showed great hatred toward us and fiercely slandered us before the tyrant, saying to him, “The congregation of the Nazarenes in the churches
sows discouragement in the souls of many, so that they will not remain faithful to the worship of the gods,
and arouses zeal for other religions, through which they rebel”—along with many other accusations
that they falsely leveled against us. For by their accusations against us, they first stirred up persecution against us.
Without delay, the merciless decree of the wicked man was rushed out against us, and his decree was put into writing
and first published against us in the royal capital. The copy of the first document published against us read as follows:
“The error of the Nazarenes, which recently spread throughout the whole territory of our dominion, has angered the gods,
in whose hands the victory of the world rests. They have withdrawn their support from our kingdom, enemies have gained power over it, and defeat has clung to us.
“Therefore, today we have taken great care to cleanse our land of the impurity of these godless, polluted people
and to wipe away and erase their crooked religion from the face of the world, and to punish them for their insolence toward the gods,
so that, through our exacting vengeance on them, the anger of the gods may be appeased, and all the territories of our dominion may dwell in tranquility and peace. A decree has been issued
therefore by Our Majesty against these guilty people: their churches are to be uprooted, and their leaders are to be sent to the mines. Concerning the rest of them, Our Majesty has decreed
that if they come to their senses, turn back from their error, and return to the worship of the gods, they shall be pardoned for their transgression,
and their lives shall be spared. But if they persist in their erroneous beliefs and profess that they are Christians,
they shall be handed over to severe scourging, merciless beatings, and various tortures of every kind. Afterward, unless they turn back from their error,

they shall suffer punishment by the sword, and their houses shall be plundered.” This was the first document published against us in the tyrant’s royal capital. When this merciless decree of the wicked man was issued against our people,
the faithful Jovinian was greatly distressed. He went home grieving, sorrowful and mourning, with his head bowed.
He ordered that none of his servants or members of his household should appear before him that day. He entered his bedroom and shut the door behind him.
He took off his official clothing and covered himself with sackcloth. He spread ashes beneath himself, threw himself face down, and rubbed his head and body in the ashes.
He wept and cried out sorrowfully, saying, “My God, why have you left me behind after my ancestors and placed me in these evil days, to witness the humiliation of your church,
the destruction and [?] of her children, and the dishonor and mockery of your holy order? If this, my Lord, has been your will, I beg you, my God,
bring your servant’s days to an end and release me quickly from life. Do not let me see the sword of the accursed butcher prevail over the blessed flock that receives your body.
For why should I have a life of anguish, sorrow, and groaning, when I see your churches uprooted and your altars overturned,
your sanctuary defiled, your priests laid waste, your order scattered, and the people who worship the cross beaten and scourged
and led like lambs to slaughter, while your church mourns and grieves over the destruction of her children? And where are they
Your glorious promises and your blessed assurances to your church, your true betrothed, to whom you promised that the bars of Sheol would overpower her.
And now the madman has threatened, with mounting threats, to overthrow her sanctuaries, tear down her enclosing walls, expose her foundations, and make her an object of contempt.
She would fall from her height and greatness, her enemies would rejoice over her, and the offspring of the crucifiers would mock her. Instead of the good things promised to her through prophecy,
afflictions have crowded upon her, evils have been laid upon her, sufferings have surrounded her, and sorrows and sighs have overtaken her. She has no comforter,
except the compassion of your mercy. For the madman has resolved to strike your church, your true betrothed, with destruction. We beg you, slain bridegroom,
who gave [?] to his betrothed to drink: do not grant the wicked man his desire, and do not bring his plan to fulfillment. Turn his scheme back upon him,
and let his tricks come down upon his own head. Let the sword he sharpened against your people enter his own heart in the land of the Chaldeans. Bring him to his knees before his pursuers,
and bring down the strength of his arrogance. At the moment of his defeat, let him know that your church has a God, O good and kind one, who does not remain silent forever.
Turn back from your burning anger, and relent concerning the calamity of your people. Deal with us as you usually do, even though we are unworthy,
for the sake of your honored name that has been invoked over us, so that pagans and unbelievers may not say, “Where is their God, who did not save them in the time of wrath?”
We, my Lord, as weak people without the strength to endure discipline, pray before you that the rod of your discipline may be taken away from us.
For the mature and steadfast, your discipline is a source of help. But for us, who are persecuted and weak,
and have no strength to stand in the athletes’ contest, your discipline is like an injury to us,
because of the [?] that grips us. Therefore, my Lord, do not turn your face away from our petition, even though we are guilty and sinful.
For your mercy, my Lord, is accustomed to granting forgiveness for sins. And since we have no confidence to ask you,
with downcast faces and a dejected spirit we ask, as a gracious gift, forgiveness for our guilt, as from a merciful father
whose compassion is mingled with his discipline. We implore you, our good and kind Lord, to grant us a little respite from our persecutors.
Stir this thought in the tyrant’s mind: may my stratagems and my agitation find acceptance before him, and may the plan I have conceived succeed.
Through the counsel of my lowly self, may the sentence of destruction against the churches be revoked, and may there be a little relief and comfort for your afflicted and persecuted people,
who look for your salvation ... And while the discerning man had been praying and pleading with God for a long time,
as though at a signal from on high, a helpful thought arose within him, one capable of quenching the tyrant’s fury
and reversing the sentence of destruction against the church of God. He rose from the place where he had been lying and shook the ashes from his face,
his head, and his body. He wiped the tears from his eyes, cast aside his grief, at least outwardly, and composed his expression.
He put on the splendid ceremonial garments of his governorship, while carrying within his hidden self weeping, anxiety, and continual sighs,
and displaying on his outward self a borrowed smile and contrived cheerfulness. He resolved to go in and greet the madman.
As he pleaded with God to open a door for his petition and to make him an object of mercy in the eyes of the tyrant[?],
and that his good advice concerning the church might be accepted. When he entered and stood before the king, he bowed down and said, “In your days, my lord the king,
may we rejoice and delight ourselves, and may heaven and earth and everything in them rejoice with us. May all nations call this kingdom blessed,
because through it vengeance and justice have come upon the wicked who defiled it.” The tyrant looked affectionately at the faithful man,
for the madman did not know that the words of his subtle speech were directed against him. Julian said to him,
“Today you appear in the eyes of Our Majesty as a lover of the gods, because joy has come to you through the favor of the gods.
For after fifty-four years, the [?] of the divinity has appeared to Our Majesty, whose worship had been denied in the days of the kings before me.”
Jovian said to him, “Still more and more, my lord the king, will the divinity be favorable to its worshipers, when there are removed from the presence
of our kingdom the wicked who defiled it, and the memory of those who denied the worship of the divinity is erased from the earth.”
But Julian felt no concern within himself about Jovian’s words, for in his madness he supposed
that he shared his pagan outlook and was a companion in his error. But that faithful and steadfast man
had not touched anything at all of the taint[?] of paganism. Rather, with a pure heart and a clear soul, he held fast to God in his mind.
To give relief to the persecuted, he appeared before the tyrant in the guise of the pagans, as a pretense,
and drew him toward his own wishes. For the madman loved him deeply and listened to him gladly.
Many times he wanted to make him his Caesar. A discussion arose between them about many matters,
and when the question of the Christians was raised, this discerning man had an opportunity to give good advice concerning the church of God.
Julian questioned him again and said to him, “What do you think of the orders Our Majesty has issued concerning the uprooted people of the Christians?”
The faithful man gave him a pleasing answer, saying, “The authority of Your Might has done well in everything it has commanded.
Nevertheless, the Nazarenes find great consolation in this decree that Your Majesty has issued, and it is a source of great joy to them.
I too think that it harms them, even though it helps us.” Julian said to him,
“How are we to learn and understand the reason for their consolation? For I desire not their benefit but their harm. It seems to us
that their own death and the uprooting of their churches cause them great suffering, and that this is a severe pain to them.” Jovian said,
“If they considered their own advantages and valued their honor, Your Majesty’s command would have been appropriate. But they do not look at things as Your Might does.
For them, their own death for the sake of their God is a good and excellent gift.
For more than the thirsty hunger and thirst for water, or the hungry for bread, they hunger and thirst for death by execution.
That which they call confession. And they are neither few nor insignificant,
those whose desire this is. But when you examine the whole army under our authority and the entire territory of our kingdom,
more than three of their divisions are Christians. Why, then, on account of confused religious beliefs that serve no purpose, to which the feeble minds of ignorant people cling,
should we destroy our forces, throw our army into confusion, empty the territories of our dominion of their inhabitants, and make those who hate us rejoice over us and our enemies exult?
Rather, if it is the wish of your mighty authority and seems good to your Majesty, let us allow the religions to continue in their customary practices for the time being.
And like strong men who are alert at their watch and concerned that their dominion should not diminish, let us turn to attending to the affairs of our kingdom and encouraging our forces.
Let us attend to the battle that lies before us. And when the gods grant us victory and we return from the capital of Assyria, let us remove the religions from our dominion.
Then there will be one single religion throughout the entire domain of our kingdom. As for the temple buildings where the Nazarenes gather, which they call churches,
if it pleases your mighty will, my lord, let them be closed rather than demolished, for they are splendid and magnificent temples.
Many of them were sanctuaries and places of worship of the gods, and in the days of former kings they were taken away
and became places of worship of the Nazarenes. Why, then, should we destroy property stolen from the gods, out of zeal for the Jews and the teaching of people who are astray like them?
With the entire treasury of our kingdom we could not manage to build temples and shrines as splendid as these. And there is not only this, but another consideration:
the Christians would much prefer, and would readily accept, that their shrines be torn down and their churches demolished and reduced to ruins,
rather than become places of worship for the gods whom your Majesty worships. It causes them great jealousy and makes their lives bitter that the houses of service and worship of the gods,
and the places in which the Christians' mystery used to be celebrated, should be used to celebrate the mysteries of Zeus and Apollo,
along with the multitude of gods and goddesses who are mingled together indiscriminately,
because they do not have temples set apart for each one of them, and males and females are worshipped together indiscriminately in a single sanctuary,
since shrines and sanctuaries have not yet been provided for them throughout all our territories, as befits the honor of each one of them.
For what purpose, then, should we demolish and build again at great expense, impoverishing the treasury of our kingdom now, when we are engaged in battles and wars?
Especially since there is no need for us to build: planted like trees and filling the territories of our dominion
are the shrines and temples of the Nazarenes, beautiful, splendid, and suitable for the gods. As an appointed servant who has received permission from his master
to give advice about the matters entrusted to him, I have offered this advice concerning what seemed helpful to us, not presumptuously, but with the freedom to speak granted by your command.
From now on, it belongs to your dread authority to examine the matter with the wisdom of the gods that is within you. And let us, without any further danger arising from boldness,
be dismissed and depart from your presence with [?] for ourselves. May the joy of our kingdom endure for many years, once the wicked who have defiled it are removed from it.
Julian remained silent and listened to him pleasantly. When he saw that these proposals were useful, he began cunningly to express his gratitude to him, saying:
“The gods,” he said, “saw how devoted you are to loving them, and made you find favor in the eyes of our majesty. They stirred our mind not to dismiss what you say as worthless,
even if it should prove unhelpful. I will not let a single word of yours fall to the ground.
For I know that your words are spoken with goodwill, and that you desire peace for our empire. Nevertheless, I desire the destruction of the Nazarenes.
I will have no rest until I have completely removed this crooked religion from the presence of my majesty.” Jovian said to him:
“That too, my lord the king, has its proper time.” On this account Julian revoked that first decree which had been published against us in the imperial city.
For it had not yet been sent out to the provinces. He issued another in its place, and it was published in Rome. It was also sent
out to the provinces. The text of the later decree that he issued was as follows:
“Because the gods, in their mercy which extends over everyone, did not allow me to carry out what I had planned against the defiled people of the Nazarenes.
For I had resolved within myself to reject their repentance, so that even if they turned to the worship of the gods, it would not be accepted.
Rather, I had determined to exterminate them from the entire territory of our empire through tortures, afflictions, and various kinds of death. For I was utterly furious with them
and desired their destruction. But the gods’ mercy overflowed upon them, although they are thoroughly unjust and provoke their anger.
The gods willed that we should be patient with these wretched people and give them time to repent,
so that they might come to their senses, turn from their error, and gain their lives. For by every means the gods seek this:
that no one should perish from their wondrous dominion and creation. We therefore owe thanks to the gods,
who stirred a helpful thought in our mind and poured into us and filled us with a spirit of understanding and discernment,
so that we might examine these matters with the sound eye of our upright judgment and recognize that it is not right for us hastily to place under a sentence of death

those who, against their will, were forcibly dragged away from the worship of their rulers into corrupt teaching and became accustomed to it. Rather, like a wise physician who thoroughly understands a sick person’s pains and sufferings,
let us offer the soothing medicine of our mercy to their ailing minds, so that they may recover from their sickness. For this too has not escaped our notice:
just as chariot wheels keep running behind their charioteers and do not lag behind them at all,
even if their driver is confused, they obey his will and are driven wherever he turns, until he is replaced and another stands in his place.
So too the affairs of the world are driven along in the course of time and obey the will of their ruler, even if his
rule is unjust. Those who take over the government after them must therefore work at these affairs,
set them right, and, with the patience that comes from their wisdom, gain possession of them rather than abandon them
to destruction. A wise charioteer, too, when his chariot is crippled by the violent recklessness of his predecessor and the mounting of its wheel comes loose,
does not throw the chariot away because it has been crippled. Rather, he takes care of it and repairs it, works on it and strengthens it.
And he harnesses and steadies it, so that by every means it may maintain the former pace it once had. Likewise, we too ought to be patient with these wretched people.
So that they may come to their senses, turn away from their error, and gain their lives. But if they persist in their erroneous thinking,
I will take vengeance on them for their contempt, and their blood will be on their own heads, because they have called destruction down upon themselves.

I and my kingdom are innocent of their blood. Therefore, what was revealed to us and spoken to us in the secret utterance of the divinity, behold, today we have openly brought to light before everyone's eyes,
Through this decree sent out by us to all our territories: from now on, Christians are not permitted to hold an assembly by any means.

Their churches are to be closed and the seal of our kingdom placed upon them, until we have time to cleanse our land of their impurity, consecrate these buildings, and make them places of worship for the gods,
As they were formerly. They themselves are to be given time to repent,
So that perhaps they may come to their senses and gain their lives before our kingdom is blamed. For through our patience toward them,
Our mercy is proclaimed throughout the whole territory of our dominion and praised among all our peoples.
This is its copy: the territory of our dominion, and it is praised among all our peoples. This is the copy of the second letter issued against us,
In all the cities under the tyrant's dominion, and through God's [?] and the good counsel of the faithful, Christ-loving Jovian.
Although the sting of our persecutor had thus been broken from the beginning, God's people everywhere were imprisoned, persecuted, beaten, seized, and plundered,
Trampled and insulted. Yet the manner of our persecution was not the same everywhere.
For among the persecutors we were not tried according to the customary, prescribed procedures laid down for judges by kings. There were places
Where, without a judge's order, they carried out their desires against us and mercilessly made God's servants endure sufferings and afflictions.
They tore their limbs apart with severe blows, and through those very blows their lives came to an end. Likewise, in other places too,
Ropes were put around their feet, and they were dragged through the streets like animal carcasses. In this way their struggle reached its end.
Others, again, they beat with sticks like dogs, without an order [?] and without the judges' permission.
Their tormentors had no fear, because there was no one to demand an accounting for their deaths. Again, in other places,
Their limbs were hewn with axes and clubs as though they were dry wood, and they [?] toward their end.
Others they pelted with stones, bringing their heads down to the ground, and they departed from the world,
Along with the other distinct kinds of death, of many sorts, through which God's servants were crowned.

For now is not the time to recount the struggle of each one of them. The deaths of individual people [?] had been recorded, and their victory was written down, along with the suffering of their struggle, the praise of their endurance, and the marvelous contest of their courage—men of integrity and steadfastness,
Who contended amid the torments inflicted by their persecutors and [?] the crown of their victory. But this condemned man, after his letters had been [?] against us in all the cities of his dominion,
Set his course to go down to the eastern regions to wage war against the kings of Persia.
For his end was pressing him to go down and meet his destruction in the land of the Chaldeans. He held a festival for his idols and a feast for his familiar spirits [?] for seven days.
He practiced augury, divination, and the consultation of spirits, asking whether he would succeed in his battles and prevail over his enemies.
His spirit-diviners told him that he could not win in battle unless he went down and renewed the kingdom on the throne
of Constantinople and uprooted from it the error of the Nazarenes, who were still clinging to the corrupt customs handed down to them by the kings before him.
He was to restore the pagan customs established in the days of the pagan and wicked kings and cleanse the city of its uncleanness.

He was to consecrate a dwelling place there for his idols and establish a habitation there for Beelzebul, the chief of the demons, along with many other things that were told him through the divinations of his spirit-diviners.
When he did these things, they said, he would prevail over his enemies and succeed in his battles, and he would gain everlasting fame and victory.
The madman did not know that his end was laughing at him, that in a little while the wretch would be no more, and that the snare of justice was set for him in Persia.
The sword of the Lord was sharpened for him. [?] But this defiled and wicked man, this priest of sin, had inclined his mind toward the deception of demons.
He was drawn into their madness and led according to their will, so that he did not do even one small thing without the permission of demons and diviners.
By this too he openly made it known about himself that it was not he, the madman, who governed the kingdom, but demons and evil spirits.
Through the workings of his error, they governed as they pleased. But the accursed tyrant, after they had been told [?], as they pleased—
But the accursed tyrant, after they had been told [?], as they pleased— But the accursed tyrant, after these things had been told him by his familiar spirits,
set his face toward going down and again issued urgent orders for his departure. He summoned the Roman nobles, the city's rulers and officials,
at whose head was Bulsinus with his fifteen companions. He took these men aside privately,
and reproached them over the burning of his priests and rebuked them for their lack of faith in the idols.
After accusing them of many things [?], he turned to pretense and reassured them with appeals, saying:
“Do not be disheartened over your transgression. I know that you did this through deception [?], that is, through the influence of the wicked Eusebius,
the head of the religion of the Nazarenes. And because I saw that you felt remorse for what you had done, I forgave and overlooked
their offenses. I did not diminish your honor in any way or remove you from your administration. What I have forgiven, I have forgiven, up to this day. But from now on
there is no mercy, forgiveness, or life for anyone who dares to defy the command of my imperial authority. Look, I warn you as a man warns his equal,
even though you are my servants and I have authority over you: if you know that your minds have been healed of the troubled [?] of the crooked religion of the Christians,
then it is well that you hold the administration of the city, and I am very glad. But if you remain in the same erroneous frame of mind,
do not cause me trouble. Hand over the administration and the accounts of the city to those who comply with the will of our imperial authority. And you, as men who have rejected our honor
and in whose eyes the authority that comes from us has become contemptible, go home in peace. You have control over your own freedom.” But the abominable tyrant—
He said this to test them, so that he might learn from them what they intended. But those faithful and steadfast men
had recognized his deceit, and they suffered no harm to their faith, nor did they waver in their steadfastness.
Instead, they openly and boldly declared that they were Christians. They held out and gave him the document containing their city's accounts, saying,
“Receive the document and the accounts of your city.” For they were asking to be released from office, since their term had ended.
For they had resolved to die for the name of their Lord. But the tyrant became furious and raged against them, answering them harshly: “You filthy and defiled men, who hate your own lives [?]!
What accounts do we need to demand from you? All the property you possess has been seized and plundered from the revenue of the empire.
You have grown rich, become unruly, and rebelled against your emperors. From now on I will take the time to call you to account for the evil you have done.
I will justly exact vengeance from you for the sacred blood of the priests of the divinity, which you shed although they were innocent. But indeed,
you who deserve death, what evil has our imperial majesty done to you, that you have asked to be released from our authority,
after I forgave your offenses and overlooked your wrongdoing, and neither took away your authority nor diminished your honor?
But in your rebellion you have repaid my kindness with ingratitude. Our honor has become contemptible in your eyes, and you have asked to be released from our authority.
Now you will be denied nothing of what you have requested.” He stripped them of their official robes and put them in irons before all their people.
He sent them to the prison where they had previously been confined, and confiscated their gold, their silver, and everything they possessed.
He left them stripped of their property until, as he said, the time should come for him to hear their case. He appointed other governors over the city in their place,
entrusted the city to them, and appointed his trusted servant Adauctus as their chief. He himself turned his attention to his departure.
He stirred his forces into hurried action. In the month of Ab, in the year six hundred and seventy-three according to the reckoning of the Greeks, on the first day of the month,
Julian set out from Rome with the might of his forces and the multitude of his armies. He pressed forward hurriedly and advanced swiftly.
For demons were leading him astray into madness, promising him in their struggles things far greater and more powerful than himself. They assured him
that, from heaven downward, he would take control of all the kingdoms of the earth, so that he alone
would be emperor over the whole world—that is, once he had laid waste to Persia and won victory there, and had bound on himself the crown of the house of Nimrod.
