The tyrant was eagerly pursuing this opportunity. He traveled double stages, and by swift marching, within a short time,
he entered and reached the region of Illyricum. From there he sent his letters to Constantinople by the hand of his uncle Julian.
He addressed his accursed letter to it under the name Byzantium, intending to deprive it of the new name that the house of Constantine had given it.
This was the text of the madman's letter: “Julian, Licinius, Julius,
Gaius, Augustus, emperor, to the whole inhabited world: greetings. Since the gods, in their mercy, have granted peace to the world,
They also stirred in our minds the desire to visit the regions under our rule, so that we might set them right and establish them in sound faith in the gods.
And we would remove from them the mistaken customs handed down to them by the kings before us, and restore for them the ancient, just, and upright customs,
which were established in the days of the steadfast and mighty kings of the house of Diocletian and Maximian,
just and upright men, whose justice and uprightness are praised even to this day
throughout the whole territory of our kingdom. Their good memory is preserved and is spoken of continually in the book of devotion to the gods.
To your well-known and famous city, then, so well nurtured by King Byzas, whose ancient victories are recounted, along with the mighty deeds he performed in the world—
and, what is still more remarkable, he laid the foundations of your city on seven hills, within the lovely embrace of the seas, and justly, according to its rightful due,
he named your city after himself, as a man who began and finished, built and completed it. And because he had no sons to appoint over its territories when he died,
he appointed in his will an heir to his kingdom: Germanicus, king of Rome. [?] the dominion of Byzas [?] the dominion of the Romans to this day.

By [?] the true name that [?] for it, the kings who built [?] I know the city [?], and not by the name [?] of those who usurped [?] glory [?] and placed their own name [?] a city in which they had not labored and which they had not built.
When its foundations were laid, even their forefathers had not yet been born into the world.
Therefore, the letter of our imperial majesty was sent first to your city—that is, as to the imperial capital—and not through insignificant and ordinary men,
but through the illustrious and powerful Julian, my uncle, who is the father of my reign, so that from this you may know with what
exceptional honor you are regarded in the eyes of our imperial majesty, now that we have learned of your faith in the gods
and of your sincere love for us. For this has not been hidden from us: what [?] and zeal [?] you have for sacrifices [?].
Nor is this [?] to us: whether [?] is attached [?] to your love for them [?] we, from seeing what good [?] you showed [?], even while we were far away.
[?] fire added [?] you in our thoughts. And day after day we long to see you, to rejoice and take pleasure with you at the great festival of the gods,
and to bestow good things upon you generously and with an open hand—not upon you alone, and not merely for the present,
but also upon your children and your children's children, for many generations. For our rule will continue for tens of generations, as the ruler of creation has promised us,
the one who is the chief ruler of demons and devils, a mighty power that cannot be described by mortal mouths.
For even the gods, they say, who formed creation, once had need of him.
They were hidden in the world, they say, and were unknown, until he, through the devices of his craft and through their delights, made them shine forth in the inhabited world.
He turned all peoples toward their good fortune, and bound and yoked creation to the practice of their worship. And because fleshly ears could not hear the hidden utterance of their divinity,

he made himself a mediator for us between the gods and human beings. Through their delights, they say, he interpreted their mysteries and revealed their hidden things. And who, they say, would call evil this one whom the gods have declared good,
except the Nazarenes alone, who recoil from his comforts and shrink from his delights, and call him evil and name him the enemy?
Together with the countless evil and hateful names they call him. “Soon,” he says, “I will avenge his humiliation on them and wipe their religion from the face of the earth.”
“For who,” he says, “would not love her company? This is the one whom the gods loved and whose company they cherished.”
“Or who,” he says, “would not call him good—this lover of the joys of creation? For he established dancing
and singing in the world to relieve creation’s sadness through them. Through his efforts, various pleasures of every kind came among the people,

so that they might fulfill everyone’s wishes according to their desires. For his pleasures are freely available to everyone, without begrudging anyone, and he is generous with his gifts in every measure.
“And to uproot the ways of wisdom,” he says, “he brought into the world a maddening desire that cannot be satisfied,
so that, through the union of secret desire, love and desire between men and women might increase [?] and burn more fiercely,
so that distress would be entirely absent from the [?] of the world. And because of these comforts and joys that he has brought about in creation,
who,” he says, “would fill his mouth with complaints against him, this worker for everyone, whose running never stops, although he labors alongside everyone freely and without pay?
“He does not grow weary in his work,” he says. “And if he is working diligently alongside a rich person, he does not stop [?] running to the poor person.”
“He is a diligent worker,” he says, “who never tires of working alongside anyone. And if he keeps company with the beautiful,
he does not consider it beneath him to work alongside the disfigured and ugly. His conscience does not recoil even from someone afflicted with sores.
“And where,” he says, “have you seen justice like this? To him, the rich are no different from the poor, nor the beautiful from the ugly,
nor the healthy from the afflicted. For his joys are spread over everyone, and he begrudges no one.”
“And who,” he says, “could give creation another provider of comfort like this, who, even when you do not ask for him, is always close by and standing at your door,
to provide the body with the comforts it desires? And because he knows that many are inclined to this—that, besides the partner with whom they are united,
they also seek another partner who is not their own—he takes care and works diligently,
using every means to give the body its comforts without [?]. He stirs up maddening desire in the hearts of men and women,
so that they stray after a partner who is not their own, so that in this too,” he says, “men and women may find relief and comfort.
“For when men become accustomed to coupling with their neighbors’ wives,” he says, “this gives their own wives a reason,
out of jealousy over their husbands, to give themselves in turn to coupling with other men, so that they may find comfort
and satisfy their desire by coupling with someone who is not their own, so that neither party wrongs their spouse at all.
“For just as someone longs for and loves a [?] that is not his own when it comes into his possession, and cherishes it more than all his possessions,
because others worked [?] on it and gathered it, so too men and women become attached to the love of secret desire.
“Like cold water to the thirsty,” he says, “so pleasing and delightful to the young is coupling with someone who is not their own.”
“What is there,” he says, “for this craftsman, this [?] of crafts, who fulfills everyone's desire according to his wishes? For his treasury is stocked and filled with desirable things of every kind.”
Even before anyone seeks him, he knocks at the door of that person's thoughts. Love him, then, who loves the comforts and joys of creation.
“In the abundant love we have for you, our Majesty has resolved to seek a dwelling for the source of all good things in your city, which is worthy,
and to settle him among you, so that through him you may have something to boast of before all nations, and all the kingdoms of the earth may call you fortunate because of him.”
These were the words of the pagan king's madness addressed to the inhabitants of Constantinople. At the end of his words he also said: “May the gods of heaven and earth,
Zeus, Dios, and Apollo, together with the goddesses of the inhabited world, Hera, Pallas, Aphrodite, and Athena, along with the multitude of gods and goddesses in the world,
come to the aid of your city and grant strength, might, and valor to your men,
and splendor, beauty, and grace to your women, and peace and stability to your city. For I know that there is never a complete absence from the city
of troublesome and disruptive people who sow divisions and strife in the city. If there are people like these among you who contend
against our command and despise our letters, our Majesty has commanded concerning these people
that they be cut apart limb by limb and their houses plundered. But to those who do good and rejoice in the stability of our reign,
may peace and well-being abound from us.” After the wicked king's letters had been read before the city's assembled crowds, everyone was terrified.
They were in great fear, and no one dared to reveal and make known his thoughts. Even the Jews and pagans who lived in the city
were afraid to say anything because of what had happened to the Jews and pagans living in the city of Rome.
While [?] the terror of the wicked man [?] at the silence of the city's assembled crowds,
Maximus, worthy of a good remembrance in heaven, was one of the city's prominent men, from the great family of the royal cupbearers, and he looked toward the kingdom of God.
At this, zeal for God stirred within him, and he set his face toward making the good confession for Christ.
He openly rebuked the wicked man and reproved him before the city's assembled crowds.
He pierced him as though with darts through his words of rebuke, saying: “What is this madness that has seized your tyrant king?
And what are these foolish letters he has sent to our city? Are these the letters of men who are kings?
Kings whose letters are like these have gone mad! Alas for the Roman Empire! What kings it has lost,
and what replacements it has found for them! Upright kings and honorable rulers have departed from it,
whose letters were as honorable as they were. In their place have arisen worthless and foolish men, whose letters are as foolish as they are.
What has become of the mighty lions of the house of Constantine, at the sound of whose roars the kings of the earth trembled,
and whose hearts mourned in fear of them? Yet today contemptible foxes scramble to lie down in their resting places and to imitate their deeds, imagining that they are kings. And it has gone astray.
Those who are not kings. For how, he says, can anyone call you kings, when kingship has been taken away from you, if only you understood? But in the blindness of your hearts you do not understand.
You are called kings in name alone. For demons and evil spirits govern all of you today, and through your hands they fulfill their desires as they please.
While secretly mocking them for your ignorance, because, like animals without understanding, you were drawn into doing their will, followed their error, and became partners in their denial of God,
you were stripped of your authority. Like foolish people whose understanding has grown dull, you subjected your authority and your government to the rulers of sin and to unclean spirits.
You have already become unnecessary to your own kingdom, and from now on you will have no success in ruling the Romans.
For throughout the time when government was entrusted to you to discipline our people because we had sinned, you defiled our kingdom with your filth.
You made it an idol of all abominations, since you have no dealings with anything except demons and idols.
Who would not ridicule you and mock your government? You have abandoned the study of the book of the wars of former kings,
from which you could learn the methods of warfare: by what ingenious strategies they won their battles and prevailed over their enemies,
and left behind them a name and victory in the world. Yet here you are, occupied like empty-headed, idle people
with the foolish, invented tales of the Greeks, with which women drive sleep from their eyes while weaving at their looms.
For who, he says, are Dios, Zeus, and Apollo, together with the rest of their companions? Worthless, corrupt men, reckless and despicable, adulterers and fornicators,
who lived most wickedly in the world, as the accounts of Homer the sage show. Your wise men boast greatly about him, although in his wisdom he did not know God.
He did not dare to withhold what duty required concerning the things he knew. For he burned as though with fire in his zeal against
those who called themselves gods in the world, and he rightly brought the account of their shameful conduct to light.
These people dishonored the common human form through their recklessness and their shameful evil deeds. He stripped away their boasting when he said:
“Under the influence of their filth, every hateful desire that entered their minds, he says, they readily carried out without concealment.
Sometimes, he says, in their filth they slept with males, without hiding it or feeling shame before the order of nature. And sometimes, he says, through the working of their sorcery,
they appeared in the form of a bird to corrupt women like themselves, and slept with them while they were soiled with the uncleanness of their menstrual blood.
For their filth gave them no patience to restrain the hateful desire of their will, and because their conscience was more defiled than that of the women,
they felt no disgust at the foul flow of their uncleanness.” These are the ones whom ignorant people today call gods.
For the same measure of shame was likewise extended equally over their males and their females, and they became a stumbling block to many
during their lives and even after their deaths. For after they had departed, he says, with their abominations,
filthy people like them, who were attached to the desire for their abominations, made [?] for them and called them gods and goddesses.
And fools went astray after them in their ignorance. Such are the accounts of Homer.
Concerning those whom you call gods today, together with the countless evils and offenses that follow them.
We need not recount their many abominations, for blood would flow from this. And if zeal over your error had not stung me,
I would not have defiled my tongue with accounts like these. But I am astonished at your king, the tyrant,
who does not feel ashamed and embarrassed by the stories of his gods. If only he were nearby now, here before me,
I would bring both my hands together and give the madman a blow in the face, because he is not ashamed to call those people gods
who lived in this world with such filthy conduct and abhorrent deeds for as long as they lived.
While he was rebuking the uncle of the defiled man with these words of reproach before the crowds of the city,
the wicked man became furious, and his anger rose. He roared like a lion ready to maul. His bile was stirred within him, and his complexion turned yellow.
He seemed like a madman because of his rage. He answered the blessed Maximus, speaking threateningly:
“Tell me, you wretch: by what power and authority have you unleashed your tongue and hurled your insults against the ruler of the world?
Like a man who has given up his life, you have reviled the king and blasphemed the gods. Perhaps in your madness you do not know
that every word your mouth has uttered will reach the king’s ears. Through the insulting behavior of your insolence, you are bringing disaster upon your entire family,
and perhaps upon your whole city. But, you wicked fool, why do you reproach the lord of the world
for worshiping those who are gods by nature? You yourself deserve death, since you are not ashamed or embarrassed to worship an ordinary human being,
whom the Jews crucified in Jerusalem with evildoers. You call him God and boast of his cross.”
When the blessed Maximus heard this wicked man’s blasphemy against God, he could not bear it. He laid his hand on the sword [?] of one of the soldiers with him
and drew it from its sheath. He raised his hand to strike the accursed pagan and [?]. But his blow did not land, because the man turned aside out of his way.
He made to pursue him, but his kinsmen and relatives seized him and would not let him follow. He turned and said to him, “Listen, uncle of the filthy man!
What do you think [?]? I warn you before the crowds of the city: if I see you in this city tomorrow, I will send your head to the madman who sent you.”
His kinsmen and relatives forcibly led him away from the crowds. In private, between themselves and him, they rebuked him
and reproached him for his words, saying, “Do you not know that you have unleashed your tongue and hurled

your insults against the king, who has power over your death and your life? And you have raised your hand to kill his uncle, whom he appointed as father of his kingdom, before the crowds of your city.
If the king learns of this, what can you possibly do? Or if he orders you to be put to death by the sword, how can we help you?
What help did the relatives and kinsmen of Rome’s rulers give them, that we should be able to help you? We are deeply distressed about this,
because there is no medicine to heal the wound you have inflicted on yourself. You alone out of your whole city have openly disclosed and made known that you are a Christian.”
And might there not be more than two hundred thousand Christians like you in this city?
Yet no one has dared to reveal and declare his convictions as you have. Instead, they have given the times their due and wisely kept them at bay until they pass and change.
Now listen to me, and let me advise you and do you some good. There is no other medicine that can heal your wound.
Go, humble yourself before this man and seek his favor. Act like a man who regrets what he has done and reproaches himself for it, and [?] a sigh over your foolishness.
Do this before the king learns about these things. We will come after you with our fellow officials and support what you say.

We will plead with him on your behalf and implore him. Perhaps, out of regard for us, he will grant us pardon for your foolishness and give us a firm promise under oath that the king will not learn about these things.
But the blessed Maximus paid no heed to the words his relatives spoke to him.
He was neither discouraged nor distressed in spirit over what he had done. Instead, boldly and with a [?] mind, he spoke out to his relatives, saying:
“Do not worry about me in these matters, and do not plead with anyone on my behalf. From this moment I myself am ready to become a sacrifice to God,
who, although he is God, did not disdain to become a saving sacrifice for sinners like me.
For a long time I have set my face toward walking the path of the crucifixion of him who, through his cross, bore our iniquity and our sins so that we might be made righteous.
Through my own sacrifice I am appointed to be a groomsman to the beloved bridegroom, who gave himself as a sacrifice for the salvation of the church. I will not deny him before others, lest
he deny me before his Father when the groomsmen enter the bridal chamber with him. For what would I gain if I acquired the whole world but lost my soul,
as our Lord said in his gospel? Or what could I give in exchange for my soul except the sacrifice of my own self? And now, my companions and friends,
has the world come crashing down on you because of this? Neither the tyrant’s threats and menaces nor the tortures of his persecution will hold me back
from the path of confessing my faith in Christ—not even if the tyrant himself were to disregard me and leave me alone.”
When his kinsmen and relatives saw that he would not be swayed by their words, they gave up and left him. They took their companions, the leaders of the city,
and went in to plead with the wicked man. With tears in their eyes and pleas on their lips, they implored him concerning what they called Maximus’s transgression,
promising him offerings and gifts if he would pardon his foolishness. His answer to them was:
“You yourselves heard with your own ears his insults against the king and his blasphemy against the gods, and you saw with your own eyes that he raised his hand to kill me.
Yet you did not rebuke [?] and discipline him as the city’s officials should. For if you had any concern for yourselves and your city,
you would have sent his head to the king whom he insulted. You would have driven disaster away from yourselves, and the sword would have ceased from your city. Now consider carefully
what you are doing, for you have heard what happened to the rulers of Rome.” When they heard these things from him,
they were greatly frightened by his words and fell silent. They no longer dared to answer him. He turned and left them in great anger
and informed the tyrant about all these things. The king became furious and raged at his uncle. He lashed out at him and drove him from his presence.
And he ordered that he should not appear before him that day, because he was filled with fury and anger against him. After some days, when his fury had subsided,
he sent for him and said to him, “When I gave you the authority of the sword, and the sentencing of those who oppose our command was entrusted to your hands,
how have you carried out the will expressed in our edicts, fulfilled the will of our sovereignty, and avenged yourself with your sword on those who dared to oppose
our will? Instead, through your weakness, our edicts have been proved false, the crown of our sovereignty has been dishonored, and the gods have been blasphemed. And what is most disgraceful of all,
if the blow that Maximinus intended to strike you had succeeded, you would probably by now have lost your life.
Our sovereignty would have suffered disgrace on your account, yet in your weakness you made no effort to advance your own case, even through petitions. This is what astonishes me most:
even if you felt no pain at our dishonor and no anger that the gods were blasphemed, should you not at least have felt pain for yourself?

The rebel made you a laughingstock before all the assembled crowds of his city, and in your weakness you were afraid to impose on him the sentence that our justice had pronounced against him. Through the confiscation of his property and the cutting off of his limbs,
he would have become an object of fear and trembling to insolent men like himself, and you would now have been spared having to shed much blood. But instead of doing this,
look, you have regretted it in vain, and you have brought reproach upon us, claiming that our great mercy leads many minds astray.
Instead of blaming yourself because, in your weakness, you were incapable of exacting vengeance for yourself,
look, you blame the mercy of our graciousness, which bears with the wrongs caused by your foolishness.” When the tyrant saw that distress and sorrow had overcome his uncle,
whose heart was filled with grief, so that he could not even draw breath under his accusations, and when he grew faint and wasted away with sorrow,
the tyrant felt sorry for him. He spoke reassuringly to him and comforted him: “From now on, do not worry about this, and let no anxiety come upon you
because of what we have said to you. Nevertheless, let no one learn what happened and took place in this city whose inhabitants are hateful,
until I have exacted just punishment from them, as their deeds deserve, lest our armies mock us and ridicule our administration. But since I have clearly perceived
that Jovian, our army commander, is concerned that our dominion should not be diminished, we have decided to reveal this to him and make our will known to him,
so that he himself may investigate the matter. For he is a knowledgeable man who understands affairs.” Then he dismissed his uncle, and he went out from
his presence, grieving and bowing his head. A few days later, Jovian came in to greet the king and pay him homage, as was customary.
In private, the tyrant revealed and made known to him everything that had happened and taken place in Constantinople.
He warned him that no one should learn of these things “until I overturn it upon its inhabitants.” But Jovian was in no hurry to plead with him.
Instead, he yielded to the tyrant’s will and, as a tactic, used flattering expressions in a deferential manner, saying,
“Because I have found favor in the eyes of Your Majesty, I have been entrusted with your secret affairs.” Julian said, “Not idly or without purpose,

but as a good servant who cares for his master’s property so that it does not diminish.” From the hint in the tyrant’s words, the faithful and steadfast man understood that he had opened a door to petition and persuasion.
Julian said to him, “What is your opinion of these things, lover of the gods?” But Jovian restrained himself and remained silent.
And he was still in no hurry to be persuaded. The tyrant said to him, “I adjure you by the victory of the gods,
not to conceal your thoughts and withhold from us whatever you think will help us and bring peace to our rule.” Jovinian said to him,
“Your Divinity knows, my lord the king, that once and twice we have laid our petition before the mighty authority of Your Majesty, concerning your dominions, that they should not be diminished,
and concerning your prosperous cities, that they should not be emptied of their splendor and deprived of their inhabitants,
because of foolish people who lack understanding and hate their own lives. For if we follow their madness,
we will devastate the lands under our rule and acquire an evil and disgraceful reputation among all the kingdoms of the earth.
For Your Majesty is not unaware that these very things were put into practice in Rome a short time ago. And had it not been for the good counsel of the wise Aptaeus,
Rome might by now have been ruined and left desolate of its inhabitants. Your Majesty would have gained no praise from these things.
And now, my lord the king, since your servant has found favor in the eyes of Your Majesty, and we have been commanded by your authority
to give advice on every matter Your Majesty considers, through our petition we present this appeal to your mercy:
like upright kings who care about the stability of their kingdom, be patient with your dominions and bear with the uproar of your city,
until Your Majesty’s kingdom grows firm and strong. And when the gods have given you rest from all those around you, and you are free from your wars,
if there are ten or twenty people in the city who deserve punishment, let them be handed over to the judges of the land and tried according to law,
as the established rules of duty command. Through interrogation and torture, they will acknowledge their offenses,
confess their crimes before the crowded assemblies of their city, and receive punishment for their offenses.
Then your justice will be praised, because Your Majesty did not threaten them idly and in vain.”
Jovinian’s words pleased the tyrant, and he received him with great favor. But concerning the blessed Maximus, the madman decided
that if he came to his senses, turned back from his error, renounced the religion of the Nazarenes, submitted to his paganism, and worshiped the idols,
he would be pardoned and his offense forgiven. But if, in that same mindset of his error, he renounced the religion of the Nazarenes, submitted to his paganism, and worshiped the idols,
he would be pardoned and his offense forgiven. But if he persisted in that same mindset of his error, he was to be cut apart limb by limb,
and his possessions were to be given over to plunder, according to the decree issued by “Our Majesty.” When Jovinian learned what the madman had decided concerning Christ’s champion,
he became deeply distressed. He left the tyrant’s presence, grieving and troubled over these pronouncements.
He secretly sent word and informed the blessed Maximus of all these things. But God’s chosen one
was neither discouraged nor saddened in spirit by what he learned. Instead, his mind rejoiced and was glad.
With joy in his heart he said, “Blessed will I be on the day when these things come upon me, for it will be a day greater for me than all other days.”

More than a bridegroom longs to reach his wedding and betrothal festivities, my mind longs for the struggle of confessing my faith. Blessed will I be at the hour when I am found worthy, through my endurance, to give
proof of my faith.” When Jovinian’s messenger returned and told him these things, he was astonished and marveled at the steadfast mind of this man of God:
a man brought up in comfort and luxury, who voluntarily, without compulsion, had called upon himself the struggle of confessing his faith.
He pronounced him blessed and praised his faith. He sent him messages twice more, warning him: “My brother, I know that you are a man brought up in comfort and luxury.
Severe trials have never come upon you, and you have not experienced the painful struggle of confessing the faith.
Now, my brother, examine yourself and consider the matter: are you strong enough to endure the sufferings of confessing the faith? If not, while you still have a little opportunity, my brother,
put your affairs in order as well as you can, before the struggle overtakes you. Move yourself and everything you own away before the wicked man’s command throws you into confusion.
For we must necessarily face one of two things: either stand our ground courageously, contend with bodily sufferings, and win a crown in this time,
or keep our faith within ourselves, move elsewhere for a while, and hide ourselves from the fury of our persecutors.
For it will not last long, as the Lord has revealed to those he wished. You know, my brother,
that not everyone can endure the sufferings of confessing the faith. It is a marvelous gift, and few are those worthy of it.
My brother, what I have told you beforehand is enough to give you an opportunity to deal wisely with your situation. For the accursed tyrant will not leave you alone.

Either he makes you renounce the faith and you yield to his wishes, or he hands you over to be killed and your possessions to be plundered. Now, my brother, if you have set both possibilities before your eyes,
it is for you henceforth to deal wisely with the matter.” But when the blessed Maximus learned how much trouble this faithful man was taking on his account,
he sent him a message to hearten and comfort him: “My brother, do not worry about this.

It is not only today that I have been looking toward this venture that has come my way. My eyes have grown weary from looking toward it until today. And now that the opportunity has come unexpectedly and offered it to me, should I ask
to be excused from it like a coward, and become a disgrace to the diligent who have undertaken it? Far be it from your brother to have a downcast face
at the hour when crowns are given to the athletes! May I not hear at that time the reproachful voice saying to me, ‘You cowardly, lazy man,
where is the profit from the purse I gave you?’ May the bridegroom not shout at me before his wedding guests when I knock at his bridal chamber, and send me away empty-handed from his door.

May his wedding guests not mock me at that hour when they delight and rejoice in their crowns, reproaching me and saying, ‘Where is your crown, you cowardly wedding guest, who lost your crown through your slackness?’
May the Son not deny me before his Father because I did not confess him before the unbelievers who rejected and repudiated the confession of him.
Far be it, my brother, from your brother to hear these words that cut off hope, at that fearful hour when there is no mercy for wrongdoers.
Instead, with confidence, bearing my victory on my limbs and wearing on my head the crown of my confession, may I enter the bridal chamber with the bridegroom,
wearing the banquet garment. May I rejoice and delight in that spiritual banquet, whose joys never end and whose guests are never dismissed.
And you, my brother in Christ, if your love for me overflows, pray this for me and ask our Lord that the door of confessing the faith may soon be opened to me.”
When Jovinian received the writings of the blessed Maximus, he placed them over his eyes and kissed them.
He wept bitterly over himself, saying, “Woe to me! I have squandered and exhausted my days, and through them I have gained no profit for myself.
Woe to me! With a downcast face I will give an account of the talent entrusted to me. Woe to me, for I have no boldness in my faith.
I have made it like a woman kept in secret who cannot show her face, and I hold it furtively, hidden in my mind.
What will I do when my faith judges me, because I concealed it within my mind and did not use it to provide for many?
While the diligent traded with it and became rich through it, I was idle by my own choice, and poverty remained with me.
I fear that, while becoming a source of help to those who share my faith, I may become a source of harm to myself and fall from the
high rank of confessing the faith, [?] when the time awards a crown to the faithful. And now I ask you, Word of the Father,
you who are beyond suffering, yet came to suffer crucifixion to lighten our sufferings: if it pleases the will of your divinity,
make me worthy to taste the sufferings of your crucifixion through the sufferings and torments of my confession of faith.
For I am not conscious of any deficiency in my faith, and my secrets are also revealed to your divinity.
It was not because of the sufferings of confessing the faith that I shrank from openly displaying the truth of my faith. Rather, zeal for the church urged me to display openly the truth of my faith.
Rather, zeal for the church urged me to take on the appearance of the pagans, so that through the counsels of my lowly self
there might be a little relief for your people, Christ, who receive your body and worship your cross, and so that the sentence of eradication against your churches might be revoked.
And now, my Lord, let not my will be fulfilled, but let the wishes of your divinity be established.” While the faithful man was absorbed in these thoughts,
an unusually deep sleep fell upon him, and, as though in a vision, the faith that he held within himself appeared to him
in the form of a modest woman. She was meek and serene in appearance, and she held two crowns in her hand.

They were exceedingly wonderful to behold, splendid in their beauty and blazing with color, so that he could scarcely face them [?]. She smiled and said to him, “Do you understand what you see in these?”
He answered her, “It seems to me, my lady, that they are the triumphs and victory of the faithful.” She said to him, “You see correctly.
In a little while, one of them will be yours. But why are you distressed, and why do thoughts arise in your heart
because you have not been called to the public struggle of confessing the faith? Had Christ not appointed you for a later time, perhaps your struggle would have preceded that of your companions.
For I know the sincerity of your mind, since you were raised beneath my wings, and from your mother’s womb your parents entrusted you to me.
So do not lose heart or let your spirit be saddened because you have not tasted the sufferings of publicly confessing the faith.
For your own confession of faith you bear secretly in your inner person. And sufficient to take the place of
torments and afflictions are your constant sufferings, your continual sighs over the churches of Christ, your good deeds, and your blameless conduct.”
And your good counsels, and all these spiritual beauties that adorn your hidden struggle—are you still sorrowful, my beloved? Cast your sorrow away.
And do not rush toward the struggle that lasts a whole day, for God’s people still need you. [?] While Jovian was marveling at the vision,
he wanted to learn who she was who had appeared to him. But she laughed and answered him, saying, “After all this time that I have been with you, do you still want to learn who I am?
“Even now, you need me to instruct you like a child! I am the true faith that you bear within your inner self.
“Persevere in me and do not grow slack, for in [a little while] the victory of your struggle will be revealed.” When Jovian awoke from his sleep and reflected on the vision,
he put his distress aside and relieved his sorrow. He returned to carrying out the king’s business that had been entrusted to him. And in those days,
trouble no longer befell the faithful man on account of God’s churches and the Christian people. [?] For there was a certain sorcerer named Gelasius.
The demons [?] him and brought him from Egypt to stir up the sword and persecution against the Christian people, and destruction against God’s churches.
For he would say to the tyrant, “The [?] have sent you a message through me: ‘How long will your sword remain inactive against the people of the Nazarenes,
“‘while the shrines in their meeting places are more splendid than the shrines of your gods? As long as your sword remains inactive against them,
“‘you will not prevail in your wars; and as long as their [?] flourish, you will not prosper in your reign.’ For this is the will of the gods.
“They themselves are witnesses that I have not misrepresented them. If I have lied to you, may the gods judge me, and may my eyes not see the vengeance that will come upon those Galileans.” [?]
When Jovian learned of these things, he set out after Gelasius to kill him, and called upon God to help him.
One day he waited for a time when Gelasius was alone, at night, lying on his bed. A large image had been set up
in his tent, and he would worship it continually and pour out offerings to it. When Jovian looked this way and that and saw that no one was there,
he took courage and went in to him inside his tent. He put a rope around him and strangled him in his sleep, then hung him on the statue of Apollo that had been set up in his tent.
He went out and grasped the statue of Apollo that had been set up in his tent. Then he went out and shut it behind him. When morning came,
Jovian went in to greet the tyrant and bow before him, as he did every day. Julian brought up the matter of Gelasius before this faithful and trustworthy man.
Jovian said to him, “Your servant agrees with everything that accords with the gods’ will and is pleasing to Your Majesty, bowing in homage and giving thanks.”
The tyrant sent someone to bring Gelasius from his tent. The messenger sent after him entered his tent,
and there was Gelasius the pagan, hanging on the statue of Apollo! He hurried back to his master and told him what had happened. [?] Julian was astonished,
and cried out, saying, “Your judgment is just, O gods, for you have repaid him as he deserved! Truly, the gods strangled this man
“because he dared to lie about them and misrepresent them. His corpse does not deserve burial; instead, let the [?] eat him!” [?]
The tyrant ordered that the defiled man’s corpse be given to the dogs and birds, and they did to him as he commanded. This report spread throughout the camp:
that the gods had strangled Gelasius because he had planned to destroy the meeting place of the Nazarenes that had been granted to the gods.
These things happened and were accomplished through Jovian, the son of Varronianus, a blessed fruit from a good tree.
Both of them served God faithfully and wholeheartedly throughout their lives, and they are to receive, in justice, the reward for their labors
from the Lord of righteousness. To him be praises and blessings forever and ever. Amen. Let us now leave aside the many things Julian did in his madness,
and briefly record the memory of the faithful men who gained renown and victory in the days of the rebel.

For, had it not been to avoid doing an injustice to the victories of these remarkable men, we would never have concerned ourselves with the history of that filthy, defiled man. For what would we have gained
from this? But because of the victories of the perfected ones, which are intertwined with his history, we were compelled to study his affairs.
These proclaim his shame and reveal his disgrace, while exalting and praising the faith of the faithful men.
Let us therefore leave aside the tangled weeds of his paganism. No one could exhaust the abundance of his madness, even if recording it were useful.
He was a man who defiled the earth and polluted it during his lifetime through the wicked counsels of his priests and his fellow combatants.
At times he would enter isolated tombs, and there, through the workings of sorcerers, he would speak with demons.
At other times he would cut open children while they were alive and take out their hearts, using them to read omens, practice divination, and summon spirits.
At times he would also cut open pregnant women and take out their unborn children, using them to perform the defiled rites of his uncleanness.
There were also the rest of his hateful and abominable deeds, which there is no need to record now, since it was not for these things that we set out to recount his history.
For our desire was not to record his hateful deeds, but to gather from his ugliness the beautiful flowers that blossomed amid the storms of his paganism.
For just as someone is compelled to approach a thornbush because of the lovely rose its thorns bear, even though it is very damaging to clothing,
so we too, because of the victory of the faithful men borne by the times of that wicked man,
were compelled to record his history, which, like a mirror, displays his blemishes, reveals his offenses, and proclaims his guilt.
Yet someone who gathers lovely flowers from the thorns of an ugly thornbush is neither blamed nor reproached,
nor is a discerning person who gathers beneficial accounts from the histories of the corrupt. Let us therefore proceed and take up the thread of our account,
and in our discourse weave a crown of praises for blessed Maximus. Our feeble speech is not adequate to recount his godly deeds as they deserve. He was a man who hated the world's glory,

its power, its wealth, and its pomp, as well as villages, houses, male and female slaves, possessions, and movable property, together with everything he owned. He chose to strip himself of everything,
so that he might possess in his soul the Lord of everything. When this chosen man of God heard that the tyrant had made threats against him and threatened to kill him,
he granted freedom to his male and female slaves, and also to the laborers in his villages. Within a few days,
he distributed everything he owned to the poor and needy. Since he still had something left,
he summoned his friend Ambrose, who also looked toward the kingdom of God, and instructed him, saying, “My brother, this little that remains to me out of much—”
If you are willing, come and be my partner in this spiritual enterprise that has come my way, and gain life for yourself as well.
Come, let me entrust to you what I have left, and use it to provide for orphans, widows, and the needy.
He entrusted what he had left into his hands, and shook off and cast away the burden of this world and its turmoil.
He himself prepared to enter through the narrow gate of confessing the faith.... When he learned that the tyrant was approaching and had already arrived, he did not delay his noble contest.
[?] some relief might be secured for him through his fellow citizens or through acquaintances who were his friends. For he knew that they were wholeheartedly determined
to urge the entire population of the city and the whole senate to present an appeal and a petition on his behalf to the tyrant when he came.
This was what the blessed man feared most: that through their intercession on his behalf, the faithful man's contest might be brought to nothing,
and he might become unnecessary for confessing the faith, in comparison with which he considered the whole world worthless....
For this reason, then, he went ahead of his fellow citizens and quickened his eager pace to attain what he desired and longed for.
He reached his goal and attained it. He made the sign of the cross on his [?] and between his eyes, and without being compelled by the tyrant's command,
he went of his own free will to the city where the tyrant's camp was established. There was no fear at all in the faithful man's mind
because of the threats and menaces of the wicked man. Before he appeared before him, the madman heard a report about him: that he had come of
his own free will, without anyone knowing. This very thing further increased the tyrant's fury against him and fanned the flame of his anger.
He thought that the man had treated him with utter contempt and mocked his authority by coming of his own free will without being summoned....
But when the blessed Maximus learned and became certain that the madman intended to offer worship to his idols the following day, he too prepared himself
to finish his race at that time and obtain the crown of his confession of faith.... The blessed man was troubled and mourned over the error of the mad king.
He prayed and pleaded with God either to turn him to repentance or quickly to bring his authority to an end and remove him from kingship.
The following day, in the morning, the entire population gathered outside the city gate.
For there stood the temple of the image of Aphrodite, to which the tyrant was preparing to offer worship that day....
Great crowds of men and women had prepared themselves and come to the festival that the madman held for the image of a corrupt woman who loved adultery....
But the blessed Maximus disguised himself and put on a soldier's uniform, so that they would not recognize him and throw him out of the king's presence
at the very hour when he had resolved to receive the sentence for his confession of faith. This was the reason why the blessed Maximus disguised himself
and put on a soldier's uniform: so that at that hour he might appear before the tyrant as one of his soldiers, until his desire was fulfilled
and he obtained what he asked for. When the tyrant set out in procession to come to the temple of the idols, the whole population was stirred up, and there arose to sound before him
all the assembled groups of the various kinds of musical instruments. The madman was puffed up, and his mind was elated by the festival of his pagan worship.
And when he saw dense crowds of freeborn women behaving wildly, dancing and singing before the image of that vile woman, and when the madman reached the temple of the idols,
the mad king took the crown from his head and threw himself face down in his purple robes before the mute delights of that mad woman.
He pleaded with her for a long time as though she were God. [?] When he rose from his worship and put his crown on his head, he turned to gladden the crowds and give
them gifts. They were all watching him, eager to hear what he would say.
As he began to speak to them, zeal stirred within the blessed Maximus. He clasped both his hands together
and struck the madman in the face, and his crown fell from his head. He quickly said to him, “So you too will soon fall from your kingdom,
because you bestowed the worship due to God on the image of that filthy woman who kills her lovers.” Before he had finished speaking, the shield-bearers guarding the king’s back
stabbed him with the lances in their hands, without an order from the wicked man. While he was still alive, a voice was heard from heaven, saying,
“You have run your race well and completed your contest, bearing victory in your own person. Sleep in peace, beloved of my crucifixion, until the voice of the resurrection calls you
and brings consolation for your slaughter.” With that voice, he fell asleep. The tyrant was bewildered and astonished at the voice that had been heard.
He began to say to his troops, “Look at the workings of these deluded men’s sorcery!
Even after their deaths their spells speak, so that you might think their God is speaking with them. I am not deceived by these things,
not even if it is as they say. For what good did the voice do this wretch? Look, it could not save him from death!
But if their God has the power to help them, let him at least rescue the corpse of his confessor from my hands,
for I intend to consume it with fire, so that absolutely no remnant of his bones will remain for those who share his faith.” [?]
When he said these things, there was a great earthquake there. The air was disturbed and became stormy, and the sky was covered with dense clouds.
There was darkness, and winds and violent whirlwinds blew fiercely. Powerful thunderclaps and terrifying lightning struck through the air.
Huge hailstones collided with one another in the wide expanse of the air. Even before they fell to the ground,
their sound could be heard in the air. In great alarm, the king and his troops abandoned the corpse out of fear,
fled, and entered the city. Each man hid wherever he could find shelter.
Those who were slow to flee were overtaken by the wrath and died from the hailstones.
Wild animals, domestic animals, and all the livestock left out under the sky likewise died from the hailstones. For the weather was so threatening and fierce
that even those who were in the city’s porticoes covered their faces with the edges of their cloaks
for fear of the thunder and the violence of the lightning. Amid all this terror and trembling, Jovinian, the military commander, who is worthy of honorable remembrance,
was ready to die for the holy man’s corpse. He took an iron tool in his hand to dig and conceal the sacred body of God’s martyr.
It was pelting down thickly with hailstones and fiery coals, mingled together.
But they did not harm him. When he approached and reached the place where Christ’s martyr had received his crown,
he threw himself upon the faithful man’s body and wept bitterly, saying, “Alas, my brother! Alas, my brother! You have left your brother to face evil days!”
He embraced his corpse and kissed the places where he had been wounded. [?] When he had somewhat eased his grief with the tears of his eyes,
he put his shoulder under the corpse and lifted it. He went about looking for somewhere to hide it. He found a secluded place on the slope of a cliff.
He set the corpse down beside him while he made a grave for it. When he raised the iron tool to dig, a secluded place was found on the slope of the cliff.
He set the corpse down beside him while he made a grave for it. When he raised his hand to dig, the place proved to be solid rock.
The discerning man was distressed and threw the iron tool from his hand. He raised the eyes of his heart toward God and prayed, saying:
“Christ, hope of Christians, for your name this man has borne the suffering of your crucifixion in his sacrifice.
Hide his precious body from the tyrant’s assault and threats. Let the faithful and true not be deprived of the blessings of the tyrant’s bones.
Let the faithful and true not be deprived of the blessings of the bones of your holy martyr. Your mighty power, which split rocks at the time of your crucifixion—
show here too the wonderful power of your divinity. Command this rock to open and receive from me the precious body of your faithful chosen one,
and to hide it within itself for a time, until your hidden command again permits it, after its appointed time, to bring him up and return him to those who promise
to bury him as he deserves to be buried.” At the faithful man’s prayer, that rock opened and received his corpse within itself.
It concealed it and closed over it. [?] Jovinian returned to the city, his mind filled with joy and gladness, thanking and praising God
because he had been counted worthy to conceal the faithful man’s body. God did not leave his labor unrewarded. [?] When he entered through the city gate,
there was calm, and the shaking subsided. The thunder fell silent, the lightning ceased, and the dark clouds rolled away. The sky grew bright and clear.
Many were seized with amazement at the changes in the weather, and at how it had grown dark at the time of the blessed Maximus’s sacrifice.
Even the accursed tyrant himself considered what had happened and understood that these things had occurred because of the body of God’s martyr.
He abandoned the search for the corpse and did not seek it again. Many things happened in the days of the wicked Julian that were not written down and recorded.
We have recorded the memory of these few things out of many, enough for you to learn from them what persecution [?] was inflicted on our people in the days of that wicked man.
For although it is said that the tyrant’s sword was not openly drawn against us, nevertheless the reputation of his paganism stirred up persecution against us in every region under his authority.
For what region or city was there where their hands were not stained with the innocent blood of God’s servants?
Many Christians died at the hands of pagans in the city, without the tyrant’s command and without the judges’ permission.
For they themselves, on their own authority, passed savage judgment on them as they pleased, while the tyrant looked the other way.
who did not dare to seek redress for their deaths through the judges of the provinces. These things were happening not only in the cities,
but also in villages and hamlets, even though they were not recorded. For who could manage to include in his account
everything that happened to God's servants in the wicked man's time? For many of them were led to death by the pagans in [?],
without their places of origin becoming known, or their names being written down, or their victories
being recorded. For it was not judges who tried them. Had they been tried lawfully before judges,
their places of origin would have been known, and their names and victories would have been entered in the records of their interrogators.
But because their confession was not written down or deposited in the [?] of the archives,
it is said that not many martyrs suffered martyrdom in the time of Julian the wicked. For had they been tried lawfully, as we said,
who could manage to count how many martyrs suffered martyrdom in his days? The defiled man's persecution was a disorderly persecution, without questioning by judges,
without answers from those being questioned, without records kept by advocates, and without sentences being handed down. Instead, in every region and city,
whatever seemed good to the pagans and suited their wishes was what they did to God's servants, through the tyrant's indifference.
Now this accursed, condemned man, after the victory of the blessed Maximus [?], had set his face toward entering Constantinople.
He sent letters of peace and reconciliation ahead of him, because he wanted to receive in their city the acclamations of praise due to imperial rule.
For he had not yet been numbered among the emperors of the Roman Empire, because the Senate of Rome had not granted him the imperial acclamations
because of his paganism. Although he was emperor in his defilement, in the record of the emperors of the Roman Empire
he was not entered until he received the imperial acclamations in the Senate of Constantinople.
For this purpose the tyrant was stirring up the people of Constantinople through his letters,
and soothing their minds from a distance, so as to bring them around to his wishes. When he arrived and set up camp by their city,
the whole Senate came out and received him with honor. He too received them joyfully and bestowed honor on them before his troops.
He behaved toward them as toward his own relatives and made great promises. When he entered Constantinople,
he distributed gifts to the city's crowds, and again sowed words of peace and reconciliation in their hearing. Through the intrigues
of his cunning, he received the imperial acclamations from them, sat on the throne of Constantinople, and was numbered among the emperors of the Roman Empire
for one year and eight months. He did what was evil before the Lord and walked in the ways of the wicked Maximinus.
He did not turn aside from them, either to the right or to the left. Had the Lord not hastened his end and shortened the span of his life,
hardly anyone from the Lord's people would have remained without either denying the faith or confessing it.
But the Lord of hosts had pity on the humiliation of the church and promptly removed him from the throne. His destruction came in the land of his enemies.
Now I wanted to rest from recounting the history of the defiled man, after gathering from his ugliness beautiful flowers fit for the church’s crown.
But the righteous conduct and fine deeds of Jovian, his commander, do not allow me to remain silent about his history and withhold his praises.
I cannot recount his history separately, because it is interwoven with the history of the defiled man—and not his alone,
but also that of the steadfast and faithful men who lived in his time, who mocked his paganism and scorned his authority,
despised his tortures, wore him out by their endurance, and through his paganism gained for themselves the kingdom above, which does not pass away,
and crowns that do not come apart. Nor was it only in one region or one city
that the valiant gained life for themselves through it. Like broad meadows planted and filled with lovely blossoms and beautiful flowers,
the whole course of the defiled man’s history was planted and filled with the victories of the faithful and the sufferings of the steadfast,
with the marvelous struggle of men mighty in their faith. Everywhere the madman set foot, he was worn out there by some of God’s servants. For what can we say
about those who suffered martyrdom in Antioch in Syria, or those who gained renown and victory under him in the land of the Christians, or about the sound faith of the people of Edessa,
or about the courage and athletic prowess of the people of Nisibis, or about the painful struggle of those who suffered martyrdom among the Samaritans—men

who were venerable ascetics, who had arranged to meet and had come from various regions, expressly to reach the holy place where their Lord was crucified, so that in the place where their Master was crucified,
they too might taste the suffering of his crucifixion through the blood of their necks. As they passed through the land of the Samaritans in the dignified clothing of their ascetic life,
the people of the towns and villages gathered against them with clubs and spears [?] and began persecuting them. When God’s servants saw that the struggle had suddenly come upon them,
they did not resist their persecutors, but gave themselves up and died for their Lord’s name. [?] to say about them, except this alone:
these men suffered martyrdom, and not even their bodies were found, because their murderers had concealed them.
It was not disclosed to those of our faith where the precious bodies of these holy men had been swallowed up.
For the persecution that spread over our people in the days of Julian the wicked was a disorderly persecution: no death sentence was openly issued by the tyrant,
nor did he call to account those who acted outrageously and, without authorization, passed judgment, oppressed, and tortured God’s servants.
Through various tortures of every kind, they met the end of their lives. For the tyrant’s negligence in demanding an accounting for the innocent blood being shed without cause

roused persecution against us throughout all our regions and gave the pagans an opportunity to reveal their hatred toward us and satisfy their desires upon us. But the Righteous One, who saw the affliction and humiliation of our people,
and the mockery and dishonor of his holy order, promptly removed the defiled man from life and brought deliverance to his church through his death.
For when the madman thought that the kingdom was secure in his hands and that he would now prosper as he wished, the Lord stirred up a ruinous thought within him
and incited him to wage war against the kings of Persia, so that Justice might hand him over to pagans like himself.
And his destruction would take place in a territory not his own. He summoned Jovian, his commander, a man who had won favor and affection
in the tyrant’s eyes. The two took counsel together about the wars and conflicts with Persia. The tyrant promised Jovian
that he would make him great throughout his life. He exalted him and strengthened his position before his nobles and officials.
He appointed him ruler and administrator, second only to himself, throughout the territory of his kingdom. He entrusted him with gifts for the entire Roman army.
He sent him ahead with a large army to go down and take up a position on the frontier and seize the boats at the crossing of the Tigris River, which separated the territories.
Jovian did as he had been commanded. He took up his position on the frontier in the month of Adar, in the year six hundred and seventy-four according to the Greek reckoning,
on the seventh day of the month. The land of Nimrod was afraid and trembled before him. The Lord was with Jovian
and cast fear and dread of him upon the kings of Persia. They were greatly afraid of him. He himself loved and cherished God with all his heart,
walked in his ways, and kept his commandments. He did not turn aside from them to the right or to the left. God rewarded him for his good deeds
and brought him and the armies with him safely up from the land of the Chaldeans. Through him he brought deliverance to the hard-pressed Roman people
and brought them out of the confinement in which they had been held in the land of the Arameans because of the wrongdoing and sins of Julian the wicked.
It was not enough for that defiled man that he had stirred up persecution against us throughout all the lands under his authority.
In his madness he also planned to renew persecution against the Christian people in Persia, although Shapur’s sword had only just subsided a little and ceased its attacks on God’s servants,
through the urging of the letter of Constantine, the faithful, Christ-loving emperor whose spirit is at rest. This condemned man, however, this hater of God and lover of demons,
was devising ways to undo the peace that Constantine had established for the churches in the land of Persia. [?] For Julian, in his madness, wrote and sent a letter to Shapur,

saying, “The whole reason that zeal has goaded me to challenge you, fight against you, and stir up war between the kingdoms is that your sword has subsided and ceased shedding the blood of the Nazarenes,
the enemies of my kingdom.” When Shapur read the accursed man’s letters, he despised and scorned him. He did not condescend even to send him an answer to his writings.
Instead, when he learned that Jovian had taken up his position on the frontier, he sent Arimhar, the chief eunuch, to him, and sent the following message through him:
“Because I have learned of your wisdom, the clarity of your knowledge, and your understanding, which is grounded in what is right, we too have desired

to lower the might of our majesty, calm the force of our power, show you our kindness, encourage you through our writings, and make known what is advantageous to both sides. Now, if your master had been upright
and had exercised his rule truthfully, we would not have overlooked this either: that it was his rightful prerogative, as Caesar, to receive letters from our kingship.
But because he has already become of no further use to the kingdom, and his authority has been dissolved from above, even though this may be hidden from him, duty has compelled us to write to you
as a man to whom the Roman kingship rightfully belongs by decree from above. Although you are still small in your own eyes, because you do not know what is to come,
to us you are already great, as has been disclosed to us through the revelation of the Magian art, which has never, ever proved false in its revelations to those who rely on it.
For the teaching of this wisdom is not from the earth. Through our offerings and our prayers it was given to the house of Nimrod, when he received the crown from heaven through its revelation.
This [?] wisdom from on high, which the God of heaven granted to our kingdom, revealed to me what was to happen before it came to light.
What you would do in our land was revealed to us, and what would happen to you in our country was explained to us. While the conflict had not yet been prepared,
and war between the kingdoms had not yet broken out, we learned the entire arrangement and character of your warfare through the courses of the stars of the zodiac.

We do not dare to challenge or struggle against what has been decreed from above, until these things are fulfilled and completed at their appointed times. For the lot fell against our lands before the Lord of battles.
The lot fell to your land to prevail over our land for ten weeks of days. And when seven days have been completed for our victory,
your land will be subjected to tribute, and you will be enslaved to our land for ten weeks of years, a year for each day. But until the days decreed against our country have been completed,
we have no right to wage war or even to seek a conflict with you. But if you have a desire for what is good in your own eyes,
lay up good pledges for yourselves in our land during the time of your victory, and treat the inhabitants of our country mercifully. Then, when the time of your victory has ended,
and defeat has settled upon you, and the strength of your arrogance has been brought low in a land that is not yours, you will have the confidence to ask for forgiveness,
and mercy will rightly be shown to you. For this is indeed justice: that a person should reap what he sows and be repaid what he lends,
and that the measure he uses should be used for him. Look, I have made all these things known to you before they happen, so that when they happen you may make use of what will help you.
When Arimhar the mobed came to Jovian’s camp and gave him Shapur’s letters, he read them and saw that they were full of madness.
He received him with great honor and gave him a designated tent to stay in, a servant [?] to attend him, and an allowance and expenses for his table and for those with him.
But Jovian examined the matter carefully and realized that he had neither authorization nor any obligation to respond to the letters that had come to him without Caesar’s command.
Jovian decided to dismiss Arimhar with a verbal reply, and, if it was also possible, through questions and the confusion caused by clever devices,
to win his confidence and learn, through the resources of his intelligence, the secret of their kingdom and the plan they had devised through the resources of his intelligence.
The secret of their kingdom and the plan that the kings of Persia had devised concerning the war between the kingdoms. [?]
He sent secretly and summoned Arimhar to him, greeted him warmly, and received him affectionately. They spoke privately together for a long time.
Jovian sowed words of peace and love in the mobed’s hearing, saying, “I wish you knew what abundant love and perfect affection I have
for you, from the moment I received you. If it were possible, I would wish that the sight of you should never disappear from before my eyes.
For my mind has become deeply attached to the love of your friendship. That a person should have his fill of the love of his friend [?], even though our mutual love urges and impels us
to be bound together by continually seeing one another at every moment. But the authority above us compels us to attend diligently to the matters entrusted to us,
lest by neglecting them we bring harm and loss upon ourselves. For it has been recognized as a duty
that it is fitting and praiseworthy for a person always to keep before his eyes the authority above him, and to attend carefully to the matter on which he has been sent,
so that he may quickly give an answer to the one who sent him, allowing him an opportunity to consider his course of action—especially when war is pressing and conflict is urgent.”
Let your fervent love for us increase, then. Let the memory of our friendship remain in your heart, and let your eyes look favorably upon our people.
Help us achieve victory, and through you the Roman Empire will gain renown and glory. When you do these things, you will be called a son of our kingdom....
These were Jovian’s words to the mobed who had been sent to him, along with many others like them. But Arimhar, being a shrewd man,
was himself aware of Jovian’s cunning and knew that he wanted to deceive him with his words. He did not fall into the confusion of his schemes.
Instead, he disregarded his request for these things and pressed him to answer the letters that had come to him, saying,
“If you are willing, answer the writings of the King of Kings, even if you treat him as your equal.
And if you find it objectionable to bring him down to your own level, return his letters to him. Then he will be great and honored in your eyes,
in return for the favor and affection you enjoy in his eyes.” But Jovian was not provoked by his words.
Nor did he answer him harshly. Instead, he replied calmly and pleasantly, saying, “My brother, do not think such a thing of me.
For I neither deprive Caesar of the duty owed to him nor withhold the respect owed to your master.
You are a wise man. Examine what duty requires and judge fairly. I have received your master’s writings, and from them I have learned what he wants.
But duty does not permit me to write him an answer to what he has sent me without Caesar’s command.
For we ought to recognize that we are appointed officials, not men who have authority to follow their own wishes. And to initiate anything on our own authority
is not permitted us by the regulations of your kingdom, nor to flare up in anger for vengeance, nor to promise forgiveness.
Nevertheless, as far as our strength allows, we will help your master’s wish be fulfilled. We will take care to petition Caesar
and offer good counsel concerning the inhabitants of your land, so that the Roman sword will not gain power over them.
For the plundering of their possessions is enough for them. Nevertheless, my dear friend, I inform you that your master is responsible for grievous devastation in our land.
Many times he has laid waste the borderlands of our empire without battle or conflict, and he has shed much blood in our territory.
These things I have now recounted to you—it is enough that their memory should remain before your eyes. If our sword is kept away from the inhabitants of your country through our intervention,
we will credit you with that kindness, for our mutual friendship has brought this about.” Arimhar the mobed marveled at Jovian’s gracious words.
He was greatly amazed at his wise patience, at how he had not been provoked by the harsh words he had spoken to him. He praised and extolled his understanding, saying,
“Happy is the Roman Empire, which has such a commander [?]! May blessing upon blessing be given to it

on the day when it is adorned with your name and made great through you. I too will rejoice in you at that hour and say to you, ‘May your royal crown shine with victory!’” But Jovian laughed and said,
“If only, in this position to which I have been called, I could bring benefit to myself and have it in my power to make peace between these two mighty kingdoms!
That would be enough for me.” Through this reply Jovian gained favor and affection.
In the eyes of Arimhar, and he loved him as himself. He trusted him in his heart and revealed to him the whole secret of the kingdom of Persia.
And that Shapur had sent gifts and presents to distant countries, to summon and invite foreign forces to support him in battle. He was urging Jovian
to engage in war quickly and prepare for battle, before Assyria’s warfare and fighting grew fiercer and stronger through them. He pressed him, saying,
“I have revealed the truth to you just as it is: Shapur has sent to summon and invite a great many barbarian forces from faraway and distant countries to come to his aid in battle.
They have not yet stirred to leave their country. But while you still have an opportunity, and time lends you a hand toward victory,
act wisely in your undertaking. Take courage and strengthen yourselves against the land of Nimrod, and put an end to the plundering of our land.
Spare the lives of its inhabitants. And I am now making a faithful covenant with you and giving you promises under oath,
that, as far as I have the power, I will secretly lend a hand toward the Romans’ victory. And if the plan I have conceived is also carried out,
I will accomplish through you a victory [?] at which the generations after us will marvel.” Jovian agreed to the wishes of the chief priest.
The two of them entered into a sworn covenant to fulfill one another’s wishes as far as they had the power. Jovian gave a great banquet for Arimhar and those with him.
They ate and drank together and enjoyed themselves. Then, after a day, when the chief priest set his face toward returning to his country,
Jovian gave him gifts and offerings with a generous hand. They embraced and kissed one another, and he sent him back to his country in peace.
Jovian wrote to Julian, informing him about what Shapur had written to him and what the chief priest had told him,
so as to occupy his attention with thoughts of his war, and turn him a little from the madness of idolatry that had taken hold of him. For he wrote him stirring words,
so that he would not hesitate at all or be delayed in answering the evil summons addressed to him: to go down and call the land of the Chaldeans to account for
the wrongs it had done him. And when the tyrant read the letters sent to him by his commander,
and learned from them how much care and concern Shapur was taking to gather a large army to support him in battle,
Julian became greatly agitated. He put all other thoughts aside and began to think about and concern himself with his battle.
He summoned Aetius, his nephew and relative, and entrusted the administration of the city to him. He himself prepared with a large army
to go down to the eastern countries. He sent letters to Antioch in Syria, to Arsaces, who was acting in Jovian’s place,
to prepare supplies and whatever was useful and necessary for the animals accompanying him. When the chief priests living in Tiberias heard that Julian had set out to go down to Syria,
they were filled with great joy. Their hearts rejoiced, and they considered among themselves how they might please the defiled man.
They consulted one another and gave gold to skilled craftsmen. They fashioned a crown for the tyrant that suited his paganism.
The seven idols that the madman worshiped most were engraved on the crown they fashioned for him, the madman.

They obtained a letter of thanksgiving from their fellow countrymen and an offering from the good produce of their land. They went up and met the madman, who was like themselves, at Tarsus in Cilicia.
wearing white, blowing trumpets, and offering him thanksgiving as though to God. But that accursed man
was not won over by their flattery. Instead, when he learned that they were circumcised, he turned his face away from them in anger
and drove them from his presence, while testing whether they would agree to his paganism. For he knew that they worshiped one God [?].
They left his presence in great distress, their faces downcast and their heads bowed. Now the Jews who lived in that city
welcomed them among themselves and gave them lodging. They argued harshly with them,
saying, “Why did you need to do this? It may stir up persecution or apostasy against our entire people. For the demand that we worship idols had been dormant and had left us in peace,
but with your own hands you have stirred it up against our entire race. For now the king has stopped thinking about the Nazarenes and has begun thinking about the circumcised.
What can we say to you, leaders of Israel, if this pagan should happen to force you to worship idols?
For the whole congregation of Jacob follows you, and you will become a cause of stumbling for the entire house of Israel. So now understand
and consider what you are doing.” The chief priests said to them, “Zeal for our ruined sanctuary and our desolate city,
and for our people, scattered and dispersed, impelled us to do this for the benefit of the whole community. But if it proves harmful to us,
you are not judging us as fairness requires. For we do not know hidden things, nor is the future revealed to us. Now stop this
and pray to God that he may open a door for our petition and that our plan may succeed. And if we must comply with the king’s wishes in pretense,
this did not begin with us. For in the days of our ancestors, too, such a thing happened and was practiced out of fear of the pagan kings who arose in Israel.
While our ancestors worshiped the true God, they also sacrificed to foreign gods and poured out libations in pretense.
Even the renowned Solomon, that ocean of wisdom, who built a house for the name of the Lord, and to whom the Lord appeared twice in a vision—
when his wives’ insistence overpowered him, and he was overcome and conquered by his love for them—gave his own God what was rightly due to him, yet complied with his wives’ wishes in pretense.
He sacrificed and placed incense upon the altars of their gods. Why, then, do we need many testimonies from the Scriptures?
Our father Jacob, too, the head of Israel’s families, burned beneath the terebinth the foreign gods that were in his sons’ encampments.
And if these ancestors and tribal leaders were not reproached for this, nor was it counted as a sin,
what is wrong with it if we, who are lesser men, are forced to sacrifice in pretense?
For behold, Adonai looks into hearts: this is being done out of zeal for our ruined sanctuary. But, my sons, let us yield to the times
and carry out the king’s wishes and obey his command. Perhaps, through our petition to him,
he will rebuild and restore our ruined sanctuary for us and repopulate the ruined and desolate places of our city.” With these empty and worthless words,
our contemptible priests silenced their fellow countrymen’s outcry against them. And from these words it came about
Julian wanted to test the circumcised with the foods of the Gentiles, to see whether they would agree with his pagan way of thinking.
He summoned Eucarpius, his chief steward, and said to him, “Go and prepare a meal for the Hebrews while they are staying [?]. Set before them all the foods that their law declares unclean for them.
Let them eat and drink in your presence.” The man did as his master said and prepared a banquet for the Hebrews.
He prepared and set before them the foods that the Lord had commanded them through Moses not to eat or use at all.
The contemptible priests, the teachers of the law, disregarded the law’s observances. They ate and drank and did not oppose the wishes of the defiled man.
When Julian learned that the circumcised had partaken of the foods of the Gentiles and had transgressed the tradition of their elders,
he went further and demanded that they worship demons and idols.
