He summoned Eucarpius again, a second time, and said to him, “Go and investigate for me the thinking of these defiled men:
whether they agree to our wishes and will sacrifice to the gods whom our imperial majesty worships. Bring me an answer quickly.”
Eucarpius did as he was commanded. He went again, a second time, to the chief priests of the Jews and questioned them, saying:
“Reassure me, Jewish men, friends of our empire, for you have found favor and mercy in the emperor’s eyes.
In this matter you have agreed to our wishes and partaken of the foods. There is one thing you still lack, and when you have completed it, you will become beloved children of our empire.”
The chief priests said to him, “Everything your authority commands us.” Eucarpius said, “We have just one request of you, Jewish men: if you worship the gods whom
our imperial majesty worships, you will receive everything you ask, and everything you request will be given to you. You will be called children of our empire,
and everything good will come to you from us.” The chief priests said to him, “Hear the truth from your servants: while we were still in our own lands,
we learned what your imperial majesty wished. Had we not resolved to obey your wishes,
we would never have dared to appear before the exalted authority of your might. And now we beg you, trusted servant of our empire, to bring our petition before the emperor,

so that he may look favorably upon us and the offerings of our lowliness may be received mercifully. Through your favor, may the crown that our wretched congregation has donated to your imperial majesty be deemed worthy of the head of your divinity.”
Eucarpius brought the words of their petition before the emperor. He rejoiced greatly at their insane words and decided
to make pagans of them in the sight of the city’s assembled crowds, so that openly, before all the people, they would sacrifice to idols
and burn spices and frankincense over their burnt offerings. Julian gave orders for the following day.
A platform was prepared for him in the middle of the city, beside the altar that had been built for his idols. The madman went up and sat on the platform.
The whole city was gathered, everyone in it. Large crowds had also gathered there from the other cities around it.
The tyrant ordered the priests and the Jews to come before him in their priestly attire, carrying their [?].
The tyrant ordered each one of them to appear before him according to the rank of his service, so that it would be clear to the spectators.
For, he said, the Hebrew priesthood had approved sacrifices and offerings for the pagan priesthood.
The servants of wickedness did as he commanded them. In their priestly attire and in the order of their ministry, they brought the circumcised men in to bow before the king.

They fell on their faces in fear and trembling and bowed before him. But that accursed man, in his arrogance and haughtiness and the extravagance of his conceit, left them lying prostrate for a long time
on their [?]. Then he signaled [?] to them to stand up. Once they had stood up, he spoke harshly to them,
to cast fear and trembling upon all who were afraid. He addressed them threateningly and said, “Tell me, you rebels,
what is this corrupt teaching [?] that you have entrusted to the world—that your scriptures proclaim one God,

while you withhold acknowledgment from the multitude of gods [?]? And what gives you such confidence that you do not keep the fear of my authority before your eyes? But now I will bring it down on your heads,
and through your punishment you will learn what royal authority is.” But those priests of sin
were terribly afraid. They could not utter a breath in answer to the questions put to them, but struck their faces against the ground
and remained silent from fear. Julian said, “Will you not utter a single breath in answer to the questioning you face, you rebels who live wickedly,

so that even in this you display your rebelliousness?” The chief priests said to him, “We appeal to the authority of Your Dread Majesty and to the exalted crown of Your Divinity, who holds dominion over the world:
relax the fierceness of your speech toward us a little, so that we may recover our strength, and allow us to utter a breath in answer to our questioning.” Julian said,
“You have permission [?] to answer what we ask you.” The chief priests said, “As for us, my lord the king,
we have scribes and scriptures, and our scriptures proclaim one God to us. We observe the customs that our fathers handed down to us.
But if something new has come to us through your discoveries, through the wisdom of the gods that is in you, we do not dispute this either. Rather, with unhesitating joy,
we carry out the will of Your Majesty. For we are not Nazarenes, that we should dare oppose the wishes of Your Divinity. And from time to time a crown is sent up to Your Majesty from us.”
Julian said, “It is difficult for me to believe that there is any truth in your lying words.
For if you were servants of our kingdom, as you have said, you would perform the deeds of our kingdom,
just as your fathers in their days performed the deeds of their kings: on every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree they offered sacrifices
and burned incense to the gods. Yet today you have said before me, ‘We observe the customs that our fathers handed down to us.’
Where have you imitated [?] their deeds and observed their customs? For if you truly held to the customs that governed their conduct,
you would have offered your sons and daughters as sacrifices to the gods, as your fathers did at Horeb. It is therefore clear
that your wisdom does not come from the heart, but is theatrical, with borrowed faces.” The chief priests said to him,
“Let not my lord the king speak these words against his servants. For more than a thirsty soul longs for cold water,
our people thirsted for the appearance of Your Majesty, and like the light of dawn that rolls away the dark gloom from the clouds.
Joy came down upon us on the day when we received the news of your rule. And [?] the troubles of our hearts, and our soul rejoiced and was glad.
We have no joy greater than this, and heaven and earth and everything in them bear witness for us.
Your Divinity can learn the truth of these things from the document of acknowledgment that the envious persecutor drew up with us,
addressed to the exalted crown of your Most High Divinity, and with these borrowed expressions, composed of artful words.
The deceivers, the children of the crucifying nation, managed to buy off the harshness of the tyrant’s decree.

He yielded to the sound of their flattery, took pleasure in their offerings, and accepted from them the documents of their acknowledgment and the crown that they [?] and fashioned for him. But that wicked man
changed his manner of speaking toward them and spoke pleasantly with them as with members of his own household, saying:
“Through the visible crown that you have presented to us, we have come to know your hidden intention: how firmly you cling to love and devotion to the gods.
For I have received, in the crown over which you labored and which you presented, the splendid images of the sacred [?] of the hidden gods. We owe thanks to your discernment,
which took care and undertook the trouble to satisfy our wishes in the things that our Majesty intended. You have not done this idly or in vain.
For I intend to decree benefits for you, so that all our peoples will call you blessed. But so that your true faith may be praised still more,
your faith in the gods, before the assembly of those who wished to see your deed, take these spices and frankincense from my hands and burn incense upon the altar of the gods.
Complete your sacrifices and offerings with your own hands, and then the words you have spoken will be confirmed for us.”
The contemptible priests of the Jews and those with them approached and took spices and frankincense from the hands of the defiled man.
They burned incense upon the altar of the demons and filled their hands with pagan sacrifices for the idols of error.
When they had finished offering sacrifices and offerings, they approached and bowed down before the madman, and they asked him
that the document of their acknowledgment be read aloud before all the people who had gathered to see them. The tyrant ordered that their wish be granted.
This was the text of the document of their acknowledgment: “To the worshipful name, beloved by the gods, honored among human beings, and triumphant throughout creation;
the immortal being entrusted with unending rule; lofty and exalted, fearsome and glorious, mighty and sublime, the god in bodily form, Julian, king forever:

Our desolate city, our ruined temple, and our scattered and dispersed people, together with the priests of our people, offer worship and acknowledgment to the exalted authority of your Most High Divinity.
We acknowledge in our writings that with fear and trembling we have dared to write a feeble acknowledgment, which cannot reach the exalted height of your greatness.
For who among those born is capable of acknowledging your goodness, which sustains the inhabited world? Like the sun, you have risen upon creation
and lifted from it the burden of its pains amid the suffering of its distress—the sickness with which it fell ill in the days of the kings before you.
Through you it has been healed and strengthened, and has rejoiced and become glad. Who among kings has brought peace to the earth as you have? Let it give thanks to the gods of heaven and earth,
who have bestowed upon creation the tranquility of your kingdom and the peace of your rule. All our mouths are insufficient to acknowledge the goodness of your compassion.”

You have lavished mercy equally on everyone, without begrudging it. Yet more than toward anyone else, your kindness toward our people has plainly been great. For more than nine hundred years, there has shone forth among you
the kingdom of the house of David, and through your hands sovereignty has been secured for Israel. For you are the king of Jacob and the leader of Israel.
Our people waited in hopeful expectation of you and looked for your deliverance, according to the revelation from heaven that came to our ancestors long ago.

And look, today deliverance has dawned for us through your hands. Our hearts have grown strong, our horn has been raised, and our mouths have opened against our enemies. Our heels have trodden on the necks of the arrogant,
who always [?] the will of your majesty. And look, today, through the zeal of your justice, their horn is lowered, their spirit is cast down, and they lurk like foxes in hiding places.
But with the establishment of your kingdom, our faces are uncovered, our voice is raised, and we receive favor and mercy in the eyes of all nations,
because their compassion has shown us favor. May the God of heaven and earth grant life and health to your sovereignty, and may the years of your reign over our people be prolonged.
And as we have been privileged to bow before your divinity through our writings, may we in turn greet your majesty face to face in victory, bowing before you in person.
After this letter had been read in the hearing of all the people, the chief priests and those with them, about two hundred men, approached.
They threw themselves down before the tyrant and said to him, “We appeal to the authority of your compassion.
Now that we have fulfilled the will of your majesty and offered sacrifices and burnt offerings of reconciliation to the immortal gods,

let the eyes of your compassion look upon our city, which has been emptied of its inhabitants, upon our sanctuary, which has been destroyed, and upon our people, who have been scattered and dispersed among all nations.”
But that accursed, excommunicated [?], with practiced cunning, put them off in their requests, saying,
“Our duty certainly does not now permit us to neglect or cease helping you, even when you do not ask us.
Our eyes are always upon you for your good. But because affairs distract us and crowd upon one another, pray and implore the gods
to lend us a hand in the war that lies before us, so that we may grow strong and defeat our enemies
and return to our dominion in peace and victory. Then everything you have asked of us will be yours tenfold, with goodwill [?] on our part.”
The chief priests and those with them said to him, “Then, my lord the king, allow us to excavate the foundations of our temple while we await your divinity’s victorious return.”
Julian allowed them to uncover what remained of their temple,
so that what our Lord had said about it might be fulfilled: “Not one stone will be left upon another in it,” together with the prophecy: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!”
But what shall we say about the deception of that defiled man? Although he had fully carried out his pagan purpose through them, he dismissed them from his presence with their requests unanswered.
They returned to their own country in shame, bearing disgrace and hiding their faces. As for what happened and befell the Jews
when they began to uncover the foundations of their temple, I would be doing something superfluous if I included these events in our history, since they have been recorded by another writer.
In their proper place I shall write about them as they happened. But after the accursed tyrant had dismissed the circumcised men, he set his face toward going down to Syria.
For he was hurrying and eagerly intent on going down to encounter his [?] in the land of the Chaldeans. … And when Antioch heard the news of his arrival,
You exulted and rejoiced; you were glad and delighted. Her streets were adorned with splendid garments of every color.
[?] For the people of Antioch had long been waiting for this, which was accomplished through Julian.
For the madness of idolatry had secretly gripped these dissolute people, even since the days of the faithful Constantine.
They were afraid to reveal themselves because of the Christian emperor’s faith. But when their opportunity came,
their madness was revealed and their paganism came to light. In all the streets and squares of Antioch they prepared altars for the idols.
At the entrance to the city as well, there were two large altars, one here and one there, on both sides of the gate
through which Julian was scheduled to enter their city. The priests of the idol Zeus also
prepared choice perfumed oil, blended with excellent spices, over which the names of demons had been invoked,
to sprinkle on the emperor’s garments and purple robes when he entered the gate of their city. But concerning the madness
of the people of Antioch and their debauchery, there would have been no need to write,
if the stories of the steadfast were not intertwined with the deeds of their adversaries. For the madness of those who were harming themselves [?]
was what summoned [?] the steadfast to become a source of benefit to themselves. And so that we might not deny the steadfast their victory because of the deeds of the contemptible,
we were compelled by duty to write about these things together, so that, when [?] the victory of the steadfast is proclaimed, the disgrace of the contemptible may also be proclaimed.
For this purpose, in the course of our account, we have taken up the story of the madman: in all the renowned and well-known cities through which the defiled man passed,
he suffered frustration and condemnation through the victory of the steadfast. For when he arrived and reached Antioch in Syria,
the entire population of the city became dissolute and went mad: men with women, boys with old men, soldiers with virgins,
together with all the [?] in their city. They began a shameful dance, men with women, for it was a city of debauchery.
The Evil One was secretly directing them. These contemptible people went out to welcome the contemptible man who was like them, behaving dissolutely and madly, males with females.
They were so entangled with one another that they were close to committing shameful acts in front of the corrupter.
When his eyes had had their fill of this shameful spectacle, he waved his hand at them to quiet them a little. When they became quiet,
he spoke to them and said, “Only now have I truly understood and become firmly convinced that you are confidants of the hidden mystery of divinity and beloved children of our imperial rule.
For you recognized your source of help and showed discernment while we were far away, and you duly offered worship to the gods.
Now too, when we are near, face to face, your discernment has shown itself unchanged toward us,

in that you have brought out your honored wives and modest daughters to welcome our arrival. You are in the heart of our imperial majesty, to receive good things from us and to have us act generously toward you,
and toward your children and your children’s children, for many generations.” Was he not a madman, with his own end laughing at him? For within four months
And the wretch is no more; his promises have come to nothing, and his memory has been erased.
Julian went on to say to them, “I am greatly amazed at the faith of your city, which has shone forth not merely among a few people, as in the other cities.
For faith in the gods has been sown among all the inhabitants of your entire city.
It has spread equally among men and women, among the elderly and children, and throughout every age group. When I considered these things,
I gave thanks and praise. I cherished you in my thoughts and pronounced your city blessed, so firmly attached is it to the love of the gods.
Rightly and fittingly, Diocletian and his household designated it in their writings as the dwelling place of the gods, for it stands through them, rests upon them, and is bound up with them.
I have read the accounts of the victories of these mighty emperors, and in their writings I found
that your city receives much gratitude from them because you were zealous in worshiping the gods.
We too, following their example, will bestow many favors upon your city.
When the gods grant us a little rest and we are free of the war confronting us, I will remember your city and will never again forget it.
My eyes will always watch over it for its good. It will find favor and mercy in my eyes, and the royal throne will never depart from it.
I will build and strengthen its walls, renew and reinforce its fortifications. I will adorn it and glorify it, and make it like an adorned bride,
so that all the cities of our dominion will envy it. For many years I will shower gifts upon its inhabitants.
I will rejoice in it, and it will delight in me all our days.” While these mad utterances were being heard from the tyrant,
the crowds of the city raised their voices in his praise, and blasphemous acclamations, foreign to his name, were directed at him by the crowd.
One of the officials with him, whose name was Elpidius, was called by another name according to the rank of his service.
This man was a Christian, but concealed it because of his official position. When he saw
the wantonness and madness of the Antiochenes, and the blasphemous acclamations with which they praised him as a god, he was distressed in his soul and deeply disturbed.
This did not escape the tyrant’s notice. It troubled him, and he was greatly offended. But so as not to mix any distress into the city’s rejoicing,
he overlooked it and did not rebuke him at that moment, but kept it in mind. When he approached the city gate,
the Jews and pagans began shouting to him, “Until today our city was a widow. The Nazarenes gained power over it and plundered it.
For fifty years its eyes have grown weary looking for your deliverance. O king of our city, remove the plunder from the church’s treasury!
For our city has become poor, while the church has become rich. Let the church’s treasures enter the imperial treasury! The church’s treasures—

let them be investigated in the hands of Theodoret, the treasurer of that pampered church! Let Theodoret the priest, who has been put in charge of the treasures of the church, of the church, be arrested quickly!
Let Theodoret, who has bristled against your authority and established a foothold in the church, be handed over to the court!” And Julian summoned his uncle.
And he placed behind him the treasures of the church of Antioch, which he had received into his custody from the priest Theodoret, who had been appointed his steward at that time.
Now the pagan priests, stained with sin, were gathered inside the city gate.
They were ready for him to enter the city gate, and were burning spices and frankincense on their altars. And the chief priest of the lord of the gods
was standing on the great step of the altar. In his hand he held a golden vessel filled with the filthy oil of demons. ...
When Julian entered the city gate, that priest sprinkled it on the emperor’s purple robes and on his horse.
Some of the spray from that anointing landed on the edge of the cloak of Elpidius the eunuch. He was deeply offended and became angry with that priest.
He looked at him threateningly, dismounted from his horse in the fervor of his faith, and kicked him in the temple, taking his life. And he fell
in front of Julian’s horse and died. The tyrant became enraged and roared like a lion bent on destruction.
He shouted, saying, “Ha! You impostor, ha! Now you have exposed your deceit and shown yourself to be a Christian!”
“From now on it is my business to deal shrewdly with you.” Elpidius said to him, “When in my life, you madman, did I ever fall into your error,
or consent to your paganism? Or when did I join in your uncleanness, or defile myself with your pollution?
Or when did I consent to the evil desire of your unbridled debauchery? Or tell me when I ever entered a temple of idols with you and worshiped demons as you do.
My soul is sheltered from your wickedness, and my senses are sealed against your uncleanness. The vessel of my being is clear of the murky sediment of your paganism.
I have not degraded myself or my mind by letting any of the filth of your apostasy touch me. Rather, I have held my faith within my soul
clearly and purely. I have been watchful over it and guarded it, so that it should not be harmed or stained in any way. For I am not an apostate like you,
who denied the faith of the church in which you were raised, fell away from your covenant, and plunged into the error of demons. From now on you will not win your battles.
For victory has been taken from you, and the sword of the Lord is against you in the [?] of Assyria, because you turned away from reverence for him and proved false to his covenant.
Justice will not leave you alone until it has exacted payment from you for what you have done to the servants of God. So do not set your sights on victory,
for it is being taken away because of your guilt. Even though the demons have deceived you and given you hope of victory, know this, madman: demons do not keep faith with anyone.
For they set snares for you with their skillful cunning. Once they had entangled you, they lifted you up and set you on the heights of arrogance.
They have laid a trap for you and will dash you to pieces. And they have taken their stand opposite you, laughing at your downfall. ...”
Julian was dismayed at the words of Elpidius and behaved like a madman. He wanted to kill him, but when he saw that his spirit was glad and joyful,
and that his face was joyful and radiant in the struggle of confessing his faith, he refrained and did not kill him. Instead, he put him in irons and sent him to the
prison until the day should come for his hearing. Now, after the tyrant had spent a few days in Antioch,
letters came to him from Jovian that alarmed him. And he summoned Arsaces, Jovian’s deputy.
And he placed at his disposal everything that was needed and useful to him and the troops with him when he was appointed over the frontier regions. He also gave him instructions concerning Elpidius:
“If he turns back from his madness, abandons his error, and comes to his senses, let him be pardoned, and let the punishment [?] be suspended.
But if he persists in his misguided thinking, why should you give him his heart’s desire? This foolish race of Christians—
death by the sword, which everyone fears and which is decreed against offenders, is to them like a gift of life. Why, then, should you fulfill his wish?
Instead, if he persists in the same thinking, as we have said, let a sentence of permanent exile be pronounced against him.” He also gave instructions concerning the rest of the Christians
who had been arrested in that city before that day, for the tyrant had given similar orders concerning them. And because he was very concerned about his [?],
he distributed gifts to the city’s assemblies. He also paid his troops their wages for their service and kept them occupied with his departure.
He had set his face toward Edessa, and he sent men ahead to make preparations for his arrival. For he had decided
to spend some days there in Edessa, so that he could remove the officials and administrators who were there.
For accusations had been brought against them before him: “They are tyrants and rebels. They openly acknowledge that they are Christians,
without fearing or trembling before the dreadful authority of your imperial rule.” The accuser of these men was
Homanas the Jew, who at that time had been made head of the synagogue of the Jews living in Edessa.
This was his accusation against them: that they had actually laid hands on some people who had embraced the wicked man’s paganism,
and had driven them out of their city. He fiercely accused them before him, saying, “Unless you remove these men
from Edessa, the entire population of the city will follow them and become estranged from the worship of the gods. For they do not allow the city’s inhabitants
to incline toward the will of your imperial rule.” From that day onward Julian threatened the administrators of Edessa
and wanted to punish them. But the faith of the people of Edessa deserves wonder and admiration: all of them, without exception, had resolved to die
rather than willingly let the unclean man set foot inside the gate of their city. And when the wicked man’s envoys arrived,
the people of Edessa would not allow them to enter the city. For they had posted guards to deal with this matter
outside their city wall, so that they would not be caught unawares. When the city’s leading men learned of the arrival of the defiled men,
they went out to meet them at the city gate, accompanied by the entire population. Rastota, the head of the city, questioned them, saying,
“Men, what do you want? Why have you come, and who sent you? Your appearance is foreign to our city, for I see the tassels
of paganism on the edges of your rags.” One of them, whose name was Colmachus, stamped his foot and shook his head, saying,
“I am deeply grieved over the destruction of this city, since you have shown such ill will. It will not be long before it is destroyed.
But now, concerning what you asked: Emperor Julian, king forever, holds authority over the world.”
He sent us to his city to announce his coming, so that it might come out to meet him and welcome him with joy, gladness, and great ceremony.
And now consider what answer you will give to this, so that we may write and inform the king of your wishes. [?] Aristota said to them:
“You men have gone badly astray and lost your way in coming to Edessa, a faithful city that is a stranger to the madness of your paganism.
What do you want with it? Or what sign of joy have you seen in it,
that you have brought it joyful news about your master? Look: its walls are covered with sackcloth, as your own eyes can see, and its streets
and colonnades are dressed in black, like a house of mourning. For Edessa is in great mourning and bitter sorrow over who has taken whose place on the throne of the Roman Empire:
Julian the apostate in place of faithful Constantine; an unjust man in place of a righteous one; a pagan in place of a Christian; a madman in place of a sensible and wise man.
And what can we say about your [?], since you neglected to go to Harran, the mother of idolatry, which suits the tyrant’s paganism, is steeped in his madness, and looks forward to his coming?
It longs to see him. As for a king who shares its false religion, it has decorated its streets for him and adorned the temples of its carved images.
Day after day it watches and waits for him, wondering when he will come and fulfill its desire, carry out the wishes of its paganism, and raise its head high in his presence.
Go to that mad city, the mother of troublemakers, and announce your master’s coming to it. It will rejoice at the news of him and exult at his arrival
and boast of his paganism. But leave our sorrowful city, which mourns over the paganism of the mad king and grieves over his error.
It is dressed in black for him as for someone dead. And who would not call him dead, this man who is dead while still alive,
who has himself taken away the glory of the living God and given it to dead idols and unclean spirits?
And who would not mock him and ridicule his paganism? Go, then, and tell the madman who sent you: ‘Who is bringing you to Edessa, the city of Christians?
It neither agrees with your paganism nor submits to your error, nor will it open its gates before you. And, more than all these things,
it does not even recognize you as king. For Edessa’s king is Christ, and he dwells within its walls.
It will not admit a stranger to displace him. If Edessa did not open its gates before the mighty kings of Assyria,
who besieged it for three years without conquering it, will Edessa open its gates to you, a contemptible adulterer and worshiper of idols, and welcome you, a madman?
Far be it from the streets of the blessed city that your unclean feet should tread them, feet that have trampled the thresholds of the temples of idolatry. But as much as
you wish, draw your sword against us and bend your bow. We will not lose heart at your frost. For we have someone who stands at our head and fights for us.’” [?]
Columcus and those with him were astonished at Aristota’s words and burned with anger at his insults.
Columcus answered the steadfast man threateningly: “Tell me, you wretch, you [?] dog barking at its masters:
are you uttering these words on your own behalf, or on behalf of all the people of your city? For we need to know,
so that we may write accordingly and inform the king of your wicked intentions.” Then the entire population of the city
They shouted, saying, “Everything that was said by the trusted men of our city was spoken by all of us.
There is no one among us who disowns these declarations, except the Jews, the enemies of Christ,
whom we will soon uproot from our city as well. Our city belongs to Christ, and the faithful Constantius entrusted it to him.”
One of the prominent men of Edessa, whose name was Ma‘nu, was at that time serving at the king’s court.
When he saw the bishops of the provinces asking him, as a righteous man, to bless their provinces and their cities,
he too presented his petition to the king on behalf of Edessa. He pleaded with him, saying, “My lord the king,
remember our faithful city, and grant it the blessing of your mouth at this time of your departure. For your divinity knows, my lord,
that our city holds fast, like steel, in the souls of its inhabitants, to the faith that your fathers handed down to it. Nor is this hidden from your Majesty:
if our sins bring this upon us—that the pagan and wicked Julian should gain power over our territory after your passing—
he has many afflictions to inflict on our city because of its faith.
For this reason we ask today in faith for a blessing from your righteous Majesty upon our faithful city, so that, like a barrier of salvation,
it may stand before us and shelter us from all that harms us.” Although the agonies of death were tormenting the discerning king,
he did not neglect the faithful man’s petition, but answered him kindly, saying, “What you have asked of us, my son, is unnecessary for your city.
For what could the blessed city gain from the blessing of our lowliness, when once, from the holy mouth and pure lips of the Word of the Father,
your city received a divine blessing that cannot be undone?” But this discerning man did not give up his petition.
Instead, he pressed his plea still more insistently, asking the king openly, “If it pleases your Majesty,
fulfill for us what our Lord said in his gospel: ‘To the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance.’ Add, then, my lord the king, a blessing to our blessing,
so that we may be perfected in our faith. Let the blessing of Edessa’s Lord be its wall, and the blessing of your Majesty its outer wall.
With the spiritual armor you have bestowed on it, may it wage war against error and overcome it, and may paganism be worn down by the truth of its faith.”
When Constantius saw Ma‘nu’s faith and persistence, he filled his mouth with blessing and blessed Edessa.
He recorded his blessings in a document and sent them to the people of Edessa. The people of Edessa held this document in great honor,
until it was taken from them through the action of the heretic Valens. ... When this document was read in the hearing of King Julian’s envoys,
the people of Edessa raised their voices in praise of the Christian kings who had passed away. They consoled themselves and extolled their faith, saying,
“Kingship truly befitted you, Christian kings of the house of Constantine! In your zeal for the faith, you uprooted the roots of sin,
cleared away the thickets of paganism, and turned all nations to the worship of Christ. The crown and the rule were glorious upon you!”
Builders of churches and upholders of orthodoxy in every region, you have fallen asleep in peace upon the bed of your lives, and you have left us
in the hands of a foul wolf thirsting for our blood. You who sleep in Christ, intercede for our city.
For although you are asleep, you are alive to God himself. Your deaths are dear to him and precious in his eyes.
Faithful Constantine, intercede for the churches whose doors are sealed and whose precincts lie deserted, you who established Christianity.
With your prayer, come to the aid of your faith. For look, the dark clouds of paganism have spread over its face throughout all our lands.
For look, the dark clouds of paganism have spread over its face throughout all our lands. Righteous shepherd, help your flock through your supplication.
For the destructive wolf has sharpened a fang against it to tear it apart. But far be it from its true shepherd, who died for it, to allow it to be torn apart.
But far be it from its true shepherd, who died for it, to withdraw his hand from it and leave it in the wolf’s hands. Rather, may he quickly bring it deliverance,
and may his sword exact vengeance on its persecutors. While these songs, together with many others like them, were being heard from the congregations of Edessa,
Callimachus wrote down these songs and sent them to Julian while he was in Antioch in Syria.
When Julian read the writings sent to him, he became bitterly angry and behaved like a madman. Yet he restrained himself for a time
and postponed exacting punishment for these things until, as he said, he had taken [?] of Assyria and finished his wars. He wrote and sent word to Callimachus:
“Leave that accursed city, and have nothing to do with it until I have time to carry out against it what I have planned.
For it is a [?] and deranged city, which neither acknowledges its kings nor recognizes its governors,
nor admits that there is any other god besides the Nazarene. And what medicine is suited to the affliction of this mad city,
except that it should be destroyed and rebuilt from the beginning? For there is no way for me to avoid destroying it and [?] rebuilding it. For it does not flourish through the [?] of the gods.
It boasts in the cross of the Nazarene, and even now it is proud and boastful in him. It trusts in him to rescue it from my hands.
I will soon make it understand and teach it what help its god provides and what discipline my gods inflict.
But until its time has come, leave this mad city and go make preparations for us in sensible Harran, the city of the gods, which longs to see us
and yearns for our arrival and rejoices in our festivals.” He also wrote things to the Edessenes that we have no need to record in this book.
For some of them were menaces and threats, while others were impiety and blasphemy.

And what need is there to repeat the impiety and blasphemy of that defiled man, which came back upon his own head in the land of his enemies? But as for the inspired words that the Edessenes wrote to him,
duty has urged us to record them in our history, to comfort the faithful, encourage the steadfast, and praise the children of the blessed city,
who endured and stood firm in their truth and did not fear the king’s fury and authority. Rather, they were deeply grieved at his error
and concerned for his peace. And when his writings were read before them in the circus, and they heard his blasphemy and arrogance against God,
They too, as far as they could, treated his letter with contempt and mocked him and his paganism.
They plunged the madman's letters into the receptacle of their city's latrine, before Diodorites, who had brought the documents.
They did not fear the tyrant's threats, nor were they intimidated by his menaces. Instead, like people firm in their faith and confident in their God's help,
they sent him replies corresponding to his letters and repaid his contempt twice over, writing to him through Diodorites as follows:
"Our whole city is utterly astonished at you: how you have gone mad, lost your senses, and become blind in the very eye of your understanding!
You do not realize that you have nothing belonging to you among us. We will neither comply with your paganism nor surrender ourselves to your error.
Nor will we take part in the filthy sacrifices offered as burnt offerings to your idols. Since you have not acknowledged God, we do not acknowledge you as king either.
What, then, do you want with our city? In your tyranny, you should rather be astonished and amazed that the king of our city dwells within its walls.
All the crowns of creation are subject to his crown. Yet you, adulterer, son of a whirlwind, are stumbling as you try to enter his city!
Far be it from blessed Edessa, the mother of believers, to bring in a stranger against her true king, through whom she has grown great and strong! His blessing has become
an impregnable wall for her. After the victory and glory he has bestowed on her, is she to deny him, you madman?

Even when she did not know him, she believed in him and acknowledged him in his humility. Through the mouths of her children she offered him entreaties and petitions, asking him to come and dwell in her
and to be king over her forever. Even before she had seen him, she accepted his lordship over her and long ago received his royal portrait with honor.
How much more today, when she sees him continually with the clear eye of faith, carries him within her soul, and has put him on in her baptism!
She cherishes his holy body, kisses it with her lips, bears it reverently in her hands, and presses it to her eyes.
She is marked with his name and stamped with his images. She worships him in his humility and acknowledges his sufferings, for he redeemed her by his death and freed her by being killed.
He promised her victory through his blessing and placed her beyond all the battles and assaults of her enemies. After all these good things he has done for her,
do you want her to deny him, you who are dead while still alive? You are greatly mistaken if you think the people of Edessa will obey your paganism,
or dress in white and come out to celebrate your arrival, or that Edessa will open her gates to you and long for you, or decorate her streets and colonnades in your honor.
Do not seek these things in Edessa. The day of your arrival is no day of joy for her; it is a day of suffering and distress.
Her walls have their lips veiled, for she mourns your madness. Her streets and colonnades are dressed in black,
for she has made a house of mourning for you while you are still alive. As for us, you are indeed dead to us. On the day when her mourning for you departs from her
and the days of mourning for you come to an end, just as she dressed in black for you, she will dress in white for you.
She will clap her hands and rejoice over you, stamp her feet, and cry out, saying, 'Aha! Aha! Our eyes have seen him!' She will mock the divinations of our paganism and say,

'Where is your boasting, madman? The lofty one has fallen, and the exalted one has been overthrown! The arrogant one, wrapped in pride, has come to nothing, has been wiped away, and is no more.' Our city will not be alone in rejoicing over you at these things.
But heaven and earth and everything in them will also tremble at your paganism at that hour, and raise a lament over your folly, because you died
in your sins. So if you are determined to hear face to face the things we have written to you,
come to our city. Otherwise, like a man who knows his own dignity, turn aside and pass us by. Look, I have exposed all your insults and thrown them behind you.
This is the copy of the letters that the people of Edessa sent to Julian through Diodoratus, his envoy,
while he was in the city of Beroea. When he read the letters sent to him, he became very angry with Diodoratus
and threw him into prison. He planned to make him suffer many evils because he had yielded to the wishes of the people of Edessa
and had agreed to bring their letters himself. For he had wanted to cool his fury
and calm his anger by taking it out on some of those who were appointed to bring him letters. When the tyrant saw that he had been mocked,
he set his face toward destroying Edessa before [?]. He grew fierce within himself and said,
“May the gods do this to me, and more besides, if I pass by Edessa before destroying it,
because they have joined together to insult our imperial majesty. When the gods give me rest and I am free from my wars, I will rebuild and restore it,
and settle in it a people who know the will of the gods and obey the will of our imperial majesty.” ... Now there was a man in the city of Aleppo whose name was Aquilinus.
He was [?] in his city and well known to the emperor, and he had great freedom to speak before the tyrant,
because he had presented Julian with many gifts and substantial offerings while he was in Antioch.
When he came to his city as well, he presented him with twice as many offerings. The emperor’s table was supplied from his own resources during the days Julian spent in the city of Aleppo.
Now this man of whom we are speaking was a Christian, but he was afraid to reveal this about himself because of the emperor’s decree.
... When he learned that Edessa had brought trouble upon itself from the emperor, he felt anguish within himself and grieved for the city.
He was waiting for an opportunity to present his petition about it before the emperor. ... When the day came for Julian to depart from Aleppo,
he called Aquilinus and said to him, “Because you have found favor and kindness in the eyes of our imperial majesty, by distinguishing yourself and honoring me in this way,
we shall yet have time to repay you kindness for kindness. But for now, whatever seems good to you, whatever your soul desires and pleases you,
ask of us, and it will be given to you. For I am determined to do you good in return for your kindness.” When Aquilinus heard these things from the madman,
he fell on his face, bowed down, and said, “Because your servant has found favor in the eyes of your imperial majesty, your divinity has stooped to ask these things concerning your servant.
Yet, my lord the emperor, what favor does a servant do by honoring his masters? Everything your servant has is yours, and what is yours has been received from what is yours.
So favor has been shown to your servant, in that I was counted worthy to serve your divinity. I myself am amazed
at how far I have been brought by your mercy, so that I may speak face to face with your divinity.” Julian said to him:
“I swear by the good fortune of the gods and by the life of my kingdom that I will grant you whatever your heart desires. Whatever you ask of me, I will do for you.” Then this discerning man,
when the opportunity came for him to make his appeal, presented his petition about Edessa before the tyrant, afraid and trembling, and said:
“I beg your awe-inspiring authority: do not let your anger flare up over my request. I am small and insignificant, and my request is greater than I am.”
He said to him, “Tell me what your request is.” Aquilinus said, “This is my request and petition:
tranquility for your kingdom, peace for your dominion, mercy for the guilty, forgiveness for offenders, and time for Edessa to repent.
For great compassion, my lord, befits your kingship.” But the accursed tyrant became very angry and was disconcerted by Aquilinus’s request.
Because he loved him, he did not wish to harm him, but merely reproached him in words, saying, “This one thing especially astonishes me:
your requests show no discernment, and you do not know what you are asking. For it is not right for us to be put to shame over this, since you have nothing to gain
by your request that you should restrain me from taking revenge on those who insulted me. Nevertheless, your request is hereby granted, to the dishonor of my kingship.”
When Aquilinus heard these things from the tyrant, he became terribly afraid, struck his face against the ground, and remained silent.
The color of his face changed from fear, and he became like a dead man. When the tyrant saw that Aquilinus had grown faint from fear,
he felt very sorry for him, reassured him, and spoke kindly to him, saying, “I know that upright and wise people
are distressed whenever devastation, upheaval, or some injury befalls one of the cities within their kings’ dominion.
Their understanding is highly praised in this respect. Nevertheless, anyone distressed over the destruction and devastation of a country or a city ought
to inquire into the cause of its destruction. Now, if you knew what letters the people of Edessa sent me, you would have urged us, even more strongly than we ourselves,
to exact satisfaction for our dishonor and the insults to our kingship. Nevertheless, since you were unaware of their outrageous insolence,
you did well to plead on their behalf [?]. Do not be troubled about this: if they repent and turn away from their twisted, rebellious thinking,
they will have gained their lives through the support of your petition on their behalf. But if they persist in their rebellious thinking,
then by their insolence they will have earned devastation for their city and destruction for themselves.” When Aquilinus heard these things from the tyrant, he fell down, bowed before him, and said:
“Now my lord has frightened his servant, but my soul has returned to me and regained its strength. I beg your awe-inspiring authority:
allow me to speak freely about my petition. It was not the destruction of that wretched city that concerned me, but that our kingdom should not be ridiculed.
For it would be a great disgrace to us and a grievous blow to our kingdom if, after an army had been stationed at the frontier
and they had proclaimed devastation for Assyria with the news of their advance, we should turn them back again from east to west,
before the kings have struck [?]. The Assyrians would mock us and heap empty words upon us,
saying, ‘Before Persia had even fought at full strength, the Romans began turning their backs on the east.’”
“And another thing, my lord the king: we would be considered weak in the eyes of the Persians.
If the Romans were to settle down to besiege a city situated within the territory of our empire, our judgment would be criticized for this: that we had left [?] in the cold that had come upon us.
Look, concern over this wretched city weighs upon us, although a camp follower of our empire could take vengeance on it whenever your command permitted him.
And now, my lord the king, leave these wretches to their miserable lives until Your Majesty returns victorious through your divinity.
Otherwise, let their blood be on their own heads; you and your empire are free of responsibility for their blood.” [?] Julian said:
“All these things would have seemed unnecessary to me, had I not been persuaded by the oaths accompanying your plea and petition.
For I do not desire their repentance as much as I desired their destruction. Nevertheless, what I have spared, I have spared for myself as a matter of [?].
For now, then, I will do as you say.” Aquilinus bowed down and departed from the king’s presence. After these things, Julian
set his face toward Harran, concealing his hatred of Edessa in his heart. He was biding his time because of the pledge made in his oaths.
He departed from Aleppo with the troops accompanying him. He traveled and advanced swiftly, without lingering on his journey.

He did not delay at any of the stopping places where he halted and then resumed his journey, until he entered Harran. [?] When the Jews living in Edessa heard that Julian had crossed the Euphrates eastward,
they slipped away and left their city, two at a time and three at a time together.

For they were afraid to go out together openly in a crowd before the eyes of the city’s inhabitants, because the people of Edessa were extremely hostile toward them and were looking for a pretext against them. When they had assembled at one meeting place,
the leader of the Jewish synagogue and those who had joined him to go with him to greet the madman
numbered about seven hundred men. They adorned themselves, dressed in white, and took trumpets in their hands
to sound before him when they welcomed him. They went and met him a very long way from their city. When he saw them, from the sound of the trumpets
he recognized that they were circumcised, and he asked them where they came from. When he learned that they were from Edessa, he snorted and uttered insults.
He rebuked them angrily and drove them from his presence, saying, “If you were not rebels like the children of the barren woman,

you would not be living in a godless city and, like them, be strangers to the worship of the gods. It has therefore become clear that you share their error and that your dealings are bound up with theirs. If it is not as I have said,
where have you shown goodwill toward us, even in a single matter?
Could you not have found some small occasion to build your house of worship for Zeus, the great god, from whom help flows to humanity?
Or perhaps we did not have the means to repay you for this favor, if your love for us were genuine? But it is just as we say:
you share the thinking of these rebels who hate their own lives. Before long I will erase their memory and wipe their name and their religion from the face of the earth.”
But the leader of the Jewish synagogue and those with him remained silent and still,
until the command permitted them to give voice to their petition. When he allowed them to speak, the synagogue leader proceeded to speak before the tyrant.
“We ask,” they said, “of your awesome authority that we not be regarded in the eyes of your divinity as those godless people who have gone astray.

For we do not worship, as they do, the Nazarene whom our fathers crucified. Nor have we committed anything hateful or deserving of death against your majesty. Yet we are made objects of hatred in our city because we have complied

with the will of your majesty. We are made objects of hatred in our city because we have complied with the will of your majesty. May the gods reveal to your might what a distressed and humiliated life
we live among these people who are estranged from the will of your divinity. For we are insulted and wronged; our [?] are seized, our houses plundered, and our places of
assembly uprooted. Our heads are crushed, and to this day there is no one to judge our case or seek redress for us.
Even when we give no grounds for an accusation concerning the gods, they pursue pretexts against us, seeking to strip us of our possessions and make us further [?] for our persecutors.
How much more, if they heard that grounds for an accusation had been established against us, would they, in their insolence,
gulp us down like dragons and swallow us alive! We therefore ask the awesome authority of your uprightness
that our people not be considered rebels in the eyes of your majesty. For rebellion has never been seen among our people,
either in us or in our fathers. Indeed, we submit to our kings and obey our governors.
Although our law permits us to serve one God, our fathers served and worshiped many gods,
conducting themselves according to the will of their kings and governors. We too, in the same way, comply with the will of your divinity,
and we serve and worship the gods whom your majesty permits us to worship. Only let the resentment that your majesty holds against us on account of the people of Edessa
be removed. Let your divinity be assured that we have never shared in the wickedness of the people of Edessa,
among whom our sins have made us live [?]. For if Zion, our true city, had not undergone a change,
our city would not have been called Edessa. Likewise, our brothers scattered throughout the world do not regard the places where they live as anything but places of temporary residence.
For we truly have only one city, which envy uprooted and jealousy destroyed.
When the gods show you favor, and you win your battles and prevail over your enemies, remember desolate Zion,
her ruined temple, and her scattered children. Raise the head of the humiliated city that has fallen, the [?] that has been overthrown.
May her spirit be lifted through you; may your years be prolonged because of her humiliation, and may your authority reign over the world.” Julian said to them:
“Your brothers also came to me at Tarsus in Cilicia and laid their petition before me concerning the land of your ancestors and also the temple, their place of worship.
I satisfied their hearts and comforted them, and they received promises that relieved their sorrow
and consoled their minds. In the same way, for you too who have petitioned us, we renew those very same promises,
to strengthen and comfort you as you hear them: if the gods are willing to grant us victory in the battles of Assyria,
when we return safely to the territory of our empire, I will rebuild your city and fortify it, and it will be called by the name of our imperial majesty.”
And I will restore your ruined house of worship and make its later glory greater than its former glory—the glory it had in the days of Solomon, who built and adorned it.
When these deceivers heard this, they suddenly threw themselves down before him and bowed to him, saying:
“Thanks be to the gods, who grant mercy before Your Majesty! May you be granted long life on account of our persecution!” Julian said to them:
“Today you have shown the goodwill you have toward us, and from the [?] of your lips we have learned
how wholehearted and sincere your love is toward the gods, who do good to their worshipers. We too will show you [?] and mercy.
For we have become truly convinced that you have no part in the rebellion and error of the children of the barren woman,
on whom I intend to take vengeance for all the evil and hateful things they have done up to this day.” The leader of the synagogue said to him,
speaking on behalf of those with him: “If, my lord the king, we had not already submitted a report to Your Justice
about the evil things being done in that city, which rebels against its kings, and how brazen its inhabitants have become toward the gods and Your Majesty,
then suspicion that we approved of their evil deeds would rightly and justly have fallen upon us. But if we are being insulted and wronged, plundered and robbed,
and our heads are crushed, these things are enough to bear witness for us before Your Majesty that they have never been at peace with us.
May the gods reveal to Your Clemency what a distressed and humiliated life we lead among them! For unless we left the city by a clever stratagem,
two by two and three by three, we did not dare, as a group,
to go out openly to greet and worship Your Divinity. The crowds of our city would beat us like dogs. The gods themselves know what happened in this affair.
For it is a brazen and insolent city, which neither fears the gods nor stands in awe of kings.”
They vehemently accused their city before the tyrant and inflamed him with zeal,
urging him to destroy and devastate their city, while giving pledges that they would hand over its southern gate. But he paid no attention at all to their words. Instead, he dismissed them with this:
“Go now, for this is not the time to exact punishment for these things. Keep quiet
until time permits us to come and deal with your city as its deeds deserve.” With this he dismissed them from his presence.
For the madman was greatly preoccupied with the route of his journey. He took the road leading toward Harran, turning aside from Edessa without entering it.
Looking toward it from opposite, he shook his head, rebuked it, and snorted at it, saying: “City, may your own fortune soon overthrow you, and may you become a mound of ruins over your inhabitants!
For you did not recognize the great things the gods bestowed on you. You withheld the thanksgiving due to them and assigned their worship to a crucified man, becoming mad with love for him.
From now on I will destroy you, and the crucified one whom you have acknowledged will not rescue you.” But the madman, that loathsome pig, did not know
that the sword of the crucified one whom he had blasphemed was sharpened for the day of his slaughter and sacrifice. As for how Harran received its mad king,
it is unnecessary to include that in our account. Those who know are not unaware of the pomp and the cries of madness with which this happened.
And with mockery and a clamor of empty praises, men with misguided tongues like their own welcomed him. Let us therefore leave these things that were unjustly done among the people of Harran.
And let us rightly praise the faith of the people of Edessa, who stood firm in their truth, hurled [?] at him, and shattered him.
For when they learned about the Jews’ journey and the circumstances in which they had left their city, they were deeply distressed. They argued with
the rulers of their city fiercely, and disputed with them, saying, “The Jews who live in our city
are being left in it for the safety of our fortress! If a crisis happens to press upon us, they will be the ones to betray it. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them
before the crisis overtakes us.” But the city’s officials and rulers knew that the tyrant was near them, encamped within the region, and threatening them severely.
And he was looking for a pretext against them. The rulers of the fortress were afraid to lay hands on those who had gone out to greet the defiled man.
Instead, they calmed the people, saying, “Our brothers, now is not the time to take revenge on the crucifiers. Rather, it is a time to perform acts of charity
and offer prayer to God, that he may remove this harsh time from his people, bring low the lofty horn of the arrogant that has grown strong, and cast down their haughty spirit.
And now, our brothers, you know that the tyrant is encamped in our region and is seeking a pretext to destroy us. Let us be patient for a while,
and, like wise people, buy ourselves time.” ... Now there were Romans in Edessa, about eighteen hundred men.
These men were known to the emperor and had served in the tyrant’s legion. And because they were believers and Christians,
they were disgusted with the defiled man’s paganism. They were looking for a place compatible with their faith, where they could find safety
and escape from the wicked man’s power. ... And when he heard about Edessa and received confirmation about it from many people—that among all the cities of the East,
it alone had stood resolutely in its truth and had persevered steadfastly in its faith, and that with one soul and one mind,
the whole city together fearlessly worshiped Christ openly and confessed him, and would not submit to paganism even if it were to be laid waste.
And when they found a place such as they had been seeking, they escaped from the tyrant’s power and came to live in Edessa.
They encouraged the entire city and strengthened its inhabitants so that they would not submit to paganism,
promising to stand on the city walls and defend them in battle. They gave a pledge
and exchanged oaths that neither side would act treacherously against the other. Now when these believing men saw that the city’s rulers
were afraid to lay hands on the enemies of the cross because the tyrant was nearby, zeal for God seized them themselves.
Before the Jews entered the fortress, they dressed and armed themselves. They took up positions against them inside the city gate and outside its walls.
They carried out a great slaughter. Whoever escaped the sword outside was met by the sword inside.
Thus these men’s swords made an end of all the Jews who had gone to greet the tyrant.
Then they once again consecrated their hands to the Lord with the Jews’ wives and children, and gave their possessions and belongings over to plunder.
They also drove out their Jewish companions—those who had not gone to greet the madman—and expelled them from Edessa.
They cleansed the city of Judaism and paganism, and did not leave a single soul in the city who did not worship the cross.
When news of what had happened reached the tyrant’s ears, he was utterly astonished. He was filled with fury and blazed with anger. He sent this message to the people of Edessa: “From now on,

I, in my mercy, have given you time to repent, but you, in your obstinacy, have squandered the time for your repentance, until the time has come to exact punishment from you for your offenses and the evil things you have done.
Hand over to me the soldiers who rebelled against me, lest an army surround your city and you seek help with no one to help you.” The people of Edessa sent him this reply:
“From now on, you have no soldier in our city. For when you search it,
there is not a single soul in it bearing the stamp of your paganism. As for the few soldiers you had here, if Your Majesty really wants them,
send wagons and carry away their corpses, lest the dogs of our country feast on them. But know, madman,
that even if you encamp against our city with the armies of all the kings in the world, we will not submit to your error,
nor will we share in your wickedness. Every one of us belongs to Christ, and we serve him truly and faithfully. He stands

at our head and fights for us, and we trust that he will give us victory. From now on, we have no concern or thought for your [?] ...” When the accursed, condemned man heard the words that the people of Edessa had sent him,
the thought stirred within him to destroy the city before the [?] of Assyria was put in order. He raised his voice and said:
“How many times have I sought to heal the stubborn ulcer of this wretched city with the gentle medicine of my mercy!
Yet it has not been healed, for its ulcer has grown worse from the medicines. Now I will check its ulcer
and apply a painful medicine suited to its wound, so that its ulcer may be cleansed of corruption and become healthy.” He wrote letters and sent them to Nisibis, to Jovian,
the commander of his army. When he read the wicked man’s letters and learned from them what the madman intended to do to the faithful city,
the discerning man groaned inwardly and was deeply distressed over Edessa. He was overcome by the grief in his soul.

He seized his clothes and tore them. He called Aphorentius, the steward of his household, and instructed him, saying: “Since I have received orders from the emperor concerning the confidential matter between us,
and intend to attend to it at once, let no one visit me today.” He took the wicked man’s letters and went outside the camp.
He came to the place where Bishop Vologeses and the entire community of the church of Nisibis were gathered for prayer.
For they had a little respite through the advocacy of the discerning man who was over them. With his permission, they had set up a cross and an altar
in a certain spacious cave in that region. There the holy mysteries of the holy church were celebrated
throughout the time that Jovian stayed in Nisibis. When he came to the place where they were gathered, Bishop Vologeses and those with him were astonished at his appearance.
For they saw that he was downcast and distressed, with sorrow written on his face. Vologeses wanted to learn the reason for his sorrow.
Jovian himself, with tears streaming down, read the letters to them. He had written to him as follows: “Since
The fate of the Edessenes has mocked them and brought them into rebellion, so that, through their failure to repent of all their transgressions,
their fate may have room to rule over them. It is therefore our will
that they be treated as rebellious people who, in their insolence, have deprived themselves of repentance and, by their evil will, have cut off their hope of life.

For these people there is no repentance from now on [?]. Rather, they shall receive punishment for their wicked deeds, as their transgressions indeed deserve. Therefore, as a faithful man appointed to carry out our will,
hurry to our deliverance. Do not let your sword delay in avenging the insult against us, lest the reproaches of our Majesty come upon you afterward. For from now on,
you are not to appear before our Majesty unless news has come to me of the destruction [?] and devastation of Edessa. See, I have made our will known to you.
When the tyrant’s writings were read [?] before Vologeses, bishop of Nisibis, and before all the faithful people of his church, they all raised their voices and wept.
They put on mourning and were greatly afraid for their brothers in Christ, who, through their zeal for their faith, had kindled the tyrant’s wrath against themselves.
They proclaimed a fast because of Edessa’s severe trial and devoted themselves to prayer and supplication for their brothers, the children of the blessed city.
Jovian himself, like a discerning man, spread the wicked man’s letters before the Lord’s altar, as Hezekiah had done.
He spread out sackcloth and ashes for himself and threw himself face down upon them before the Lord’s altar. In the anguish of his soul,
he asked for death for himself, saying, “Please, Lord, bring your servant’s days to an end, and release me quickly from life.
For I am very sick from the sorrows and groans that come upon me every hour, through my zeal for your church and your faithful people, who receive your body and blood.
How much can your servant’s soul endure suffering? I am sick and weak, and I have no strength to fight against the pagans. If your mercy does not come to our aid,
defeat remains our lot. But I beg your abundant mercy: do [?] one of two things for your servant. Either take my soul from me and release me, so that I may sleep
with my fathers and find rest, or take the cruel evildoer away from us, who has placed us under the dominion of paganism and afflicted us. For he gives us no peace,
and he has no other business than dealing with us. He has drawn up his furious battle against us and fights against our faith at all times. But if your strength joins our strength,
we have hope of victory. For what can we weak people [?] do by our own strength? Without your strength, our Lord, nothing at all.
For it was in reliance on the promise of your blessing that Edessa hurled scorn at the tyrant and was not afraid,
because the promise you made to her is faithful and sure: that an enemy would never gain dominion over her. O [?] faithful one, who does not lie,
preserve peace for the blessed city, as you promised her. Turn the wicked man’s onslaught away from her, and quench the violence of his anger against her, so that he may not harm her.
Sprinkle the dew of your mercy upon the city that has kept your faith, and spread the wing of your mercy over its inhabitants, who trust [?] in your cross.
Remember, my Lord, this city and her true faith: although she did not know you, she believed in you.

Although she had not seen you in the flesh, she acknowledged your lowliness. She despised and abandoned the worship of her idols and carved images, and offered her worship to the lowliness of your cross.
Who would not praise the faith of Edessa? Even today, when stormy waves rise against her, she has not weakened in her steadfastness.
or fallen away from her faith. Rather, trusting in your promise, she stoned the tyrant with her rebukes as though with stones.
And she pierced him with her words of reproof as though with arrows. Who would not share the suffering of this faithful city?
For look, the wicked man threatens her and vows to destroy her. No, my Lord, I beg you: do not grant the wicked man his desire, and do not let his plan succeed.
Turn his evil scheme away, my Lord, from the city that worships you. Let those delivered through the help of your blessing give thanks, my Savior. Yes, I beg you, the hope and expectation of my soul.
Hear the prayer of your sinful servant, and accept the petition of this guilty man, for I have cried out to you from the pain of my heart and the anguish of my soul.
My sins did not hold me back from standing at your door, for your encouraging voice, which urged sinners
to stand at your door, gave me a hand, drew me along, and brought me to your door. For in my suffering, my Lord, I forgot my sins.
And because of my soul’s sorrow, I did not even bring before my eyes the fact that I am sinful and guilty. Instead, with a downcast face, I boldly knocked at the door of your mercy.
I beg you, good one, whose hand gives generously: do not send me away empty-handed from your door. Rather, as a reward for my tears, grant tranquility
to your Church, peace to her children, and deliverance to the city of believers that has taken refuge in you. And as for me, my Lord, who have grieved over the humiliation of your Church,
grant that I may see her exaltation. And when my eyes see the deliverance of your Church, command that I depart to the dwelling of the dead
and lie down in peace beside the bones of my fathers.” … When Jovian finished his prayer, he stood up and shook off the ashes that lay upon him, and saluted the altar.
He comforted the chaste religious community of the church of Nisibis with his words, bowed his head for Bishop Vologeses to lay his hand upon him, and returned to the camp.
He carried within himself the suffering and sorrow of Edessa, as well as the thoughts and anxiety caused by the letters sent to him. He did not know what to do.
For to carry out the tyrant’s will distressed him greatly because it meant the destruction of the faithful city. But to oppose the will of that guilty man
would kindle anger upon anger against him and against them. While this faithful man was absorbed in these thoughts, sorrow came and filled the righteous man’s heart.
His mind bore such a weight of suffering that he was close to becoming ill from his sorrow. When God saw the toil and suffering of this discerning man,
he wished to comfort him in his distress. Since there was no manifest vision at that time, he cast stillness upon him, and he fell asleep. During his sleep upon his bed,
he sent him a dream and comforted him. For there appeared to him, as in a wondrous apparition, one of those forty blessed men who suffered martyrdom in the ice
in the days of the wicked Maximinus, whose name was Mercurius. Even before he came to martyrdom, this holy man had been zealous for good deeds.
He had been fiercely opposed to the pagan faction and filled with fury and anger against them. It was this holy man whom
Jovian saw wondrously in his dream, coming to him in his military uniform, holding a bow and three arrows in his hand.
He seemed cheerful toward him and smiled. As though he did not know, he asked him, “My brother, what is this sorrow in your heart and anguish in your mind?
For I see that you are deeply distressed and mourning.” Jovian answered him in the dream, saying, “Should I not, my brother, grieve and mourn over the humiliation of our people,

over the ridicule and disgrace of our religious community, over our churches that are closed and their altars that are torn down, over our priests who are persecuted, and over the crown of our glory that has fallen?”
Yet you ask about all these things that have happened as though you knew nothing about them. Are you really the only one left in the Roman Empire who is unaware of these things?
The blessed Mercurius said to him in the vision, “It is right and entirely fitting that you grieve over your church, your true mother.
Your faith is all the more praiseworthy because of these things. But now put away your mourning and free yourself from sorrow.
Your prayer, together with that of Julian the Elder, has now come before God. He has sent me to reveal and explain to you the truth of the matter.
Twelve weeks of days from today will be allowed for the humiliation of our people, so that the perfect may be tested and the wicked man's sins may reach their full measure.
And furthermore, vengeance will be taken on the assembly of the Assyrians, who attributed their victory to the stars of the zodiac.
After these twelve weeks of days, deliverance will dawn for the church through those to whom it has been granted by the Lord.
For the wicked man's time has already run its course, his measure is full, and the measure of his sins has overflowed. These twelve weeks
the decree of the Most High has granted the rebel to live in this world. And after these weeks, with one [?] this fugitive,

who, in the hatred of his [?], intended to defile the holiness of our worship. With these two arrows that remain in my hands, I will take vengeance on two of the wicked man's officials, Bagris and Eugenius, who
were especially urging him to uproot the churches and also to persecute the Christians. Once these wicked men have perished, peace will reign in the church,
and no one will stir up trouble against it for a very long time. ... And you, Jovian, what you asked of the Lord in your petition concerning your departure from life
will be granted to you at its proper time, as the Lord wills. When your time is complete and the full measure of your days has been reached, your departure will take place on a bed of rest.
You will be gathered to your fathers in peace. As for Edessa, do not entertain any anxiety about it. For the faith of the city has come before God
and has gone forth victorious. For Truth rebuked the wicked man through his own people, so that he would not wage war against the city blessed by God.
For the entire company of the left, to whom the tyrant gave his allegiance—his magicians, diviners, and soothsayers—continually prophesied to him as though with one voice
that he should not attack the city to which victory had been granted from above, lest, they said, he suffer defeat there along with his soldiers.
Through the members of the very faction responsible for his error, Truth mocked him and turned his evil purpose away from the city. And so that you may believe the words spoken to you in the dream,
at daybreak you will receive the wicked man's letters rescinding the sentence against Edessa. Now that I have made these things known to you, remain in peace, my brother.
For I have also been sent to Julian the Elder, to bring him this good news as well.” When Jovian awoke from his sleep,
he was somewhat comforted in his mind by the dream he had seen. He rose from his bed and poured out his soul in prayer before God until the morning light.
When he rose from his prayer in the morning, at that very hour he received the wicked man's letters rescinding his earlier letters:
“Since it has been the will of the gods that we should not exact punishment from the offenders until Karsan has been taken in its entirety, we have taken care to write to Your Might about this,
so that no force should be moved from the frontier until Karsan has been secured and our armies have joined one another.” ... And when Jovian read
the wicked man's letters, he rejoiced greatly. He gave thanks and praise to God because what had been told to him in the dream had actually happened.
He sent word to Bishop Vologeses and those with him about the change in the tyrant’s plans [?], saying that this had come from the Lord and had been brought about by him.
When the illustrious priest and those with him learned of the wonders God had performed, they set aside a contribution and held a service.
They offered the oblation for the deliverance of the faithful city. Many things happened in our own days, in the days of Julian the pagan.
If only we were able to record them all in our history! But it was not possible to include them all in our history,
lest our account lose its way in the vastness of their number and scarcely be able to reach its conclusion.
These things that we have written, a few out of many, are enough for discerning lovers of learning to understand the many from the few:
what a fierce struggle befell the Church in the time of Julian the wicked ... Now this evil man, after he had behaved recklessly and gone mad in the worship of demons in the city of the fighters,
and had satisfied himself with the unclean sacrifices he offered there to the idols, summoned the priests of sin.
He entrusted to their hands all the treasures of the church of Harran and the vessels used in its holy service,
to be used in the service of its idols. He assigned the church’s endowments and income to meet the expenses of the temple of idols.
He burned its holy books in the fire. He turned the chaste ascetics of the church of Harran to his paganism.
As for the few among them who persevered, stood firm in their truth, and openly proclaimed their faith, after he had oppressed and tortured them and they had not been drawn into his paganism,
he cast them into a copper mine. This was among the many things provoking God that the madman did in this city of pagans.
Then he wished to leave it, after all his evil desires had been fulfilled.

The people of Harran were deeply distressed at his departure from them, for they had found in him an opportunity to display their paganism openly. They accompanied him as though accompanying a dead man, when he prepared
to leave their city. They cried out to him, saying, “Light and sun of our city, why are your hours hastening toward sunset? Remain shining upon us,
lest the shadows of Christianity fall upon us and the dark night of the Nazarenes settle over us as before.
Only with difficulty did the gods answer our prayers and arrange to bring you to our city.
Why are you hurrying to travel on like a passerby? Either stay with us and let us have our fill of you, or take me with you wherever you are going.
After fifty-four years our joy has come back to life through you. Yet before you have spent even a day or an hour in our city, look, our joy is already eager to depart with you.
Until when must we watch and wait for you, the pride and glory of our city? Even while you are still inside our city’s gate,
our eyes are looking for your coming. And now, since you are indeed leaving, may the gods of our city go with you.
