May Sin, the great god, accompany you in your battles and quickly bring you back to us victorious.” The madman turned toward them and heartened them, saying,
“Because I have seen how firmly you cling to your love for us, and how your wishes depend upon ours, we are confident that the gods will help us,
so that we may soon return to you victorious. What we owe your city today we will repay many times over with joy.”
For we owe your city, more than all the cities under our rule, repayment for its kindnesses. And he distributed gifts with a king's generosity.
He set out on his journey. As he went out through the city gate, he bowed his head on his horse to worship the image of Sin that was fixed above the gate of the citadel.
His crown fell from his head, and he became deeply distressed. He questioned the wise men with him and the adherents of his false religion,
asking, “What is this omen that has met us today at the beginning of our journey?” But they, in their cunning,
deflected the tyrant's inquiry from themselves and shifted it onto the priests, saying, “They are always engaged in the mysteries of divinity,
and they know the secrets of the gods and understand their hidden things. For [?]
they have been entrusted with revealing and interpreting the things about which Your Majesty has inquired through us.” And the wicked, defiled man sent
and summoned the priests and [?] of Harran. He questioned them, saying,
“What is this omen that has appeared to us today at the gates of your city? For this unusual sign is no ordinary thing.”
The priests told him, “Do not let your heart be shaken or your spirit distressed over this, my lord, my lord the king.
This happened to many kings before you, and they suffered no harm in their battles. So now, do not lose heart in your battles,
or let your hands grow weak in combat. For the gods have [?] victory for you. But, my lord the king, cleanse your army of Nazarenes.
There are many Galileans with you who openly wear the uniform of your service but worship the God of the Christians.
Drive these men away from you, lest they become a stumbling block to you in your battles and you suffer because of their sins.” And at that very moment,
a herald [?] in the tyrant's camp: “Anyone who is a Nazarene must withdraw from our battle, lest he bring the sword upon himself.”
About twenty-two thousand warriors, men experienced in battle, withdrew from the army that was with Julian.
Their company headed for Edessa, and they were welcomed there joyfully. When Julian learned that they had headed for the city he hated,
he was greatly displeased and regretted that he had not put them to the sword. In anger he mounted his horse to depart, but his horse stood still and would not move.
He urged it strongly to go, but it did not move from its place at all. Julian became angry and pulled on his horse's [?]
to force it to move from its place. His horse put its mouth to the cloth of his purple robes
and tore it from end to end. It trembled beneath him, fell, and died. Fear and trembling seized all his troops,
and their spirits were distressed about their coming battle. The accursed man blasphemed and said, “Leave me alone, Nazarene! Leave me alone!
For our battle today is not being fought against you. Wait for me until I have finished my battle, and fight with me as much as you can.” But the defiled man was inwardly broken,
and madness gripped him. He did not know what to do. He decided to kill all the wise men, sorcerers, and diviners with him,
because they had been unable through their craft to explain to him the extraordinary sign that had appeared to him. He also planned to destroy the priests of the false religion with the sword.
Because they had lied to him and spoken insolently before him. And when the order was already about to be issued, Aplatus the wise man
dared to enter the tyrant’s presence, for he enjoyed great freedom to speak before him. He threw himself facedown at his feet
and pleaded with him, saying, “I appeal to the awesome authority of your divinity: do not let your anger flare up against your servant.
I lay my petition before you. If even you, my lord the king, who possess the books containing the wisdom of creation
and have been made chief priest of all the gods of the world, and have been entrusted with the key to the treasury of divine revelations,
have not been shown the explanation of the things revealed to you, then we, who are insignificant and unlearned, who possess only bits and pieces from the books of wisdom,
a little out of much—should we be put to death over this affair? Far be it from your mercy to do this!
Instead, let your Majesty give orders for the sentence against us to be revoked. Now, we have learned that in the temple of the goddess Athena there is a young virgin who has a spirit of prophecy.
Let us send for her, for perhaps the explanation of what has happened has been revealed to her.” The accursed man acted on Aplatus’s advice
and sent for Dionysia and brought her from the temple of idols. The young woman was beautiful to look at and lovely in appearance.
When Julian saw her, he was astonished at her beauty and marveled at her appearance. He entertained a thought about her. But she sensed it within herself, and [?] in her eyes.
Through Aplatus he asked her, “What does this omen that has appeared to us in your country mean for us?” But she scorned him and gave him no answer.
Instead, she stood calmly and silently before him. Julian said to her through Aplatus,
“Do not suppose, young woman, that you were summoned before me because of your beauty. Rather, because I learned that a spirit of prophecy
is in you, we wished to learn from you what the outcome of our campaign will be.” Dionysia said to him,
“Keep your eyes on your battle, like a disciplined king whose thoughts are on his campaign. For a king is contemptible
when he lets his gaze wander: the nakedness of shame is depicted in him during his campaign, especially if it happens that people do not obey him. But, king,
why do you inquire about omens? If you concern yourself with omens, you will establish no frontier in the east and fight no battle.
For mighty kings who have set their faces toward battle do not concern themselves with omens. If they do concern themselves with them, they are unfit for battle.
But battle is fitting, and campaigning is becoming, for warlike kings clothed in strength, whose faces are always set toward death,
so that they may win victory over their enemies and extend the borders of their dominion. A peaceful life and a quiet residence, however, are much more helpful
to fainthearted kings who watch for omens and shrink from campaigning. Look, I have set both alternatives clearly before your eyes.” Julian said to her,

“I did not ask you about these things, young woman. There was only one thing I wished to learn from you, if possible: what will be the outcome of our campaign and the conclusion of our battle?” Dionysia said to him, “This is the outcome of your campaign:
peace along the borders, reconciliation between the kingdoms. For through you the hostility and hatred between the kingdoms will be removed.
The east and the west will rejoice and delight in you because they have been brought to peace through you, even though today they are gloomy and distressed at your coming.
But at your departure the West and her sister the East rejoice, celebrate, and clap their hands together. This is the end of your [?],
and the outcome of your battle.” While Julian was waiting to learn the force of her statement and the explanation of her riddles, she fell silent after these words.
She gave him no further answer, but returned to the temple of the idols. He went on his way, distressed and weighed down in his soul
by thoughts of what Dionysa had said to him. When he had traveled a day’s journey from Harran, some Jewish men came from among the inhabitants of Nisibis.
They accused Bishop Vologeses and those with him, and also Jovian, his army commander, saying,
“The Christians have great freedom in our city. They hold their assembly quite openly, three miles outside the city.
They gather their fellow believers around them and celebrate the mysteries. Several times we have brought complaints against them to the victorious and glorious Jovian, your army commander,
but our complaint against them was not accepted.” They made many accusations against them. But the tyrant did not accept their accusations against Jovian.
Instead, he became angry with them and drove them from his presence. Inwardly, however, he wondered whether what he had been told about Jovian might already be true.
He was waiting for an opportunity to discover the truth of these reports. Jovian, meanwhile, was unaware of the accusations made against him.
But when he learned that Julian had left Harran, he secretly sent for Bishop Vologeses and said to him, “You know, my father, that the tyrant threatens our faith,
and there are many accusers. If it seems good to you, [?] your message to your flock and instruct them that, from now on,
they should hold no assembly until the tyrant leaves the city, lest some harm come to your flock on account of the assembly.”
Bishop Vologeses said to him, “[?] Does Your Excellency suppose that we are not distressed and deeply concerned for you,

lest you receive some reprimand from the tyrant on account of [?]? Every hour we shed sorrowful tears before God for Your Excellency, that you may not be diminished, and for your authority, that it may not be brought to an end.
For like a pillar you bear the weight of our persecution, and like a protective barrier you stand before Christ’s church everywhere.”
Jovian said to him, “Do not be concerned about me in this matter, for the tyrant cannot harm me.
Even if he does mistreat me, I am not troubled, for this is my whole desire. But you must take care of yourselves,
lest you perish miserably. In this I have made my own position clear: it is for you that I am troubled. This concern of mine was not for myself.”
Bishop Vologeses said to him, “May God establish you at the head of his churches. As for us, we will not give way. Even if we are afflicted,
or even if we die, we would not consider it a great thing. For how can we repay Christ, who died for us?
Even if it were possible for us to die ten thousand times for him, we would not be able to repay Christ, who died for us.
Yet we are all ready, according to our strength, to share a little in the suffering of his crucifixion by confessing our faith. Our regular daily assembly is for this purpose:
that our public gathering may give us a good opportunity to confess our faith. We do not lose heart in our afflictions.
Our entire flock shares this united resolve. Examine the whole flock that Christ has entrusted to my hands, and you will not find in it a single scabby or sick sheep.”
Nor is anyone lacking in faith. For all of us together, with one soul and one mind and one faith, to taste the suffering of his crucifixion—
the Son of God's—we are resolved in our confession, and we desire and long for it. Therefore, do not take this sorrow upon yourself,
lest it prove harmful to us. Instead, accept the plea of our petition and allow us to gather as usual, without being hindered from the service of God.
And whatever accords with the Lord's will and is pleasing in his eyes for us to do, we will do.” When Jovinian saw the faith of Vologases and those with him,
he was astonished and greatly amazed at their firmness of mind. His compassion welled up, and his tears flowed.

He comforted them and said to them, “My children, may Christ, for whose name you have set your faces toward death, stand before you and spread the wing of his mercy over your souls.” He permitted them to gather as usual, while he prepared to go out to meet the tyrant
with his many troops. He sent his heralds throughout all the Roman territories
and summoned to himself all the forces that had come down to the frontier. He went out to meet the madman with a great procession. He saw that the tyrant's expression toward him was not
as it had been yesterday and the day before, for anger covered his face. Jovinian knew that accusations had been made against him.

Nevertheless, the faithful man did not neglect this either: he sent secretly to inform Bishop Vologases and those with him that they should save themselves wherever they could, before the ordeal overtook them.
But when those faithful and steadfast men learned these things from Chrysorus, Jovinian's servant, they were neither frightened nor disturbed, nor did they move elsewhere.
Instead, they remained calm, and so they continued together in harmony, with one soul and one mind,
bearing the burden of the service themselves and serving God with all their strength in psalms and songs of praise.
Contrary to their custom, the sound of their worship could be heard openly, so that the very sound of their worship would become the occasion for their confession of faith.
But the enemies of the truth, the pagans and the Jews, when the tyrant entered their city, fiercely accused Vologases and those with him.
They clamored and said, “Let our words be believed by you at least now, my lord the king! For look, above the great [?]
the sound of their worship can be heard, with the freedom granted them by your commander. See how far their insolence has gone!

Face to face, openly, they have defied the authority of your kingdom. Contrary to their custom, they have raised the sound of their worship to show by this that they are not placed under the yoke of your authority.” ... But Julian paid no attention to these things,
because Jovinian, the commander, had about a hundred men belonging to a great clan,
and these men had a force of their own numbering about seventy thousand. For they were well-known and renowned men,
and they were not subject to the tyrant. For this reason the tyrant restrained himself and did not wish to harm Jovinian,
lest the war on the frontier turn against him. When the clamor of the pagans and Jews against him grew stronger, saying, “Either wipe this religion out of our city,
or allow us all to become Christians,” the tyrant, to quiet the violence
of their shouting, gave his ring to Pamphilus, his trusted servant, and said to him, “Go quickly to where these misguided people are gathered,
and if you find matters as they have been reported concerning them, imprison them in those caves in which they have been gathering.”
And block the entrances of the caves with large stones, and affix seals to them with the seals of my [?].
The man did as the king had commanded him. ... But Jovian was overcome with sorrow and mourned deeply.
He wept bitterly, saying, “Woe to me! I have become guilty of shedding the innocent blood of God's servants. I have brought this upon them,
because I allowed them to hold an assembly.” He was deeply distressed. ... But after the accursed tyrant went to his quarters and was alone,
he reflected that it was no help to distress the soldiers who were with him, bearing the burden of his campaign, and to follow the wishes of troublesome, disruptive men.
He was especially concerned about Jovian, his army commander, lest he lose heart in his campaign. He decided to use a cunning pretext to dismiss the affair.
He sent for Jovian and said to him, “Tell me, son of Aronianus, what are these reports about you that I have heard in the streets of Nisibis?
What is this insolence that has seized you, so that you have assumed the command of my kingdom and allowed the Nazarenes to hold an assembly, when I gave no such order?
What astonishes me still more is this: by what power or authority did you do this, without trembling in fear before the authority of my kingship?
Perhaps, because your relatives are here with us, a surge of arrogance seized you, and you did this without our permission. From this moment I will humble your pride
and bring down your mighty arrogance. You will recognize that you are a weak man who was appointed to office and entrusted with authority through the favor of our mercy.
From this moment I will take back what is mine and leave you with what is yours. For the sake of your relatives, we grant you your life.” ... But Jovian said,
“My lord the king, I have never boasted of the authority entrusted to me by Your Majesty, nor has my heart become proud because of the command
that you placed in my hands. Never in my life have I presented myself as a great man. Your troops are my witnesses
that I conducted myself among them as one of them. If I did not exalt myself or act proudly toward my fellow servants who rank below me, should I have exalted myself above you, my lord the king?
Why, then, should Your Majesty accept lies about me? I have not broken your commands, and deceit has never been found in me throughout my life.
Nor have I done anything hateful. But if the Jews are stirring you up against me, there is one thing I owe you, and it is you who are holding it back.” Julian said,
“Let us know what it is that you owe us.” Jovian said, “You have long been thirsting for my lifeblood. Pour it out, my lord the king, and satisfy yourself.”
Julian became angry and said, “You deserve death, you who have denied the favor of our kingship! I brought you from insignificance to greatness,

and made you second only to me, a ruler with authority over all my troops—and I thirst for your blood, you wretch?” The tyrant gave an order, and they stripped him of the insignia of his military office.
He clothed him in ordinary clothes and removed him from his command. Jovian left his presence with no thought or concern about anything in his heart,
except for Vologases and those with him. He stayed awake all night, praying for their deliverance.
But God, who always accompanies those who worship him and never neglects to help them, soon sent consolation to this discerning man.
Following his trial, he added to his triumph. For a short time after Jovian had been dismissed from military service, letters came into the tyrant's hands,
sent by Arimhar, Shapur's chief magus, to Jovian, commander of the Roman army, concerning the victory of the Roman Empire.
For they had love and affection for one another ever since he went up to visit him in the border region ... For a wondrous vision appeared to Arimhar
in Jovian’s tent, while they were [?] together. For he saw a right hand holding a crown above Jovian’s head.
He knew that the kingdom and the rule of the Romans would be his. He did not, however, reveal the vision to him, but asked him under oath, “Which God
do you worship?” When he learned that he was a Christian, the veil of error was rolled away from Arimhar’s heart.
True repentance began to dawn within him. When he returned to his own country, he was fully instructed in the way of the Lord
by Jacob, a priest and abbot who lived in the city of Beth Lapat. He secretly received from him the seal of baptism,
and he admitted him to communion in Christ’s divine mysteries ... When Jovian learned of the conversion and repentance of this magus,
he did not hesitate to write him a letter of encouragement, urging him on in his resolve and strengthening his faith. Along with this letter,
he also sent him a letter urging him to work for the Romans’ victory. In it he set out this argument for him:
“My brother, the coming of the Son of God, in whom you have recently believed, took place in the Roman Empire.
From it he took bodily existence for his hidden being, from our visible existence. He was entered in the census of this empire, and he was also recorded in the genealogy of his family.
He paid the poll tax so that it would be clear to discerning people like you that the human birth of the Son of God belonged to this empire.
Therefore, as this empire is pleasing to the God in whom you have believed, help it as much as you can, my brother, and strive for its victory.
Pray for the peace of our empire more than for the empire in which you live. For, like one who cherishes children, it asks you to become a son and heir within it.
When God grants it victory through your hands, you will be proclaimed a son of our empire, and you will be great within it all your days.” ... After writing many things to him,
he wrote at the end of his letter: “If you have truly put on Christ, my brother, and have believed in him with all your soul,
give proof of your faith by bringing about the downfall of Shapur, the enemy of our faith, and desire the death of that wicked butcher,
whose sword has been drawn against us for thirty years and has still not had its fill of our blood.

Yes, my brother, take up zeal for Christ, in whom you have believed, and set a deadly trap for this man who has mocked our religious garb, dishonored our order, defiled our holy things, abolished our worship, burned our churches, and profaned
the glorious name by which we are called. My brother, put a noose around the head of this wolf who has torn apart and scattered Christ’s holy flock.
It is known, my brother, that your wisdom can accomplish this, and it is easy for your understanding to see that, by slaughtering this unclean man, you will establish peace and reconciliation
between our two mighty empires. Nor is this a small sacrifice that you will offer to God when you do this.

The grateful memory of this kindness will not fade from our minds ... My brother, be sound in spirit and steadfast in your faith, and bring the comfort of peace to the churches in your days.” ... When Arimhar read Jovian’s letter,
he composed a reply and sent it to him. But the bearer of the letters was arrested at a Roman guard post, and they summoned him before Julian as a spy.
When he was examined with questions and pressed to reveal the truth, he admitted without hesitation that he had been sent to Jovian with letters from his master.
which helped secure the Romans’ victory. When the truth of these things had silenced the tongues [?], he received Aspabar, Arimhar’s envoy,
with the honor due to him. He gave orders for him to be kept under honorable guard until he had made peace with Jovian and restored him to his position
and returned his authority to him. He attended to the letters that had reached him. The copy of the letter sent by Arimhar was as follows:
“I have received your letter, my brother. My spirit was uplifted by it, and my mind rejoiced. I valued the greeting in your letter like a precious gift.
For when I examined the contents of your letter, I was greatly astonished and marveled at you, at the fidelity you show toward your king.
I counted the Roman Empire fortunate to have you as its commander, and I marveled greatly within myself
at the zeal you have for the Romans’ victory. For from the indications in your letter I learned what you desire.
I have taken care, my brother, to write to you, who truly love and cherish us: do not burden yourself with anxiety over the matters about which you wrote to me in your letter.
Do not let concern about them trouble your thoughts at all. For our word to you is true: before Persia’s army is prepared, your empire will gain renown and victory
in your war—not through your strength or the force of your fearsome power, but through our humble efforts and the opportunity afforded by our stratagems. For I will bring reversals
upon Shapur, the enemy of your empire, and he will be delivered into your hands without war or battle, without shouting or horns that stir up combat,
without fully drawn bows discharging arrows, and without sharpened swords flashing between the ranks,
and without massed legions destroying and being destroyed. The fighting between the empires will come to an end, and the hostility along the borders will be removed.
The kingdoms will dwell in peace. But you, my brother, as far as you can, urge Caesar to muster an army while, for a time, there remains quiet and inactivity
in Assyria’s great army. For the force subject to us has not yet assembled here to wage war against you. But be assured
that before long you will not be able to face the ranks of our army, for our empire’s military power is stronger than yours. Rather, do what you can while our warfare is quiet:
win victory and gain renown and triumph. Be well in spirit, my brother, and always keep a kindly remembrance of us in your mind.” ... When Julian read Arimhar’s letters
and learned from them of Jovian’s faithfulness in the authority entrusted to him, and of his zeal and concern for the tyrant’s victory,
he regretted his threat and became angry with the Jews who had slandered them. He sent and seized ten of their leaders, the very men who had slandered Jovian,
and crucified them on wooden crosses opposite his camp quarters.
He wrote notices and placed them above their crosses: “Anyone who dares to slander before me any one of the religions within the dominion of our empire shall die as these men have died.”
He drove the Jewish community living in Nisibis out of their city and gave their possessions over to plunder.
He demolished their synagogue and burned their Sabbath house [?]. That same day he granted an amnesty to all the religions. He released Bishop Vologases
and those with him from imprisonment in the caves. He threatened them, warning them not to hold such a gathering again.
They covered over the caves in which they had gathered and sealed them up, as they remain to this day. ... But Jovian, because he knew that the tyrant was investigating him,
He kept himself hidden where he had been received [?], with no one aware of him except Sargdanius, the head of his clan.
When Julian looked for him and did not find him, and the camp of his forces was searched and he was not there, he placed responsibility for finding him upon the members of his clan.
They were to go out in search of him and bring him from wherever he was. But they put him off, saying, “We do not know,” and bring him [?].
But they put him off, saying, “We do not know where he is.” [?] Julian said to them, “If you were honest and upright,
and loyal to us, it would have been your responsibility to call him to account for his transgression and, as members of his clan, to present an appeal to me on his behalf.
For it was not my responsibility to demand him through you. Since you did not do this, even now, when I have demanded him through you,
take responsibility for him and bring him, so that I may entrust him with his authority.” Sargdanius said to him,
“What hateful or evil thing has Jovian done during your reign, that you have dismissed him from his service and removed him from his position of authority?
Or how were we supposed to call him to account—a man against whom no transgression was found throughout his administration?
Or how can a man whom you have belittled before your forces and humiliated before the officers of your kingdom serve as your commander?
Know, then, my lord the king, that Your Majesty has distressed us as well by this.” [?] Julian said to him, “Do I not have authority as king to exalt and to humble?
Or is it perhaps beyond my power to give him greater rank than his former rank and to strengthen his authority beyond his former authority,
and to make the forces with me fear and tremble before him? And now, let all the members of his clan know:
unless he comes today and appears before me, I can no longer believe that you are loyal to me.” Sargdanius promised to bring him so that he would appear before him,
as he had commanded. Julian rejoiced greatly and promised gifts to all the members of his clan.
He urgently commanded Sargdanius to bring Jovian quickly, so that he might appear before him.
Sargdanius did as he had been commanded. He brought Jovian, who appeared before the king. The king received him affectionately and spoke kindly with him.
He reassured and comforted him, saying, “Look, your wish has been fulfilled: your enemies have been removed, and their accusers and slanderers, the Jews, have been crucified.
I have also released those defiled Nazarenes from their prison, and on their account I have granted freedom to all religions.”
Jovian said to him, “Everything Your Clemency has commanded, you have commanded well. But, my lord the king, why was Your Majesty angry with me

because I neglected to investigate the gathering of the Nazarenes? Let Your Glory learn from Fabrinus, a servant of your kingdom, with what intention I refrained from prosecuting these wretched people.

For I sent him to them to establish for us the truth of the Jews’ accusation against them. He found that what I had been told about them was indeed true, and he found them assembled. But I also learned this:

with great earnestness, tears, and prayer, they were pleading with their God for the victory and return of Your Majesty. And I thought to myself [?] that this very thing Your Majesty has also commanded is helpful: that we should allow the religions to plead with their gods
for the peace and stability of our kingdom, rather than oppress them, so that they complain against us to their gods and become a cause of stumbling for us in battle against our enemies.
For Your Divinity knows, my lord the king, that we are about to enter a land that is not ours, where we may be confined as though in a prison.”
Therefore, release the prisoners, so that the land of Nimrod does not rise against us. For mercy is acceptable to the gods.
And now, my lord the king, if it pleases your merciful majesty, let an order be sent to our territories that the captives and prisoners of every religion be released.
Let no one oppress them or harm them until your majesty returns to your realm in victory and peace. For this has not escaped the divine wisdom within you:
In all our territories there are troublemakers and agitators, unruly men who devise pretexts to plunder and seize
their neighbors’ possessions, especially now, when your majesty is not in the country.” Julian said to him:
“Since your loyalty to us has been revealed, and your zeal for our victory has become evident through the writings of Armahar the mobed, from now on I have no reason to reject your word
or to turn down your request without granting it.” And the tyrant ordered that all the captives and prisoners of every religion be released.
He imposed the death penalty on anyone who oppressed or harmed them in any way until he returned from his campaigns.
His order was sent in writing to all the territories of his dominion. Through the efforts of this discerning man, the Christian people had a little respite.
Jovian gained favor and affection in the tyrant’s eyes, and he loved him as himself. He honored and exalted him in the eyes of his nobles
and in the eyes of the entire Roman army. He made him lord and ruler, second only to himself, over all the affairs of his kingdom.
He also appointed him commander-in-chief and leader of all his armies. Jovian grew great and powerful in the tyrant’s kingdom.
His reputation continued to grow, and without him no one dared to ask the king for a gift or present a petition to him.
When Julian set his face toward crossing into the land of the Chaldeans, he summoned Jovian and said to him, “Do not bring to mind again
that occasion the other day when I caused you distress, for I intend to repay you with many good things in return for it. You yourself and the gods know
how you intend to conduct yourself toward our majesty in a land that is not ours. May the gods themselves be with me, just as I intend to act toward you for your good.”
The two of them made a covenant with one another under oath at the frontier. Jovian was trusted by the king, and he entrusted the war to his hands.
They set a day for crossing into the land of the Persians. He wrote a letter to Shapur and sent him this message: “Hurry! Look to yourself,
attend to your duty, and be prepared for our attack, lest our army fall upon you suddenly and you blame us and say, ‘I was utterly
taken by surprise.’ Look, I have warned you beforehand: defend your land as well as you can, and prepare for your battle. For I am already determined to take vengeance on your country
and exact repayment from your land for the damage you have inflicted on ours.” He mocked his armies, saying, “The Romans are straw, and their words are leaves.
When they rattle, they make a noise; they turn their backs on battle. The Sun, the god of the East [?]
who are splendid on the march but weak in battle [?]” He composed a reply to Julian’s letters and sent him this message: “You, feeble Roman, are no man for these things,
and you are weak in battle. If arrogance has driven you to challenge a kingdom of mighty warriors, know for certain that your doom is making a mockery of you:
Your end will come in a land that is not yours. For you do not know your own weakness, and that is why you are puffed up. If the humiliation of your expedition were revealed to you,
Your mouth was filled with lamentation in your anger. But because these things are hidden from you, you have not recognized your obligations at all. Now I bear witness to you in my writings:
If you are determined to stir up war between kingdoms, then, according to the laws and regulations established for kings long ago, observe the proper rules of battle.
Set a day for him on which to fight. When side stands against side, and battle line against battle line, and battle breaks out between the lines,
the victorious side gains the upper hand over the other and rightfully extends its territory. Whichever king wins, let his mercy be praised.
When he has triumphed and prevailed, he graciously grants pardon. This is the proper order and manner of warfare between kings.
But if, in your tyranny, you are carried away by the fury of arrogance and rush like a raiding band to plunder our land,
know, tyrant, that you will have to give an account for plundering it. For I have confidence in the sun, my mighty god, that if you cross the borders toward the east,
you will never see the face of the west again. See, I have warned you beforehand. ... When Julian received Shapur’s letters and read them,
he scorned them and mocked their sender. He summoned Jovian, the commander of his army, and instructed him to cross into the land of the Persians.
He pressed upon him the command to hurry his troops along. The tyrant wanted to know how many troops he had with him.
Jovian counted the entire Roman army at the River Tigris, which separates the territories.
The number of the army appointed to cross with Caesar into the land of the Persians was three hundred and ninety-five thousand fighting men, skilled hunters,
men of war: one hundred and forty thousand horsemen armed with lances and bows, and one hundred and fifty thousand infantrymen,
bearing shields and checking the onslaught of battle; and twenty thousand craftsmen of every kind, skilled men thoroughly versed in everything needed for war;
and eighty-five thousand who loved battle and were eager for slaughter, who rode whirlwinds and raced with the winds, who fought with death and did not turn back from battle.
This was the number and total of the army appointed to go down with Julian into the land of the Persians, apart from the mixed crowd who joined them as they went down:
villagers skilled with slings, who lived along the banks of the Tigris and were neither included in the count nor entered in the reckoning.
Of their own free will they committed themselves to go down with them for the sake of plundering the land. Jovian assembled the entire Roman army
at the River Tigris, which separates the territories, in the month of Iyar, in the year six hundred and seventy-four according to the reckoning of the Greeks. On the first day of that month,
the entire Roman army crossed the River Tigris eastward and entered the land of the Persians. They found the land prosperous and dwelling in peace.
For the inhabitants had not been given time to flee before them: a raiding force of Arabs from Roman territory had swept through the country and seized it,
until the Romans entered and took control of the land as they pleased. They laid waste, plundered, and took captives as they wished, and conquered defiant fortresses,
high and strong towers, and fortified villages
on the plains, and cities with their fortifications. They conquered high mountains and concealed places among the cliffs.
They uncovered the caves of the land and the hiding places in the strongholds, and brought out the Persians’ hidden treasures.
They carried away all their valuables and possessions, and the Romans gained great wealth from the land of Nimrod.
None of them could handle all their plunder, for it had become far too much for them. For they were taking all their plunder for themselves,
except for the gold and silver, which went into the king’s treasury as the share assigned to the king by earlier kings.
The gold and silver brought to the king from the plunder of the land became so abundant that he could not weigh it or finish counting it.
For no fortress, city, village, or small rural estate remained that had not been delivered into the hands of the Romans, from the River Tigris on the borders
as far as the borders of Aramean territory. The terrible suffering that the wicked king had inflicted on the sons of the righteous king was repaid through the hands of the unjust king.
As Holy Scripture says, “The wicked will be punished by the wicked, and the Lord will punish them both.” When the Romans’ eyes had had their fill of the country’s plunder,
they again set their hands to taking women and children captive and putting men to the sword. This conduct displeased Jovian.
He brought the petition of the country’s inhabitants before the king and pleaded on their behalf, saying:
“I beg your victorious majesty, my lord the king: let your gracious compassion be stirred by the humiliation and plundering of the country.
Let the slaughter and captivity of the country’s inhabitants be stopped. For what will we gain by drawing our sword against new subjects
who have today been brought under the yoke of service to our kingdom? Nor is it an act of bravery to lay waste the territories added to our dominion.
For the land we have conquered is ours, according to the customs, regulations, and laws established for earlier kings.
It is no advantage to turn our sword against the land we have acquired with our own blood. For the troops with us will have no need
of the land once the war is over and each of them has gone home. But when our Caesar [?] departs, we will have greater need than we do today
of the land and its produce.” The proposal pleased the tyrant, and he ordered that the slaughter and captivity of the country’s inhabitants be stopped.
The Romans were to carry away only plunder and then withdraw. The king’s command prevailed over the army commanders, the commanders of thousands, and the commanders of hundreds.
Everyone released the people they had taken captive. The slaughter of that land’s inhabitants ceased, and its inhabitants were left there,
stripped of their property, their possessions, and their supplies for the year. When Julian saw that the land had been deprived of its produce
and the country emptied of its possessions—and there was no compassion in him—he decided to resettle the land. For Jovian’s advice pleased him.
He traveled through the land and resettled it. He distributed some of the land’s plunder among the villages, cities, and rural estates to provide a livelihood for the country’s inhabitants.
He also left some of the oxen and other livestock in the country for cultivating the land.
He made a covenant with them, confirmed by oaths, that he would no longer harm them, promising their land an exemption for four years,
so that they could cultivate the land and support themselves from its produce. The inhabitants of the land agreed to settle in it.

Through their wisdom, the king and his army commander succeeded in resettling the land of the Chaldeans after they had laid it waste. ... When Shapur learned that the Romans had brought these calamities upon his land,
He was troubled in his heart, and sorrow seized him, and he seemed like a madman. Yet even this was not hidden from him:
that through Jovian’s intervention, the sword and captivity had been kept from his country, and through the care of his compassion, mercy had been shown to its inhabitants.
He acknowledged Jovian’s kindness before his nobles and his leading officials.
And he gained favor and compassion in their eyes. [?] The king, his nobles, and his leading officials wrote [?] that they should devise a plan concerning the land of Beth Aramaye.
For the Romans had not yet gained control of it. They took counsel with one another. They all devised a plan and agreed
to it: [?] with the forces of infantry and armored soldiers stationed near the approaches and royal residences of Persia, always available to the kings, receiving pay and bound to its service,
Shapur should advance and appear in the land of Beth Aramaye, to serve as a defense for his royal residence and seize the entrances to the country,
until the force being assembled at his royal residence grew strong, lest the Romans gain strength, come down, and seize the cities of his kingdom.
Shapur’s leading officials encouraged him, saying, “The king of kings must not lose heart over what has happened.
Such things happen many times in war. This will prove to be the Romans’ undoing.

For they have been caught as in a net in the land of Nimrod, and they have entered and been confined as in a prison in a territory not their own, so that not a single survivor will escape from among them.”
Shapur said to them, “I have never been abased in my battles. You, my nobles and leading officials, are my witnesses.
For you have not forgotten the massacres I carried out in the Romans’ land in the days of Constantine’s sons.
Although they were warlike and powerful kings, three times I prevailed over them in their own territory and laid waste their borderlands. They could not rescue their land from my hands by force.
And if kings, sons of kings, could not withstand my strength and stand before the uplifted arm of my might, would this lowest of men,
this [?] dog barking at his masters, have dared to set foot within our borders if he had not stolen a march on me?
Yet I am fully confident in the sun and fire, the gods of the East, that he will not defeat me and escape from my hands. Having trampled the borders of the East,
he will not live to see the West that made him king. But you, my nobles and leading officials, have thought me like that lowly, feeble man
by offering me consolation over what the Romans have plundered and carried off from our land. I will have occasion to remind you of this.”
His leading officials trembled and were alarmed, and they were very afraid. Shapur summoned his army of soldiers and appeared in the land of Beth Aramaye
with seventy thousand infantry and fifty[?] thousand armored soldiers. He seized the entrances to the country.
He built up and fortified the cities of his kingdom. [?] Julian was told that Shapur had appeared with his armies in the land of Beth Aramaye.
He too assembled his forces to go down against him into Beth Aramaye, so that in the land in which Shapur placed his confidence and in the cities of his kingdom
he might fight him, ridicule him, and make a mockery of him. When the plan Julian had devised became known to Shapur,
he sent spies to the Roman camp disguised as merchants, to spy out and investigate how many tens of thousands of troops Caesar had with him.
Shapur’s envoys returned and brought him news that dashed his hopes: “Hurry! Save yourself, and withdraw your army before the sword of the Romans,
before battle is forced upon us and the army surrounds us on every side, and we try to save ourselves but cannot.
For Caesar has vast numbers of troops with him, fierce men experienced in warfare. It is not only Caesar’s own soldiers who are with him,
but men from every nation are mingled and massed together in his camp—tyrannical and savage men, clothed in fury and wrapped in anger.
They do not know what peace is. However many troops we gather [?], we cannot withstand their assault, for Caesar has more than five hundred thousand men with him,
besides the slingers who have joined them from place after place.” When Shapur heard these things from his envoys, astonishment fell upon him, and he was bewildered and groaned.
He did not know what to do. He was afraid to remain in that country, because he did not have enough troops with him to withstand an assault.
He left a small part of his army in Seleucia and Ctesiphon, the cities of his royal residence, and moved his army’s camp, and from Beth Aramaye
they traveled about five days’ journey [?]. When Julian learned that Shapur had become afraid of him and had withdrawn, he urgently issued orders to the Roman army
and urged them to pursue him. But Jovian restrained him and would not let him go. For he said, “It is not advantageous for us to abandon this land before us, which is delightful in every
way, planted with crops and full of fortified royal cities, filled with every good thing, in which the treasures of kings are stored,
and pursue a man who has grown old and experienced in battles and assaults and knows the hidden places of his country.
For [?] he is already lying in ambush for us in his country and attacking us from behind. Moreover, we do not even know the way into his country. But if it pleases you, my lord the king,
let us first cross into the territory of Beth Aramaye, carry off the country’s plunder, mark it off, and bring it within the borders of the kingdom.” Julian said to him,
“We have done well to extend the borders of our kingdom this far.” They built a monument there and marked out the boundaries. Then the unclean man began to say to the commander of his army,
“From now on, I want to devastate every land we enter, strip it of its inhabitants, and tear down the walls of its cities.
I will leave it a wasteland for the Persians, and I will take rightful revenge on them for the terrible destruction they have inflicted on our country.”
But Jovian, because he wanted to save lives, said to the tyrant, “Everything that Your Majesty has planned,
you have planned well. But [?], if it seems good to you, my lord the king, let us not bring the sword upon the inhabitants of the land we enter.
Instead, let us deport them from their country and settle them in Arzanene, in the territories that our sword has taken from the control of our enemies,
which are strong and spacious but sparsely inhabited. For it is fitting and glorious for our kingdom that its borderlands should resound with inhabitants and abound in people.
Let [?] the borderlands of Persia lie in ruins and its villages be emptied of their inhabitants, just as he devastated the borderlands of our kingdom.” This proposal pleased the tyrant,
and he acted according to Jovian’s advice. Julian went down into the land of Beth Aramaye with his vast army and the might of his kingdom,
as they charged forward on their horses and drove along with whirlwinds. From the sand stirred up by the horsemen’s steeds, a cloud of darkness gathered over the country.
It was as though ashes were being sifted over the inhabitants of the country, for the sunlight had grown dim. And the gates of the fortress and of the cities
The rest of the inhabitants of the country, those who lived on the plains, were seized. Fear and trembling gripped them.
They abandoned all their valuables and possessions and resolved to leave their country themselves. A force of Arabs was stationed behind the departing exiles.
They turned back and stationed it on the northern side of Ctesiphon, in the open area where Caesar’s camp had been established.
The Romans exercised control over the country as they pleased, and the land of Beth Aramaye was given over to plunder. The Romans could not cope with the plunder of the country,
because it was too abundant for them. For all their valuables and possessions, when they had resolved to leave their country—
For many days the Romans were occupied with the plunder of the country and the taking of its inhabitants captive. When the taking of captives had ended and the plundering was finished,
only the two great cities of Shapur’s royal domain remained, over which the Romans had not gained control,
until the plundering of the country and the taking of its inhabitants captive had ended. When there was quiet and the army had assembled,
Julian gave orders, and the army was deployed against the whole of Ctesiphon. They began to wage war against it, and its inhabitants were in great distress.
For the armored soldiers of the fortified city were not sufficient to defend the wall. Many of the city’s inhabitants, who were standing on the wall and helping the armored soldiers,
were struck by arrows and died. Fear gripped the inhabitants of the fortified city, and they no longer appeared on the wall,
because they were afraid they might be [?] by arrows. As the battle against them grew fiercer and their distress and hardships increased,
the Romans began to capture part of the wall. The inhabitants of Ctesiphon went up and saw
that, despite their resistance, their city’s wall was being overcome by the devices and machines of the skilled craftsmen who were with Caesar. The city’s leaders concluded
that it would be better to submit voluntarily to Roman rule and save their lives than to remain defiant and let their defiance cause their destruction. The leaders took counsel with the inhabitants
of the fortified city. They went out at night to Caesar’s camp and threw themselves face down at Julian’s feet, pleading with him to spare their lives
and those of all the inhabitants of the fortified city. He received them, reassured them, and comforted them, saying, “Take courage and do not be afraid.
For you have saved yourselves and secured your lives. From now on, not a single hair from the heads of the inhabitants of the fortified city will fall to the ground.
But keep away from the king’s soldiers stationed in your city, lest you perish because of them.” The inhabitants of Ctesiphon did as Caesar commanded.
They handed the fortified city over to the Romans during the night. The Romans entered quietly and slaughtered all Shapur’s soldiers,
whom he had left to guard the fortified city. In the morning, at sunrise, Julian entered Shapur’s royal city,
in a great procession, with people proclaiming his praises ahead of him, carried away by arrogance and clothed in pride.
When the inhabitants of Seleucia learned that the inhabitants of Ctesiphon had surrendered, they too wanted to surrender.
But Shapur’s soldiers, who had been stationed there to guard the city, would not let them.
For they said, “You must not destroy our lives through your negligence. Instead, be patient, so that we may all reach the same decision and be of one soul and one mind.”
Whether for death or for life. And if what happened to our brothers in Ctesiphon should happen, perhaps their deaths will be investigated and their blood avenged, for Caesar has not yet met his end.
As long as Shapur is alive and standing, there is no victory for the Romans, and their rejoicing will not reach its fulfillment. Rather, like good servants who remain faithful to their master,
let us be patient for a full seven days. Let us expose ourselves to the risk of surrender. And if deliverance dawns for us from [?]—
otherwise, we will surrender the fortress as you say.” The inhabitants of Seleucia argued fiercely with them, quarreling and saying,
“Go away, you counselors of evil, who have ruined the land by your tyranny! Who is Shapur, and who is the son of Hormizd?
The blame is on you and on Shapur your king, because you broke the peace between the kingdoms and brought disaster upon our country.”
The words of the fortress's inhabitants prevailed over those of Shapur's armed soldiers, and it submitted to Caesar.
They opened the gate of their city to the Roman army. The Persian troops who had been stationed to guard the fortress
were put to the sword and destroyed. The Romans took control of the cities in Shapur's kingdom
as they pleased. They plundered their possessions, emptied their treasuries, tore down their walls, and carried their inhabitants away into captivity.
The sound of their cries and lamentation rose to heaven. Jovian was grieved for them and presented a petition to Caesar on their behalf, saying,
“If I have found favor in the eyes of Your Majesty, let the cries and lamentation of the captives come before your compassion, and lavish mercy upon them in their distress.
For the troops with us are oppressing them severely. Your compassion will be praised all the more if Your Divinity issues a merciful decree
concerning this oppressed people, whom distress has surrounded.” Julian said to him, “Look, you have received from us authority over this matter,
so that you may command whatever seems good to you and be obeyed. For I have appointed you leader and commander over all my troops.” Jovian said,
“Although authority has indeed been given to me by Your Divinity, I do not dare to do anything at all without your command.”
Julian acted according to the wise man's words and commanded, “No one among the troops with us is to harm the captives,
for this is our will.” The tyrant also ordered that their clothing should not be taken away, but that each person, in whatever clothing was found on them when they were captured,
should be left in it, whether a man or a woman. No one was to dare to remove anything from their clothing
or lay a hand on the captives' jewelry and ornaments. Julian commanded that women should not be dishonored by their captors in front of their husbands, nor
were the captives to be separated, a man from his wife and children. He gave strict warnings [?]. All these things happened
through the efforts of faithful Jovian, who deserves to be remembered well for his good deeds.
But Julian, because he still intended to wage war against the king of Persia, wanted to move the captives [?]
to the regions he had conquered earlier, in accordance with the advice of Jovian, his commander, lest the captives become spies against him during the war.
He gave orders, and a platform was prepared for him in a spacious place on the north side of Ctesiphon. And when he sat on his platform,
He signaled to his trusted men, and, following the command they had received from him, they carried in gold and silver and piled it before him like rocks.
He ordered the captives to pass before him, while his troops stood armed on his right and on his left.
The captives from the land of the Arameans passed before him in the order and arrangement he had commanded, each man together with his household. According to the number of people,
gold and silver were given to them for their support until they could settle in the land and eat its produce. When the procession of captives had finished and come to an end,
his troops raised their voices in his praise. They sent up empty glory to him with their voices, and for a long time they acclaimed the madman.
But that accursed, damned man, when his ears had had their fill of the acclaim and empty praises they were lending him,
waved his hand at them and silenced them. When silence had fallen over them, he began addressing them with borrowed words,
to repay them for the empty words they had lent him. He began speaking graciously to them: “It is we who ought to offer you praise today
“for the deeds of valor you have displayed in the land of mighty men. For we are not unaware that what has happened was not accomplished by our own strength or our own might,
“but first through the help of the gods who accompany us, and then, after the gods, through the strength of your valor.
“Our empire has gained this renown and victory. For who among all the nations and languages has achieved the renown and victory

“that you have achieved? You have trampled beneath your feet the empire of mighty men that trampled all kingdoms, and you have made it an object of mockery and disgrace among all kingdoms. Who would not call you heroes,
“when the lofty leg of the house of Nimrod has bowed before you? And who would not name you mighty men, when the Roman Empire has secured its borders through your hands?
“To you, to you indeed, belong strength and valor: you made Shapur the tyrant, who overpowered all kingdoms, flee before you like a lowly weakling. To you belong skill in battle and courage,
“for you have raised the head of our empire and brought it victory. What can be given in return for these things except gratitude alone?
“Even if I gave all the treasures of our empire together with the plunder our sword has carried off, we could not adequately repay what has been accomplished through your hands.
“Look, a high place has been established for us in Shapur’s land, and we have been acclaimed in his domain, while he is a fugitive, driven from his country,
“like a weak and wretched man. But thanks be to the gods, who have granted this to our empire through your hands. And now it is right for us, too,
“to fill our hands with sacrifices and offerings for the gods, because of Assyria’s defeat and our empire’s victory. And now, as sensible and discerning men,
“let us set apart an offering for the gods who have given us victory, and hold a festival for them to celebrate our victory in our enemies’ land for seven days.
“Let us rejoice and enjoy ourselves with our enemies’ plunder, and feast on the abundant produce of their land.” He summoned the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds
and the commanders of fifty. He measured out gold and silver and gave it to them by the measure, generously and lavishly, to each man his due according to his rank,
so that they might rejoice and enjoy themselves at the festival of his idols. … But Jovian was mourning and distressed over the delusion of the mad king,
who had not abandoned his paganism or subsided from his madness even in a foreign land that was not his own. So that he, a pure man, would not be stained by the defiling [?] of the pagans,

he devised pretexts by which he could find shelter and keep himself apart during the evil days the tyrant had set aside for his idols. He said to the wicked man, “It is not [?], my lord the king, that on the great day of the gods
in which all your troops rejoice. Through it, may the cries and howls of the inhabitants of the country rise to the ears of Your Majesty and the ears of your nobles.
But if it pleases Your Lordship, allow me personally to remove them from their country, so that their [?] do not harm them,
and so that the allowance which your compassion granted them for their livelihood may be withdrawn from them. This pleased the tyrant, and he permitted him to do as he had requested.
Jovinian took the captives from the land of the Arameans and brought them to the regions of Arzan and Armenia. He settled them on fertile land
and gave them livestock for cultivating the land. He treated them kindly and compassionately. They acknowledged his kindness and prayed for his victory.
And not only they, but also throughout the whole country of the Armenians and the Arzanites,
the kindness of this discerning man was acknowledged. [?] When the righteous man again intended to travel through the country and provide for its distressed people from his own resources,
good men urgently pressed him and held him back from his undertaking. For discerning men came from among the inhabitants of the country
and secretly disclosed this to him in confidence: “An army beyond counting,” they said, “has been stationed on the border

and has blocked the entrance to Assyria, so that no one can bring provisions to your forces. In this way the strength of your army will be weakened by hunger, and then they will fight you. Now, before the enemies learn
that you have encamped in our country with a small force—” [?] Jovinian, being human, was deeply concerned. But the accursed tyrant knew nothing of these things.
He was encamped in a country not his own as though it were land under his own rule. Without a care, he reveled and behaved madly at the festival of his idols. When the days of his madness were over,
he held a banquet and summoned his nobles. He seated them at his couches. All Shapur’s [?] and the vessels used at his table
the tyrant had brought out of his royal palaces in the city of Seleucia. Caesar used them, he
and his nobles. When the madman’s heart was delighted with boasting, he lifted his elbow from the cushion
and imposed silence on all his guests, for they knew that the king had something to say. “Thanks,” he said, “to the immortal gods,
who have granted our reign this day, which the kings before me longed for but were not permitted to see.
The members of Constantine’s house were certainly not weak men: they were men who defeated five kings. But because they lacked faith in the gods,
they were not granted what has happened today. For who would not testify that they were mighty, warlike kings,

who by the strength of their valor defeated tens of kings, none of whom could stand before them? Their heels trampled the necks of their enemies, and there was no kingdom that fought against them which they did not conquer,
except only this kingdom of mighty warriors, which fought against them and defeated them. Yet even this kingdom
was not able by its own strength to wrest victory from them. For it was the gods of our empire who lent this rebellious kingdom a hand and made it victorious.
Because their kindness was despised in the eyes of the kings before me, who withheld worship from them, the gods in turn turned their faces away from the empire of Constantine’s house
and withdrew their support from its dominion, and defeat clung to them. For from the beginning of those kings’ rule,
they had given them support, and they triumphed in their battles. Wherever they turned, they were victorious. But in the blindness of their hearts they neither knew nor understood.

For they were victorious in their battles through the help of the gods who accompanied them. But because they did not recognize their help, they credited their victory to the man whom the Jews crucified.
Their insolence was not satisfied with denying the gods’ kindness and depriving them of praise. They went further and laid hands on the temples and shrines of the gods.
They uprooted their high places, overturned their altars, and plundered their treasuries. But the gods, in their great patience,
although they saw the error of these kings, did not hurry to exact vengeance. Instead,
they gave way and withdrew from the Roman dominion. They reserved vengeance for the appointed time of these kings’ end.

They did not allow them to leave heirs to their dominion after their death. During their lifetimes the gods were angry with their dominion, for they had abandoned the Roman Empire and left it without a god.
They had gone down to the kingdom of Persia, which, through their help that is with us today, has been defeated and overcome before us. And when the Roman Empire was emptied of divinity,
it was left without a god. Once and twice the house of Constantine dared to seek victory on the battlefield of Assyria, but they did not obtain it.
When the time of these kings was over and they departed from the world, the favor of the gods called me to assume their administration,
and to sit on the throne of the gods, to assume their administration, and to sit on the throne of their kingdom. And when the kingdom was established in my hands,
I had no other concern before setting myself to appease their anger by the means I knew and by the clamor of my sacrifices and offerings.
[?] I brought them up from the land in which they had been angry and returned them to the land of their inheritance. And by these means,
we were barely able to appease the anger of the gods. Our Majesty ordered the sanctuaries of their temples to be opened,

their sacrificial high places to be rebuilt, and altars for their honor to be established. I appointed priests for their service and attendants to honor their dignity. I gave orders, and all the treasures taken from them in the days of the kings before me were returned to them.
I bestowed on their temples all the adornment and splendor of the churches of the Nazarenes.
Praise thundered in the temple of their dwelling. They emerged from their hiding places and shone forth, and I held a festival of renewal for them in every city.
I fulfilled their will everywhere, and their latter glory became greater than what they had in the days of Diocletian
and in the days of Maximian, who loved the gods. Through them our kingdom grew, and through them our dominion became strong.
Through their hands this victory was given to us. Our heel trod on the proud neck of this arrogant kingdom, and it trampled our borders
and grew strong against the sons of Constantine. And look, today, with the help of the gods who accompany us, in the renowned regions of the kingdom of mighty warriors,
our armies rejoice and delight in the plunder of their land. They cannot muster the strength to meet our battle line. But these things did not happen through our own strength.
Rather, thanks be to the gods, through whose hands this triumph came about. So, my brothers, let us not deny the kindness of the gods as the kings before me denied it,
lest their condemnation cling to us. For our contest is not yet finished: battle and conflict between the kingdoms are reserved for their appointed time ...
Therefore, as people whose victory and defeat in every contest lie in the hands of the gods, let us hold faith in them wholeheartedly.

Let us persevere in worshiping them, take upon ourselves the burden of their service, and attend diligently to their sacrifices, firstfruits, and offerings. And again, when we have fulfilled these things,

We are indebted for their kindness [?]. For what can human beings offer to repay their debts to the gods for their kindness, except thanksgiving from their mouths alone? ... And the madman finished his speech.
He ordered all the groups of musicians of every kind to come before those reclining at the banquet, so that his guests might be entertained by the sweet sounds of every instrument.
When the preparations were finished and he had called his guests, he lay on his bed, preoccupied with thoughts of his campaign. By then it was already night.
Sleep fled from him, and he became deeply troubled in thought because he had encamped in a land not his own and did not know what outcome his campaign would have.
For he knew that Shapur was biding his time until he had gathered to himself the army being prepared for him. The madman carried the anxieties of his campaign within himself.
After his thoughts had disturbed him for a long time, calm fell upon him, and he slept and sank into a deep sleep. And amid the stillness of his sleep,
terrifying dreams and frightening visions settled upon him. Terrifying dreams and frightening visions disturbed him more than his waking thoughts.
Dreams disturbed him in his sleep more than his waking thoughts. For there appeared to him a fearsome band of mighty men,
forty in number. They were threatening fiercely to kill him. One of them, however, was threatening
him more than the others. He drew his bow fully to strike him, but one of his holy companions stopped him.
He said, “My brother, do not honor the slaughter of this abominable pig by striking him in his sleep, lest his armies and even his enemies suppose
that the madman tasted the natural death decreed for everyone, like anyone else. Instead, let the insolent man be struck while awake, so that his paganism may be put to shame through his wound,
and those who assented to his apostasy may be terrified by his slaughter.” When the tyrant awoke from his sleep and remembered the dream, his heart trembled,
and all his limbs shook, and he became greatly afraid. He summoned his magicians and diviners and recounted the dream before them,
and demanded its interpretation from them. Following the customs of their error, they strung together empty and foolish words
and offered them to him to calm the trembling of his heart, saying [?], “The heaviness of the drink with which you filled yourself remained with you while you slept, my lord the king.
It brought you disturbing dreams and false visions. Do not burden yourself with anxiety or concern about these things,
for the dreams of the night are fantasies and shadows: even as your eyes are upon them, they are gone.” But that accursed, condemned man
paid no attention at all to the nonsense his magicians had told him. Instead, he carried within himself the terror of the things that had been said about him in the dream,
and the thought of them tormented him. While the madman lay there amid these distressing thoughts,
sorrow upon sorrow and terror upon terror were added to him. For Jovian returned from his reconnaissance and broke the wicked man’s heart.
For he spoke harsh words to him, concealing nothing, and said, “You are not attending to your campaign like a king conducting a war.
You sit here at ease in a land not your own, occupied with matters that there was no need to attend to today.
The enemy’s army surrounds you on every side, and you are unaware of it. For a large Persian army has been stationed along the borders,
and they have seized the entrances to the country, so that no provisions at all can come from our land to our armies. And now, moreover, even
Shapur has hemmed us in on every side with a force greater than ours. Now let us look to ourselves and attend to our provisions [?], lest we perish of hunger and fall by the sword of our enemies.
When Julian heard these things, he groaned in his heart and was greatly alarmed, and his hands grew weak. But Jovian, a righteous man,
was deeply grieved for his countrymen. In the turmoil of his soul, he bore the burden and suffering of his entire army.
He undertook a fast before God and continued it through the night. He did not fast for just one day and leave it at that, but fasted for many days,
praying before God for the deliverance of his countrymen. One day, during the middle watch of the night,
while he was kneeling and praying before God at the entrance to his tent, he dozed during his prayer and fell asleep.
The blessed Mercurius appeared to him in a dream—the one who had revealed himself to him in a vision in the city of Nisibis.
He encouraged and comforted him and said to him, “Why are you anxious and mourning over this madman, who has exalted himself against God his Maker and turned away from his care?
Of his own accord, he has withheld the praise and worship due to God Most High, and in his error has bestowed it on demons and carved idols. His own sin was not enough for him,
but through his tyrannical power he also brought many others, against their will, into following his error. From now on he will have no victory.
For victory has been taken away from him [?] and given to another.” Jovian said to him in the dream, “My lord, holy one of the Lord,
it is not over this tyrant, who is devoid of faith in his Maker, that I grieve. I myself know that he will not have a peaceful end,
because he has emptied himself of the fruits of repentance. It is for my own countrymen that I suffer—the innocent sheep who have been drawn into the paganism of the supposed shepherd.
I fear that, because they have strayed from the true Shepherd, they may fall by the sword in a land not their own.” Saint Mercurius said to him,
“This is not yours to manage; it lies in God's hands. Rather, pay attention to the matters about which I have been sent.
Now Arimhar, Shapur's chief magus, in accordance with the promise he made you, has deceived Shapur and brought him
to the village of Beth-Nisbat with a very small force. He deceived him with this plan: that he should go in disguise,
and, dressed as a Roman, enter your camp himself at night and inspect it,
and learn how many tens of thousands and troops you have with you. This morning the magus will send word to you to set an ambush for Shapur
and capture him alive, according to the agreement he made with you. But do not let him draw you into this, for this is not God's will.
For this is the will of the Most High: that Julian's condemnation should first be proclaimed throughout the whole world. And when Shapur's time has run its course,
he too will be delivered into the hands of wicked men like himself. Your clean hands must not be stained with the blood of an unclean man.

Instead, a defiled hand like his own will be raised against him. His sword, which has been drawn against God's holy people, will pierce him, the unbeliever, so that what is written may be fulfilled concerning him:
‘Their sword will enter their own hearts,’ together with that other passage which is written: ‘They will fall into the pit they have dug.’ But you, man of God,
pay attention and consider what I am telling you, so that when their time comes you will remember these things. Fourteen weeks of years.
The kingdom of Persia will grow stronger than your kingdom and subject it to tribute for this number of years. And after these weeks,
the yoke of Persian tribute will be lifted from your kingdom, and both kingdoms will remain at peace for seven weeks of years.
After these weeks of years, the rebel against Persia will stir up turmoil and dissolve the peace between the kingdoms.
Both sides will wage war against each other, and their warfare will last for two weeks of years.
Afterward, the hand of your kingdom will grow strong; it will rise and gain ascendancy over Persia. Persia will be subjected to tribute to the Romans for ten years.
Here the message ends. These are the things I was commanded to tell you, and that is enough. Even these things
were told to you provisionally. It is enough for you to keep them in mind. When the present war comes to an end,
and both sides reach an agreement, and the fortified city of Nisibis is given in exchange for your lives for a specified number of years—twenty-one weeks—
you are to reach an agreement according to this outline that I have drawn for you, and arrange that, according to this outline that I have drawn for you, you reach an agreement
and make peace between the kingdoms through a written treaty. You will place the people of your nation under tribute to Persia for the years I have marked out for you. But you, man of God,
comfort yourself and put sorrow away from you. As for anxiety over the [?] that lies upon you, do not suppose that the war will end with the slaughter of this unclean and defiled man,
and that the kingdoms will remain at peace for the years I have marked out for you.” When Jovian awoke from his sleep and reflected on the dream,
he was greatly distressed, and his spirit was grieved. For he knew that condemnation would cling to them, and this discerning man was saddened
that through their hands Nisibis was destined to be handed over to the Persians. When morning came, he received a letter sent to him by the chief magus,
in keeping with the revelation that had come to him from God. For he wrote to him as follows: “My brother, since you have urged me, and I was obliged to write to you about the things that concern us,
I inform your loving self through this letter that God has today fulfilled the promise I made to you.
For Shapur, the enemy of your kingdom, is now encamped here with a small force at the village of Beth Nisbat, through the working of God
and through the resourceful schemes of our humble self. Bring a force of armored men with you, and come take vengeance on this [?] for the oppression
and the [?] that he has made God's servants endure. Exact vengeance for the holy blood of Christ's martyrs, which was shed by his hands though they were innocent.
Be zealous for the churches of your Lord, which he uprooted, demolished, and burned. Bring down upon his head what his crimes deserve. When you do this,
your valor will be proclaimed, your faith will be praised, and your army will be delivered. We will rejoice in your victory. Be strong in spirit and steadfast in your faith.”
But Jovian did not wish to conceal the truth from the man who had exposed himself to death for the sake of Roman victory.
Instead, he wrote and informed him of the truth of these matters. He marveled within himself and offered praise and thanksgiving
to God, who was faithful and revealed his will to his faithful servants. He also wrote to him a second time:
“[?] now, my brother, since this has been God's will, and his wishes must always be fulfilled, listen to me, my brother, and give me counsel.”
So that our journey here will not be entirely fruitless, some of our men have been sent to you disguised as Romans.
They are to investigate your secret plans and inspect your camp. You can therefore, my brother, earn Shapur’s gratitude even while you are far away.
Let this favor be credited to you in advance. Those we have sent have been instructed to spend this night on the outskirts of your tent,
to investigate and report what is being discussed among the army commanders in your tent. You, however, according to your wisdom,
should dismiss the army commanders from your presence tonight. Arrest these men who have been sent by us, without anyone knowing.
Bind them and compel them to tell you what you have learned from us, so that Shapur will believe that they revealed the secret under compulsion.
Once you have learned it from them, show them mercy and release them to return safely to their master. Put words in their mouths,
such as ought to be spoken to Shapur, so that he will take upon himself the obligation of repaying your kindness. For, as your letters indicate,
the victory is his.” Jovian did as the chief priest had instructed him by letter. He arrested these men and subjected them to harsh coercion.
When they confessed to him the truth about their coming, he showed them mercy. Food was set before them, and they ate and drank.
He gave them gifts and said to them, “Go to your master and tell him: ‘This is what Jovian, Caesar’s army commander, says:
Today I have granted you your life as a gift. Your life was in my hands tonight, had I desired your death, or had I wished to capture you alive.
You would already have been held among Caesar’s prisoners. For your own cunning turned back and cast you into our trap without bait or hook.
But your life was precious in my eyes, and I had no desire to make a mockery of your old age. Hurry, therefore,
and save yourself and those with you, before this news spreads through our camp and you seek to save yourselves but cannot.’”
These men went to their master and told him all these things. Shapur was shaken and became very afraid.
He blamed his chief priest for bringing about this [?], which threatened death. In haste, beset by anxiety and fear,
he mounted his horse and returned to his camp with those accompanying him. He was thinking to himself, “What can I give the Roman army commander in return
for my life and deliverance? All the treasuries of my kingdom are not enough for this.”
Shapur secretly treasured Jovian’s kindness in his heart and kept it in mind until the right time, for he loved him as himself.
When the leading men and nobles of Persia learned of these things, they were filled with indignation. They grumbled among themselves about Shapur, saying,
“How long will we remain silent about our [?], while our kingdom bears disgrace among all kingdoms? Our land has been devastated and emptied of its inhabitants.
Now enemies are growing fat on its produce in their place. The splendid and renowned palaces of our royal house have today been made into [?] for the Romans.
They ridicule us and mock our kingdom, while we ourselves still regard it as though it were only a story.” Tamshapur, king of Adiabene, brought
