the nobles’ complaint before Shapur, king of kings. He pressed him to remedy the [?]. Shapur ordered the nobles and leading men of Persia to come before him.
When they entered and bowed before him, he reassured them and comforted them with his words: “If I had not taken into account the force that was being prepared for me,
our battle would already have come to an end. Now devote yourselves to pleasure, and do not worry about this, for before a week has passed,
our sword will take vengeance on our enemies. Before a week has passed, our sword will take vengeance on our enemies.”
When he had calmed their minds and dismissed them, and they had left his presence, he sent envoys to the Roman camp and threw it into turmoil with the sound of his pronouncements.
For Zurand spoke great, boastful words before Caesar: “Thus says the great king, the Magian and mighty god, Shapur, feared above all:
What is this confidence on which you have relied, that you have dared to challenge our fearsome authority, our uplifted arm, and our mighty hand?
You have crossed into a land that is not yours, and like a thief and a raider you have devastated the territories of our kingdom. Perhaps now, in your stupidity, you imagine
that you have won a victory worthy of kings. In your error you fail to see that in this you have shown yourself a lowly king, and your victory is a women’s victory.
For warlike and powerful kings, when they have given proof of their valor in battle against their enemies
and carried off victory in the ranks of combat, then their victory is proclaimed and their courage praised. They are not like you, a lowly man
who is shut up like a robber in a prison, in a land that is not yours. Even if you wish to flee, your place of escape is lost to you,
because the exits from our country have been closed against you. But if you have strength for war, and might and valor for battle, stand firm like a warrior
and face the great battle force of Assyria. But if you have no strength to face our battle force, throw away your weapons, bow before our crown, and acknowledge your defeat with your own mouth.
Ask forgiveness, return the plunder of our land, and give, as ransom for your lives, every territory from the sea
to the Tigris, the river that divides the borders. Place the yoke of our tribute upon the neck of your kingdom. Take your armies and return in shame to your own land.”
When Zurand the Magian had finished saying these words to Caesar as though from Shapur’s own mouth, he asked him for an answer to the letters.
Julian said to Zurand the Magian, “Go and tell your master who sent you: Truly, I am deeply ashamed on your behalf,
because [?] has already been devastated and laid waste, while you, like a child foolish in its understanding, rattle off empty words like the leaves of trees.
There is no reason to marvel that your understanding has grown foolish: the devastation of your land has driven you mad. Nevertheless, do not be angry about what has happened.
For if I had not been detained by the festival of my gods, our army would already be encamped in Gurgan today. If,
then, you are a mighty king and possess strength of arm and valor, show yourself, appear with your armies, and give proof of your courage.
Rescue your land from my hands. When you are confident that you have won, then lift your downcast face and speak. Until now your face remains downcast,
if only you understood. For your words are great and forceful, but you have not considered the outcome at all. You retreat before us like a weakling,
with no firm footing.” The envoy returned and reported all these words to King Shapur. Shapur became furious and was deeply angered by Caesar’s words.
He sent for the nobles and leading men of his kingdom and had Caesar’s words read aloud to them. The nobles of Persia grumbled against Shapur, saying:
They said that Caesar was rightly and justly exalted and raised up over our country, and that his boasting was splendid and fitting.
He plundered our country and devastated our land. His armies grow strong and fat on its produce, and he has drained its inhabitants’ [?] from within it.
Shapur was being pierced, as though by [?], by the words of the nobles. He had already set his mind on waging war against Caesar.
He summoned all his armies for war against the Romans. All the forces of Persia gathered to him, thousands and tens of thousands beyond counting,
together with foreign troops from all the peoples whom he had summoned and called to help him in his battle. When the entire army set out to march into Mesopotamia,
the land trembled before them, for, like locusts and creeping locusts, they covered the face of that land because of their great numbers. Like locusts and creeping locusts,
they covered the face of that land because of their great numbers. When news of their gathering was heard in the Roman camp, the Romans were shaken and greatly afraid.
For fear was lashing them, as though with a whip, for two reasons: first, because they were stationed in a land that was not their own,
and second, because famine had grown severe among them. For the grain in Mesopotamia had run out,
and they had nowhere to find relief. For the entrances to the country had been closed against them, and, as though in a trap,

they were confined in distress. When Shapur returned to Mesopotamia with his numerous armies, on the fourteenth of June in the year six hundred and seventy-four according to the reckoning of the Greeks,
on that very day the armies of the Persians and the Romans confronted one another.
The two kings saw one another face to face, and the armies of both sides were stationed on the Tigris River,
opposite one another, on the northern side of Ctesiphon. They were ready and armed, maintaining their ranks for their kings and awaiting the command.
Silence lay over them, and no one made a sound except the two kings alone, who had reached a decision
and appointed a day on which to fight [?]. While everyone was straining to hear when the signal for battle would be sounded,
out of the silence a voice came to them from heaven, saying, “An arrow of deliverance for the Roman army!
And [?] injustice shall be removed from their midst, and peace shall reign between the kingdoms.” [?] When this voice was heard, amazement fell upon both sides,
because they did not know upon whom this lot had fallen. Even Shapur, although he was very wicked and cruel,
was shaken when he heard this voice and became greatly afraid. But Julian, in his arrogance and hardness of heart,
paid no attention to this. Instead, he mocked the voice and blasphemed, saying, “Oh, these deceptive voices,
and how children go astray after them!” He turned his attention to his troops and said, “Take care that you are not led astray by this deceptive noise
and fall by the sword in the land of your enemies. For the voice that was heard does not belong to one of the gods, but to the Nazarene who called himself God.
But if he truly is God, let him provide proof of his divinity through a clear sign, and we will believe in him.” [?] At the very moment the wicked man spoke,
the sentence of justice overtook him. An arrow flew through the air from the place where the voice had been heard and struck the wicked man.
beneath his breast and delivered him to death. The wretched man wailed and cried out, and caught some of the blood from his wound in his hands.
He sprinkled it toward heaven, blasphemed, and said, “Have your fill, Jesus! Have your fill now and be satisfied! Look, kingship too has been given to you, along with divinity!”
While agony gripped him and the pangs of death struck him, the Romans snatched him up and brought him into their camp. At the time of his death, he said to those beside him:
“Now that I am dying, immediately make Jovian, the army commander, your king in my place.
For you have no man as fit for kingship as he is, who is able, through his knowledge and skillful resourcefulness,
to bring you out of the confinement in which you find yourselves.” When he had said these things in his brokenheartedness, his soul left him, wretched man that he was.
He became [?], and already here he received a foretaste of the torment reserved for him and of the Gehenna promised to him and to those who acted wickedly as he did.
Thus Julian the wicked reached the end of his life, in accordance with the prophecy spoken about him by upright and faithful men,
who suffered martyrdom during that evil man's persecution. The prophecy they had spoken about him was fulfilled in him, and his destruction in death took place in a land not his own.
What is written also applied to him: “The end of the wicked is destruction, but the Lord is the deliverer of the righteous.”
For God truly brought deliverance to the church and her children through the destruction and death of this man, who was truly pagan and wicked.
Even in the land of his enemies, he did not [?] turn away from his paganism. While his hands were stained with his pagan sacrifices, his end overtook him; and while his mouth was full of blasphemy,
the sentence of justice caught up with him. Truly, this is the worker of deceit who completed his days in the service of sin and cut short and severed the hope of his repentance.
He went away carrying the load of his sins on his shoulder—a merchant dealing in losses, who gained for himself the fire that is not quenched and the worm that does not die.
An ignorant sailor, blind in understanding, he drove the ship of his own self into the sea of sin, and it sank in the flood of paganism.
It rose up and reached the harbor of outer darkness, where weeping and gnashing of teeth are promised
to wicked people like him. Let us bring the account of the evil man to an end, just as his pagan sacrifices were poured out at his slaughter.
Let us briefly describe the severe distress and terrible famine that pressed upon the Romans in the land of the Persians,
and what toil and struggle fell to the faithful Jovian for the deliverance of those with him, and how he was able, through his knowledge and the [?] of his wisdom,
to bring them out unharmed from the confinement in which they had been trapped. For their distress had grown severe, and hunger had overpowered them,
until they ate their horses and livestock, and the carcasses of their dead animals. Their strength weakened and gave out, and their spirits failed.
When they also saw that Julian their king had died, their hands grew slack in battle. Their hearts trembled, and they were very afraid of the Persians.
They considered laying aside their weapons and surrendering to the Persians to save their lives. But Jovian rebuked them and said to them:
“Take care that you do not lose courage and lay aside your weapons, only to fall by the sword in the land of your enemies.
The few of you who remain will become slaves to the Persians forever. Instead, take courage and be men!”
Fight for your lives, and do not be afraid. I have hope in the God of the Christians, in whom my fathers put their hope:
if you listen to me, turn away from your error, turn to the mighty God, serve him with all your heart and all your soul, and believe in him,
not a single hair from the head of any one of you will fall in the land of the Persians. Only set your hearts toward God,
and he will fight for you.” On that very day Jovian openly declared that he was a Christian.
And [?] seized everyone who heard him. They were strengthened by his words and comforted by what he said. They wanted to make him king that day.
But he did not yield to their wishes. He addressed them, saying, “Today, when war with our enemies is upon us,
leave this alone. Let us concern ourselves only with [?].” The Romans said to him, “Whatever seems good to you and whatever
you desire, we will do. Only bring us out of this confinement unharmed.” Jovian said to them,
“When we please God, we will find mercy.” Now the Persians were [?] to fight the Romans that day.
But Shapur would not let them. For he said, “I will not defy the voice as the king of the Romans defied it,
and his destruction came suddenly. I will not share in his punishment.” For he kept in mind the thought of what had been said:
“Let the wicked man be removed from among us, and let peace reign between the kingdoms.” It was this that restrained him from waging war,
not compassion, which he did not possess. Shapur ordered that fighting should cease that day. But his nobles and the satraps of his kingdom
grumbled bitterly against him because a day of vengeance had come their way, yet he would not allow them to fight.
For they saw that the Romans were brokenhearted over the death of their king
and had given up fighting. They were chafing at being held back. When Shapur learned that his nobles were grumbling against him,
he sent for them and rebuked them harshly, saying, “If you were just and upright,
you would not be grumbling [?] and pointlessly against my decisions. You heard with your own ears what was spoken,
and you saw with your own eyes what happened. You yourselves know that because Julian defied the voice,
a terrible, merciless sentence overtook him, and he was struck by a spiritual arrow that no fleshly hand had shot.
Now understand and consider what you are doing, lest through your zeal against the Romans you bring disaster upon my kingdom.
And perhaps, time and again, it is my own destruction that you desire.” His nobles were afraid and could not answer him a word.
Shapur summoned the wise men and magi of Persia and questioned them in the presence of his nobles:
“What was this voice that was heard? Which of the gods thundered with his voice and revealed his will to human beings?”
The wise men and magi said to him, “As for the things Your Majesty asks of us, unless it is granted to us from above to speak about them,
They are. We cannot say anything about them, because they are concealed and hidden from us. ... Shapur said to them:
“Then go, search your books, and examine the treasury of the revelations of the Magian religion. Consult the calculations and reckonings of Chaldean astrology,
and bring to light for us the truth about the event, just as it happened. When you do this, you will receive honor and gifts from us.”
The Magi and Chaldeans left the king’s presence and searched the books of the Magian religion. They consulted the calculations and reckonings of Chaldean astrology.
When the revelation dawned on them, they were afraid to disclose to Shapur the actual truth, just as it was.
For the revelation disclosed to those versed in the books of Chaldean astrology was foreign to the faith of the mad king.
They took counsel with one another, cobbled together worthless and hollow words, and acted deceitfully. They changed their account before the king and said:
“The sun, the god of creation, became angry with the Roman emperor. It thundered against him with its voice and struck him with the arrow of its ray,
and deprived him of life because he overstepped the bounds of proper conduct and crossed into a land that was not his.” ... Shapur said to them:
“Now I know for certain that you are liars and that there is no truth in your words. For the sun of which you spoke
has never made its voice heard by human beings, because an ear of flesh could not endure hearing its mighty voice.
For we have not recognized that it is a god through its voice, but through its constant help toward us. For it rises over the created world,
and evil vanishes and disappears before it. It makes the roads peaceful for merchants, unties knots, and resolves disputes.
It pursues spirits and drives away harmful beings. It cleanses springs of the filth of disease. It makes the hours known and distinguishes the seasons. It shows human beings
when to begin their work and when to finish, and travelers on the roads when to set out and when to stop. Besides these things,
with the gentle warmth of its heat it ripens fruit, makes crops grow, and brings forth flowers. And with the fervor of its burning heat it also checks the severity of winter
and softens its bitterness. And what is greater and more exalted than all these things: in a full day’s journey, from one end to the other,
it flies on the spiritual wings of its divinity. There are also many other wonders of its that we cannot fully recount. It is through these things, then, that we have recognized that it is a god,
and not through its voice, as you claimed. But I am even more astonished at this: I entrusted my affair to you as trustworthy men,
but you, like deceivers, decided to utter a false and empty statement before me. You neither trembled nor feared before me.”
The Magi and Chaldeans answered, saying, “We beg your fearsome authority, my lord the king, not to become angry with your servants over this.
For we dare not bring to light before your authority the account of the things we encountered among the luminaries of the zodiac.
Their account is foreign to the faith of our kingdom, and for anyone to introduce something foreign concerning our gods brings great fear of your authority,
since it is sheer insolence.” ... Shapur said to them, “If this prevents you from telling the truth, here is my pledged word to you:
you will suffer no harm at all over this matter about which I have questioned you, for I wish to learn the truth.”
They said, “Now that this has been your divine will concerning us, we will make the truth of the matter known to you face to face.
The voice that spoke does not belong to one of the visible gods, nor is he numbered among the gods from heaven downward.”
Shapur said to them, “Whose, then, is this voice that was heard?” The magi and sages said to him:
“It belongs to Hormizd, the God of heaven, who is concealed and hidden in the highest heights, whom no investigation can reach ...” Shapur said to them:
“I have heard that there is a God in heaven. But I have never devoted myself to seeking him,
nor to investigating his being. In the writings of our kingdom, however, I found that his nature is fire, and we have long worshiped this likeness of him.
Nevertheless, I would like to hear an account of his true nature, if that is possible ...” The [?] sages among them said to him—
those who were especially well versed in the books and revelations of Chaldean learning: “How could you hear an account of his true nature, when the account of him is high and exalted above
the understanding and thought of mortal human beings? No knowledge is capable of grasping and reaching the height of his greatness. The inquiry into him is hidden and inaccessible,
bounded and enclosed within silence. For he is God without beginning, the One who exists without end, above the ages that he created.
Within time he appeared as he pleased. It is difficult for us to explain him, since we are strangers to his worship. If there were someone who could instruct us
about him, our sword would have been drawn long ago ...” Shapur said to them, “What you have said is new to us, and I demand its explanation from you.”
But knowing that his disposition was contrary, they ended the inquiry with this statement: “An explanation of this has not been given to us.
This alone has been revealed to us: that it was he who thundered with his voice.” “Tell us what his will is, so that we may learn it ...” The magi and sages said to him:
“This is the will of the Most High: now that the enemy of our kingdom has been removed, warfare must cease and the camp must be broken up.
Our sword must be put back into its sheath, and peace must reign between the kingdoms. This is the will of Hormizd, God. Now take care of yourselves,
and understand and consider what you are doing. Even if you are unwilling, his purposes are fulfilled at all times, and whoever challenges his will wages war against himself.
For who has resisted him and remained unharmed?” When the sages had finished speaking, Shapur said to his nobles:
“What do you think about what you have heard? Give definite advice about it.” The freeborn men and nobles of his kingdom said:
“What advice can we give about matters that are not determined by our will? Our sages have presented them as determined by the will of Hormizd, God.
How can we reject his voice, accompanied as it is by the rod of discipline? Even if we were resolved to wage war, victory would not be granted to us,
according to the revelation that came to our sages. Nevertheless, so that the Romans do not boast and say, ‘Not even [?], when we have no king,
do the Persians have the strength to face our Caesar’s battle line,’ if it seems good to you, my lord the king, let us put a face on the matter and not be hasty to show them this
mercy of ours, lest pride carry them away. Instead, let us first make them hear harsh words and torment them with hunger.
Let us persuade the inhabitants of our land to sell them, as though from friends, ground [?] mixed with [?].”

that they might eat and grow weak. And when their strength had weakened and failed, and the force of their arrogance had been brought low, they recognized their condition and acknowledged their defeat.

They handed over the booty taken from our land: the fortified city of Nisibis, which had been seized from our fathers, and the territories subject to the Armenians. They also laid upon their kingdom the tribute due to our kingdom.
Then, as though to lavish mercy on them generously and hurry to send them out of our land in shame, [?] Shapur said to them:
“What you have planned is good, and I have carried out your plan. But if it seems good to you, let us first allow them to appoint a king for themselves,
so that they have no way to console themselves over their defeat and make false claims, saying, ‘If we had had a king, we would not have been defeated
and would not be surrendering to the Persians.’ For when their king is at their head, they have no excuse to take refuge in.
Their disgrace will increase still further, and their shame will be greater than it is now.” And the nobles and great men of Persia approved
the king’s plan and agreed to it. [?] But this accursed, damned man did this cunningly, to put Jovian under an obligation of gratitude,
in return for the kindness he had shown him in the village of Beth Nisbat, and thereby to repay him for the great ravages he had inflicted on his land.
Shapur had conceived the idea of making him king over the Romans through a stratagem involving his troops. [?]
Shapur sent messengers to the Roman camp and sent them this message: “Because the mighty hand of Ohrmazd, the God of heaven, has come against you for harm,
and, as justice requires, he has sent distress and famine upon you,
because you have insolently defied what is right and crossed into a land that is not yours, we, as disciplined and wise men, have considered the matter properly.
It is right that we make room for God’s discipline, so that his wrath may grow strong against you and
his fury may gain power over you. Then we too, in keeping with the high rank granted us from above, will justly exact vengeance from you for the evil ravages you unjustly inflicted upon our land,
so that at the moment of your destruction you may know that you have thrown a pebble against a great [?], and against the divine kingdom that received its crown from heaven.
But so that we do not become presumptuous like them and share in your punishment, we have decided, out of our compassion,
to grant [?] a respite of thirty days, during which you may take thought for yourselves and appoint a king for yourselves,
and be comforted over the death of your lord—although I am even more distressed over his death than you are. For I did not desire his death
as much as I longed to capture him alive, so that I could carry out my wishes on him and show him what the strength of his heroism amounted to.
For I was not in a hurry for his death. I had resolved to imprison him for a long life full of misery,
with him bound in irons and both his eyes blinded, as my fathers did to the kings of Judah,
so that through his tortures and afflictions he might learn and become wise, realizing that nothing helps a person except doing what is right.
That was what I was looking toward and hoping for. But now, since this was the will of the God of heaven,
everything is justified by his will. For I wanted to act harshly against you as you did, but the decree from above did not permit me to do this today.
But he taught us through his voice to make room for his discipline, as his wishes are fulfilled among you. Let this, then, be certain to you
and set before your eyes: when the thirty days that our mercy has granted you have passed,
we will wage war against you without respite. [?] Therefore, seek out among yourselves a man who knows how to govern your kingdom well
and is strong enough to stand at your head and face the onslaught of our fierce battles, and who is worthy of kingship
and will fight on your behalf. I have also learned that Jovian, their commander, is a man of knowledge and understanding.
He knows his duties, and he knows the order and forms of government, and [?] what causes harm, and recognizes
what causes injury. Nothing escapes his knowledge. He is mighty in strength and has a heroic arm with which to face battle.
I have long wished that I had a man like him, and I would have made him the [?] of my kingdom.

Make this man your king, if you wish, for we too have granted him your kingdom—that is, to help you, so that he may stand at your head and fight on your behalf, and give proof of his knowledge and demonstrate his leadership
in the battle that lies before us. For my part, I have set before your eyes what seemed helpful to me.
From now on, it is for you to make whomever you wish your king. For after the days we have mentioned,
we will wage war against you.” When this letter was read aloud to the whole Roman army, they rejoiced greatly.
They said to one another, “Jovian has truly found favor and compassion with the king of Persia.
Perhaps this has come from the God of the Christians to help our camp.” These words were being spoken about Jovian
throughout all the Roman camps. All the people looked to him to reign over them. Shapur, meanwhile, wishing to show kindness to the Romans,
moved his camp away from them and went two days’ journey away, to give them an opportunity to appoint a king for themselves.
Jovian, wishing to fulfill the customary duties and the rites prescribed for Roman kings when they died, gave orders to the physicians who were with them.
They embalmed the wicked man’s body. He had a coffin made for him and placed him in it until he had an opportunity to send him to Roman territory.
[?] Then the army commanders, the centurions, and also the prominent men in the army gathered and formed a plan concerning Jovian:
they would seize him by force and make him king, for he was unwilling to offer himself as king. When Jovian learned of this,
he hid from their sight and took refuge in a burial ground, where no one would expect or think to look for him
there. There was great uproar and confusion among the Romans over his disappearance. They went about searching for him everywhere.
When they had searched for him and failed to find him, they spread a false report, saying, “These ten commanders who rank below Jovian
formed a conspiracy against him and drove him away, so that they would not make him their king and their own authority would not be diminished.” The whole army rose against these men
and demanded that they hand Jovian over. They argued fiercely with them, saying:

“Give us the man whom you spirited away from us through your skillful schemes, so that he would not reign over you and your authority would not be diminished. For we know that you did this out of envy.
It is plain to everyone that you have coveted the kingship. Can all of you possibly become kings?
For the kingship belongs to him, and we have no one else to be king over us except Jovian, the commander of the army.
Both kings declared him entitled to the kingship: Shapur in his letters, and Julian as he was dying. Now give us the man!
Otherwise, your blood will be shed in our camp today!” Vitalis, who was next in command after Jovian, said to them:
“Men, what is this disturbance today? Why are you quarreling with us for nothing and to no purpose?
You accuse us unjustly of things that never even entered our minds. For we have bound ourselves under oath
not to eat bread or drink water until we [?]. We are worried about his disappearance and are in great distress over him,

lest our oaths prove false. Yet we hope and trust that our oaths will not be dissolved before your wish is fulfilled. Now stop oppressing and troubling us—you have pelted us with false reports as though with stones—and give us a little room
to go out and search for him, if you wish.” ... When Vitalis said this, there subsided, only with difficulty,
the people's uproar and shouting. When they had dispersed and each had gone to his tent, these officers went out
in search of Jovian. They searched for him throughout the Roman camps, and the contents of his tent were searched, but they did not find him. His absence now became a matter of uncertainty.
These men were afraid to remain in the camp, lest the people discover them, and they resolved to flee. While they were bewildered and frightened,
someone came secretly and disclosed to them, “I saw Jovian throw himself into a [?] in the cemetery, with no one there to see him
except me, who happened to be opposite him. Go quickly, and you will find him there.” They kept careful hold of that man
and said to him, “Come, go and show us.” That man went with them and showed them the place, and they went down into that enclosure.
They found Jovian hiding in the cemetery. They argued fiercely with him, complaining against him and saying,
“Oh, man! Why have you done this to us? You have thrown the whole Roman army into confusion, and they very nearly stoned us because of you.
Do you not know that our entire camp has set its sights on you, so that you may be king over them and bring them out of the distress of the confinement in which we are trapped?
Why did you set your heart on doing this and sinning against your God? Look, the people are crying out and weeping because you have departed from them.” ... Jovian said to them:
“Why are you accusing us for nothing and to no purpose? Yesterday and the day before, this was what I told you: I will not approach the rank of king.
For I have not come down here from a royal line. Rather, like one of you, I was entrusted with authority to be commander of the army.
Nor do I yet withdraw from this authority entrusted to me. As commander of the army, as far as I am able,
I fight for the victory of the Romans. I have hope that not a single hair from the head of any one of you will fall to the ground
in the battle and conflict that confront us.” Vitalis said to him, “We must impose the kingship on you by force, unless you willingly accept it when called.”
This is what you were called to. Or is there someone else above you who can compel your will? Why, then, have you lowered yourself by withdrawing from us?
Come, then, go with us to the camp, and explain your withdrawal to the people who look to you. Our camp is not without someone to govern the kingdom.
But he would not be persuaded at all to go with them, saying, “I am not capable of this, for I am uneducated and an ordinary man.
I do not know how to govern the kingdom.” When they saw that he would not be persuaded to go, they seized him and brought him to the camp by force.
They gathered the whole Roman army around him. They were shouting and reproaching him, saying, “You have not dealt justly with your servants.
You brought us in and trapped us in our enemies’ land. When our distress grew severe and troubles surrounded us on every side,
and times turned against us in a territory not our own, you withdrew from leading us and hid yourself from our sight.
You left us like sheep with no one to gather them. This is not justice! Had it not been for your promises to us,

we would probably already have surrendered to the Persians and saved our lives. For it would have been better for us to serve the Persians as slaves and save our lives. For it would have been better for us to serve the Persians as slaves
than to suffer and perish from hunger. Is this, then, the whole of your justice—that you have poured out your compassion on foreigners and shown them abundant kindness,
but have treated us, your servants, as foreigners, and have yourself withheld our deliverance?” Jovian said to them,
“Do not complain against me, for it was not through me that you came to this. Instead, go and complain against the corpse of your king, whose paganism you were drawn to,
whose error you followed. You sacrificed to demons and evil spirits, and worshiped images and idols,
thinking that they were gods. If, then, they are gods, let them rise now and help you and become your protectors.”
The Romans said to him, “We have never heard these things before—only since yesterday.
Now, if you want anything, first become king and do everything with authority. [?]” Jovian said to them, “I did not want
this repentance of yours to be forced, but voluntary. Nevertheless, I have withdrawn once and for all from being your king. Make whomever you want your king.
As for me, I will fight on your behalf as an army commander, as far as I am able.” The Romans said to him,
“If we did not know for certain that the kingship had not been rightfully granted from above, and that both kings, though unwilling, relied on you,
someone else would probably now be reigning in your place, and we would have no dispute with you now. Put an end to everything now,
for whether you wish it or not, the kingship is yours. Accept the kingship at our [?], and not under compulsion.”
When Jovian saw that nothing was helping and that he could not get away in any direction, because they were watching him very closely,
he went up to a high place where all the people could see him. He waved his hand to them to be silent, and when they became quiet,
he spoke to them and said, “What is this uproar and commotion today? You have gathered needlessly and pointlessly.
For I have only one thing to say to you: unless you turn back from your error and renounce your paganism, I will not become the leader of a godless people.”
And I will not be called king over pagans, even if I must die at your hands.
I am a Christian, the son of Christians. Far be it from me ever to have shared in Julian’s paganism.
Even though I had taken on the outward appearance of pagans, it was only borrowed, as an expedient. So if you are determined to remain in your paganism,
look, there are strong men among you, followers of your error, who can govern the kingdom with strength. Let your king be one of the followers of your own faith,
and do not lay this burden on me. All the people answered and said, “We have no other king besides you, and we will do everything you tell us.
Only let us not serve as slaves in Persia.” Jovian said to them, “If it is me you want,
put away the foreign gods [?] from among you, and direct your hearts toward God, for he has the power to rescue you from the hands of your enemies.
Turn toward him, so that he may turn toward you. Seek him, and he will be found by you. Call upon him, and he will answer you.
For he is always near to those who call upon him, and he opens his door to those who seek him. Return to him with all your heart, and believe in him with all your soul.
And if you are truly and sincerely looking to him for salvation, give proof of your repentance by bowing before the cross.
For it is the sign of salvation for all who believe in him. Let Christ reign over you first, invisibly, as God.
Then afterward I too will reign over you visibly, as a human being.” The Romans willingly agreed to this.
For many of them were Christians, and out of fear of the wicked man’s decrees they had submitted to his paganism. When Jovian saw their good willingness,
he took the cross that used to go at the head of the army, raised it, and set it up in a high place so that the rest of the people could see it.
There was much discussion of this among discerning people. They asked why Julian, although he was a thorough pagan and an apostate, had not abolished this arrangement
and the custom established for the Christian kings before him, that the cross should go at the head of the army. They thought that the tyrant had reasoned as follows:
the kings before him had gained strength through this sign and had won their battles. If he removed it and defeat befell him,
the Romans would have grounds to say, “The whole reason we were not granted victory
is that the sign of our kingdom’s victory was taken away.” Perhaps it was with this strategy in mind that the tyrant had neglected the matter
and had not removed this sign from the Romans’ camp, so that, if there was a victory, he could attribute it to his paganism,
and if defeat befell him, he could attribute it to that sign of victory through which salvation came to all creation.
This was the view that learned men took of this affair. But, my brothers, one must marvel and wonder at the faith and understanding
of the faithful Jovian, who used every possible means to win over to repentance the thousands and tens of thousands who were with him.
For they had approached to place the royal crown on him, according to the established law and ceremonies observed by the Romans.
But to make paganism contemptible in their eyes, he did not accept it from their hands. For he said, “Far be it from me! May it never happen!”
that the pagan's crown, which he wore when worshiping idols, should be placed on a head before it is placed on the top of the cross.
And when Christ has become king over you through his crucifixion, and the crown of our kingdom has been blessed and sanctified through it, then I too will receive it fittingly and rightly,
from the blessed right hand, full of holiness, through which the unclean have been sanctified and sins have been forgiven.
So approach and place the crown that is in your hands on the top of the cross. Come, let us implore Christ, worshiping before his cross,
for the peace and stability of your kingdom.” The king's servants did as they had been commanded. Jovian bowed down and worshiped before the cross.
All his troops worshiped with him. Jovian poured out his soul in prayer before God. He shed tears as he pleaded,
so that the ground was soaked with his tears. He cried aloud, wept, and implored God for the peace of the churches and the salvation of their children,
and for the victory of the Romans and the stability of their empire. After he had lain facedown praying for a long time,
[?] he rose from the ground, spread out his hands toward heaven, and called God as his witness, saying:
“You, Lord God, mighty and holy, know what is in everyone's heart. Be a witness for your servant today,
that I have not desired this authority, nor this kingdom that passes away. For I look toward and await the one that does not pass away.
And now, Lord, since this has been your will, and your grace has called me to be ruler and king
over the guilty who have taken refuge in your cross and look to your salvation, I beg you, mighty Lord:
let this authority not bring harm to my soul, injury to my spirit, or condemnation upon me, but rather atonement for my soul,
forgiveness for my spirit, confidence for me, satisfaction to your divinity, reconciliation for your people, and peace for your churches,
and the return of their children, the establishment of faith in you, and victory and salvation for those who went astray
but have turned back from their error and clung to you. And to me, a sinner and a guilty man, whom your divinity has called to the royal crown although I am unworthy,
grant this, and make me worthy by your grace: that I may receive this crown from your blessed right hand, full of holiness,
so that through you I may have reason to boast among all the kingdoms of the earth.” When Jovian had finished the words of his prayer,
he bowed down and paid homage to all his troops. He marked his chest and the space between his eyes with the sign of the cross.
He approached with fervent faith and bowed his head before the cross. The royal crown came down and was placed on his head,
although no human hand had touched it. All the Roman people were greatly astonished and marveled at this great miracle that had taken place.
They shouted, saying, “From now on, Christ is king over us in heaven, and Jovian is king over us on earth.”
Fear and awe of Jovian fell upon all his troops, for they knew with certainty that the Lord was with him. On that very day,
Jovian, son of Varronianus, became king over the Romans in the land of the Persians, in the region of Beth Aramaye.
On the Tigris River, on the northern side of Ctesiphon, in the month of June in the year 674 according to the Greek reckoning, on the twenty-seventh of the month, on Friday.
When Jovian became king, he was zealous for God, and he ordered that the seven priests of sin be brought before him,
who had gone down with Julian into the land of the Persians, together with the seven golden idols that the madman had especially worshiped and offered sacrifices to.
[?] But the faithful king Jovian was still standing in the very place where he had become king, with a cross set at his right hand.
They brought these priests and the idols of their error before him. Jovian looked at them angrily and rebuked them, saying to them, “Tell me, you guilty men, what is
this madness that has seized you? Even now that the time of your error has ended, you have not abandoned your preoccupation and taken refuge in God.
Was Julian’s time alone [?] not enough for you, but you persist even in ours? Know, then, that you will certainly die, and your blood will be on your own heads, because you
have brought destruction upon yourselves.” He ordered that they be thrown into the Tigris. But when these priests saw that the order against them was being hastened [?]
they approached and clung to the cross for deliverance [?]. It was fixed at the king’s right hand.
They grasped it and held tightly to it with their hands, saying, “Save us, cross of Christ! Save us, for through you salvation came to the whole world.
For us too, Christ, who have taken refuge in your cross, forgiveness of our guilt is fitting. Do not let us be beyond the reach of your salvation.”
The king’s soldiers wanted to throw stones at those priests and pull them away from the cross.
But the king’s command restrained them, for Jovian said, “I will not establish this wicked law during my rule:
that anyone should violate the sanctuary of the cross, even if the person taking shelter in it deserves death.”
Jovian said to these priests, “Tell me, you priests devoid of faith,
for what [?] have you taken refuge in the cross today, when only days ago you spoke blasphemous words against that worshipful name of the one who was crucified upon it?”
These priests said to him, “We appeal to your mercy, my lord the king. Is our wrongdoing greater than that of the Jews who crucified him?
As their writings show, your God asked forgiveness on the cross [?]. And now the descendants of those who crucified him are allowed to remain in the world, although they do not acknowledge him,
and no one calls them to account. Yet we, who are determined with all our soul to [?] in him—will he reject our repentance and refuse to accept us?” Jovian said to them,
“If your repentance were true and genuine, there would have been [?] in your hands. It is clear

to those who understand that your repentance comes not from faith but from fear of death.” These unbelievers said to him, “Far be it from us, from now on, to be false in our repentance or, from this day forward, to be strangers to the worship of the cross.
For a sign of mercy appeared to us in it and amazed us—a sign that perhaps has not appeared to you.”
But the righteous king, because he desired their repentance more than their destruction, admonished them, saying,
“What have you ever done that deserves forgiveness, that [?] you expected forgiveness [?]?
Or how can anyone accept your words that you saw [?] mercy in the cross? For look, you are enemies [?] through the working of your error.”
Those priests said, “For where has [?], and when has an astonishing miracle like this one that happened among us ever been seen? For look, we are awake
[?], and a flame of fire came down [?], yet we were not scorched. If Christ had wanted our destruction, he would already have consumed [?] all [?] at once,
from the [?] of the burning of the cross in which we took refuge.” [?] Jovian was astonished at their words, but he doubted their repentance. Yet the merciful God, who desires
at all times the repentance of sinners, [?] the true [?], opened the eyes of the believing king, and he saw that cross burning and blazing like a fiery torch. [?]
[?] the hands of those priests [?] being scorched. When Jovian saw that their repentance had proved itself,
mercy dawned within him. He decided to spare them and began to say to his troops, “What are we to do with these condemned men,
since they have now grasped the cross and taken refuge in it?” When his troops saw that his words were full of mercy and that he wanted to spare them,
they agreed to the king’s wishes. They cried out to him, saying, “On the day of your joy, forgiveness befits you,
and mercy becomes you. On the opening day of your reign, it is right to grant life to those condemned to death, comfort to the brokenhearted,
joy and gladness to those distressed in spirit, and mercy and forgiveness to offenders. On the day when
the royal crown was bound upon you, let no one die. Instead, let joy reign over everyone, and let your mercy be praised by all.” Jovian said to these priests,
“To fulfill the wishes of my troops, and still more because you have taken refuge in the cross, I have granted you your lives today.
That is, if you remain steadfast in your repentance. But if you return to your error,
know that you will certainly die.” These priests said to him, “Far be it from us to return to our error and deny the God of the Christians,
who alone today has spared the blood of our lives. [?]” Jovian said to them, “If you have truly and sincerely come to believe,
put your hands to work for him against your idols.” He gave them axes and said to them, “Come forward and break the images of your error.”
The priests took the axes, and with their own hands they broke the idols of their error. Jovian melted down these images
and ordered that they be given toward the expenses of the churches that had been destroyed during the persecution of Julian the wicked. As for the priests themselves, he ordered that they be placed
in monasteries and receive full instruction in the faith of the righteous, and then come for baptism. Jovian gave gifts to his troops

and spoke reassuringly to them and encouraged them. He said to them, “Be strong and do not be afraid, for Christ will not withdraw his hand from you and leave you in distress. From now on, he cares for you.
He fights secretly on your behalf and openly brings you deliverance through my hands. For if Shapur wishes to make peace and friendship with us,
we will deal with him gently and humbly. But if he persists in his tyrannical intentions,
do not lose heart or become discouraged even at this. For I have hope in the God of the Christians, in whom we have taken refuge,
that even if his army exceeds ours by three hundred thousand, victory will be ours and defeat will be theirs.
So do not let distress or sorrow rule over you in any way, even by a single hair’s breadth.
“Not a hair will fall from the head of any one of you in the land of the Persians.” The Romans took heart at his words,
and their spirits were at ease. The weight of their distress was lifted from their minds, and they were very glad and joyful,
because a good remedy had been found for their wound. When Shapur learned [?] that Jovian had become king in Julian’s place,
he wanted to engage him through letters that would test him and reveal what his intentions were.
He decided to write him arrogant and insulting words, to inflame the righteous man’s mind with indignation, so that he would disclose his thoughts and make them known to him.
For this purpose a messenger was sent to him, carrying letters that called for the sword and stirred up war.
But he was shrewd and knew what was appropriate. When he received the tyrant’s letters, he placed them against his eyes,
kissed them, and treated them affectionately. He instructed the messenger: “I [?] in these matters, and heaven and earth are witnesses. But if this comes from your side,
and your kingdom forcibly wages war against us, I trust in the God whom I serve, in whose hands lie the wars and conflicts of the world,
that you will soon ask our kingdom for peace, and it will not be granted to you. For no [?] has defied his fellow and remained unharmed.”
… Then the messenger Gudfar returned to Shapur, carrying letters of peace from the Roman emperor.
He reported to his master everything he had seen and heard in the Roman camp. He spoke favorably to him about Jovian
and praised him before his master. When Shapur read the letters sent to him, he marveled at Jovian’s intelligence and praised him,
because the gentle words he had sent were mingled and interwoven with harsh ones. Shapur sealed the letters brought to him and returned them to the messenger.
He warned him, saying, “Let no one learn about these things unless you are summoned before me.” He put words into his mouth to say before the nobles
and dignitaries of Persia when they were summoned. The messenger left the king’s presence under strict orders to remain silent.
Shapur sent for the elders of his kingdom and the nobles and dignitaries of Persia, and said to them, “The messenger has returned from the Roman camp,
and he has with him letters from the new king whom the Romans have made their ruler. We have decided that they should not be read unless we are all assembled.”
Shapur’s proposal pleased the elders of his kingdom, as well as his nobles and dignitaries.
Shapur sent for Gudfar the messenger and said to him, “What did you see in the Roman camp? Bring the truth to light, and do not lie.”
Gudfar said, “I appeal to the exalted crown of your kingship, King of Kings. How [?] your servant
to dare to speak a false word before the might of your divinity! My lord, I went to the Roman camp as you commanded,
and I was greatly astonished at how calm and quiet they were. There was no fear or thought of battle in their hearts.
Instead, they were glad and joyful and rejoiced greatly in their king. I presented Your Majesty’s letters to the Roman emperor, and he eagerly reached for them as though for a precious gift.
He rose from his royal throne and received them in his purple robes. He placed them against his eyes, kissed them, and treated them affectionately.
He received them warmly and paid us great honor. His officials also came to greet us and spoke with us in words of peace and reconciliation.

They bear within themselves [?] the kindness of Your Majesty and constantly give thanks for your mercy, which has prevailed over them. You entered their minds, searched their thoughts, and learned the truth:
They are not determined to wage war against us, not even if we fight them violently. For they have entrusted their war to Ohrmazd, the God of heaven,
through Jovian their king. For he found favor and mercy before the God of heaven, as his officials told me about him.
They said that he had appeared to him many times in dreams at night.
And in all his battles victory was granted to him. [?] These things I saw and heard in the Romans’ camp, and I am not lying. Look, Caesar’s letter bears witness to my words. [?]
The envoy stretched out his hand and gave Jovian’s letters to Shapur, and he too rose from his royal throne.
He honored Caesar’s writings and remained standing on his feet until Jovian’s letters had been read. Then he sat down on his throne.
He said to his nobles and officials, “What do you think about what you have heard? Let us consider it.”
His officials said to him, “What deliberation is needed about this? It has already been settled for us by Ohrmazd the god,
that there is to be no war with them, for such was his will. But indeed, my lord the king, even apart from this,
what quarrel would we have with them after what they sent us—people who placed themselves under obligation in the document they drew up for us,
and called themselves servants of our royal authority? After what they sent us—people who placed themselves under obligation in the document they [?] for us,
and called themselves servants of our royal authority—even if we fought them, devastated and were devastated, struck and were struck, we would have had no course of action [?].
But now, look, [?] their freedom [?] to this, without [?]. From now on we have nothing to do with them except to offer entreaty and petition on their behalf,
that they may receive forgiveness from us, and that we may show them favor for the sake of Jovian their king, who through adoption called himself the son of Your Majesty,
and in his writings also called you his father. Who, from now on, would dare to sow discord between a son and his father and remain alive?
Rather, my lord, if Your Majesty commands it, let there be peace from now on between the kingdoms.” But that accursed tyrant, in his cunning,
gave the affair a favorable appearance, so that the nobles and officials of the kingdom would not blame him for it later.
For he was ready to tell them, “I had one thing in mind, while you thought something else. I did not expect the war between the kingdoms to end in this way.
For I had resolved to exact retribution from the Romans and take revenge on them for the offenses they committed in our land.
But since your mercy has overflowed toward them, I too have agreed to your wishes. Perhaps the gods stirred this in your minds, so that we might not suffer
because of the Romans’ sins. For it is not right to pursue them with the anger that has lasted until today, since they were subjects acting under orders.
For they did what they were commanded. Let us therefore not look at what happened through the tyrannical ruler, but let us look at what has happened today through the wise king,
and at the goodwill he has shown us in his writings. Indeed, it is not only from today that our royal authority owes him gratitude.”
Even before he became king, he had placed our land under many obligations. So you have advised well, and as is fitting.
I too have agreed to your wishes, if indeed you have asked me with such great goodwill for peace between the kingdoms.
Go now and give written proof of your goodwill by pardoning the offenders,
as a memorial of your compassion for the generations that come after us. Then the nobles and dignitaries of Persia went out from Shapur’s presence,
though they were not fully reconciled to what they had been commanded. For they did not wholeheartedly desire peace with the Romans.
For the slaughter the Romans had carried out in the land of the Persians was no small thing.
And if the Persians had not feared what had happened to Julian—who had incurred a terrible sentence of judgment because he had defied the command of the Most High—
the Persians would have inflicted slaughter in the Romans’ own camps worse than the devastation the Romans had inflicted in their land. For this reason the Persians refrained from taking revenge.
They submitted to the king’s will [?] and drew up a document of agreement [?], confirmed by their signatures [?], and gave it to Shapur. When the tyrant received the document they had drawn up,
he spread it out toward heaven. He too sealed it with his signature, raised his eyes toward heaven, and said in a loud voice:
Sun, god of the east, in whose hands the kingdom of mighty warriors stands, be my witness concerning this document: the nobles and dignitaries of my kingdom
have of their own free will called for peace with the Romans, although I myself had no intention of doing this. But for the sake of one
person whose life I desire, I yielded to their petition, agreed to their wishes, and sealed their document.
I pledge myself with oaths before you, Sun, light of the world: from now on we have nothing toward the Romans but love and friendship.
If anyone, after this document, dares to ask us for anything [?] that would cause unrest, and [?], let him be cut apart limb by limb, and let everything he has be given over to plunder.
For we have sanctioned peace between the kingdoms once [?]. When his dignitaries heard his words, they threw themselves down before him
and pleaded with him, saying: [?] King, live forever, and may your crown remain secure on your head! We ask of your fearsome authority
that we too may first present our petition concerning the plundering of our land. Then you may pass judgment on us.
For your divinity knows about its revenues. Even if they compensated us for the plundering of our land from the Euphrates to the Tigris,
the plunder taken from the land would still exceed their gift. And now, my lord the king, since the Romans have obtained such favor and mercy in the eyes of your compassion,

let them at least return to us the fortified city of Nisibis and the [?] to its east as compensation for the plundering of our country, according to the agreement your majesty made. For that fortified city itself
was ours from ancient times, and it was forcibly seized from our fathers in the days of the tyrannical kings who arose among the Romans. [?] Shapur became angry at his dignitaries’ words.
He was furious with them and said to them: It is not you who have dishonored me. I have dishonored myself by stooping to take advice from you,
when I had the right to do everything by my own authority as king. Nevertheless, you wise men,
why, then, are your minds so slow? Do you not understand that a king’s word can never be revoked, and that after a pardon there can be no demand for retribution?
I asked this of them before the document was drawn up, sealed by the laying on of our hands, and confirmed by oaths, with the sun, the god of the world, as witness. And as
knowledgeable and wise men, then, should you not have understood that, after the agreement we made concerning the Romans’ years,
the request you made of me is unjust and improper? Your request has no justification. How can I agree to what you have asked of me,
after the document granting you pardon was proclaimed in the sight of the sun and before all the constellations of heaven, and your mercy was praised among the ranks of the heavenly lights?
Now you have turned back to make a request which, if we agreed to it, would bring us trouble among the ranks above.
Therefore put away your resentment over the things that have happened up to this day, and, like merciful people,
set your hearts on the peace and pardon you have granted. I will ask Caesar for what you have requested, so that, without difficulty, of his own free will and without coercion,
[?] he may fulfill your request. [?] For [?] good [?] and discerning. And not [?] his [?] from [?]. But by force, or coercion, or authority,
we have no claim against the Romans, according to the agreement made before the gods.” And Shapur’s nobles fell silent.
No one dared to ask him about this again. [?] Then Shapur again wrote letters to Jovian
and sent him this message: “The Romans incurred a debt to the Persians greater than their ability to pay, through the tyranny of the king who preceded you.
The territory [?] of your kingdom would not have been enough to pay off the bond of your debt. But the freeborn men and nobles of my kingdom resolved
that the great bond of your debt should be erased with your own blood. But when I examined the matter with the clear eye of my [?],
I judged truly and determined what was right: it is not just before the gods to pursue servants under orders for payment of their dead master’s debt,
but rather to pursue the one who has become heir to his dominion and inherited his crown and throne. He must pay with his own blood for the outrage against our land,

and the servants under his authority should receive pardon. Therefore, if you are resolved and consider it right to secure life for your army through the blood of your own sacrifice, come to me with a few men, dressed in your royal attire,
so that a king may exact satisfaction from a king for the outrage, and the armies of both sides may withdraw from one another in peace.
I swear by my royal crown, by all the gods beneath heaven, and by the mighty god above it,
that the moment you appear before my royal presence, Persia’s anger and [?] will be appeased, and the troops with you will receive pardon through you
and return peacefully to their own territory. Not a single hair from the head of any one of them
will fall to the ground within the territory of our kingdom—not even from those appointed to accompany you.
For your death is sufficient to pay for the outrage committed by your entire army, since your blood is more precious in my royal eyes than that of the four hundred thousand troops
who came down into Persia with Julian. Now consider what answer you will give to what we have sent you.”
For Jovian had been informed secretly and confidentially about the arrangements [?] for peace concerning the Romans in the Persian camp,
and his mind was greatly encouraged. When this document was read aloud to the Roman people, they all raised their voices and wept.
They scattered dust on their heads and cried out sorrowfully to God, saying: Oh, we beg you, good and gracious one! We have sinned and angered you by our sins.
Do not hold against us the sin we have committed against you at this time of distress. Instead, turn toward our repentance and look upon our humility.
For our distress is known to you alone. The harsh affliction surrounding us is not hidden from your eyes.
It is devouring us. But even the lamp that your grace lit for us, so that we might walk by its flame—the winds and storms of Persia have blown upon it, to deprive our eyes of the light of its flame.
We beg you, Lord of times and seasons: do not let the lamp of our camp go out, or let the thick darkness of Assyria’s night settle over us.
Do not let the name of our kingdom perish, or let Persia’s gloomy shadows descend upon us. And since we have no boldness to ask you,
act for the sake of our faithful king, who fears you with all his heart. Grant him compassion in the eyes of the kings of Persia, and stir
in their hearts the intention to seek peace for our kingdom. … And when Jovian saw his troops tormented by sorrow,
he spoke to their hearts and comforted them, saying: Take courage, you who are fainthearted! Take courage and do not be afraid, for the Lord’s hand is not too weak to save.
For what you have now despaired of is held in his hands. Soon deliverance will dawn for you. And if it truly pleases Shapur
that through my own blood there should be [?] for you—for you are weak men and cannot meet the [?] of Persia by force.
His troops turned away from him, feeling [?] and anxious. Jovian went on his way, he and the men with him.
When the lookout stationed by Shapur saw the emperor and the men with him approaching,
he informed Shapur that the emperor had appeared with a few men and baggage for thirty men. The king of Persia was astonished and amazed.
He said to his nobles: This seems very astonishing to me. If the emperor has already given himself up to be captured by the Persians,
his undertaking is a great one, if he has trusted our battalions and entrusted himself to us. While they were wondering about this affair,
the emperor and the men with him came into view of the entire Persian camp. His face was smiling and his expression cheerful.
His lips seemed to express peace. Astonishment came over all the Persian troops when they saw him.
For they had not been certain that Jovian would entrust himself to them. Their zeal immediately subsided, and their fury diminished.
They looked kindly upon the discerning man, for the Lord had granted him compassion, and he found favor and mercy in their eyes.
When Jovian saw the king of Persia and his troops, he dismounted from his horse, as did the men with him.
He took the crown from his head and, like an ordinary man, bent forward and bowed down before Shapur and his entire army.
Through the humility of this discerning man, the Persians’ fury was extinguished, their anger subsided, and zeal was removed from their minds.
In the Persian language they adjured Shapur by the bones of his ancestors not to devise any treacherous scheme
against the emperor, nor to entertain any thought of killing him. Shapur, for his part, was very pleased with their request.
He had not made his intention known to them beforehand. Shapur rose from his throne and came on foot to meet him affectionately.
At last the two kings met and threw their arms around each other’s necks. They wept, embraced, and kissed one another, rejoicing and celebrating.
The armies of Persia surrounded the two kings, while the nobles and dignitaries of Assyria rejoiced and celebrated with them.
They were greatly astonished at the unprecedented event that had taken place between the mighty kings of the Romans and the Persians. They said to one another,
“Nothing like this has ever happened or taken place in all the days of our ancestors.” Shapur said to him, “Now put your crown on your head.

For your humility today has erased the record of the debt your kingdom owed us, which could not have been repaid without the blood of your lives. Through the wisdom of your understanding, our sword has been withdrawn from the Romans,
though it had been sharpened to kill them. And now, through your personal act of homage, our sword has been restrained in its sheath. It will not be drawn again against your people in our lifetime.
So that the nobles and dignitaries of my kingdom may know the favor you enjoy with me, I felt compelled to bring this into the open:
what took place secretly a little while ago, so that everyone may know that I have not loved you without reason or to no purpose.
For I openly acknowledge your kindness, without concealing it. Had you desired my lifeblood and my destruction,
I might already have become a bare skeleton today, and my bones would have been laid in the burial place of my ancestors. Or, had you wished to humiliate and ridicule me in my old age,
I would have been held prisoner in your camp with the [?], and through me the kingdom of mighty warriors would have suffered disgrace.
My life lay in your hands at the village of Beth Nisbat, when I rashly attacked your armies with only a few men. Yet my life was precious in your eyes,
and you granted me my life anew. Nor is this the only kindness for which our kingdom is indebted to you, but also

the kindness shown to the inhabitants of our country. Through the working of your compassion, our desolate land has become inhabited, and through the good counsel of your understanding, the sword was kept from it, and it was not emptied of its inhabitants.
And now, kings and dignitaries of Persia, what kindness could we have offered this man in repayment for his kindness, except what has happened today?” When the Persians heard these things,

they were greatly astonished and groaned inwardly over what had happened to Shapur at the village of Beth Nisbat. They said to one another, “The king of the Romans has proved himself better than our king,
and great is the kindness he has shown him. For who could have removed the disgrace from our kingdom if Shapur had fallen into Roman hands?
They would have subjected him to disgrace in their country and made a spectacle of him in every city of their dominion. And not only that, but something worse than this:
the Romans would have massed against our country and laid our land waste.
Persia would never again have been inhabited in our lifetime. Yet this man’s kindness remained hidden from us until today, because he had not disclosed his deed to us.”

When Shapur saw them discussing this with one another, he asked them what they were discussing and why they were astonished. They said to him, “My lord the king, we are astonished at what happened to you at the village of Beth Nisbat, and we find ourselves asking
about the kindness this man has shown us, for he has still not been repaid as his deeds deserve.
For we should not count it as a kindness to him that he appeared in our camp today and we did not harm him.

Even if our kingdom had owed him no debt of gratitude, we would have had no grounds for mistreating him. A man who came of his own free will to greet your majesty and pay you homage—were we to harm him?”

How much more today, when disgrace has been removed from our kingdom through his hands and he has helped us to victory, should we take upon ourselves the burden of repaying his kindness! For the treasuries of our kingdom
are all insufficient to repay the good debts he has laid upon our land.” Shapur said to them, “Now that this is your wish, consider the matter justly,
and determine what is due to the man. I will gladly grant him what justice requires.” His nobles said to him, “Then, my lord the king, this is what justice requires:

that the man who saved your life and helped our kingdom to victory should be second in your kingdom, a partner in your throne, and a son-in-law to your royal house. Let a record of his kindness be written

in the book of the chronicles of our kingdom for the generations after us. Indeed, duty itself calls for this: that a crown should be bound upon his head within the dominion of our kingdom.” Shapur said to them,
“And what shall we do with the Romans who made him king over them?” The nobles and magnates of Persia said to Shapur,
“If you have no enthusiasm in your heart for what we have said, it is enough for the Romans
that the offenses they committed in our land should be settled by the hostages our kingdom takes from them, and that they should leave our land for their own in peace, unharmed.
Within the dominion of their own kingdom, let them make themselves a king.” Shapur said to them, “You have judged well. But if it seems good to you,
let us first learn what the man wishes and what would satisfy him, and let us agree to that.” When Jovian learned of these things,
he presented a petition to them, saying, “I too am truly the servant of everyone. But in your kindness you have called me a son of your kingdom.
So I ask you for a favor, as I would ask fathers: that in the land of my ancestors, upon the throne of my kingdom, I may reach the end of my life
and lie down with my fathers, and that my bones may mingle with the bones of my departed relatives. This is my entire desire.” Shapur and those with him said to him,
“Now that this is your wish, and this is what satisfies you, we acknowledge that we are indebted to your kindness

in every degree. [?] yourself.” Shapur prepared a great banquet and drinking feast for Caesar and the men with him. He invited the nobles of Persia and the magnates of his kingdom to share his banquet with them. And when
they had eaten and drunk, and their hearts were merry with wine, the nobles of Persia said to Jovian,
“Look, we are granting both things you desire, as [?]. You, in turn, grant at least one thing we desire.”
They said to him, “Make us happy by becoming related to us through marriage. Take a wife from among our daughters, and the power of our kingdom will be entrusted to you.” Jovian said to them,
“Look, this is a drinking feast, and the things being said about me are jokes. Morning is a better time to speak.
Whatever your royal majesty commands us, we will do.” That night Jovian spent the night near the king’s guard,
he and the men with him. Early the next morning he went to Shapur’s tent, where his nobles were gathered around him.
He approached, greeted them, and said to them, “If I have found favor in your eyes, tell me what you wish concerning the things that have happened up to today.
We will willingly obey your command. Allow me to leave your land, for we are staying shamefaced in a land that is not ours.” Shapur said to them,
“Today, since you have come of your own free will to make peace with our kingdom, we have no claim to press against you concerning the war or the plundering of our land.
Instead, return in peace to the camp, you and the men with you. On the third day we will meet at the place where your army is encamped.”
Both sides [?] their thoughts about the unjust things done in our land. Both sides reach a decision and make peace with one another.
The war is ended and hostility is removed. You return in peace to your land and to the dominion of your kingdom.” Jovian bowed and returned to his camp,
he and the men with him. Now it is fitting to marvel and be astonished at Queen Astina, the daughter of pagans,
whose story we mentioned a little earlier in our account. Although she was indeed a daughter of Magi,
she bore in her soul the sorrow of the persecution of the Christians and anguish for their lives over the grievous deaths of God's servants.
For she was a compassionate woman, full of kindness toward everyone. She had found favor and affection in Shapur's eyes, and he loved her deeply. She was a woman
of beauty and lovely appearance. Although he loved her so much, she was afraid of his paganism,
so as to petition him face to face on behalf of the Christian people without an intermediary. When she learned that Jovian was a Christian,
she secretly wrote him a letter, sealed it with her ring, and sent it to him through Zurand, her trusted servant, who was in charge of her entire treasury
and was privy to all his mistress's secrets. She also put other words into his mouth, besides the letter she had written,
and sent him this message: “I have long desired to see you, if only it were possible for my hunger to be satisfied from your fullness,
and for me to quench my thirst from your clear spring and fulfill my desire. But since this is difficult for me,
here, in the letter I have written to you, I have covered and buried my plea like a dead person. For my plea is dead without an intermediary.
Open up before it, then, so that it may be brought to life through you and find mercy in the eyes of Your Majesty. When you do this, my brother, you will also put my compassion at ease,
and your heart's desire will be fulfilled. …” When Jovian heard the words Astina had sent him, he made the sign of the cross over himself
and declined her letter, refusing to accept it. For it seemed to him that [?] a corrupt intention had been devised against him as a trap.
When Zurand saw that the faithful man had turned his face away from his mistress's letter, he was deeply distressed. He answered him sternly, saying,
“It was not right for you, O king of the Romans, to hold in such contempt the writings of the woman who holds authority as queen of Persia.
More than all the other queens, she has found favor and affection in the eyes of the king of kings, and she has great freedom to speak before him.
It is within her power to do you good, just as she has the power to do you harm. So, as a wise king who understands what is proper,
you ought to have read this letter secretly, in private, by yourself. And if what she has sent you seems good to you—
otherwise, you could have returned it to her without reproach.” Zurand's words seemed good to Jovian, and he accepted them fully. He took the letter from him and went
into his tent. When he opened it and read it, he was grieved in his soul and sighed, filling his mouth with lamentation. He reproached himself, saying,
“Alas, we have not even taken to heart the sorrow of our brothers' persecution as this daughter of pagans has!” The letter she sent him
was as follows: [?] “Know, O king of the Romans, that your descent into the land of the merciless was not [?] empty and futile.”
Bring to mind [?] the God of the Christians whom you worship, so that you may go down and visit him in the prison of Persia, where he has been for more than thirty years.
His back is stretched out for lashes, his sides for iron combs, and his limbs for cutting off, together with the body, the parent of the limbs, which is beaten and battered with tortures
and afflictions of many kinds. Do not doubt this: your God is scourged and suffers in his servants.
For truly, when their persecutors say to them, “Deny your God and escape the tortures,”
it is clear to those who understand that the name of their God, which they bear, is scourged in them. And if a king, who is a mortal human being—
if someone strikes his image, those who see it feel insulted, as though the king himself had been struck through it—how much more does God feel the suffering of his servants,
who have given themselves over to torture and death for his name! If, then, you hold fast to your God wholeheartedly, with all your soul,
take the suffering of his servants upon yourself, and help them through the request you make. Perhaps it was for this that God chose you as king
and placed a crown on you in our land: that you might help the people of our land who are oppressed because of the truth of your God,
using the freedom to speak that your God has given you before the King of Kings. Do not shrink from doing good because they are Persians,
for they have become strangers to us, and their name bears witness to this: they are called Nazarenes.
Take care, then, not to neglect helping them and bring the blood of their lives upon yourself. For if I had the power to accomplish this without an intermediary,
I would not have burdened you with these matters. But because this is difficult for me, while it is easy for you, I have informed you in my letters of the harsh persecution
that has arisen against the people of your faith in our dominions. God will hold you accountable for this
if you neglect to help them. For the King of Kings is coming to you on the third day, as he promised you, and he intends to ask you to give him voluntarily
the fortified town of Nisibis and all the territory east of it, on this condition [?]: that you, in the same way, should ask him for whatever your heart desires.
Consider, then, O king, and see what your request is [?]. Weigh the treasures of our kingdom and the cities of our dominion against the love of your God,
and choose what seems [?] to you to outweigh the other. Set your mind on requesting it. But to me, a daughter of the Magi,
it seems that you have no greater request than this: to rescue, through your request, the persecuted and upright servants of God.
For it is no small thing that, in exchange for the one fortified town requested from you, the sword of our kingdom should be lifted from the people of your faith,
that its terror should subside and it should grow rusty [?]—the sword that for forty years has been drawn to slaughter Christians and has still not had its fill of their blood. When you do this,
you will please and comfort your own God, and you will also do me a kindness. For I am a woman overflowing with compassion,
and my insides are already writhing in pain over what has unjustly been done to the servants of God. As for these things I have written to you,
I have arranged for my letters to take my place and urge you on my behalf concerning this. For all my hunger, thirst, and longing are for this:
the day when these things will be removed from our dominion. ... Be at peace, you and your army, and pray for me to your God, that he may absolve my soul of the innocent blood shed in our dominion.
who had done no wrong. This is the copy of the letter sent to Jovian by Queen Astina through Zorand the eunuch.
