He, in turn, composed a reply to her letter and sent her words of faith suited to her repentance and capable of strengthening her understanding.
But consider the faith of this discerning man: although he had firmly resolved in his heart to do this without Astina’s favor, in the letter he wrote
to her he nevertheless praised her and extolled her compassion. In his letter he thanked her as though she had been his good reason for this action.
Many things happened and were done in this war, whose history your love urged me to write down for you.
We have passed over many things that were not relevant, and from the multitude we have recorded a very few things worthy of remembrance, setting down their memory in this book
for those who enjoy studying accounts like these. But so that you may know, my dear friend, how the war between the kingdoms came to an end,
we have considered and resolved to bring our history to a close by recounting everything briefly, and to refrain from a lengthy proliferation of words.
… And on the third day Shapur appeared before the Romans’ camp, as he had promised, with his vast army,
accompanied by the nobles and magnates of Persia, and pitched his camp opposite.
Both kings came out of their camps and approached one another between the camps of the two sides, to consult with one another about peace between the kingdoms.
Orders were given for the nobles and magnates of both kings to come to the kings’ council, and this was done.
Both kings and their magnates sat down between the two camps. They consulted with one another about entering into negotiations and reaching a settlement.
There was extensive discussion between them about the wrongs committed in the territory of both sides. They reckoned up the places Shapur had devastated in Roman territory
in the days of Constantine’s sons, and the places Julian had devastated in Persian territory. The Roman side slightly exceeded the Persian side.
Nisibis was given to the Persians for a hundred years, together with all the territory east of it. This was done voluntarily, without compulsion. For Shapur said to Jovian:

“Although Nisibis has been given to us as justice requires—first, because of the plundering of our land, and second, because the fortified city was ours of old and was forcibly seized from our people—
nevertheless, even though this is so, in the love you have desired us to have for one another, I have accepted as a favor this deed
that has been done, so that I owe favor in return for favor and will repay gift with gift.
I swear to you by all the gods, and by Hormizd, the god of heaven, whose dominion rules over all the gods:

do not let grief over Nisibis enter your heart. Instead, ask for whatever your soul desires from our territory, and it will be given to you in exchange for the fortified city taken from you.” … Jovian said to him:
“What is there in the world that a person holds as dear as his own life, O king of kings, my brother?” … Shapur said, “Nothing at all.”
Jovian said, “If, then, I have entrusted you, my lord the king, with my life, which is dearer to me than anything, and have placed it in your hands,
and have not been distressed over Nisibis, would you suppose that your request has distressed me? Know, then, my lord the king, and believe my word:
if you had wished to ask us for everything from the sea as far as the River Tigris, which separates the territories, your request would not have distressed me. For I am a son of your kingdom.”
And the father has authority over his son's inheritance. Now the nobles and magnates of Persia, when they saw the goodwill of the king of the Romans,
raised their voices in praise of him. For a long time they acclaimed him in the Persian language. They called him a son of their kingdom and said,
“As a son, ask for as much as you wish from your father's inheritance, and it will be given to you. Do not take the sorrow over Nisibis upon yourself.”
When they had finished their praises, Jovian spoke with them and said to them, “You have shown your goodwill well today.
We likewise hold your kingdom in honor, and we feel no sorrow in our hearts over the surrender of Nisibis.
And through the love we have for one another, what is ours is yours, [?] ours. And as for your urging us to ask for a gift,
our request of you is a small one. 2. Your dominion will not be diminished by it, for we do not seek to ask for territory in exchange for territory, or a city in exchange for a city,
but only mercy and relief for those oppressed by your hostility. By this your kingdom will be praised all the more, and your compassion will be acclaimed.” ... Shapur said to him, “What is
your request? Tell me, and it is granted to you from this moment.” ... Jovian said, “My lord the king, this is my request: for the number of years for which Nisibis has been given to your kingdom,
let peace reign over the Christians in your dominion, and let the harsh, merciless sentence be revoked
that Your Majesty has imposed upon them. Let no one stir up persecution against them during this period of one hundred years
for which Nisibis has been given to the Persians. Rather, let them live peacefully in your dominion, with no one harming them. Through the care of your compassion,
let their churches be restored to them, and with the freedom you grant, let them openly perform the prescribed order of their worship. When you do this,
we will be indebted to your kindness all our days.” ... Shapur said to him, “And is this your entire request, king of the Romans?”
... Jovian said, “It is indeed greater and more glorious in my eyes than all gifts, for they are my brothers in the faith,
and I do not desire their destruction.” Then Shapur wrote and sent orders to the regions of his dominion that persecution of the Christians should cease in every region under his authority.

“For this is our will: that they should receive kindness and mercy in the eyes of all who fear us, just as they have received kindness and mercy in the eyes of Your Majesty. From now on, their places of assembly also

shall be restored to them. And if [?] any have been uprooted and demolished through the zeal of the Magi, they shall be rebuilt and restored. The expenses of their construction shall be paid from the treasuries of our kingdom until they are completed. If anyone has seized or plundered anything from the Christians,
he shall willingly restore it to them and thereby preserve his life. But if anyone acts defiantly after this command and persists in plundering the Nazarenes,
he shall be cut apart limb by limb, and everything he owns shall be given over to plunder. ... We have also decided, because of the love and kinship we have with the king of the Romans,
to show him favor because he is a Christian, and to exempt from taxation the members of the covenant who are in the churches of the Christians
throughout the entire dominion of our kingdom. The bones of their departed shall also be handed over to them, so that they may build memorial tombs over them,
according to the custom among the Romans. I, Shapur, king of Persia, son
of Hormizd the Elder, [?], have issued this command and decreed this ruling: the kings who come after me shall not be permitted to dissolve the peace I have established between the kingdoms,
or to stir up and renew persecution against the Christians before one hundred years have passed since the surrender of Nisibis.”
For this was the will of Hormizd, the great and mighty god, and of the Sun and Fire, the gods after him: that there should be peace between the kingdoms for a hundred years.
From now on, the Persians are permitted to exchange goods with the Romans, to buy and sell, and to trade with one another.
May the peace of our kingdom endure for many years. ... Then the Romans raised their voices in praise of Shapur.
They praised him for a long time, and from their camps they sent him flattering cries that captivated his heart.
They called him the father of the kingdom. And when the tyrant’s ears had had their fill of their praises,
both kings rose from their thrones and returned to the camp with the nobles accompanying them. Then, on the following day,
at dawn, according to the secret arrangement made between the two kings, a drum sounded between the camps.
The troops of both kings laid aside their weapons, and immediately all the companies of Persian and Roman musicians began to play their various instruments.
There was joy and rejoicing in the camps of both sides, and they were greatly amazed at the change that had taken place.
They clapped their hands, stamped their feet, and cheered one another. The sound of their rejoicing could be heard far away. Both kings led their armies forward,
and the two sides approached one another, their mouths full of laughter and their tongues full of thanksgiving. They made peace and were reconciled with one another.
One embraced another, and another kissed his fellow. And this had been so since ancient times. After these things had happened,
Jovian said to Shapur, “If you wish, let the memory of this day be set down in writing for those who come

after us, together with the things that have happened and taken place up to today.” Shapur said, “It is not advisable, my son, nor is it fitting that this document be drawn up in the territory under our rule,
lest many people suppose that Nisibis was taken from you by force because of the distress of the confinement in which you were held in our land. Instead, let us go out to the border,
and let this document be drawn up there. Let it be confirmed by our signatures and those of our nobles, so that everyone may know
that after the two sides were reconciled and made peace, and ate and drank together, Nisibis was given to us in return for the plundering of our land, by the free consent of the Romans,
with their [?] set, and acknowledging our kindness.” The proposal pleased Caesar, and he agreed to it. Both kings departed from Beth Aramaye to go to the border,

with their troops in procession and their numerous armies. As Shapur passed through the land in his dominion that the Romans had conquered, he saw that the land was inhabited and bustling with its people.
He leaned down from his horse and, with both hands, expressed his gratitude for Jovian’s kindness. The inhabitants of the region, too, who had willingly come to greet these kings,
expressed their gratitude for Jovian’s kindness before Shapur their king, and before the nobles and dignitaries of Persia.
Through this very thing, the Persians’ affection for Jovian grew greater still. When they came to the border,
they found Nisibis emptied of its inhabitants, for the entire population of Nisibis had migrated to the region of Edessa
as soon as it heard that the fortified city had been given to the Persians. Both kings renewed the covenant with oaths concerning peace between the kingdoms.
At the border they drew up a document concerning Nisibis and concerning peace for the churches in Persian territory for a hundred years.
How an agreement was made between the kings, and Nisibis was handed over to the Persians, emptied of its inhabitants.
In the month of August in the year six hundred and seventy-four according to the Greek reckoning, Jovian succeeded, through his understanding, in making peace between the two powerful kingdoms.
Through his wisdom he managed to bring his armies out of the confinement in which they had been trapped, without hardship or loss. And although he had not yet
set foot in the territory of his kingdom, news of the deliverance of the churches was spreading throughout the land of the Romans.
For his command went out to the territory of his kingdom that the churches should be opened and that peace should abound for their children.
The holy priests who had been driven from their cities because of the truth of their faith were to return with honor to their churches,
together with God's holy covenant community. In his letters he authorized the bishops of the churches to put seals and stamps on the treasuries of the idols
and on the treasury of the teaching of error, until he returned safely to his territory and restored to the churches the treasures that had been taken from them
by Julian in his madness. One must marvel at the faith of the faithful king: before entering the territory under his authority and attending to affairs in his kingdom,
his first concern was for the church of God, and he gave her support through his letters.
He strengthened her and lifted up her head. Her horn grew strong and was [?] above all religions, and her heel trampled the neck of her accusers.
For the news of the Christian king's coming threw all the forces of error into confusion,
especially the people of the crucifiers. Just when they thought they had prospered and their horn had been raised,
their joy left them, their horn was brought low, and their spirits fell. What is said in the psalm was fulfilled in them: “They were suddenly filled with astonishment.”
Give thanks to the Good One, who judged mercifully and did not neglect to discipline us, but looked upon the humiliation of his church and took the wicked king from among the living.
He brought her deliverance through a faithful king. Now the blessed legions of the faithful and steadfast Romans who were stationed in Edessa,
when they learned that Jovian had reached the frontier, put on white clothes, took gifts, and went down to meet him and gladden him. When the discerning king saw them,
he [?] them wholeheartedly and received them affectionately, acknowledging them as friends in his kingdom.
They told him about the faith of the people of Edessa, and how they had given themselves over to death
for the truth of their Creator. Jovian cherished them in his heart, intending to do them good
in keeping with what their labor for the faith deserved. Since he had decided to travel up to his royal city by the desert road, so as not to burden the cities on his journey,
he wrote letters of encouragement and peace to the people of Edessa, thanking their city,
extolling and praising their faith, and promising them on oath in his letters: “If God gives me time, and I sit peacefully on the throne of my kingdom,
I will remember your city and will not forget it. I will make it greater and stronger than all the cities in my territory.
I will do good and generous things for you, as your deeds deserve. For we must not fail to reward your labor for the faith, you who gave yourselves over to death.”
As for how deeply my soul longed to come to you, if it were possible!
But duty restrained me from doing this, so that we would not throw the city into turmoil with the great number of troops accompanying us.

But if the Lord is willing to let me dwell peacefully in the territory of my kingdom, my pledges and the promises I made in writing to your city will soon be fulfilled. Be sound in spirit and steadfast in your faith...
When the people of Edessa learned from the king’s letters that he did not intend to pass through their city, they were deeply saddened and greatly distressed.
For they wanted him to come and longed to see him. They sent him five men from among [?] the city’s prominent citizens,
to ask him to come to Edessa, so that through his hands it might offer to God the offering it had vowed on his behalf while he was in the land of his enemies.
When those sent to him arrived, Jovian welcomed them gladly and received them with great honor. He kept them with him,
and praised the city before the nobles of his kingdom, saying, “There is no other city in my dominion as dear to me as Edessa, or one that has found favor and affection
in my eyes as it has—that is, because of its true faith.” The men who had been sent to him said, “Then, my lord the king,
if our city has truly and sincerely found favor and affection in the eyes of Your Majesty, surely you will not frustrate the faithful city’s pride and expectation,
and turn aside and pass it by! Day after day it watches and waits for you to brighten its face with your coming,
and to take pride in you before the pagan cities around it. And if the wicked king, because he saw that Harran clung to his paganism and was steeped in his madness,
turned back from the road he was traveling and turned aside to that city of debauched people [?], and held a festival there for his idols and a feast for his carved images,
and the city of carved images took pride in him, the mad king, for a period of time, how much more fitting is it today that the faithful city should take pride in you—
the city that is marked with your image, stamped with your faith, and constantly looking to you to enter it and hold there a joyful festival celebrating peace for the churches,
and to offer there offerings and sacrifices of thanksgiving to Christ, who bound the crown upon you and through your hands granted peace to his churches.
But so that you may learn, my lord the king, how closely the people of our city cling to the divine love of affection for you,
let Your Divinity ask the faithful Romans who stayed with us how deeply our city longs to see you.
For it is certainly true that the people of Edessa thirst even more than a blind person thirsts for light,
waiting for the time when they will receive the radiance of Your Majesty. For constant prayer is offered to God in our church for the peace of your reign,
and that your years over our territory may be prolonged, because of the orthodoxy of your true faith. Still more astonishing are the young children of Edessa,
who have left off studying their books at school; and the church hymns that learned men composed in honor of the orthodoxy of your faith—
these are what the children constantly study in their school. When their teachers dismiss them, they first go outside the gates of our city,
the one that leads here to the border [?], and bow three times before the exalted crown of Your Majesty. Then they disperse from their groups to go
to their families’ homes. And not only the children, but also the men and women and all our fellow Christians in our city have no other thought or concern.
But only that your Majesty should appear to them and to a people who long so deeply for your coming—this is their entire request. Far be it from your compassion,
my lord emperor, to deny their request yourself! Rather, let our city, rejoicing and celebrating, welcome your Majesty with love. ... Now Jovian, because he was a sensitive man,
when he heard these things from the men who had been sent to him, his eyes filled with tears, and he wanted to weep. He went into his tent and wept.
When his weeping had eased the tears in his eyes, he washed his face and came out to them, saying kindly, “It was for the welfare of your city
and of our entire realm that I decided to travel through the outlying territory of the nations, so that we would not burden the cities of our realm in any way.
But now that I have learned what you wish, I will carry out your wish and fulfill your desire.” He summoned Arsaces, the commander of his army,
and entrusted to him the entire Roman army, apart from twenty thousand troops who remained with the emperor.
He sent him ahead to Constantine’s imperial city, by the northern road leading up from the frontier.
He himself, with the cavalry force that remained with him, decided to come to Edessa. When Edessa received the news of his coming,
it rejoiced, celebrated, and was glad. Its streets were clothed in white, and its porticoes shone with silks. The city’s gates too, both outside and inside,
were adorned with doorway hangings combining every color. Throughout all the streets and porticoes of Edessa,
ropes were stretched in close rows for the many lamps and lanterns that the people of Edessa had prepared,
so that this faithful man’s entry into their city would be accompanied by a splendid procession of light. For the arrival of this discerning man was very precious to them.
Just as though a divine light had dawned upon them, so the news of the Christian emperor’s coming dawned upon them and made them rejoice. They thoughtfully took upon themselves
the burden of serving him. They had assigned skilled craftsmen to the palace of the house of Abgar, so that, with great care, they would prepare quarters for him worthy of the honor of attending him.
Also, outside the city’s eastern gate, through which the emperor was to enter, at a distance of two stadia from it,
they erected a canopy for him of fine linen and purple cloth, beautiful to behold and finely made by skilled craftsmen.
Above the columns supporting the canopy, around its lower edge resting on the columns, the craftsmen had placed
three rows of gold and silver apples. At the very top of the canopy a gold cross was fixed,
which had been made with painstaking care for King Abgar and had been mounted in his royal palace during his lifetime. Inside the canopy,
a large platform had been set up for the emperor’s seat, so that he could be seen by all the people of the city. ... When the city had been decorated and adorned,
the leaders of the church and the city’s officials dressed in white and went out to meet him, to welcome him while he was still a great distance away.
When they reached him and he saw them rejoicing and exulting, resplendent in their clothing,

he recognized from their appearance that they were people of Edessa. When they approached to bow before him, he leaned down on his horse and acknowledged their homage with his hand. He spoke with them as though with his brothers and relatives, smiling and cheerful as he said,
“Because of your request [?], I have imposed great labor and endless trouble on you—and not on you alone, but on the other cities as well.”
which lie along the route of our passage. “And this, then, is what you wanted?” The bishop of Edessa said to him:
“We ask justice of your royal authority. My lord the king must not say such a thing. May Christ, who dwells in you, reveal to you
that the cities long for the time when your righteous rule will dawn upon them more than a blind man longs to see the light.
For all the regions of your dominion are truly Christian, even though for a considerable time, out of fear of the tyrant king, they were drawn into his paganism
and submitted to his will. Your Divinity can learn the truth of these things from the letters sent to us from Antioch
and from the other cities situated along the route of your journey, my lord the king. And, as to a city [?] that had found favor and mercy in the eyes of Your Majesty,
they wrote letters of entreaty and sent them to us, so that we too, like servants who have found favor and mercy in the eyes of their master,
might offer entreaty and petition to Your Divinity on their behalf, so that they might not be deprived of the joy of your arrival. Truly, however, my lord the king,
all the regions under your royal dominion cannot offer sufficient thanks for your service to righteousness
and the wholehearted labor of your faith on behalf of the churches of God, and your sorrowful weeping over the persecution and affliction of our people,
and your repeated groans over the subjection and humiliation of our order, and your constant prayers over the dishonor and mockery of our habit.
What need is there for more? For even in the land of our enemies your faith has done its work and granted a hundred years of peace to the churches of Persia
and well-being to their children. Your wisdom has succeeded in bringing reconciliation between our two mighty kingdoms.

And after these victories achieved by your faith, and the good and splendid things for which our kingdom is indebted to you, do you suppose, my lord the king, that your passage is a burden to the cities of your dominion?
Do not, then, my lord the king, let this enter your mind again. You have become a source of great joy to the cities through your arrival.”
Jovian, however, gave thanks to God for these things, for pride was deeply hateful to him,
and arrogance was repugnant in his eyes. For he was a humble man, and his humility came from choice, not from natural disposition.
But consider, discerning one, how far he showed the good will of his humility: he carefully regulated the pace of his horses
according to the pace that the mount on which the bishop of Edessa was riding had the strength to manage,
so that he could carry on a conversation with him. For he was telling him what God had done through his hands for the churches of God that are
in Persia. While they were talking and traveling along the road, the nobles and leading men of Harran came toward them to approach and bow before him.
But when he saw that there was no one from the ranks of the church with them, he turned his face away from them in anger
and dismissed them from his presence. He did not allow them to approach and bow before him.
Instead, through an interpreter, he questioned them about the clergy of the church of Harran, asking what had prevented them from coming to greet the king.
They, fearful and trembling, answered and confessed, and did not deny it.
Many of them, it is said, because they had yielded to the will of Emperor Julian out of fear of his decree, moved elsewhere.
For they were ashamed to be seen again in our city by those who knew them. The few of them who endured and stood firm in their faithfulness
were banished to the mines and to harsh, remote places. Their appointed time to return home had not yet been completed when Jovian became angry with them and said:
“I myself remember the evils that the people of Harran committed against God's innocent servants. With words of praise and extravagant flattery,
which they offered to the tyrant full of filth, they captivated the mind of the deranged emperor, and he was induced to slander them. Through their assaults on the churches,

the church's treasures were taken away, and it was deprived of its worship. The honored priests who had been brought up in it, because they had not abandoned their steadfastness and denied their faith,
were banished to the copper mines by the decree of wretched Julian. But now I will exact vengeance from them for the crimes they committed,
and I will bring their paganism down upon their own heads.” He ordered them to be put in irons and sent in chains to Edessa,
so that their interrogation and sentencing would take place there. But the Edessans who were with the emperor asked him not to send them to their city. For they said to the emperor:
“If Your Majesty sends these men to Edessa, before they are interrogated and their sentence is pronounced,
their destruction in our city will be very terrible, and the Edessans will consign
them to the flames. For Edessa burns as though with fire in its zeal against Harran, because of the paganism of its inhabitants.
For they did not begin practicing paganism only under Julian. Even in the days of Christian emperors,
their paganism lay hidden within them like a viper in its hole, although fear of the Christian emperors kept them from revealing it.
And now, my lord emperor, if you are willing and it seems good to you, let these men be sent to the city of Constantina,
and let their interrogation and sentencing take place there.” But some men from Tella who were with the emperor argued fiercely with the Edessans.
They accused them before the emperor, saying, “What is this audacity that the Edessans have assumed,
that they should improperly give orders to Your Divinity? And how could anyone not be angry at the scheme the Edessans have devised against our town?
They rolled this heap of weeds out of their own city and threw it away, and like troublesome men they have thrown it onto our city—or so they thought!
But far be it! May the feet of these unclean and defiled troublemakers never tread within our town!
Like blind guides, they have become a stumbling block to their own city. Let them be sent to that very city of theirs, with irons upon them and bound in chains,
and let their trial and interrogation take place there, so that the punishment of these defiled men may strike fear and trembling into all the inhabitants of their city.”
The proposal pleased the emperor, and he did as they said. He sent them in chains to Harran, pending his dispatch of a judge to hear their case.
When a certain question concerning the faith of the church arose, the emperor praised Edessa highly, saying:
“Although today, because of fear of our authority, faith in Christ has spread uniformly throughout our dominion,”
But Edessa, he said, gave greater proof of faith than all the other cities. For at the time when paganism broke out and openly revealed itself,
and the truth of the faith was concealed for fear of the wicked king’s command, and the cities succumbed and submitted to his error, blessed Edessa, the city
of Christ, remained steadfast in its truth. Its faith shone openly like the sun, and it did not shrink from the onslaught of the tyrant’s fury.
Nor was it frightened by his letters. Instead, it scorned him for his writings and mocked his paganism.
It dipped the letter he had sent it in the filth of its menstrual discharge. And when he again made many threats to destroy it and set his face toward entering it in anger,
it poured contempt on him in the letter it wrote to him, pelting him with insults as though with stones. Fury seized the madman, and he swore by his idols that he would not enter it.
And who would not praise the anointed city in which Christ has placed his blessing, and accord it honor? And if it received kindness and mercy in its Maker’s eyes,
how much more should it be exalted and honored in our lowly eyes! While he was praising Edessa at length, he raised his eyes and saw it before him.
He stretched out his right hand, blessed it, and made the sign of the cross over it, saying: May the Lord bless your surroundings and make your inhabitants fruitful and numerous.
May your name become great, and may your faith be praised throughout the world. May the Lord give me time to reward you for the labor of your faith.
I will raise your head, strengthen you, and place you above all the cities of my dominion. I will set apart an offering to the Lord on your behalf,
when he grants this to me and I sit upon the throne of my kingdom. When Jovian had finished blessing Edessa,
the Edessenes who were with him approached and asked him to send them ahead of him. They said to Jovian: We have learned, my lord the king,
that a great many people have willingly gathered in our city from the whole region of Mesopotamia, to welcome your arrival and pay homage to you.
If, therefore, it pleases your Divinity, command your servants to go ahead of you, so that we may arrange the crowds in our city and separate the men from the women,
and the young men and children from the old men and old women, as well as the pregnant women together with those carrying children in their arms,
so that the great crush of the densely packed crowds may not mingle any distress with our city’s joy when your blessed arrival dawns upon them.
We have also learned this for certain: the Edessenes have even brought the sick out on litters beyond the gates of our city, so that they may have relief from their suffering
when the faith of your righteous reign overshadows them. The king agreed to these men’s request
and sent them ahead of him to announce his arrival. As for the glory, pomp, and cries of praise with which Edessa welcomed the faithful king,
we have too little time to describe them as they deserve. For God brought great joy to Edessa through the arrival of the righteous man.
And wondrous were the things that took place there during these days of celebration that Jovian set apart for God,
a celebration of joy at the peace of the churches. For on the very first day of the celebration, God performed a manifest sign through the hands of the faithful king.
For there was a believing woman from the city itself whose name was Mary, [?] well-known and distinguished people.
She had been bedridden with a severe illness for eight years. Because of the severity of her illness, she constantly asked for death for herself.
It happened on the first day of the feast, while her servants were carrying her in a sick person's chair to take her to the church, that she might ask in her prayer for death for herself.
And behold, the king met her on the way. Caesar's attendants rebuked her and pushed her away from his presence.
But when the righteous king saw her suffering from her illness, he felt sorry for her and ordered them to bring her near him.
For he supposed that she was asking him for some gift. But the sensible woman considered within herself
and said, “Perhaps this is a summons from God.” When her servants brought her before him, he asked her what she wanted.
But because of the pains and afflictions that surrounded her, she could barely manage, with great effort, to answer the king.
In a weak voice she pleaded with him, saying, “I beg you, merciful king, full of kindness:
have mercy on me and relieve me of this affliction I am in. For it has tormented me for eight years, and it has still not had its fill
of my limbs.” The king was startled by these words and said to her, “Woman, why have you spoken this blasphemy
against my lowly self? I am a sinful man. Had your request been known to me, I would not have allowed you to appear before me.
For I am not a prophet, that I should free you from your illness, nor am I an apostle, that I should give you healing.” The woman said to him,
“My lord, I beg you: I am not asking for healing. For I know that my sins make me unworthy of this.
But because I have learned about you from many people, my lord, that you are a righteous and holy man, and that your prayer is heard and accepted before God,
my distress begs you, and my misery pleads with you: pray to God for me, that he may quickly bring my life to an end.
For I have become miserable from illness, and my soul has been tormented by affliction.” But he, discerning and full of kindness,
felt sorry for her, reassured her heart, and said to her, “Go, woman, and put your hope in God. Do not give up hope of your recovery.
For it is within God's power to come to your aid quickly in his mercy.” He comforted her and dismissed her from his presence, and entered the house of the Lord,
grieving and bearing in his soul the suffering of the stricken woman. He ordered a haircloth to be spread for him before the steps of the sanctuary.
His servants did as they had been commanded, and the righteous king earnestly approached to labor in prayer for the stricken woman.
He bent down and placed his head between his knees, and pleaded with God with discernment. When the time came for the reading of the Scriptures,
the bishops, observing protocol, waited for the king to rise from his prayer, so that they could then go up to the seats on the platform. When the king continued at length in his prayer,
the bishops were astonished and asked one another, “What can be the reason for the king's earnestness?”
But one of the bishops, whose name was John, who had met the king as he was entering the church, put his companions at ease by saying,
“A stricken woman, whom illness has tormented for eight years, presented a petition to him as he was entering the church, asking that he should offer
a petition to God on her behalf, so that she might have relief from her affliction. This, my brothers, is truly the king's concern.”
The bishops who were his companions, nine in number, had learned from Bishop John the reason for the king’s concern.
They were greatly astonished and marveled at the discernment of this faithful man. They reproached themselves over it, saying:
“If a king, who is a layman and is not charged with responsibility for the sick and infirm, has humbled himself so deeply before God because of the suffering of a wretched woman,
how much more ought we to take upon ourselves the burden of the flock entrusted to us, praying without ceasing and pleading without growing weary,
for the sick, the afflicted, and those who are suffering terribly!” The bishops took counsel with one another, and that day they did not go up to their seats on the platform.
They remained bowed in prayer until the time for the reading of the Gospel of our Savior ... This whole supplication had become known.
Everyone was earnestly offering a petition to God on her behalf, that he might give her relief. When the time came for the priest to stand at the altar and consecrate the offering,
Jovian poured out his soul in prayer before God on the haircloth upon which he was standing.
He prayed with deep concern and pleaded before God for that woman, that she might have relief from her suffering.
When he had risen from his prayer and received communion, and the service had ended, he gave gifts to the churches,
with royal generosity, and also to the crowds of the city who were gathered in the church and in its outer and inner courtyards.
To them too he gave substantial gifts, so that they might rejoice and enjoy themselves at the joyful festival celebrating the peace of the churches ... As he moved to leave the church,
the congregations of the church raised their voices in praise of the faithful king ... For a long time they praised him and extolled his faith.
As he was going out through the church door, the afflicted woman met him. With tears and sobs she pleaded with him. When he saw her, he did not turn away from her, but
motioned to the crowds of the city and quieted them, so that her petition could be heard. She pleaded with him, saying:
“I beg you, my lord, the pride and glory of the church: do not let me be excluded from the joy that has come throughout your dominion.
Let me too rejoice and delight in the wedding feast of the church, in which the cities and villages of your dominion are rejoicing!” ... Jovian said to her:
“Believe me, woman: if the concern in my heart for you were known to you, you would not have pressed me so much with your petition.
For you ought to understand clearly that what you ask lies in God’s hands, not in human hands.
My daughter, I have done what lay within my power as a mortal human being: I have offered prayer and supplication to God on your behalf.
It is now for his divinity to visit you in his mercy, if it is his will. For he alone has abundant compassion for what he has formed,
and from him help flows to those in need. Plead with him and ask him to help you.” ... That woman said to him, “I beg you, my lord,
you too, together with God, do what lies within your power to attend to my distress.” That faithful and upright man, thinking that she was asking him for something to meet her material needs,
gave her generous gifts. But she would not accept them from him, for she said to him, “This is not what I am looking for, my lord the king.
Nor do I have any need of it. There is just one thing I ask of you in faith: that I may have relief from my afflictions.” ... Jovian said to her:
“Woman, I have already told you once that what you ask rests in God’s hands.” The woman said to him, “Indeed, I see, my lord,
that the Lord’s hand is with you, and that within your right hand is hidden the right hand that gives health to the sick and healing to those in pain.
Why, my lord the king, do you withhold healing from me? Just stretch out your hand, and I will be healed of my pain.” ... These bishops were astonished
and marveled at the woman’s faith. They begged the king not to deny the believing woman’s request. For they said to him, “Do not look lightly
upon this matter, my lord the king. Perhaps this is from the Lord, who wishes everyone to know openly
that the Lord’s hand is with you to heal.” Jovian said to them, “Why, my brothers, when you yourselves [?] have rightly received the gift of healing,
and, like faithful stewards, have been entrusted with the keys of the heights and the depths, have you now placed, as a loan, the gift entrusted to you
upon a weak and wretched human being? I alone know my sins and am troubled by my shortcomings.” ... The bishops said to him,
“Far be it from your righteous Majesty that anything at all of sin’s defilement should touch you.
Rather, with your faith pure and your righteousness clear, you will appear with unveiled face before Christ when he is revealed at his coming,
when the Church acknowledges your kindness before her Lord: you became her help in her trial and sprinkled upon her the blessed dew of your blessed promises.
You kept the tyrant’s fury away from her, and through the mouths of her children she continually offers prayer to God on your behalf,
that he may prolong your years upon your royal throne, for her peace and that of her children.” ... At these words, Jovian
gave thanks and praise to God, who had granted deliverance to his Church through his hand. ... But the woman did not stop wearying him with her pleading.
He, however, faithful and steadfast, was not puffed up by her petition, but comforted her with gentle words, saying to her,
“Woman, why do you weary yourself in vain over this, asking me for things beyond my power? Call upon God instead of me,
so that he may send you healing for your suffering. For difficult things are easy for him.” The woman said to him,
“Is this too beyond your power, my lord the king, merely to stretch out your hand toward me in my distress? Or have you perhaps recoiled in disgust from my pain

and drawn away from me so as not to come near me? Yet Christ, who dwells in you, did not shrink from the foul disease of the suffering woman who approached him. And if that beautiful and radiant Holy of Holies
did not recoil from a woman—that pure and radiant Holy of Holies did not recoil from an afflicted woman—was it right for you, my lord the king, to recoil from your servant?
Far be it from you, my lord, to do this, for you are a compassionate man.” Then Jovian felt the force of the woman’s words and was moved. In the fervor of his faith,
he approached her, stretched out his hand to her, and said to her, “My daughter, may the hidden right hand that took on our visible form and gave health to the sick
visit you in mercy through the hands of our lowliness and give you health.” At the very words of this discerning man, she gained strength despite her illness and stood up.
Her complexion brightened, and she became well, as though illness had never touched her. She gave thanks and praise to God, who had visited her in his mercy.
She knelt and bowed before the faithful king and kissed his feet, weeping. But he pushed her away from his feet, saying,
“Offer thanks to God, my daughter, for it is he who has visited you in his mercy, not I.” ... Then the people of Edessa raised their voices in praise of him.
They poured out praises to him, and cries of praise of every kind were offered to him by the crowds of the city.
So that the people of Edessa scarcely allowed him to reach his lodging that day.
But the faithful man was embarrassed by these cries of empty praise, and he feared that, because of this passing and perishing worldly glory,
he might be deprived of the everlasting glory toward which he looked. ... God performed many other deeds through the hands of this faithful and steadfast man,
but there is too little time for our account to extend to them all. These few out of many, whose memory we have recorded for those bound together in love,
are enough for them to learn that the hand of the Lord was with Jovian in all his deeds.
He was a man who loved and cherished God with all his heart and all his soul, kept his commandments, fulfilled his wishes, and did what was pleasing before him all his days.
He walked in the ways of Constantine and did not turn aside from them, either to the right or to the left. He exalted and honored the churches,
and gave them back the treasures that Julian the wicked had taken from them. He exempted God's holy clergy from taxation and wrote letters of peace and reconciliation,
of pardon, honor, and exaltation to all the churches in his dominion. [?] He wrote letters to other kingdoms
concerning the peace of the churches and the relief of Christians. He cleansed the Roman Empire of the pollution of pagan sacrifices.
He overturned its altars, uprooted their shrines, and persecuted false teachings. He demolished their meeting places and brought their treasures into the treasuries of the church.
He imposed heavy taxes on the people who crucified Christ. He issued orders concerning the nobles of Rome who had been persecuted for Christ,
that their property should be restored to them in double measure by those who had taken over their offices after them. But those faithful and steadfast men
would not consent to receive more than they had possessed. Jovian sent for them and brought them from Rome with great honor.
He accorded them honor as people more worthy of honor than himself. He would kiss the places where their hands and feet had been bound. But they pleaded with him
not to empty the labor of their faith of its value through temporary honor. Jovian, however, would not consent to their request,
but compelled them, against their will, to become the heads of his entire senate.
... Jovian loved to walk in the straight paths of the Lord and to practice justice and righteousness throughout the whole period of his rule.
He reigned for eight months after he sat on Constantine's throne in the city of Byzantium.
The empire was put in order under his hands, his fame spread throughout all the lands, and peace reigned in the churches in his days,
as in the days of Constantine. When his spirit was glad and his soul rejoiced in the deliverance that God had accomplished through his hands for his churches,
he petitioned God in prayer, saying, “Oh, I beg you, mighty Lord, God of my fathers, if I have found mercy in your sight,
now that my eyes have seen the deliverance of your church, bring your servant's days to an end in peace. And after me, my Lord, spread the wings of your mercy over your church.”
But God, who is always with his worshipers, hears their petitions, and fulfills their wishes, heard the prayer of the righteous king and granted the petition of the
faithful king. His death took place on his bed of rest, in the year six hundred and seventy-five according to the reckoning of the Greeks. He died righteously.
He was buried with the honor his conduct deserved. Now I, the lowly servant of Jesus Christ, Aploris, the trusted servant of King Jovian,
made copies of these accounts for the virtuous friend of God, Mar Abdiel, abbot of Sandron, the town.
This discerning man, who loves learning, asked us through his [?] to write down for him the history, sequence, and manner
of this war that took place in our days. He asked us to begin our history with the sorrowful death of the faithful Constantine
and continue until the life of Jovian, the restorer of the churches, came to an end. We fulfilled the request of the pure priest,
who holds fast to a chaste way of life. We wrote these accounts in their proper sequence and order, one after another, just as things happened and took place,
neither adding to nor taking away from what happened before us and what we witnessed.
But we refrained from recounting the history of the unjust and wicked things done in Emesa, through the agency of Julian the tyrant,
during the few days when he interrupted his journey and turned aside to it. This was because he had heard about the splendor of the church sanctuary
that Constantine, the lover of Christ, had built there—may his memory be blessed forever, amen—to provoke the jealousy of the pagans,
who boasted of the great temple built for their idols on the height of their city. On this pretext, jealousy goaded the mad Julian
to come to the city of the people of Emesa, intending to lay hands on the church sanctuary and destroy it. But when he entered and saw it,
he marveled at the beauty of its construction, praised its builder, and shrank from destroying it. He decided to make it a house of worship for his idols.
He offered sacrifices in it and performed the mysteries of his pagan religion. He shut it and sealed it with his signet ring. Then he returned once more to Antioch and set out on his journey.
Now I wished, O man of God, to include in this history an account of the repentance of Queen Astina as well, if possible, because there is benefit
in it for those who repent. But because the king’s affairs have already occupied us and we are pressed for time, I have therefore written you a little out of much, my beloved,
for you to study until we have a suitable opportunity to take up anew the history of the wonderful repentance of this daughter of pagans, an ugly vine from a bramble,
which, from among harmful thorns, brought forth beautiful flowers of repentance. At the wafting of their sweet fragrance, the heavenly beings marveled and rejoiced.
Jovian too, when the fragrance of her repentance reached him and he heard that Shapur was threatening her, returned once more from Edessa to Nisibis,
so that through the persuasion of his good counsel he might support the repentance of this daughter of pagans. And the faithful king succeeded
in changing the evil intention Shapur had formed against Astina. Through his skill he even managed
to bring Shapur to a favorable disposition and to have him leave Astina free to exercise her own liberty. Therefore, to that good shepherd,
who always cares for his flock, rejoices in finding the lost, and desires the repentance of sinners, be glory, honor, worship, praise, and exaltation.
Now and always and forever and ever. Amen and amen. Or do I crave power? I am a philosopher.
I will not even [?] remain in the royal capital at all. I am going up to Athens, from where I came down. When the king heard these things, he became angry and said:
“Anyone who brings Eleuthera’s case before me is an enemy of the kingdom.” And no one dared bring up this case again.
One day, during evening prayer, Eleuthera, distressed by her grief, threw herself down beneath one of the bases of the church’s columns and fell asleep. And when
the service ended and everyone went out, her servants looked for her but did not find her. At the third hour of the night, she woke from her sleep.
She looked around and saw that there was no one there. She got up and went out alone. As she wept to herself and walked up the street called the Golden Street,
a demon spoke to her and said, “What is wrong, Eleuthera, daughter of Licinius, my friend? Has Julian not given you back what he took from you?”
She said to him, “No, my lord.” She thought he was one of the street guards. He called her, and she approached, trembling with fear. He said to her:
“Because of my love for your father, who used to worship me, offer me incense, and sacrifice to me, I will restore to you everything Julian took from you.
But go to the king and tell him, ‘Let Julian come and swear to me by that statue that keeps the city’s hours.’
Then I will seize him, and he will not escape from my hands until he restores to you everything he took from you.”
First thing in the morning, she went in to the queen and told her. The queen told the king.
When the king heard, he said to her, “Then do not tell me these things, but tell Samdron the lawyer.”
The king was astonished and amazed at this affair. He summoned her [?], and she came before him, fell at his feet, and bowed to him, weeping bitterly.
She pleaded with him, saying, “Have mercy on me, my lord. I am not a stranger to you. You, my lord, are my true brother. My parents [?] me to you.
I have no other refuge, my lord, except Your Majesty. I am your sister in affection, my lord, and your own flesh and blood by birth. It is not godly
for you to disregard the injustice done to me. I have no other heir, no family, and no close relative. Consider, my lord the king,
that my ancestors governed the kingdom. Do not turn your face away from me because my father was a tyrant.
Instead, have mercy on me for the sake of my mother, who was your father’s sister. For it was not merely the wealth of one of the nobles that Julian took and seized for himself,
but a throne, a diadem, and a crown. His sights are set on the kingdom, and he is scheming [?] to become a king above you.” When
the king heard these things from Eleuthera, he became deeply embittered and said to her, “What, then, shall I do for you now?”
She said to him, “Let him swear to me by that statue that keeps the city’s hours, and I will never again have any dispute with him.”
When the king told the senate what that demon had said to Eleuthera, they were greatly astonished. When Julian heard these things,
he told his friend Magnus the sorcerer. Magnus took him at night and went to the house of the hours. As they were entering through the doorway,
that demon began to howl, saying, “Where are you going, Julian, you thief, robber, and liar?”
Woe to you from God, whom you have deceived! You swore by the holy cross and by the Eucharist. You lied by these, yet they did not expose your deceit.
By the great name of God, I will proclaim your deceit throughout this whole city and make you a laughingstock throughout the earth!
You coveted the wealth of my friend Lycanus, and you seek to become great through that wealth which was given to him by [?].
Woe to you! Into whose hands have you fallen! No, by that great radiance of God, you will not escape from me in peace or safety!
When Julian heard these things, he became greatly disturbed. Magnus the magician appeased that demon and said to him, “My lord, do not let Your Greatness trouble yourself over him.
He will do everything you command him. Only do not let him be exposed and become a laughingstock, for he is no ordinary man.”
That demon said to Magnus the magician, “As for the inheritance of Lycanus, who used to sacrifice to me—to anyone who does not sacrifice to me and offer me incense,
I will not give it [?]. But if Julian listens to me and does what I tell him, I will make him lord over the whole earth.
Sovereignty over the entire Roman dominion will be given to him, and his name will be proclaimed from one end of the earth to the other.
His kingdom will continue victoriously for hundreds of years, while he holds authority over all kingdoms.
But if he wants to avoid being exposed, having what he has done revealed, becoming a laughingstock, and having the Christians burn his body with fire as they did to his brother,
let him immediately cast frankincense before me.” Magnus the magician said to Julian, “Look, my brother,
now—which of these two things are you prepared to do?” Julian said, “Two great calamities have befallen me.
If I am exposed, I will become a laughingstock and have a bad name throughout the earth.
I am a man educated in wisdom and known as a philosopher. Throughout the whole senate, they used to present gifts and honors to me, as befits a philosopher.
They, their sons, and their wives used to bow before me as before a king. And after this great reputation,
this will be proclaimed in the royal city, where there are people from all over the earth: ‘Julian, the son of Asclepius, who was known as a philosopher—
because of his love of gold, stolen goods were found in his possession. He brazenly swore falsely by the cross and by the Eucharist.
He denied the God who made him and became a stranger to the mysteries of the Christians and to the holy seal of baptism.’
Woe to Julian! Into what ridicule, shame, heartbreak, and distress has the love of gold brought him!
So it is better for me to cast frankincense and offer sacrifice, rather than become a laughingstock and have a bad name.”
Magnus the magician immediately ran and brought frankincense. He gave it to Julian, who offered it before the demons.
He bowed his head and worshiped them. That demon said to them, “Go in peace, and after three days
come to me, for I have something to tell you.” After three days, Magnus the magician took Julian
and brought him down to the house of [?]. Magnus the magician opened the book of destruction, in which the names of all the demons were written.
Immediately the demons gathered from every direction and came. When Julian saw them flying and entering,
he trembled and became afraid. He hurriedly made the sign of the cross on his forehead, and immediately they all fled.
Magnus said to him, “My friend Julian, why did you make the sign of the cross on yourself?” Julian said,
“I did not know that they flee from the cross and fear it. Otherwise I would not have done it.” Magnus said to him,
“If you want to see them and have them gather around you, show you hidden things, teach you secret things, and let you enter into their mysteries,
and become fully initiated through seeing them, and become their covenant partner, and have them show you what is hidden, teach you what is concealed, and make you king of kings,
and subject the nations and all the kingdoms to you, exalt you above everyone, and obey you as slaves obey their masters—this sign of the cross,
never make it again.” Magnus called them again, and they came with their master Satan.
Julian bowed his head and worshiped them. The ruler of the demons ascended and sat on a throne of deceptive illusion.
It was, they say, a throne of fire, and armies of demons stood before him in fear.
He spoke and said to them, “You know that I hold the kingship and authority over this whole world.
The kings of the whole earth used to worship me and offer sacrifices before me: the kingdom of the Babylonians, of Persia,
of Media, of Sheba, of Seba, of India, of Cush, of [?], of Philistia, and of all the barbarian nations
who live in the far reaches of the earth. They belong to us and worship us, along with their wives and children, and great Rome.
Since the beginning of the world there has not been a single nation or kingdom that did not worship me, except for this Constantine,
who, in his lack of sense and his deficient knowledge—and because I had leisure and went out to all the regions at the far reaches of the earth,
and traveled around all these kingdoms of the nations and visited them, and established peace throughout all my dominions, and while I was returning here—
this Constantine renounced the religion of his fathers and threw himself into the error of the Galileans. He claimed the title of king for himself and his sons alone.
When I saw that they had abandoned me and worshiped the one whom the Jews crucified on the wood, out of love for his fathers I was patient with him for a long time.
When I saw that he would not turn back from his error, I deprived him of life, and both his sons as well, who wanted to take possession of the kingdom after their father.
As for the one who remains of them, in these very days I will deprive him of life and remove him without sons to inherit from him. Now I am establishing Julian as king.
I will make him emperor over the whole earth. He alone will be king, from east to west.
His kingdom will endure for hundreds of years, and all the kingdoms of the earth will be subject to him.
What I did not do for his fathers, I will do for him. All the armies of those who serve me will rest in him as on a comfortable bed.
He will be a temple for me, and I will dwell in him. I will never leave him, because I have found him alone remaining in the whole kingdom under my authority.”
And he will carry out all my wishes. Rise, Julian our king! Be strong and prosper!” He immediately rose and offered sacrifice that very night.
All the demons came and bowed down to him. On another night, Magnus the sorcerer took Julian and went outside the wall, the two of them [?].
To the temple of Beelzebub. He took with them Kozo, Magnus the sorcerer’s young female servant, who was pregnant. They stripped off her clothes and hung her up in the temple.
They cut her open from her womb to her navel and, while she was alive, took a nine-month-old infant out of her belly.
They practiced sorcery, summoned spirits, and performed divination with him. Spirits rose from within the earth—that is, the demons below [?].
Magnus the sorcerer spoke with them and said to them, “The ruler of the world and all his forces were pleased to grant kingship and authority to Julian, who shares your faith.
Do you agree that he should be king, and will you help him? For you hold authority over that lower region.”
They all answered, “We submit to him, for the entire kingdom under heaven belongs to him.
His authority reigns above all kingdoms, and his kingdom will continue victoriously for hundreds of years.”
After practicing sorcery and divination with that infant, they put him back into his mother’s belly. They took her down from the rope by which she had been hanging.
They laid her on the sacrificial pyre and put frankincense on her. Julian approached and set fire to the laurel wood laid on the pyre.
He spoke and said, “Ruler of this world, and mighty power of the rulers of demons and evil spirits, those above the earth and those beneath
the earth, I beg you to accept this new and first sacrifice from Julian, your new king, for the peace of his kingdom, the well-being of his dominion, and the preservation of his life,
for the hundreds of years for which you have granted him kingship.” Immediately Satan entered him. As into an idol shrine, he entered, settled, and dwelt within him.
Immediately the Spirit of God departed from him, as it had from Saul. The spirit of Satan reigned in him and took control of him.
From that hour onward, everything he did was done under the influence of the demon. On that very night when Julian sacrificed to the evil spirits,
this vision appeared to one of the holy men. He saw Julian standing in the public baths of Athens.
He was sweating sweat that smelled sweet like spices. An angel of God held a fiery sponge in his hand and was wiping that sweat from his entire body.
The man who had been found worthy to see him in this way said to the angel, “Why are you wiping this sweet fragrance off him?”
He told him, “I am wiping off the holy anointing with which he was clothed at his baptism.” The holy man said to him, “For what reason, my lord?”
The angel answered him, “Because the Spirit of God has departed from him.” The man who saw this kept silent and told no one anything.
Many days later, the king pressured him to swear [?] to Eleuthera by that statue that keeps the hours.
He said, “It is enough for me that I have sworn twice by the Christians’ Eucharist and by the cross they worship. If she wishes,
I will swear to her a thousand times by the Eucharist that Christians receive and by the cross they worship. But I will not swear to her by the statue above.”
The entire senate rose against the king and said to him, “This is not reverence for God.”
that a Christian man should abandon God and bind himself by oaths to the idol worshiped by the pagans. For the members of the king’s court were not aware
that Julian had denied God and offered sacrifices to demons. The king remained silent and gave no answer.
Eleuthera approached again and pleaded with the king, and he was [?] by her. Immediately there came to
the king a war against the barbarians. And because the Romans had no commander,
the king appointed Julian commander over all the Roman forces for the war. When he went to war against the king’s enemies,
he summoned Magnus the sorcerer, who invoked spirits and practiced divination for him to determine whether he would win or not. The demons told him to hold a festival
and offer sacrifices to Hadrius, Zeus, Hermes, Serapis, and Baalshamin. “They,” he was told, “will fight on your behalf.”
After offering sacrifice in secret, he set out for war. He fought and defeated the barbarians. Immediately his heart swelled with pride, and he forgot God, who had made him.
In those days, while Julian was in the upper regions, the son of Constantine, the victorious king, departed from this world.
Then Julian openly revealed his paganism and stirred up persecution against us. For they had already foreseen with discerning eyes
what was going to happen to him. One of the holy men had once seen him, while he was still a little boy,
sleeping on a bed, with a venomous snake, the kind called an asp, coiled around his head like a crown. Immediately he said to himself,
“This boy will become an accursed man.” Again, when he was reading from the Apostle, those near him would see him
looking bewildered, turning aside, and changing color. And he turns all the spheres [?], and the days of [?]. “More than all those who were before me,

I will magnify your festivals, and I will be your brother, friend, and beloved companion.” He stretched out his right hand in his sleep, gave it to Satan, and said to him, “You are our master, and [?] your disciple.
And if I deny you, may God deny me. You are mine, and I am yours forever.” Immediately he kissed his right hand.
When Basil woke him, he said to him, “Tell me, who were you speaking with in your sleep? To whom did you give your right hand? With whom did you make
a covenant? And who was it who spoke with you?” After a long while, when he remembered his vision,
he said deceitfully to Basil, laughing, “You and Gregory are my brothers forever.
It was to you that I gave my right hand, and it was with you that I was speaking.” And Theon the philosopher, who had received Julian from the baptismal font,
often said to him in front of us all, “If my dreams do not deceive me, judging from the visions shown to me concerning you,
you will die an evil death. For [?] before God, a merciless sentence has been decreed against you. But watch yourself.
For I believe in my heart [?] that your lot will be with Satan.” One day, when all the philosophers and wise men of Athens were seated,
and Julian and all their students were standing before them, Bion the philosopher said to Julian,
“Look, there is no one in this whole assembly of royal descent except you alone. Consider whether an opportunity might arise and you might become king.”
Do not repay anyone in this gathering with evil. Let your eyes watch over them for good.
For tell me, if [?] and you become king—as for me, who received you from the waters of baptism and have now taught you wisdom—
what will you do to me?” Julian laughed and said, “I would crucify you above the great public baths and burn your body inside them.
And I would skin Sosipater alive.” They all laughed, but Theon, his teacher, said to them, “Do not laugh, my brothers.
Pray that not one of you lives to see the fourteenth year of the Athenian reckoning, because in that year there will be a great persecution.
In that year, one of those present in this gathering will deny God and worship demons. Then he will persecute those who have confessed Christ.”
Because not everyone knows how Julian’s downfall came about, I took care to write for the members of the holy church
the whole unclean course of the paganism of Julian the Apostate, just as it happened. The account of Julian the pagan is finished.
